<margin>Traces of secrets are found in every science and condition of human affairs: Theology, Jurisprudence, Commerce, the art of Painting, and warfare. Examples of them.</margin>
And I do not know if there is any science, or any condition in human affairs, in which traces of this kind are not found. Hence, Nicephorus Gregoras <note>A 14th-century Byzantine historian</note> in Book 11 of his *History* calls them the "secrets of Theology," which the common people gape at just as herds gape at grass and pastures. And Justinian <note>The Roman Emperor famous for codifying the law</note> says: *Jurisprudence is legitimate when it is filled with secrets;* and in Law 5 of the Code regarding the Julian Law of Majesty, he mentions the *secrets of counsels.* So too in commerce, or in contracts, there are deceits <term>deceits: *doli*, technical legal terms for fraud or strategic misrepresentation</term> in which one thing is done and another is simulated to be done, as Servius <note>A Roman jurist</note> says in Book 1 of the *Digest* regarding deceit. The art of painting has its own tricks of colors <note>original Greek: *σοφίσματα τῶν χρωμάτων*</note>, the inner secret <note>original Greek: *ἐνδόμυχον*</note>, or the pretenses of colors, which are used in shading or darkening an image. In matters of war, there are stratagems <term>stratagems: *stratagemata*, clever maneuvers designed to outwit an enemy</term> devised for circumventing the foe. For this reason, they are called "inventions of war" by Ammianus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus, a 4th-century Roman historian</note>; "exercises" by Tacitus; and by Marcus Tullius [Cicero] and Livy in Book 4—most magnificently of all—*tactics and the skills of a General.* Valerius Maximus calls this part of cleverness "distinguished" and far removed from all blame; such as inducing a suspicion of flight, leaving enemy fields untouched, and many more of that kind. So in domestic affairs, there is the inner secret <note>original Greek: *ἐνδόμυχον*</note>, that is, the secret of the household, about which Cicero writes in *Letters to Atticus*, Book 5, Letter 14. Physi—

<meta>This page continues from the previous page, completing the word "Medici" (Doctors). Clapmarius is arguing that just as doctors use "pious frauds" to heal patients, so too must rulers use "arcana" (political secrets or maneuvers) to maintain the state.</meta>

### On the Law of Empire. Chap. 2.

<margin>Medicine.</margin>
Doctors (who, as Plato says, are the image of the Republic within the Home) have their own deceits, by which they circumvent the sick for the sake of restoring their health. Therefore, as the most elegant Lucretius sings regarding children:

> *When healers try to give foul wormwood to children, they first touch the rims around the cups with the sweet, golden liquid of honey: so that the improvident age of children may be tricked as far as the lips; meanwhile, they drink down the bitter juice of wormwood, and though deceived, are not harmed.* <note>original: *Abſinthia tetra medentes...*</note>

And Pliny in his *Letters*: *For if Doctors provide healthy foods that lack pleasure with flattering words, etc.* So too Horace in *Book 1 of the Satires*:

> *Just as flattering teachers once gave cookies to boys, so they would be willing to learn their first elements.* <note>original: *Ut pueris olim dant cruſtula blandi...*</note>

In almost the same way, the Tribunes in Livy (Book 5) call the granting of pay "a gift from enemies smeared with poison." Mathematicians also
<margin>Mathematics.</margin>
use certain fictions, which Aristotle calls *divisions* <note>original Greek: *χωρισμὸς* (chorismos)</note>. Yet falsehood <note>original Greek: *ψεῦδος* (pseudos)</note> is absent from these. Similar to these are those fictions of the Legal Scholars, and those imaginary sales <term>imaginary sales: *imaginariæ venditiones*, a legal procedure in Roman law where a formal sale was staged to achieve a different legal result, like a transfer of power</term>. 
<margin>Law.</margin>
Furthermore, Marcellinus writes in *Book 14* that even walls are conscious of secrets, and the Tragedian in the play *Octavia* mentions *hidden senses.* <note>A play formerly attributed to Seneca</note> So also Virgil says: *to entrust even hidden senses to you.* Furthermore, most frequently of all, 
<margin>Logic.</margin>
disputants—or Logicians—employ their own contorted and prickly sophisms <term>sophisms: clever but fallacious arguments used here as a tool for training the mind</term>; as Cicero calls them in the *Academics*, by whose benefit the window of truth is opened. Following the example of all these, political men <note>original Greek: *πολιτικοὶ* (politikoi)</note> and Princes in any Republic make use of secrets.

## CHAPTER III.

*Arcanum (Secret), to shut away, archive, secret thing <note>original Greek: ἀπόῤῥητον</note>, sacred secrets, secret books <note>original Greek: Βιβλία ἀπόῤῥητα</note>, secret soldiers, Prefects of Secrets, how the secrets of princes were usually sealed, the secret of Quintus Cicero, place of storage <note>original Greek: τεχόφυον; likely referring to a place where secrets or treasures are guarded</note>, the Emperors' chamber.*

<margin>Etymology of the word "arcanum".</margin>Festus says that *Arcanum* (secret) is derived from *arx* (citadel), which is the safest part of a city. Or it comes from a type of sacrifice performed on the citadel by the augurs <term>augur: a religious official in ancient Rome who interpreted the will of the gods by observing the flight of birds</term>, which was so far removed from common knowledge that it was not even committed to writing, but celebrated through the memory of successors. Or it comes from *arca* (a chest or box), in which things are shut away and remain safe; the origin of this word itself depends on *arcendo* (keeping away or shutting in). The best explanation of all is that it comes from *arca* and *arcendo*. From this also comes *arcus* (a bow or arch), from the Greek "to be strong enough" or "to ward off" <note>original Greek: παρὰ τὸ ἀρκεῖν</note>. 

<margin>What "arcivum" signifies according to its etymology.</margin>For to "shut away" (*arcere*) is the same as to contain; what Tacitus calls "to restrain" (*coercere*). He speaks of "the plan for restraining the Empire." From this comes *arcivum* or *archivum* (archive), called an *archeion* <note>original Greek: ἀρχεῖον</note> by the Greeks, in which secrets of this kind are preserved. In ancient glossaries, *Arcanum* is defined as "that which is not to be spoken" <note>original Greek: ἀπόῤῥητον</note>. *Arcanum* means secret, unheard of, and "hidden away" <note>original Greek: ἀπόκρυφον</note>, concealed, or tucked away. Furthermore, "secret counsels" are loosely defined as those things which it is a sin to make public. Valerius Maximus writes: *All were held by such great love for the fatherland, that the secrets...*

<summary>Clapmarius defines the term "arcanum" (political secret) through its linguistic roots, linking it to citadels, locked chests, and the necessary "beneficial deceptions" used by statesmen like Cicero to protect the state.</summary>
<keywords>arcanum, etymology, Cicero, Tacitus, archives, political secrets, Festus, statecraft</keywords>

--- Page 147 ---
<meta>This page continues Clapmarius’s exploration of the word "arcanum" (secret), moving from its basic etymology to historical examples of political, religious, and military secrecy.</meta>

On the Right of Empire. Chapter 3. 7

...no Senator in any age revealed the wise <note>original: *cana*, literally "gray-haired" or "ancient"</note> counsels of the Enrolled Fathers <term>Enrolled Fathers: *Patres Conscripti*, a formal title for the Roman Senators</term>. And Tacitus, in the 12th book of the *Annals*, mentions a "secret treaty" <note>original: *arcanum fœdus*</note>; and in *On the Manners of the Germans*, he speaks of "secret rites" and "marriage gods." Hence we find the "secrets of Venus" and "secrets of Ceres" <note>Ceres: the Roman goddess of agriculture and motherly love, whose mystery cults were strictly private</note> among the poets. Horace, in Book 3, Ode 2, writes:

<margin>Secret counsels which are so called broadly.</margin>
> I will forbid the man who has made public 
> the sacred secrets of Ceres <note>original: *Cereris sacrum / Vulgarit arcana*</note>

Justin, in Book 5, speaks of "him who calls away the mysteries of Ceres." So too in Suidas <term>Suidas: a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia</term> there are "books containing something secret" <note>original Greek: βίβλια τὰ ἀπόρῥητόν τι ἔχοντα</note>; that is, secret books; and in Ammianus Marcellinus, "secrets of atonement" <note>original: *arcana piacularia*</note>.

<margin>Confirmation of the explanation.</margin>
For this reason also, "secret soldiers" <note>original: *arcani milites*</note> were formerly those who, according to the same Marcellinus, ran back and forth over long distances to report the movements <note>original: *strepitus*, literally "noises" or "din"</note> of neighboring nations to the Roman generals. Others call these men "investigators" and "scouts." Suetonius calls them "scouts" <note>original Greek: κατόπτας</note>. They were also called "scultatores" <note>likely a variation of *sculatores* or scouts</note>, as Cujacius <term>Cujacius: Jacques Cujas, a famous 16th-century French legal scholar</term> corrected. From this, we find "Prefects of Secrets" in the same Marcellinus. For this reason the English, when going to war, swear they will not reveal secret counsels, as Froissart <term>Froissart: Jean Froissart, a 14th-century chronicler of the Hundred Years' War</term> testifies. And the Turk, when something has been decided, is said to lead his Pashas or Viziers <term>Vizier: a high-ranking political advisor or minister in the Ottoman Empire</term> into the hunt or the wilderness for a time, so that the opportunity to spread decrees or war secrets is taken away from them. And formerly, as Curtius testifies in Book 4, it was the custom of the Persians to hide the secrets of kings with wondrous loyalty; neither fear nor hope drew out a word by which hidden things might be betrayed.

<margin>The secrets of princes, usually sealed.</margin>
Secrets of this kind were sealed by the Roman Emperors in double tablets. Herodian writes regarding Maximinus: "He twice gave sealed letters in folded tablets, through which secret and hidden messages are sent to the emperors" <note>original Greek: δὶς ἔδωκε κατεσφραγισμένα γράμματα ἐν πυκτοῖς πίναξι, δι᾽ ὧν τὰ ἀπόρῥητα καὶ κρυπτὰ ἀγγέλματα τοῖς βασιλεῦσιν ἐπιστέλλεται</note>. By these tablets, they were accustomed to signify secret and hidden matters—

# Regarding the Right of Empire. Chapter 4.

...ments <note>The text completes the word *delinimenta*, meaning soothing charms or inducements used to manage the public</note>: "Many allurements," he says, "were given to the common people at that time." In the same place, he mentions skill: "One must act with skill <note>original: *arte*</note> in the face of a hatred already grown old with age." Therefore, those who were well-versed in these secrets he calls "Craftsmen" <note>original: *Artifices*</note> in Book 6: "Craftsmen [skilled] by the use of so many years in managing the minds of the common people." This is, as Cicero says, "those whose minds have grown hardened by experience, just as a hand is by labor." The same author, Livy, calls them "soothing charms" <note>original: *delinimenta*</note> in Book 4. Sometimes they are called "weapons of the Fathers" <note>The "Fathers" refers to the Roman Senators; original: *Patrum tela*</note>, as in Book 5: "The Fathers would find another weapon." Likewise, "mockery" <note>original: *ludificationem*</note> in Book 6. 

Cicero calls them "Secrets of the Republic" <note>original: *Arcana Reipublicae*</note>. Tacitus, in Book 1 of the *Annals*, uses "Secrets of the Empire" <note>original: *Imperii Arcana*</note>. "There was no doubt," he says, "that the secrets of the Empire were being tested." In the same work, he mentions "Secrets of dominance" <note>original: *Arcana dominationis*</note> and "Secrets of the House" <note>original: *Arcana Domus*</note>. Elsewhere, he speaks of the "secrets of the Empire." Polybius calls them "hidden things" <note>original Greek: ἐπίκρυφα (*epikrypha*)</note>, or as in the glossary, "concealed things" <note>original Greek: ἀπόκρυφα (*apokrypha*)</note>. 

Of the same sort are those phrases in Tacitus: "empty secrets" and "deceitful secrets." Also "images of the Empire" <note>original: *Imperii simulacra*</note>. The glossary translates these as "representations" <note>original Greek: ἀπεικονίσματα (*apeikonismata*)</note>, "acts of hypocrisy" <note>original Greek: ὑποκρίσματα (*hypokrismata*)</note>, or "appearances" <note>original Greek: φαινόμενα (*phainomena*)</note>. To these, Plato’s "masks" <margin>masks</margin> <note>original Greek: προσωπεῖα (*prosopeia*)</note> are not dissimilar, nor the "visible law" <note>original Greek: ἐνόφθαλμος (*enophthalmos*)</note> of the Milesian, which you might call a "masked law." Likewise, the "masks" <note>original Greek: προσωπεῖα</note> and "swinging masks" <note>original: *Oscilla*, small masks hung from trees during festivals</note> of Aristophanes. From this, Nonius says: "*osciculatim*, that is, feignedly or by way of pretense." 

For public actions are like comedies, in which a mask is put on and taken off, and, as the Satirist <note>The Roman poet Juvenal</note> sings: "The true face returns, the feigned one perishes." 

<margin>Commonly called hidden counsels.</margin>Commonly they are called "hidden counsels," although these are usually understood in a negative sense. Cicero, in *On the Response of the Soothsayers*, says: "The same men warn that the republic should not be harmed by hidden counsels." And Tacitus in *Annals* Book 2: "Some believed that hidden mandates were given by Tiberius." Hence also Tacitus says: "To test the secrets of the Empire," and "To make public the secrets of the Empire." And Juvenal: "To betray a secret." Even in private business, the law speaks of "stripping bare the innermost things and opening the secrets of the business" (from Law 3 of the Digest on receiving arbitrators), and "to reveal the secrets of the estate."

<note>The text begins with a legal reference: Law 2 of the Code regarding the provision of maintenance.</note> To this are added the **Rights of Dominance**. Or, as Curtius calls them, the **Rights of the Kingdom** <note>original: *Iura Regni*</note>; the Italians call it **reason of state** <note>original: *ragione di dominio*</note>. The Germans do not use the term "secrets of the Empire" <note>original: *arcana Imperii*</note>, as far as I know, unless perhaps by **secret imperial matters** <note>original: *geheime Reichssachen*</note>; nor do they speak of "secrets" or "Rights of Dominance," except through **Imperial Reservations and Sovereignty** <note>original: *Keyserliche Reservaten vnd Hochheit*; these were specific legal privileges held by the Holy Roman Emperor</note>. For I see no reason why you should not refer all these things to the secrets of Republics. Yet each of these differs greatly from one another, and they must be distinguished so subtly that it will become clear from the following sections.

### CHAPTER 5.

*The definition of Secrets. Their purpose. The meaning of the public good, the common benefit <note>original Greek: τὸ κοινῇ συμφέρον (*to koinē sympheron*)</note>, and the good for the city <note>original Greek: τὸ πόλῃ ἀγαθὸν (*to polē agathon*)</note>. The distinguished public interest and its dignity. The use and necessity of simulation in great affairs.*

<margin>The Secrets of Republics are defined.</margin>
I define the **Secrets of Republics** <note>original: *Arcana Rerumpublicarum*</note> as follows: they are the innermost and hidden reasons or plans of those who hold the leadership in a Republic, used both for their own tranquility and for preserving the present state of the Republic, and done for the sake of the public good. And they are generally such things for which, as Velleius says in Book 2: "one thing is said, another is understood." Or, as Servius writes regarding deceit: "one thing is done, another is feigned to be done." Let us consider each of these elements, if you please, somewhat more accurately. 

<margin>Why they are called hidden plans.</margin>
They are said to be **hidden plans** for this reason. They are certainly **difficult to unravel** <note>original Greek: δυσέξύματα (*dysexerymata*), likely a variation of "hard to track"</note>, both because the common people do not easily perceive them (for what the poets say of sacred rites—"I hate the profane crowd and keep them away"—we may not undeservedly use regarding these Secrets), and also because they are mostly imposed secretly upon those who seem to hate the current state of the city.

<vocab>Arcana Rerumpublicarum (Secrets of Republics), Iura Dominationis (Rights of Dominance), Iura Regni (Rights of the Kingdom), geheime Reichssachen (secret imperial matters), Keyserliche Reservaten (Imperial Reservations), bonum publicum (the public good)</vocab>

<summary>Clapmar defines "Secrets of State" as the hidden strategies used by leaders to maintain peace and preserve the government’s structure for the public good. He notes that while different nations use different terms, such as "reason of state" or "imperial reservations," they all refer to the necessary use of secrecy and redirection in politics.</summary>

# On the Law of Empire. Chapter 5.

-> A 6 <-
<meta>catchword: is</meta>

Furthermore, their purpose is twofold: the safety and longevity of the current Republic (that is, ensuring it is not changed into another form of government); and the security of those who command. For so says Herodian in his life of Maximinus, <note>original Greek: τὰ ἀπόῤῥητα καὶ κρυπτὰ δοκοῦντα ὑπὲρ σωτηρίας τοῦ βασιλέως (*ta apporrhēta kai krypta dokounta hyper sōtērias tou basileōs*)</note> **"Secrets and mysteries pertaining to the safety of the prince."** That goal is the **public good**, as the term is used by Velleius Paterculus in his second book. Gracchus revoked the command of his colleague Octavius because Octavius was standing in the way of the public good. You might call it the "good of the people," or, as it appears in the ancient glossaries, the **populic good** <note>original: *bonum populicum*, an archaic term for public welfare</note>. This is why only the goods belonging to the Roman people are called "public." <note>References to the Digest of Roman Law: Book 50, Title 16, Law 15; and Book 41, Title 3, Law 1.</note> For example, **usucapion** <term>usucapio: a legal method of acquiring ownership of property through long-term undisturbed possession</term> was introduced for the **public good**. Aristotle, in the fourth book of his *Politics*, chapter 8, calls this "the common advantage" <note>original Greek: τὸ κοινῇ συμφέρον (*to koinē sympheron*)</note> and "the good for the city" <note>original Greek: τὸ πόλεϊ ἀγαθόν (*to polei agathon*)</note>. Tacitus, in the third book of his *Annals*, calls it the **distinguished public interest**; this stands in opposition to what Livy (Book 2) calls the **worst public evil**, and what Velleius calls **the public harm**.

<margin>To what extent they are tolerated.</margin>
Indeed, these state plans and counsels sometimes have the appearance of fraud or injustice when considered simply on their own; yet, they are tolerated out of respect for the public good and the stability of the Republic. And why shouldn't they be? For there is such a sacred duty and care for the public good that we rightly place it above all human emotions and all personal plans. This is a standard that should by no means be measured against private affairs, which (as Livy witnesses in his second book) have always hindered, and will always continue to hinder, public business. Furthermore, certain forms of **simulation** <note>the act of pretending or creating a false appearance</note> are among the secrets of Republics; these are drawn over the eyes of the citizens like a **glaucoma** <note>original: *glaucoma*; used here metaphorically to mean a blurring of vision or a "smoke screen" intended to deceive</note>, so that they believe they possess something which they actually do not. In this way, relying on that belief, they do not disturb the current state of the Republic. Concerning this, Livy writes in his second book: **"The moneylenders had prepared with such great influence and such art that they frustrated not only the common people, but even the Dictator himself."** But...

It argues that the stability of the state and the safety of its leaders may require "simulation" or "fraud" that would be unacceptable in private life but is necessary for the common advantage.</summary>

<margin>The use and necessity of simulation.</margin>
There exists an honorable and lawful form of **simulation** <term>simulation: the act of pretending to have or feel something that is not there; creating a false appearance</term>. If this is permitted in private contracts (as the jurist Labeo says in *Digest: On Fraud*, book 4, title 3, law 1, stating that one thing can be done while another is simulated without it being considered "evil fraud"), then how much more is it permitted in public affairs? These matters are of greater weight and higher dignity. This is what Marcus Tullius Cicero advises in his *Letters*, book 10, epistle 9: <note>original: "Ut ad effectum consiliorum suorum veniant, multa oportet simulent inviti, dissimulentque cum dolore"</note> **"To achieve the intended effect of their plans, leaders must often simulate many things against their will, and dissimulate others with pain."** And as the Poet says in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*:

-> **They should prepare their arms, and the reason for** <-
-> **changing their affairs** <-
-> **they should dissimulate.** <-

Livy also speaks to this aptly in his fifth book: "At the elections for the Military Tribunes," he says, "the Fathers [the Senators] struggled with all their might to ensure Marcus Furius Camillus was elected. On account of the wars, they **simulated** that they were preparing a leader; but in truth, an opponent was being sought to block the Tribunician proposal." <note>This refers to a political maneuver where the ruling class used the threat of war as an excuse to put a strong leader in power who would oppose the laws favored by the common people.</note>

We even see this in the immortal God, for whom nothing exists except what is just and good. In the book of Wisdom, chapter 11: **"You have mercy on all because you can do all things, and you dissimulate the sins of men so that they may repent."** <note>original Latin: "dissimulas hominum peccata, ut resipiscant"</note> And regarding Saul, in the first book of Samuel, chapter 10: **"But certain wicked men despised him and brought him no presents; but he held his peace as if he were deaf."** <note>original: "ipse verò erat veluti surdus" — Saul "dissimulated" his knowledge of their insults to maintain peace.</note>

From this, Aeschylus says: <note>original Greek: Ἀπάτης δικαίας οὐκ ἀποστατεῖ θεός (*Apates dikaias ouk apostatei theos*)</note> **"God does not distance himself from a just deception."** To this same point are the words of Tacitus: **"The tricks were understood, but part of obedience consisted in this: not letting them be detected."** And elsewhere in the first book of his *Annals*: **"The Senators had but one fear: that they might seem to understand."** <note>Tacitus is describing the oppressive atmosphere under the Emperor Tiberius, where people had to pretend they didn't see the Emperor's obvious manipulations just to stay safe.</note> And finally, that line from the comic poet Syrus to Dromo: **"What you know, you do not know; if you are wise, Dromo."**

...weavings and repetitions <note>original Greek: "πλοκὰς καὶ παλιλλογίας"</note>, impenetrable words <note>original Greek: "ἀμβάτους λόγους"</note>. In an old glossary, this is defined as [things] phrased circuitously <note>original Greek: "παραπεφρασμοινθέντα"</note>. Plautus calls it *twisted speech*. Cicero calls it *word-coverings* <note>or "veiled words"</note>. Dio [Cassius] calls it *obsequiousness and hypocrisy* <note>original Greek: "ἀρέσκειαν καὶ ὑπόκρισιν"</note>. Perhaps you would not so strongly detest some of these things if you carefully consider the position in which both Tiberius himself and the Roman Republic then stood. Although, as Augustine says, they are not without fault. 

But Plato, in the 5th book of the *Republic*, says that *rulers must use frequent lies and deception* <note>original Greek: "συχνῷ τῷ ψεύδει, καὶ ἀπάτῃ δεήσει χρῆσθαι τοὺς ἄρχοντας"</note> *for the benefit of the subjects*. And who is so master of himself, yet so forgetful of another's safety, that he would demand of a great man that he express every thought according to his mind's conviction in front of anyone? How much more correctly the Philosopher <note>meaning Aristotle</note> says in the 3rd chapter of *Ethics*, Book 4: *A great man*, he says, *uses freedom in speaking and truth, but does not speak according to the will of others: he also remains silent and dissimulates among the lowest, namely those unworthy of him opening or communicating all his plans, words, or deeds.* Therefore, in an old glossary, "to dissimulate" is *to keep silent* <note>original Greek: "σιωπᾶν"</note>.

<margin>*The limits of the art of simulation.*</margin>
But indeed, there are limits to this art, which it is not permitted to cross with impunity; such as faith, honesty, and virtue. He who forgets these no longer deserves the name of a "prudent man" or a "politician," but of a sly, cunning, and wicked man. If such a person is to be called a politician, then there is a greater harvest of politicians in this day and age than of the petty masters who weep in the schools and, as the saying goes, *teach for three coins* <note>A reference to low-paid, common schoolteachers</note>.

<margin>*The methods of Political Science are other than the common people think.*</margin>
The methods of political science are far different than the common people think; such as occupying the minds of others, extorting a decision in marvelous ways, enticing others to one's own opinion, and other things of that kind. Just as in

Sallust <note>The Roman historian</note> records that the famous Metellus approached the ambassadors of Jugurtha <note>A King of Numidia who fought Rome</note>—who had come to him with pleas for mercy—one by one, separately from each other. By gradually testing them, once he recognized they were favorable to his aims, he persuaded them by promising many things. Certainly, these are the arts required in great and public affairs.

## CHAPTER VII.

Men of the times. The middle way in public business. Base simulation. Open simulation. Overly suppressed simulation. The difficulty of simulating, naked mysteries <note>original Greek: "ὄργια γυμνά"</note>. Suspected dissimulation, disordered dissimulation.

Regarding Francesco Soderini <note>A Florentine Cardinal and diplomat known for his political maneuvers</note>, a Cardinal and a man of sharp intellect, it has been handed down in memory that he was accustomed to say: nothing is better in practice or more expedient for a man seeking high things—especially one navigating the fortunes of a court in precipitous affairs—than to sit on two chairs at once; or, as that man says, to hold the middle line <note>original Greek: "τὴν μεση γραμμήν"</note>, if it can be done without certain offense. It seemed to him that a wise man should never risk any of these things by casting them entirely upon a single roll of the dice. Thus, while the other Cardinals were falling away from the Pope, this Soderini alone remained, acting as a kind of observer <note>original: "speculator"</note> of the Pope’s plans. Claudian <note>A late Roman poet</note> depicted such "men of the times"—as they are called by Cornelius <note>Referring to the historian Tacitus</note>—in a certain passage:

> He balanced the twin powers, with the outcome as his judge, 
> a client to the turning points of affairs, ready to surrender himself 
> to the victor.

This is truly an arduous and perilous matter, especially in great and precipitous affairs. In my <margin>For it is the most solid</margin> judgment, that famous Pontius <note>The Samnite leader who famously trapped the Roman army at the Caudine Forks</note> in Livy’s 9th book speaks more truly: <margin>The middle way</margin> The middle way is that which neither prepares friends nor removes enemies.

<margin>What must be avoided by one wishing to feign.</margin>
But truly, whoever wishes to play this part <note>original: "scenam agere," literally "to act this scene," treating politics as theater</note> decently must beware of two things: first, from shameful simulation <note>pretending or feigning</note>; second, from open simulation. For there is a type of feigning that is not only placed on the border of vice, but even enters the very territory of crime and disgrace. Then, effort must be made so that the simulation is not excessive—for what is too tightly pressed will burst out—and also so that the act of hiding is itself hidden. For, as the Comic poet <note>The playwright Plautus</note> says:

> Deceptions are not deceptions, unless you cultivate them with craft. <note>original Latin: "Doli non sunt doli, nisi astu colas."</note>

And the Lyric poet <note>Horace, in his Art of Poetry</note> says beautifully:

> If you bring anything untried to the stage, and dare
> to form a new character, let it be kept until the end,
> just as it started from the beginning, and let it be consistent. <note>original Latin: "Si quid inexpertum scenæ committis..."</note>

Otherwise, they become naked mysteries <note>original Greek: "γόργεια γυμνά," likely a reference to "orgia gymna" or exposed secrets</note>. Tiberius, otherwise a most cunning prince, having killed Germanicus <note>The popular Roman general and nephew of Tiberius</note>, pulled the mask off himself when he put on a show of mourning against his true feelings. This was partly because he did not cover it in a simulated way (and indeed at that time he could not: for Tacitus says, "adulation was absent since everyone knew that the death of Germanicus was joyful to Tiberius")...

<margin>
2. Those things which serve the security of Princes are of three kinds.

and these are threefold; some are secrets of royal rule, others of aristocratic rule, and others are of popular rule. Kin to these are what are called either the "Rights of Rule"—which are like restrictions on the Right of Empire—or the **Shameful Acts of Rule** <note>original: "Dominationis flagitia"</note>, or, as Tacitus <note>A Roman historian famous for his cynical analysis of the exercise of power.</note> calls them, **Secrets of the House** <note>original: "Arcana domus"</note>: and these are transgressions against the Empire. And I categorize these just as many times, that is, threefold. For they are either the rights and shameful acts of royal rule, or of popular rule, or of aristocratic rule. 

Of the third kind are those which are called **Shadows of Empire** <term>Shadows of Empire (simulacra Imperii)</term> <note>Political "illusions" or empty titles given to people to make them believe they have power or that the old form of government still exists when it has actually changed.</note>, or of Republics, and these are improperly called "Secrets." 

<margin>
Improperly called shadows of empire are again varied.
</margin>

Therefore, Tacitus calls them "empty secrets": which vary repeatedly according to the form of the Republic. For they are either Royal Shadows—found in both aristocratic and popular states; or Aristocratic Shadows, in royal and popular states; or Popular Shadows, in kingships and aristocracies. Of all these, some are specific and suit a single form of Republic; some are common and apply to all. To all these are added the secrets called military; likewise private secrets, that is, the intimate counsels for establishing a common and private life happily and decently in the public eye. 

<margin>
This distribution contains almost the summary of the work.
</margin>

Add to these certain other abstruse and hidden counsels for administering a Republic, all of which are observed both from reason and from the outcome of many events (which, as Livy <note>Titus Livius, a Roman historian; the quote refers to how fools only learn from results after they happen, rather than planning ahead.</note> says, is the teacher of fools).

### CHAPTER IX.

->*The foundations of secrets, and the <note>original Greek: στοιχεῖα (stoicheia)</note> elements; and in how many ways the secrets of Empire differ from the Right of Empire; <note>original Greek: ἀφορισμοί (aphorisms)</note>. The citadels, or the bulwarks of Majesty and Empire.*<-

<margin>The Rights of Empire are the foundations of this doctrine. What they concern.</margin>
In order that these Secrets of Republics may be more rightly understood, it is worthwhile to know what those highest **Rights of Empire** <term>Rights of Empire (Iura Imperii)</term> <note>The legal and sovereign powers that form the basis of a government's authority.</note> are, which are like the elements and foundations of this doctrine. Aristotle (in *Politics*, Book 4) teaches that these revolve around five things: public assemblies, magistrates, the courts, arms, and the use of arms. For these secrets are nothing other than the hidden arts through which seditious men are kept away from the Right of Empire and from the exercise of rule itself. This close relationship is why many people confuse these secrets of Empires with the Right of Empire.

<margin>How the Secrets of Empires differ from the Right of Empire.</margin>
Furthermore, they differ in more than one way. First, because the Right of Empire—or <note>original Greek: πολίτευμα (politeuma)</note> the form of government—is that which belongs to whoever holds the primary position in the Republic; it is what Cicero calls the "extreme" and highest right. However, the Secrets of Republics are the methods and reasons for preserving that **Majesty of Empire** <term>Majesty (Majestas)</term> <note>The supreme authority or sovereignty of the state, which Clapmarius argues must be protected through secret means.</note>, lest it be seized by others. For all the power of Empire consists in the consent of those who obey, as Livy <note>Titus Livius (64 BC – 17 AD), a Roman historian who wrote a monumental history of Rome.</note> excellently says in Book 2.

I will speak more clearly: the Right of Empire is that it is not permitted for anyone to take up arms, or to handle them without...

<summary>Clapmarius distinguishes between the legal "Rights of Empire" (Iura Imperii), based on Aristotle's five pillars of governance, and the "Secrets of Empire" (Arcana Imperii), which are the practical, often hidden methods used to protect and maintain that legal authority.</summary>

<margin>Secrets of Empire are like the citadel and bulwark of the sovereign Majesty.</margin>
...and the consent of the Prince; a **Secret of Empire** <term>Secret of Empire (Arcanum Imperii)</term> is to devise strategies by which the common people, being kept content and as if under a spell, abstain from the use of arms. Thus, the right of public assemblies is a **Right of Empire**; but a **Secret of Empire** is to exclude others from that right of assembly through some permissible deception. For the Right of Empire is like a citadel or a palace; however, the Secrets of Empire are like the walls and bulwarks, or the tunnels, which defend this citadel from the assaults of the factious. This is similar to how that famous Icilius <note>Lucius Icilius, a Roman tribune who defended the rights of the plebeians.</note> in Livy <note>Titus Livius (64 BC–17 AD), author of a monumental history of Rome.</note> (Book 3) calls the aid of the tribunes and the right of appeal for the Roman people "two citadels for protecting liberty"; and in Book 6, he calls the consulship the "citadel and pillar of liberty."

<margin>They vary according to the variety of Republics.</margin>
Secondly, the Right of Empire is almost one and the same in all Republics of whatever kind, and it does not vary. But the Secrets of Empire vary according to the form of the State. For there are certain secrets for the Turkish kingdom, others for the kingdom of France, others for the Venetians, others for the people of Nuremberg <note>original: "Noricorum"</note>, and others for those of Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentinensium"</note>; that is, some belong to a monarchy, some to the common people, and others to the Patricians <note>The ruling noble class in aristocratic republics.</note>.

<margin>Secrets of perfunctory action.</margin>
Finally, the Right of Empire is pure and genuine, not simulated. But a Secret of Empire occurs when one thing is done while another is pretended to be done; which is beautifully described in the gloss as *acting for form's sake* <note>original Greek: ἀφοσιοῦσθαι (aphosiousthai)</note>, that is, to act perfunctorily and not according to one's true intention. For example: the appointment of a magistrate is a Right of Empire, as witnessed by Modestinus <note>Herennius Modestinus, a celebrated Roman jurist.</note> and Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras, a 12th-century Byzantine chronicler and theologian.</note>. However, ensuring that magistrates do not serve five-year terms is a Secret of Empire; see Tacitus, *Annals* Book 1. For this reason, Tiberius—because he understood that the Secrets of Empire were being tested by these five-year elections—postponed them, yet acted as if the Imperial power were being increased. <margin>
The Rights of Empire are called by various names.
</margin>
Therefore, the **Rights of Empire** <term>Rights of Empire (Iura Imperii)</term> are not the **Secrets of Empire** <term>Secrets of Empire (Arcana Imperii)</term>, but rather their first principles <note>original Greek: στοιχεῖα (stoicheia)</note> and foundations. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero, the famous Roman orator and statesman.</note> calls these the "Rights of Majesty"; Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> calls them the "Rights of Supreme Command." He says, "The right of supreme command has been handed down from the Fathers." And in Book 3, "the command of royal majesty." And Curtius <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, historian of Alexander the Great.</note> in Book 10 says, "The Right of Empire must be consecrated by the death of Perdiccas." Livy likewise speaks of the "rights of the Consuls" and the "rights of the kingdom." Tacitus <note>Roman historian known for his analysis of power.</note> refers to them as the "sacred things of the realm" <note>original: "sacra regni"</note>, just as one might speak of the sacred things of an embassy, of treaties, or of the household gods. Livy sometimes calls it "the highest state of affairs" <note>original: "summa rerum"</note>; in Book 2, he writes: "The highest state of affairs and the majesty of the consular command had come to them."

<margin>
How the terms for Supreme Command differ.
</margin>
The legal experts <note>original: "ICti" (Iurisconsulti)</note> call them the sacred rites of the most high, inseparable sacred things, or the Sublime Rights. Aristotle calls it the *politeuma* <note>original Greek: πολίτευμα, meaning the civil constitution or the governing body of a state.</note>. The scholars of feudal law call them **Royal Prerogatives** <term>Regalia</term>, though these terms are broader in scope. The Germans generally call it "Princely Territorial Authority" <note>original German: "Fürstliche Land Obrigkait"</note>, and there are many other names for supreme command.

Yet these terms differ greatly from one another. For **Majesty** <term>Majestas</term> is proper to the Supreme Prince—and was formerly proper to the Consuls, the Senate, and the Roman People—

# On the Rights of Empire. Chapter 10.

...the Romans. Law 2 on the origin of law <note>A reference to the *Digest* of Justinian, a foundational collection of Roman law</note> and Livy <note>Titus Livius, Roman historian</note> in book 2: "It had already nearly come to the point that not even the majesty of the Consuls could restrain the anger of the men." From this, Cicero says, "Majesty is the greatness of the supreme **Power** <term>Empire (*Imperium*)</term>." Majesty is even attributed to a governor, but improperly <note>original: *abusivè* - meaning the term is used loosely rather than in its strict legal sense</note>. Supreme command is also used with this same meaning. Properly, however, "Empire" is taken to mean military command, as Sigonius <note>Carlo Sigonio, a 16th-century Italian humanist and historian of the Roman Empire</note> noted previously.
<margin>Command used for military authority.</margin>
Cicero says: "The same day gave both the end of command to the victors, and the end of life to the vanquished." And elsewhere: "We therefore grant command to Caesar, without which military affairs cannot be conducted." And in his *Oration on the Consular Provinces*: "A war against the greatest nations and tyrants of Syria was then finished by the consular army and command."
<margin>Command is also attributed to a Magistrate.</margin>
Thus Curtius <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, historian of Alexander the Great</note> in book 4: "Then the soldier, still unarmed, awaits the command." It is also attributed to a Magistrate by Ulpian <note>A famous Roman jurist</note> in Law 32 of the *Digest*, "On Injuries." "Lesser magistrates," he says, "have neither command nor power." Hence Varro in his *Satires*: "To seek the command of the people and to strive for honors."
<margin>Leadership is a general name.</margin>
Thus, **Empire** is generally a name for **leadership** <term>Principate (*Principatus*)</term>, which is also a specific type of **Beginning** <term>First Principle (*Principium*)</term>. Therefore, Caesar in book 6 of the *Gallic War* says: "The leadership and the command were handed over to Cingetorix." Yet they are used without distinction in the commentaries. The Greeks use the word **authority** <note>original Greek: ἀρχή (*archē*)</note> for command, office, governorship, and leadership.
<margin>Leadership is distinguished from a kingdom.</margin>
But **leadership** <note>The *Principate*, the early Roman Empire where the ruler acted as "first citizen"</note> is also distinguished from a **kingdom** <note>A *Regnum*, or absolute monarchy, which the Romans traditionally detested</note>. Suetonius says of Caligula: "Nor was it far off from him immediately taking up the diadem and converting the appearance of a leadership into the form of a kingdom." And Tacitus in *Annals*, Book 2, distinguishes one who rules as a master from one who leads: "He added instructions," he says, "so that he might think not of a mastery over slaves, but of a ruler and citizens." **Power** <term>Potestas</term> also differs from **Command** <term>Imperium</term>; see the aforementioned Law 32 "On Injuries." Hence, in Ammianus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus, a 4th-century Roman historian</note> and others, those in whose hands are military rights are called "Powers"...

But formerly, it was used to refer to the supreme magistrate who held the command of affairs, according to Law 13 "On Jurisdiction," which Paul even calls the **governing authority** in his Letter to the Romans <note>original Greek: *ἐξουσία ὑπερέχουσα* (exousia hyperechousa), a reference to Romans 13:1</note>.

<margin>What Dignity is, and how it differs from Power.</margin> **Dignity** is a far different thing. For any urban honors, as Cassiodorus <note>A Roman statesman and writer of the 6th century</note> testifies, are called dignities. Pomponius and Tacitus call it **estimation** <term>worth (*dignatio*)</term>: in Book 2 of the *Annals*: "But they should excel in places, ranks, and estimations." In Church histories, this term is assigned to those who today are called *Reverend*. Therefore, the Papal interpreters call the Papacy the "pinnacle of dignities."

<margin>Authority distinguished from Command.</margin> In this same way, **Authority** is distinguished from **Command** <term>Empire (*Imperium*)</term>. Livy says in Book 1: "Evander ruled those places more by authority than by command." But also Senate decrees <note>original: *Senatusconsulta*</note>, which were made while Caesar was absent and had not yet been delivered to the treasury, were called "Authorities," as others have noted from the historian Dio.

<margin>To what extent Senate decrees are called Authorities.</margin> Indeed, Tacitus calls the Senate decrees made under the Emperors not only "authorities," but even "flatteries." In Book 2 of his *Annals*: "Whose authorities and flatteries I have recounted." Otherwise, Authority is mostly attributed to the Senate. Cicero says in Book 2 of *On Duties*: "When all things were held by the domination of one man, there was no room for counsel or authority." And Tacitus in Book 12 of the *Annals*: "Whether he should yield to the orders of the people, or to the authority of the Senate." Sometimes it is even attributed to the Prince. Pliny writes in Book 4 of his *Letters*: "With Caesar as the author <note>original: *autore*</note>, the Senate took counsel." And in an inscription from Brescia: "By a decree of the Senate, and by the authority of Caesar."

<margin>Necessity distinguished from Command, as is Counsel.</margin> In this way, Caesar separates Command from **Necessity**: "Because they were absent," he says, "and were constrained neither by any necessity, nor by command." In the same manner, **Counsel** is separated from Command. Livy says in Book 1: "That was not my command, but my counsel, and a simulation of command." And in Book 6: "But Com-" <meta>catchword: -mand (rium)</meta>

<summary>Clapmarius distinguishes the legal nuances between "Command" (military or magistrate power), "Dignity" (honorary rank), and "Authority" (moral or senatorial influence). He provides historical examples from Roman law and historians to show how these terms functioned in different political contexts.</summary>

# On the Right of Empire. Chapter 10.

...command <note>The word "Imperium" (command/empire) began on the previous page</note> was slower than counsel. And in Book 22 [of Livy]: "Acting not only by command, but also by counsel, and almost by prayers." But **command** is also called **discretion** <term>judgment or will (*arbitrium*)</term> by Tacitus <note>A senator and historian of the Roman Empire</note> in Book 6 of the *Annals*: "Soon he held the discretion of Roman affairs for nearly twenty-three years." And Justinus <note>A Latin historian of the 2nd century</note> in Book 1: "The discretions of princes stood in place of laws." Hence, the "arbiter of affairs." In Book 2 of the *Annals*: "If he were the sole arbiter of affairs, if he had been so by the right and name of kingship." 

<margin>The saying of Empire and Discretion.</margin> 
These are those whom Livy <note>The author of the monumental history of Rome, *Ab Urbe Condita*</note> in Book 9 calls "Masters of things and times." I discuss all these matters more fully in my *Notebooks* <note>original Latin: *tumultuariis meis*, referring to his own miscellaneous scholarly writings</note>, Book 5, chapter 3. For these terms of **principate** and **powers** ought to be distinguished with subtlety.

Furthermore, Gunterus <note>Gunther of Pairis, a 12th-century Cistercian monk and poet</note> graphically describes this **Majesty** in Book 4:

> Truly, the royal majesty of a just ruler possesses
> This force of dread within itself; whether far or near, present
> Or absent, it is always terrible, always to be feared,
> And remains full of its own vigor; it is believed 
> That it cannot be suppressed by anyone with impunity, 
> And it is always feared by all, and everywhere.

# Arnold Clapmar, Book I.

<margin>The Rights of Empire ought to belong only to those who command.</margin>
More justly in Tacitus <note>Cornelius Tacitus, a Roman historian and senator</note>, Book 1 of the *Annals*, [Tiberius] warned Livia not to dissolve the force of the **Principate** <note>The early period of the Roman Empire where the ruler acted as "first citizen"</note> by referring all matters to the Senate; for he argued that the condition of ruling is such that the accounts only balance if they are rendered to one person alone. This passage seems to me to have been borrowed by Tacitus from Aristotle. For so it says in Book 4 of the *Politics*, chapter 4: "all offices are dissolved" <note>original Greek: καταλύονται πᾶσαι αἱ ἀρχαί (katalyontai pasai hai archai)</note>; that is, as Tacitus translates it, *to be dissolved*. To this principle the poet <note>Virgil, in the *Aeneid*</note> repeatedly looked:

->*Fastened and clinging to the tiller,*<-
->*he never let go, and kept his eyes*<-
->*upon the stars.*<-
<note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.852-3, describing the helmsman Palinurus; here used as an allegory for the singular focus required of a ruler.</note>

Furthermore, majesty consists primarily in two things.

<margin>Majesty consists in two things.</margin>
1. First, that the prince be released from the laws; 2. second, that he imposes laws upon the citizens and subjects.

<margin>How necessary it is in a Republic for someone to be released from the laws.</margin>
That both of these occur is for the benefit of the Republic <term>the state or commonweal</term>, especially in a principate or a turbulent Republic. Wherefore, when the Roman Consuls were rebuked because they had permitted the bribes of Spurius Maelius <note>A wealthy Roman accused of seeking to make himself king by feeding the poor</note> and the gatherings of the common people to take place in a private house, Titus Quinctius <note>Titus Quinctius Capitolinus Barbatus, a Roman statesman</note> said that the Consuls were undeservedly rebuked, since they were "bound by the laws concerning the right of appeal—laws passed specifically to dissolve the absolute Command—and they did not possess as much power in their office to punish the matter according to its atrocity as they had courage." <note>This refers to the *lex de provocatione*, which limited a magistrate's power by allowing citizens to appeal to the people.</note> "Therefore, there was need not only of a brave man, but one who was free and released from the bonds of the laws." (Livy, Book 4). For this reason, a Dictator <term>an emergency magistrate with absolute power</term> was created, against whose power the Tribunes of the people, or the common people themselves, did not dare even to raise their eyes or open their mouths. (Livy, Book 6). The second aspect is that he gives the law to others. These two things are held by the King in a kingdom, by the people in a Republic, and by the Patricians in an Aristocracy—or, as it is in the gloss, the "enlightened citizens" <note>original Greek: φωτοπολίται (photopolitai), literally 'citizens of light' or 'men of the city's light,' referring to the ruling elite</note>.

# Arnold Clapmar, Book I.

## On the Right of Empire. Chapter 11.

<margin>Eleven categories of supreme power.</margin>
Furthermore, majesty is a broad concept. However, it can be narrowed down to more or less eleven types: namely; 1. Giving the law to others, and not receiving it from them; 2. Being exempt from the laws; 3. Creating magistrates <note>high-ranking government officials</note>; 4. The right of sending and receiving ambassadors; 5. The right of life and death; 6. The right over sacred matters <note>control over religious institutions and practices</note>; 7. The final appeal; 8. Waging war and making peace; 9. Minting money; 10. The right of Markets <note>the legal authority to establish and regulate trade fairs</note>; 11. The right of taxes.

Ligurinus <note>Gunther of Pairis, a 12th-century poet who wrote the *Ligurinus*, an epic about Frederick Barbarossa</note>, in his eighth book, included some of these in the following verses, and even added others which are properly called **Regalia** <term>royal rights or prerogatives</term>, though I do not list them all here:

> *And first the Italians <note>original: "Ligures"</note>, being asked by the king about this,*
> *[Granted] the tribute, the harbors, and the rights of minting money,*
> *Along with the customs houses for mills, the rivers, and the bridges,*
> *That also which they call "fodder" <note>original: "fodrum," a medieval tax for the maintenance of the king’s court or army while traveling</note> in the royal name,*
> *And the head-tax <note>original: "capitolitium"</note> paid at a certain time;*
> *All these the Italians granted to the sacred treasury.*

For the power over these matters ought to belong to those who command in a Republic: and these points must be explained and illustrated a little more at length in order to understand the nature of the **Secrets** <term>the "Arcana Imperii" or secrets of state power</term>.

# Arnold Clapmar, Book I.

<margin>The Rights of Empire ought to belong only to those who command.</margin>
More justly, in the first book of the *Annals*, Tacitus <note>a Roman historian and politician</note> advised Livia <note>the wife of Emperor Augustus</note> *not to weaken the power of the Principate <note>original: "Principatus," the early Roman imperial system</note> by referring everything to the Senate; for the condition of ruling is such that the accounts only balance if they are rendered to one person alone.* It seems to me that Tacitus borrowed this sentiment from Aristotle. For in the fourth book of his *Politics*, Aristotle says that **all magistracies are dissolved** <note>original Greek: "καταλύονται πᾶσαι αἱ ἀρχαί"</note>—which is exactly how Tacitus translates it with the word *resolvi* <note>meaning to be loosened, weakened, or dissolved</note>. The poet <note>Virgil, in the *Aeneid*, describing the pilot Palinurus</note> repeatedly looked to this same idea:

->*Fixed and clinging to the tiller,*<-
->*He never let go, and kept his eyes on the stars.*<-

Otherwise, majesty consists chiefly in two things.

<margin>Majesty consists in two things.</margin>
1. *First, that the prince be free from the laws*; 2. *second, that he lay down the laws for the citizens and subjects.*

Both of these are for the benefit of the Republic, especially in a monarchy or a turbulent state. For this reason, when the Roman Consuls were rebuked because they had allowed the bribes of Spurius Maelius <note>a wealthy Roman accused of seeking kingship by distributing grain during a famine</note> and the gatherings of the common people to take place in a private house, <margin>How necessary it is in a Republic for someone to be free from the laws.</margin> Titus Quinctius <note>Titus Quinctius Capitolinus Barbatus, a Roman consul</note> *said that the Consul was unjustly rebuked, for being bound by the laws of appeal <note>laws that allowed citizens to appeal a magistrate's decision to the people</note>—which were passed to dismantle the Empire—he by no means possessed as much strength in his office to punish the matter according to its atrocity as he had the spirit to do so. Therefore, there was a need for a man who was not only brave, but also free and released from the bonds of the laws.* This is from Livy, Book 4. For this reason, a **Dictator** <term>in Rome, a magistrate with absolute authority appointed during emergencies</term> was created, *against whose power the Tribunes of the plebs, or the plebs themselves, did not even dare to raise their eyes or open their mouths.* This is from Livy, Book 6. The second point is that he gives the law to others. These two powers are held by the King in a monarchy, by the people in a Republic, and by the Patricians—or as it is said in the Greek glossary, the **leading citizens** <note>original Greek: "πρωτοπολῖται"</note>—in an Aristocracy.

<summary>This page defines the core of "Majesty" as the ruler's dual power: being exempt from the laws himself while holding the sole authority to impose laws on others. Clapmar uses Roman history and classical philosophy to argue that divided authority leads to the dissolution of the state.</summary>

Plato says this: <gloss>a ruler according to the laws is not unaccountable.</gloss> <note>Plato’s point is that a ruler governed by law is held responsible, whereas the "Princeps" discussed here is above such accountability</note> In this sense, those words of Tacitus in the second book of his *Annals* must be understood: *Tiberius*, he says, *rejoiced when the Senate debated between his sons and the laws; the law was defeated, without doubt, but not immediately and with only a few votes; just as even when they were in force, the laws were sometimes defeated.* In the same way, Livy says in Book 3: *So that it might clearly appear that if it were permitted to act thus, the law was defeated.*

As recorded in *Tacitus, Annals Book 1*, Augustus designated Gaius and Lucius as consuls before they had even laid aside the purple-bordered toga of boyhood <note>The *toga praetexta* was worn by Roman boys before the *toga virilis* marked their entry into manhood</note>.

He claimed the same decrees had been granted to himself and his brother at Augustus's request. 

In a similar way, the Pope released Ambrose, Nicholas, and Severus from the law so that they might be made Bishops without first having been initiated into the lower sacred orders <note>This refers to the practice of "per saltum" ordination, skipping the traditional steps of the ecclesiastical hierarchy</note>. Furthermore, Tiberius granted a Roman knight a release from his oath so that he could divorce his wife, who had been caught in adultery with his son-in-law, even though the knight had previously sworn he would never divorce her. This is recorded by *Suetonius in his Life of Tiberius.*

<margin>
The Empresses were not released from the laws.
</margin>
However, you will find nowhere that the Empresses <note>Latin: *Augustae*</note> were released from the laws, though many people believe they were; for their power was indeed very great. Examples of this, to omit others, were seen in the cases of Urgulania <note>A powerful friend of Livia</note> and Plancina, the wife of Piso; Livia rescued them from the judgment of the Senate. Following her example were several others, such as Theodora, the wife of Justinian, and especially that Agnes, the mother of Henry IV <note>Agnes of Poitou, who served as regent of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, who acquitted the Duke of Swabia after he was accused, doing so with the consent of the Emperor and the Archbishops. The author of this account is the chronicler of Aschaffenburg <note>Referencing Lampert of Hersfeld, a medieval historian</note>.

<margin>
The Prince leads by the example of his ancestors.
</margin>

From this came obedience to the Prince, and a desire to emulate him that was stronger than the punishment of laws or fear.* And Pliny says in his *Panegyric*: *We do not need command so much as example. ### CHAPTER XIII.

->*Giving laws, not receiving them. Commanding by laws. No one is permitted to defraud the laws. Tiberius as a discoverer of new law. To be invincible by the laws.*<-

<margin>The second branch of supreme Sovereignty: to make law.</margin>
To make laws belongs to supreme Sovereignty, and it is the characteristic of the one who holds the first place in the Commonwealth. <margin>The Prince receives laws from God alone.</margin> For he gives laws, he does not receive them, except from the Most High God, as the Prophet and King <note>King David</note> says: *Against you only have I sinned.* <note>original: "Tibi soli peccavi" — Psalm 51:4. Historically, this was interpreted by legal scholars to mean that a king is accountable to no earthly judge, only to God</note>. The Romans carefully exercised this majesty against their enemies. Thus Quintus Cicero <note>Brother of the orator Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>, as witnessed by Caesar in the fifth book of the *Gallic War*, responded to the Nervii: *it is not the custom of the Roman people to accept any conditions from an armed enemy.* And Curtius <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, historian of Alexander the Great</note> says in Book 8: *I confess that they are indeed the victors if we accept from them the laws by which we live.* In this same vein, Charles V wrote to the Pope: It is not in keeping with the dignity of the Emperor <note>original: "Augusti"</note>, by far the greatest of Princes, to receive laws and be terrified by threats, especially from those who to his Empire...

<meta>The catchword "sub-" indicates the next page begins with "subiecti" (subjected) or a similar word, continuing the thought that the Pope's predecessors were once subjects of the Holy Roman Empire.</meta>

<summary>This page argues that the defining power of a sovereign is the ability to give laws without being forced to receive them from others. It uses examples from Roman history and the Holy Roman Empire to show that a true ruler is accountable only to God.</summary>

# On the Right of Sovereignty. Chapter 13.

...subjected, and with fortune as the judge, they were so often conquered in war and found ungrateful, that they were finally judged worthy of a heavier punishment. *Giovio in the Life of Leo X.* <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552) was a famous Italian historian and biographer of the Renaissance.</note>

<margin>It belongs to the same person to abolish laws.</margin>
Furthermore, he whose task it is to decree a law, to him also belongs the power to abolish it, and even to substitute one for another <term>subrogation: the act of replacing an existing law with a new one or amending it</term>; for this is **not only to rule according to the laws, but also to rule over the laws**, as Plutarch says in his life of Flamininus <note>original Greek: οὐ τῷ τοῖς νόμοις μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν νόμων ἄρχειν</note>. Therefore, Tiberius, in the case of Piso—because an ancient Decree of the Senate <term>Senatus-consultum: a formal decree of the Roman Senate</term> prohibited a capital inquiry <note>a trial involving the death penalty</note> against a master based on the testimony of his own slaves—ordered that the slaves be sold individually to the public official. <note>By selling the slaves to the state, Tiberius bypassed the law that prevented slaves from testifying against their owners.</note> He did the same in the case of the young daughter of Sejanus; because it was considered unheard of for a virgin to suffer the punishment of the Triumvirs <note>the *triumviri capitales*, officials in charge of executions</note>, she was assaulted by the executioner next to the noose before being strangled. *Tacitus, Annals, Book 6.* Thus,
<margin>Abuse of the same power in Tiberius.</margin>
the Triumvirs, so that a minor could be punished according to the law, first dressed him in the man’s toga <note>the *toga virilis*, the garment symbolizing adulthood</note>. These examples, although they pertained to the security of the Princes, were nevertheless devised as a mockery of the laws and joined with cruelty; as such, they should be attributed to the crimes of absolute rule. This is why Tacitus calls Tiberius "shrewd" and a "discoverer of new law."

<margin>No one is permitted to defraud the law, scarcely even the Prince.</margin>
Otherwise, no one is permitted to commit a fraud against the law. Therefore, Gaius Licinius, as Livy records in Book 7, was fined ten thousand pieces of copper under his own law by Marcus Popilius Laenas, because he possessed a thousand acres <term>jugera: a Roman unit of land area, roughly 0.6 acres</term> of land together with his son. <note>Licinius Stolo passed a law limiting land ownership but tried to bypass it by registering half the land in his son's name.</note> Fabius Maximus says of this in Book 10 of the same author: *What is the point of laws being passed if they are defrauded by the very men who passed them? Then the laws are ruled, they do not rule.* For this reason, when notorious women—in order to avoid the penalties of the law and be released from the status and dignity of matrons—began to register themselves as prostitutes, and when the most dissolute of the youth did the same to avoid appearing in plays...

Justinian likewise said: "The one has always needed the help of the other; military matters are preserved by laws, just as the laws themselves are preserved by the protection of arms." Thus, the Constitutions state that the laws are **armed with the sword**; and Livy, in his sixth book, writes: "They themselves arm the cause of the common people with great spirit."

<margin>The third head of supreme sovereignty: the creation of magistrates and the right of the assemblies.</margin>

Therefore, the <term>Decemviri: the "Ten Men," a Roman commission of the 5th century BCE</term>, according to Livy, made a secret pact so that no elections would be held, and they might retain the power they had once possessed through a perpetual Decemvirate.

# On the Right of Empire. Chapter 14.

This right, moreover, almost always belonged to the Roman people. Once the Republic was changed, it was transferred from the Field <note>original: *campo*; referring to the *Campus Martius*, where the Roman people historically gathered to vote</note> to the Senators, as Tacitus testifies, and finally to the Prince <note>the Emperor</note>. As the jurist Modestinus writes in the single law of the Digest regarding the *Lex Julia de ambitu* <note>The Julian Law concerning bribery/corruption in elections</note>:
> The creation of magistrates pertains to the care of the Prince, not to the favor of the people.

And Zonaras <note>A 12th-century Byzantine chronicler and legal scholar</note> says:
> The creation of magistrates is the greatest part of the Imperial duty.

Maecenas, according to Dio <note>Cassius Dio, the Roman historian</note>, advised Augustus long before this that he alone—without the commoners, the people, or the Senate—should create the magistrates. For this reason, according to the same Dio in his 58th book, Tiberius reserved for himself alone the title and the official announcement of all consuls (whose office was once the highest in the Empire); yet he indulged the other magistrates by interposing his own recommendation.

<margin>Tiberius's authority in the recommendation of Candidates.</margin>
Caesar used this same form of recommendation:
> I recommend to you this man and that man, so that they may hold their dignity by your vote.

But in truth, this was merely a <term>sophism: a clever but false argument</term> and a pretense, lest he should amputate the whole Empire from the Roman people with a single blow while their servitude was still raw <note>i.e., while the memory of lost liberty was still fresh</note>; this is discussed further in the final book.

Certainly, this "recommendation" carried a certain necessity. For such is the condition of Princes—as Quintilian says in his 4th Declamation—that whatever they do appears to be a command. Gaius <note>The Emperor Caligula</note>, either through an ignorance of ruling or a desire to mock the commoners, attempted to return the right of voting to the people by reviving the custom of the <term>comitia: the formal public assemblies</term>. However, he later abandoned this. This is noted by Tranquillus <note>Suetonius</note> in his *Life of Caligula*.

<margin>A confirmation is sometimes sufficient.</margin>
Nevertheless, sometimes a mere <term>ratihabitio: a legal confirmation or ratification</term> by the one who holds supreme power suffices in the creation of magistrates. For instance, as Cassiodorus records, King Theodoric of the Goths wrote to the Senate:
> Our assent, O Conscript Fathers <note>the traditional title for Senators</note>, follows your judgment.

For just as Plato says regarding the government of the world...

Afterward, however, with complete harmony, both the clergy and the people granted the bishopric to Uto. *Jacob of Schaffenburg.* <note>Also known as Lambert of Hersfeld, an 11th-century chronicler</note>

### On the Law of Empire. Chapter 15.

...conciliates, I refer to the supreme power of the state. And the most ancient kings and princes diligently cultivated this.
<margin>According to Justin, the Jews had the same men as Kings and Priests.</margin>
Justin, writing on the Jewish Commonwealth, says: "After Moses, his son Arvas <note>original: "Arvas." Justin the historian likely refers to Aruas; note that historical accounts of Moses' lineage vary significantly across ancient sources</note>, a priest of Egyptian rites, was soon created king; and from then on it was always the custom among the Jews to have the same men as both Kings and Priests." And the Poet <note>Virgil</note> says of King Anius in the third book of the *Aeneid*: "The same man was both king of men and priest of Apollo." For religion, as that African Bishop <note>Likely Optatus of Milevis, an influential 4th-century bishop who argued for the state's role in church affairs</note> used to say, ought to be within the Commonwealth, not the other way around. I believe this is the reason why the Turkish Emperor <note>The Sultan</note>, even when he grants many rights of empire back to kings who have come under his protection, always reserves for himself a few specific rights, including the sacred and public prayers that are conceived in the temples for the safety of the Prince.
<margin>Among the Romans, public thanksgivings for deeds accomplished could only be decreed by the Senate.</margin>
Hence also among the Romans, public thanksgivings <note>original: "supplicationes," formal days of prayer or thanks</note> for things successfully accomplished at home or in war could only be decreed by the Senate.

Indeed, I do not find that this right in the Roman Commonwealth belonged to any others than the kings and Emperors, and that supreme and greatest
<margin>That law belonged to the Roman kings.</margin>
Senate. In the Royal Laws <note>The *Leges Regiae*, legendary laws attributed to the early kings of Rome</note>, it is written: "Let the King be the overseer of sacred rites." For the role of the Pontiff <note>The High Priest</note> was only to administer the rites and to know, as Livy says in his first book, which sacrifices, on which days, and at which temples the rites should occur, and from where the money for those expenses should be drawn.

<margin>Among them, the King was the overseer of sacred rites. After the kings were expelled, it was the Senate.</margin>
Once the kings were expelled, it is established that this power resided with the Senate, as seen from a decree of the Senate <term>Senatusconsultum: a formal decree of the Roman Senate</term> which instructed the <term>aediles: Roman officials responsible for public order and buildings</term> to ensure that no gods except Roman ones were worshipped, nor in any way other than the ancestral custom. And there is the matter that Marcus Aemilius proclaimed before the assembly: that whoever possessed prophetic books, prayers, or written instructions on the art of sacrificing should bring all those books to him, so that no one might sacrifice in a public or sacred place according to a new or foreign rite. Especially from that text, it appears that caution was taken so that there would be no Bacchanalia <note>The Roman festivals of Bacchus, which were suppressed due to their perceived threat to public morality and order</note> in Rome or in Italy. If anyone considered such a sacred rite to be traditional and necessary, and felt they could not omit it without religious guilt and a need for atonement, they were to declare this before the Urban Praetor <note>The magistrate responsible for legal matters within the city of Rome</note>. The Praetor would then consult the Senate; if permission were granted—provided that no fewer than one hundred members were present in the Senate—then the rite could be performed, as long as no more than five people participated in the sacrifice.

After the Republic was changed: The Emperors.

<margin>
By whom certain matters of sacred law were initially granted to the Senate.
</margin>
This is testified by Tacitus in *Annals*, Book 2: *a decree of the Senate <note>original: "Senatusconsultum"</note> was made regarding the expulsion of Jewish and Egyptian rites.* And under Claudius, a decree of the Senate was made that *the pontiffs should see which practices of the Soothsayers <term>Aruspices: ancient Roman priests who interpreted the will of the gods from the entrails of animals</term> were to be retained and strengthened.* For we know that the Senate decree passed against Tiberius—lest Christ be counted among the gods—is unique and mysterious <note>original: "μυστικὸν" [mystikon]</note>. 
<margin>
The Decree of the Senate that Christ not be counted among the gods.
</margin>
Similarly, when Alexander Severus intended to build a temple to Christ, our only Savior, and to receive him among the gods—which Hadrian is also said to have considered, as he had ordered temples to be built in all cities without idols—he was prevented by those who, consulting the sacred rites, had discovered that all people would become Christians if his wish were fulfilled, and the remaining temples would be abandoned. *Aelius Lampridius in his Life of Severus.* But this, as I said, is mysterious. For afterwards, the sacred law belonged solely to the supreme Prince. *Pope Leo to Emperor Leo: "You must," he says, "Emperor, realize without hesitation that royal power was bestowed upon you not only for the government of the world, but especially for the protection of the Church."*

To this end serves that response of *Demetrius Chomatenus* <note>A 13th-century Byzantine archbishop and expert in canon law</note> in the *Eastern Responses*, which I am surprised others have neglected. *The Emperor,* he says, *existing and named as the common* <term>Chief Overseer of Order</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπιστημονάρχης (epistemonarches). <margin>The Empire was made two-headed by the Roman Pontiff.</margin>
But in truth, the Roman Priests or Pontiffs <note>The Popes</note>—either inflated by a tide of ambition or led on by the leniency and religious devotion of the Princes—have seized this Right; so aptly does that saying of *Otto* <note>referring to Otto of Freising, a medieval historian and bishop</note> in *Tacitus* apply here: *The Empire, through its love of religion, has exhausted itself.* Hence, from one head, it was made two-headed, regarding which *Gunther* <note>Gunther of Pairis, a 12th-century Cistercian monk and poet</note> writes in book 5:
> *Those whom, with serene praise,*
> *The miter or the sword makes to be feared in the world.* <note>The "miter" (infula) represents the Pope’s spiritual authority, while the "sword" (gladius) represents the Emperor’s secular power</note>

This might be tolerable, if they did not moreover "thrust their sickle into the business of the Republic" <note>An idiom meaning to meddle in affairs that do not belong to them</note>; indeed, they even summon the Prince to trial. Thus it has passed into a proverb, as *Guicciardini* <note>Francesco Guicciardini, a famous Italian statesman and historian</note> witnesses in his *Political Commentaries*: *To fear and to hate the Caesars is the characteristic of the Church.* This impiety and ambition was heavily and sharply criticized in many places by the illustrious writer *Otto of Freising*, who was otherwise a pro-Papal Bishop. And following him, that other "Poet of the Emperors" <note>referring again to Gunther of Pairis</note> wrote in book 6:
> *Now it delights [the Church] not to bear the cross of the Lord, but to hand over kingdoms,*
> *And prefers to be held as an Augustus rather than a prelate.* <note>The verse critiques the Papacy for preferring the power of an Emperor (Augustus) over the duties of a high-ranking clergyman (prelate)</note>

And yet, this is the very same man who once called the Emperor his "Lord," as is evident from that diploma <note>A formal state document or charter</note> mentioned by *Guicciardini*...

### CHAPTER XVI.

->*To coin money. To mark coins with one’s own image. To melt down signed coinage bearing the face of the Prince. The religion of the Romans concerning coins.*<-

<margin>The fifth head of supreme Empire: to coin money.</margin>
To coin money is also a Right of Empire. This right, while it formerly belonged to the <term>Masters of the Mint</term> <note>original Latin: Triumviros monetales. A board of three officials in the Roman Republic responsible for overseeing the minting of coins</note>, the Caesars transferred to themselves. Hence, in the acclamations of the Princes: *“Let the name of Antoninus be restored to the coinage.”* As Aelius Lampridius writes in the life of *Severus*. And *“When Antoninus Diadumenus was elevated to the Empire, money was immediately struck at Antioch in the name of Antoninus.”* So too Vopiscus writes in the life of *Firmus*: *“While he claimed that Firmus was merely a petty thief, not a Prince; I, on the contrary, argue that he—having both worn the imperial purple and struck coinage—was called Augustus; Severus Archontius even produced five of his coins.”* For besides the Prince, it was permitted to no one to coin money, or
<margin>And to mark it with his own image.</margin>
to mark it with his own image. For this reason, Commodus punished Perennius, his close associate, with the death penalty because he had marked public coins with his own image. This is recorded by Herodian in his life of *Commodus*. Herodotus reports the same regarding the King of the Persians, who for the same reason ordered Ariander, the prefect of Egypt, to be struck with an axe <note>beheaded</note>. Otto of Freising notes the same regarding the Hungarian State: *“No one,”* he says, *“in such a vast territory, except for the King, dares to have a mint or a custom-house.”* Whence the Poet says in his third book on Frederick I:

> *That the money shaped by the King is the King’s is clear,*
> *The image of Caesar shines under Caesar as Lord.*

Which same Right the Turk <note>The Ottoman Sultan</note>, according to Bonfini <note>Antonio Bonfini, a 15th-century Italian scholar and historian of Hungary</note>, grants to no one...

<margin>The sixth head of supreme Empire: the power of life and death.</margin>
*The power of life and death. The dagger. The sword. To pardon the condemned. To restore the rights of one's rank. To grant safe passage. The Great Council of the Venetians. To delay punishment.
