<margin>
A judge cannot change a sentence but is bound to carry it out immediately.
</margin>
A Judge, however, cannot change a sentence once it has been entered into the official records (Law "what he ordered," Digest, *On Judgments*), and his sentence is to be handed over for execution immediately (Law 15, Code, *On Punishments*). This is for two reasons. The first is that often, with the passage of time, the severity of those in power is softened. Regarding this same Emperor *Theodosius*, *Aurelius Victor* says: "He was indeed angry at shameful things, but was quickly turned," whereby he was moved to mercy by a modest delay. *Ammianus Marcellinus* calls this a "second deliberation" in his 15th book. This delay, however, was in vain in the case of the Emperor *Tiberius*. For, as *Tacitus* says in the third book of his *Annals*, he was not softened by the passage of time. Secondly, the Judge did not possess the <term>right of life and death</term> <note>original: "jus vitæ & necis."</note>, but the Prince alone:

> From whom the accused, though redeemed by no gold, 
> Often receive their own lives when their crimes are forgiven.

As is written in the *Ligurinus* <note>A 12th-century epic poem by Gunther of Pairis regarding the deeds of Frederick Barbarossa.</note>, Book 4. And *Tacitus* notes in Book 1 that the Senate did not have the liberty to change its mind. The reason is given in Law 18 of the same Code: lest there be an opportunity for petitioning the court, or for obtaining an acquittal through "wicked arts" <note>This refers to using corruption, bribery, or complex legal maneuvers to escape a finalized sentence.</note>. How a Judge might actually be able to soften a delivered sentence may be seen in the *Observations* of *Cujas* <note>Jacques Cujas (1522–1590), a towering figure in legal humanism who applied historical analysis to Roman law.</note>. Hence, he is called by *Aristotle* the **Mesotēs** <note>original Greek: "Μεσόδης," meaning a "mediator" or "middle-man" who stands between the law and the parties.</note>.

<margin>The seventh head of supreme power: The Right of Embassy.</margin>

# Arnold Clapmarius, Book I.

### CHAPTER XIX.

->Final appeal. The supreme judge of a case.<-
->To hold the laws in one's hand.<-

<margin>The eighth point of supreme Power is final appeal. First used by the Roman kings, then by the people.</margin>
The final appeal displays no less Majesty [than other rights]; and the Roman kings formerly used this right, as has been learnedly shown by others. Afterward, the people seized it, and this, according to the testimony of Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note>, was their strongest bulwark. For this reason, Appius says in the same author: *He says that these are the threats of the consuls, not their Power, when it is permitted to appeal to those who had sinned together.* <note>original: "Minas esse consulum, non Imperium dicit, ubi ad eos, qui unà peccaverant, provocare liceat." Appius Claudius is arguing that if a consul’s judgment can be appealed to the common people, the consul has no real power, only the ability to threaten.</note> The same Livy, in book 3, concludes that liberty was removed from the fact that appeal had been removed. For, he says, *besides the fact that there was no protection among the people, with appeal removed they also took away intercession by consensus, since the earlier Decemvirs <note>The Decemviri were a ten-man board appointed to codify Roman law; they were eventually seen as tyrants.</note> had allowed laws they had issued to be corrected by an appeal to a colleague.* However, appeals were rarely made to the people, and only in cases of major crimes. I speak of the *final* appeal. For at other times appeals were also made from praetor <term>a Roman judicial officer</term> to praetor, or even to the Tribunes, as the most learned Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius, a famous 16th-century humanist scholar.</note> noted.

<margin>Final appeal to the Prince [the Emperor].</margin>
When the Republic was finally changed, Augustus, by right of his Tribunician power, reserved the final appeal for himself, as is clear from Dio <note>Cassius Dio, a historian who wrote in Greek about the Roman Empire.</note>. This is especially clear from Tacitus, *Annals* book 4: *And with them pressing on, he says, he appealed to the Prince.* <note>original: "Iisque instantibus... ad Principem provocavit."</note> For what Gaius [Caligula] changed afterward did not last long; just as the fact that Tiberius, as Tranquillus <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, the biographer of the Caesars.</note> relates, allowed certain things to be decreed against his own opinion, is more a shadow and a mask of former liberty. In those times, appeals were made to the Prince from almost the entire world; as seen in *Law 45 of the Digest, under the title "On conditions and demonstrations"* <term>The Digest was the primary collection of Roman legal precedents</term>. Thus it is a wonder that there are those at this time who think that the Cham-

# On the Rights of Empire. Chapter 19.

<margin>Which today are the supreme judgments.</margin>
...that the judicial power of the Empire is unequal to deciding the disputes of Germany. <note>The author is likely referring to the Holy Roman Empire's struggles to centralize judicial authority amidst the various German states.</note> Yet today, even in the Empire, as the legal practitioners <note>original: "Pragmatici"</note> testify, appeals are made by nearly all orders to the Chamber; <note>The Reichskammergericht, or Imperial Chamber Court.</note> just as among the French, appeals go to the eight major courts; <note>The regional Parlements of France.</note> among the Spaniards, to four courts; and among the Venetians, to the Council of Forty. The kings of France have valued this right so highly that when Charles V, King of the French, <note>Charles the Wise (r. 1364–1380).</note> granted many Imperial rights to John, Duke of Berry, <note>original: "Ioanni Duci Biturigum."</note> he reserved the final appeal to himself by a singular exception. Likewise, Conrad, King of the Romans, <note>Likely Conrad III (r. 1138–1152).</note> held the people of Utrecht <note>original: "Trajectenses."</note> to be guilty of Lese-majesty <note>High treason against the sovereign.</note> because they had appealed from him to the Roman Pontiff. This is recorded by Otto of Freising in his deeds of Frederick. <note>The *Gesta Friderici I Imperatoris* by the historian-bishop Otto of Freising.</note> Furthermore, when Pope Julius III, through his legates, testified before King Henry III of France <note>The text says Henry III, though Julius III was contemporary with Henry II; the author may be citing a specific later legal precedent or there is a transcription error in the original Latin.</note> that God would be the avenger, and said he appealed to Him, the King agreed and promised that he too would be present before the tribunal of God—but added that he knew for certain the Pope would forfeit his bail. <note>original: "Pontificem vadimonium deserturum." A witty legal jab suggesting the Pope would not actually show up to face God's judgment.</note>

<margin>The Prince is the supreme Judge.</margin>
Hence the Prince is called the supreme Judge. For such a one is he to whom the final appeal is made. As Pliny says in his preface to Vespasian: *To such an extent does everyone make the one they choose the supreme judge of their cause; whence it is called an appeal.* <note>original: "Adeò summum quisque causa sua judicem facit, quemcunque elegit. unde provocatio appellatur."</note> And as Gunther <note>Gunther of Pairis, a 12th-century Cistercian monk and poet.</note> writes in book 2:

> — *So that he, present as if the greatest Judge of all,*
> *Should close the laws in his hand and cut short all disputes,*
> *And every judge, every power,*
> *And every magistrate should fall silent in his presence.*

Hence that famous line regarding Paul in the Acts of the Apostles: *This man could have been set free, if he had not appealed.* <note>Acts 26:32. Paul appealed to Caesar, which removed him from the jurisdiction of the local governors.</note> Now the Poet says "to close the laws in his hand"; which is nearly the same as what Pomponius <note>Sextus Pomponius, a 2nd-century Roman jurist.</note> calls "acting with a royal hand." Indeed, the word "hand" <note>original: "manus." In Roman law, 'manus' signified power or legal control.</note> is familiar even to <term>Jurisconsults</term> <note>Legal experts or scholars of the law. original: "ICtis," an abbreviation for Iurisconsultis.</note>. Whence it is said in the Laws of the 12 Tables: <note>The foundation of Roman law, dating to c. 450 BCE.</note> *If any join hands in law* <note>original: "Si quei in jure manum conferunt." This refers to the 'manum consertio,' a preliminary ritual in a property dispute where both parties laid hands on the object in the presence of a judge.</note>; concerning which we speak elsewhere.

# CHAPTER 20.

### Ninth: To decide on wars; to make peace. The Caudine and Numantine Treaties. It is High Treason to take up arms without the Prince’s command. The rights of a triumph.

<margin>The ninth head of supreme power is to wage war.</margin>
This is indeed perhaps the greatest right of Sovereignty of all. Certainly, among the Romans, it was not permitted to declare war except through the centuriate assembly of the people—that is, the highest assembly. For, as Plato says in the second book of his *Laws*: "If anyone makes peace or war privately with others, without the common authority, let death be the penalty." <note>original: "ἐὰν τις ἰδίᾳ ποιῆται πρὸς τινας εἰρήνην, ἢ πόλεμον, ἄνευ τοῦ κοινοῦ, θάνατος ἔστω ζημίας"</note> And once the Republic had changed, anyone who waged war without the Prince's command was held liable under the Julian Law of Treason. <note>original: "Lex Iulia Majestatis." This was the Roman law governing crimes against the state and the dignity of the Emperor.</note> (See book 3 on the Julian Law of Treason and the single law in the Code regarding the use of arms, etc.).

<margin>It is not permitted to carry arms except by the Prince's permission.</margin>
"To no one," it says, "should the means of moving any arms whatsoever be granted entirely without our knowledge and consultation." And in the *Novels*, 17, it is not permitted to carry arms unless one is on active military service. And in the *Authenticum* regarding arms, it is forbidden by Justinian's constitution <note>A collection of laws by the Emperor Justinian.</note> for weapon-makers <term>Fabricensibus: state-appointed manufacturers or workers in imperial armories</term> to sell weapons to private citizens. On this charge, among others, Piso <note>Gnaeus Calpurnius Piso, a Roman governor who famously clashed with the popular general Germanicus.</note> was accused because he had sought to retake by force of arms the province from which he had been ejected.

<margin>It is not permitted to sell them to private individuals;</margin>
This was also the reason why Cato <note>Cato the Younger, a staunch defender of Republican tradition.</note> judged that Caesar should be handed over, naked and bound, to the Germans: though I do not know if that was not perhaps too harsh; see others on this point. For I do not care "to recount again what has been told so harshly." <note>original: "αὖτις ἀμελιχήλως εἰρημένα μυθολογέω." This is a literary flourish, likely echoing Greek epic style, to avoid repeating grim details.</note>

The same reasoning applies to the making of peace; which among the Romans could not be entered into except by the consent of the Senate and the people, and later of the Emperors. Therefore, that famous Posthumius said that "the Roman people are not bound by the guarantee <note>original: "sponsione." This refers to the "Caudine Forks" incident in 321 BCE, where Roman generals made an unauthorized peace treaty to save their trapped army.</note> which was made without the command of the Roman people," as found in Livy and Tacitus’s *Annals*, Book 15.

<margin>Likewise, making peace is a Head of Supreme Sovereignty.</margin>

Unlike a treaty (*foedus*), it did not legally bind the Roman state unless ratified by the Senate or the people. Thus, it was not a deception, but the law and the command of the people. Furthermore, as **Pliny** says in the *8th book of his Epistles*: to deceive, according to the customs of the times, is prudence?

<margin>Royal prerogatives differ from the Right of Sovereignty.</margin>
As for the rest, which are called **Royal Prerogatives** <term>Regalia: Specific rights, lands, or revenues (like mining or tolls) that belonged to the crown, distinct from the broader legislative powers of sovereignty.</term> in the second book of the *Feudal Laws*, title 16, I do not include them here; for they differ from the **Right of Sovereignty** in many ways. Partly because prerogatives—whether major or minor—are granted to others as fiefs, just like immovable property; however, the **Rights of Sovereignty** are not easily granted (as they are reserved for the supreme Prince as a mark of his superiority). Partly also because prerogatives, especially the minor ones, do not display such great majesty; rather, they serve to increase the personal estate and domestic wealth: such as **riverbank tolls** <note>original: "ripatica"</note>, **silver mines**, **port duties**, **salt-tax revenues**, etc. Add to this that the purpose of feudal matters and Royal Prerogatives is almost solely the administration of war: therefore, he who has the right of war can share these prerogatives.

### Arnold Clapmarius, Book I.

<margin>From the "heads" of supreme power, the secrets of Empires are extracted.</margin>
...of the Empire, from which are drawn those **Secrets of Empires** <term>Secrets of Empires: *Arcana Imperiorum*, the strategies and hidden mechanisms used by rulers to maintain power and stability.</term> that we are investigating. These are like the ramparts for preserving the state, toward which factious citizens often creep gradually and, so to speak, by indirect steps. Their greed is so insatiable that once they have cut away some small piece of the Republic and welded it to their own body, they always scrape away more, never finding rest.

<margin>Most authors refer the right of establishing public transport to the heads of Empire. Royal couriers.</margin>
To these heads of Empire, most authors also refer the **Right of establishing public transport**; or, as the Laconian <note>Likely referring to a concise or Spartan-style author, or a specific commentator on ancient law.</note> calls them, *royal couriers*, known today as *posts* <note>original: "postas"</note>. Regarding these, see the *Code on Public Transport* <note>A section of the *Codex Iustinianus*, the Roman legal code.</note>. For the Emperor alone possesses this right; thus, not long ago, he strictly forbade a certain German Duke who had organized public routes into Belgium and Italy from doing so. Concerning these "posts," as they are called, consider what **Caesar** says in the third book of the *Civil War*: *Messengers on horses stationed at intervals (for this is what posts are) brought word of Caesar's victory to Messana.* Consider also what **Capitolinus** <note>Julius Capitolinus, one of the historians of the *Augustan History*.</note> wrote regarding a messenger who, by changing animals, ran to tell the Romans of the murder of Maximinus. Truly, this system provides the greatest security for the Prince. Therefore **Augustus**, so that he could be notified and learn more quickly and directly what was happening in each province, first stationed young men at moderate intervals along the military roads, and later vehicles. This seemed more convenient, so that those who carried the letters from the same location could also be questioned if the situation required it. Thus writes **Tranquillus** <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, the Roman biographer, in his *Life of Augustus*.</note> in his biography of Augustus.

<margin>The right of granting citizenship, as well as the rights of fortifying and closing the gates; where these should be categorized.</margin>

### CHAPTER XXII.

*Military command is not a matter of the Law of Sovereignty. The military rights of a General. The free administration of war by Roman generals. Deciding according to the moment. To have full power <note>original German: "Volligen Gewalt haben"</note>. Modern methods of warfare based on directorates. The Turkish military.*

<margin>The military rights of a supreme commander are not part of the supreme Sovereignty.</margin>
Military command <term>Military Command: *Imperium militare*, the authority granted to a general in the field, which Clapmarius argues is distinct from the civil sovereignty of the state.</term> belongs here even less. Its use and force apply only in the camp, outside the civil state, and rests with the generals of war. Indeed, military command includes the **Right to punish the soldier**. This is how **Agamemnon** acts in **Homer**, as **Aristotle** reports in the third book of the *Politics*: *For with me is death* <note>original Greek: "παρ' γὰρ ἐμοὶ θάνατος". This refers to a general's absolute power over life and death during a campaign to maintain discipline.</note>. And **Venulenus** <note>A Roman jurist frequently cited in the Digest.</note> says (*On the custody and exhibition of defendants, law 9*): *He who takes command of an army also has the right to punish common soldiers* <term>Common soldiers: *milites caligatos*, literally "booted soldiers," referring to the rank-and-file who wore the heavy military sandal called the *caliga*.</term>. <margin>What is included in that right.</margin> It encompasses the power to start a battle at will, to lay out camps, to decide on sieges and assaults, to keep captives, to issue camp edicts, to receive hostages, and finally, to do everything necessary to wage war. However, this excludes the right and privilege of **making peace**, which belongs, as I have said, to the state administration <note>original Greek: "πολίτευμα". The author distinguishes between tactical control of an army and the sovereign political power to end a conflict.</note> of the Republic. <margin>The power of Roman Generals over the Senate.</margin> For the Roman Generals exercised the other military rights even against the decrees of the Senate <note>original: "Senatusconsulta"</note>, as we read in the histories of **Fabius** and **Livius Marcatus**. Indeed, they even acted against the commands of Emperors, as **Procopius** notes in the *History of Belisarius and Narsis*. For both of them fought beyond the limits of their orders, and by doing so, secured victory.

<summary>This page defines military command as a specialized power distinct from civil sovereignty, granting generals absolute authority over soldiers and tactics but excluding the right to negotiate peace. It cites classical examples like Agamemnon and Roman generals to show that field commanders often acted independently of the central government's decrees.</summary>

# On the Rights of Empire. Chapter 10.

<margin>In war, the rule of a single person is superior.</margin>
...[he said] that as the sole arbiter of affairs, if he had held the title and right of a king, he would have achieved military glory much more readily <note>original: "solus arbiter rerum... nomine regio"</note>. In war, indeed, nothing is more effective than the rule of one man. As a certain colleague says in **Livy**, book 6: *The management of all affairs, whenever any military terror looms, resides in one man; and I have determined in my mind to submit my command to Camillus, believing my own majesty is in no way diminished by yielding to the majesty of such a man.* <note>Marcus Furius Camillus was a legendary Roman general and dictator celebrated for saving Rome from the Gauls.</note> And in book 4: *Three generals, having been chosen, set out for Veii, and they served as proof of how useless a command held by many is in war; as each clung to his own plans, and while one thought one thing and another something else, they opened up an opportunity for the enemy.*

<margin>Sinan Pasha's supreme command in war.</margin>
Hence, among the Turks in recent years, **Sinan Pasha** <note>Koca Sinan Pasha (c. 1520–1596), an Ottoman Grand Vizier and influential military commander.</note> exercised supreme command of war in the camp for an entire seven-year period, even in the presence of the Prince <note>Referring here to the Sultan</note>, with the same power as the Emperor himself, as witnessed by Soranzio in his work on the Ottomans. > *many a page was found among them as empty sheets.* <note>original: "Impresso plurima signo / Deprensa est vacuis apud illos pagina chartis." This refers to the practice of providing "carte blanche" to trusted officials.</note>

### CHAPTER I.

->*Threefold civil prudence, threefold state of the Republic. From this arise as many types of Secrets of the Republic. Why Aristotle passed over royal secrets in deep silence. The principal authors of Secrets.*<-

<margin>
Secrets specifically so called are divided according to a threefold state, which is either
1. Popular.
2. Aristocratic.
3. Royal.
</margin>

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' entwined with stylized floral vines and leaves.</image-desc> I categorize "Secrets," specifically so called, into three types, based on that threefold state of Government <note>original: "Imperii"</note>. For all nations and cities, says **Tacitus**, the people, the leading men, or individuals rule. Hence **Aristotle**, **Cicero**, and especially **Tacitus** in the third book of his *Annals*, noted a threefold prudence. *Formerly*, he says, *when the common people were powerful in the state, or when the fathers <note>The "patres" or Senators of Rome</note> prevailed, it was necessary to understand the nature of the masses and by what means they might be managed with moderation; and those who best understood the character of the Senate and the aristocrats were considered clever in their times and wise.* Thus, with the state of the Republic having been changed, and there being no other condition of affairs than that one man should command, it has become useful for these things to be sought out and handed down. That is, to speak plainly <note>original: "crassâ Minerva" — literally "with a thick Minerva," a Roman idiom for using common sense or plain speaking rather than subtle, poetic refinement</note>; it is one thing to know the method of governing a popular Republic, another an aristocratic one, and another a kingdom or principality. This is what historians have noted regarding the citizens of **Florence**: that some of them were favored during the time of the Republic but were hated by the Princes; while others, while the Republic stood, were less... <meta>catchword: ca mi- (likely "minus," meaning "less," continuing the comparison of Florentine citizens)</meta>

<summary>Clapmarius introduces a taxonomy of political secrets (Arcana) based on whether a state is a democracy, an aristocracy, or a monarchy. He cites Tacitus to argue that political wisdom must change when a government transitions from a republic to the rule of a single prince.</summary>

<page-num>55</page-num>

<header>On the Secrets of Empire. Chapter 1.</header>

...[common things] that are least pleasing to the masses, but most welcome to princes; others, however, had no place neither under a princedom nor while the Republic <note>Clapmarius uses "Republica" as a general term for any state or commonwealth, not just a representative one.</note> stood. Concerning which matter I think it is established in a few words.

According to this variety of Republics, and the prudence <note>In this context, "prudence" refers to "political science" or "statecraft."</note> concerning them, the **Secrets** of the Republics—or **Sophisms** <note>original: "sophismata"; here meaning political stratagems or clever maneuvers used to maintain power.</note>—also vary. For they are either **Aristocratic**, **Democratic**, or **Royal**. In this [Royal] Republic, danger to the King comes either from the common people or from the nobility; in that one [Aristocratic], either from one man who might invade the empire, or from the patricians; in that other one [Democratic], either from the common people, or lest one man draw the sum of the entire Republic to himself. For civil dissensions of this kind, says **Cicero** in his *Oration against Catiline*, pertain not to destroying the Republic, but to changing it.

<margin>*Why Aristotle omitted royal secrets.*</margin>
Regarding the first two, the **Philosopher** <note>A standard academic reference to Aristotle.</note> treats some things in his *Politics*; but of the royal secrets he hardly makes mention. Was it because they were kept in the dark? Or was it because he hesitated to give them out to the common people, and thus make the private thoughts of Princes subject to the people, so that he might look out for the rule of King Alexander, his [pupil]? As **Cassiodorus** says in the 10th Letter of the 8th book of *Variae*: *It is a difficult thing to have earned the secret of a Prince, where, if anything is known, its betrayal is feared even by another.* And **Tacitus** in the 3rd book of the *Annals*: *The deep thoughts <note>original: "sensus"</note> of a prince, and whatever he prepares in secret, are illicit and risky to explore; nor might you even then attain them.* There are, however, certain things in the 5th book of the *Politics* concerning "Tyrannical arts," some of which, correctly understood, you might refer to the secrets of royal rule without danger: of which I will speak later.

<margin>*The principal authors of popular and Royal secrets.*</margin>
Furthermore, many examples of popular and Aristocratic secrets can be excerpted from **Livy**, **Sallust**, and other historians. But royal secrets, most sharply and frequently of all, [noted]...

## CHAPTER II.

->*Aristotelian secrets of the nobles, or Patricians, against the common people. The meaning of the common people. The common people prefer to be deceived rather than compelled.*<-

<margin>The secrets of the Patricians against the common people are defined.</margin>
The secrets of the Patricians against the common people, then, are hidden counsels through which the common people are so baited <note>original: "inescatur"; a metaphor for enticement, like a fish to a hook.</note> in the Republic that they believe themselves to possess that which they do not.

For the people must be enticed with this deception, as it is most dangerous to impose anything upon them against their will. As **Livy** says in Book 4: *Indeed, to be prohibited by law and to have the right of marriage between the fathers <note>The "patres" or Senators/Patricians.</note> and the common people taken away, that is finally an insult to the common people.* I speak of the common people <note>original: "plebe"</note>, not as they were among the **Gauls**, who—according to **Caesar** in Book 5 of the *Gallic War*—are held almost in the position of slaves, who dare nothing on their own and are admitted to no council, and against whom there are all the same rights that masters have over slaves. Rather, I speak of a people who love liberty—as **Tacitus** testifies of the Romans, **Guicciardini** of the Florentines, and **Crantz** of certain German Republics—who can endure neither total liberty, nor total [slavery]...

...[nor] can they endure such servitude. Moreover, the **Secrets of the Patricians** <note>original: "Arcana Patriciorum"</note> against the common people <note>original: "plebem"</note> are generally these, according to **Aristotle** in Book 4 of the *Politics*, chapter 13, whose words it is right and proper <note>original: "jus & fas"</note> to record here.

<margin>The principal secrets found in Aristotle are recounted.</margin>
<note>The following passage is translated from the original Greek in the text.</note>
There are five things that are clever devices <note>original: "sophizantai"; used here to mean political tricks or pretexts.</note> used in constitutions for the sake of a false front toward the people: regarding the public assembly, the magistracies <note>government offices</note>, the law courts, the bearing of arms, and physical training. Regarding the assembly: it is permitted for all to attend. But a fine is imposed on the wealthy if they do not attend, while the poor are either not fined at all, or the fine for the wealthy is much greater. Regarding the magistracies: those who meet the property qualification are not permitted to decline an office under oath, but the poor are allowed to do so. Regarding the law courts: there is a fine for the wealthy if they do not serve as jurors, but the poor have immunity; or the fine is large for the wealthy and small for the poor, as in the laws of **Charondas** <note>A 7th-century BC lawgiver from Sicily known for his strict and sometimes unusual legal codes.</note>. In some places, everyone who has registered is permitted to attend the assembly and serve as jurors; but if they register and then fail to attend or serve, heavy fines are imposed. This is done so that people will avoid registering to escape the fine, and because they are not registered, they then cannot serve in the courts or attend the assembly. They legislate in the same way regarding the possession of arms and physical training: for the poor are allowed to not possess arms, but the wealthy are fined if they do not have them. Similarly, if they do not engage in physical training, there is no fine for the poor, but it is punishable for the wealthy. This ensures that the wealthy participate because of the fine, while the poor, having nothing to fear, do not participate. These, then, are the oligarchic clever devices of legislation.

These are the secrets or "sophisms" <note>original: "arcana sive sophismata"</note> which are used as a pretext by the aristocrats <note>original: "optimatibus"</note> before the people, and they are five: Public Assemblies, Magistracies, Law Courts, arms, and the use and training of arms. Concerning assemblies: everyone is allowed to be present, but a greater fine is established for the Patricians, or the wealthy, if they are not present, than for the common people. Concerning magistracies: those who possess a high property rating <note>original: "censum"</note> are not allowed to renounce a magistracy, whereas the common people...

<margin>Legal judgments.</margin>
...but it is indeed permitted for the poor. Regarding the **Legal Courts** <note>original: "Iudicia"</note>, they decree a penalty for the wealthy unless they dispense justice to the citizens; for the common people <note>original: "plebi"</note>, however, there is impunity, or they might decree a large fine for the former and a very small one for the latter, as is found in the laws of **Charondas** <note>A 7th-century BC lawgiver from Sicily known for his strict legal codes.</note>. In certain places, it is permitted for all who are registered to be present at the assemblies and trials: those who do not obey face great penalties, and so out of fear of punishment, they neither register their names nor come to the gatherings and trials. They establish the same method regarding arms and **gymnasia** <note>term: "gymnasia" — In antiquity, these were places for both physical education and military training, essential for those holding full citizen rights.</note>.
<margin>Arms and gymnasia.</margin>
The common people and the poor are not permitted to have arms; for the **patricians** <note>The hereditary noble class of Rome; here used generally for the ruling elite.</note>, however, a penalty is established if they do not possess them. If the former do not exercise themselves in arms, they are not punished at all; the Patricians, however, are punished; and so the latter are compelled by fear of penalty to handle arms, while the former, unpunished, abstain from arms. These are the arts of the **aristocrats** <note>original: "optimatum"; the "best men" or upper-class faction.</note>, or the secret counsels against the common people. **Aristotle** says the same in Book 4, chapter 9: <note>The following is translated from the Greek.</note> "For in oligarchies they impose a fine on the wealthy if they do not serve as judges, but for the poor, there is no payment;" <note>original: "ἐν μὲν γὰρ ταῖς ὀλιγαρχίαις τοῖς εὐπόροις ζημίαν τάττουσιν, ἂν μὴ δικάζωσι· τοῖς δ’ ἀπόροις οὐδένα μισθόν"</note> that is, in the power of the few, a penalty is decreed for the aristocrats unless they dispense justice, but for the common people, there is no reward. Thus far the Philosopher <note>Aristotle was often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in early modern scholarship.</note>.

**Livy** hints at the same thing in Book 4 when he says: *It happens through the ambition and the arts of the Fathers <note>The Senators or Patricians.</note> that the path to honor is blocked for the common people.* Indeed, each of these points comes under investigation:

### On the Secrets of Government. Chapter 2.

...by the common people <note>original: "plebe"</note>; for if they are entirely removed from the government, they become most hostile to the present state of the Commonwealth. As **Aristotle** testifies in the *Politics*, Book 3, Chapter 7: *“When,”* he says, *“a multitude of the needy is in the city, and they are excluded from honors, it is necessary that city be full of enemies of the State.”* <note>Aristotle's *Politics* is a foundational text for this author's analysis of power dynamics.</note> From this come so many dissensions and civil wars in all histories among almost all nations. For example, in the **Roman Republic**, when the common people were excluded from all honors, they were an enemy. Indeed, they rose up against the Fathers <note>The "Patres," or the Senate and patrician class.</note> to such an extent that they preferred the Roman Republic to be overwhelmed by hostile arms rather than be entirely removed from the Republic. 

There have also been very frequent examples of this matter in the Christian Republics, as **Guicciardini** <note>Francesco Guicciardini (1483–1540), a Florentine statesman and historian.</note> testifies regarding the **Florentine Republic**, **Lambert of Aschaffenburg** <note>original: "Scaffnaburgensis"; an 11th-century chronicler.</note> regarding the state of **Trier**, and **Albert Krantz** <note>A 15th-century German historian.</note> regarding others. And as **Justin** <note>A Roman historian.</note> says in Book 13: *“When,”* he says, *“the Knights also had done the same, the foot-soldiers, indignant that no part of the deliberations was left to them, named Arrhidaeus <note>The half-brother of Alexander the Great.</note>, Alexander’s brother, as king.”*

<margin>Keeping them from the administration of the State by subtle arts.</margin>
Furthermore, lest a window be opened to the common people in an **Aristocracy** <note>term: "Aristocratia" — A government ruled by a small, elite class of "best" citizens.</note> for the creation of magistrates (for in such a way a change and overthrow of the present State would eventually occur), they must be kept away and deterred from the administration of the State by subtle arts and slow pressure. First, the path must not be closed to the common people; rather, they should be admitted. As **Livy** writes in Book 4: *“And the leaders of the common people preferred those elections in which they were not taken into account, rather than those in which they were passed over as unworthy.”* <note>Livy suggests that people find it less insulting to be ignored by the system than to be officially rejected by it.</note> But truly, a penalty must be declared for the patricians and the wealthy unless they come to the assemblies; for the common people and the poor, however, the penalty should be waived.

<margin>What those arts are.</margin>
Fascinated by this "beautiful lie" <note>original: "speciosa fallacia"</note>, the common people, occupied with their domestic labors for the sake of supporting themselves and their families, will easily stay away. For it is enough for the common people...

...opportunity is given to them to participate in the Republic, from which they nevertheless abstain on account of private business, with which men are more occupied than with public affairs. As **Tacitus** <note>Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), a Roman historian known for his cynical analysis of power.</note> says in the first book of his *Histories*: *“The people were excluded from common concerns by the excessive magnitude of those very cares.”* <note>original: "Magnitudine nimia communium curarum expertem esse populum."</note> And in the same place: *“Each person has their own private motivation; public honor is held in low esteem.”* <note>original: "Privata cuique stimulatio, vile decus publicum."</note> The **Patricians** <note>The hereditary aristocrats of Rome.</note> and the wealthy, however, who are sometimes rather negligent in exercising their authority, prefer to administer the Republic rather than be punished by a financial penalty. Whence, both outcomes occur which benefit the state: that is, the patricians are industrious in governing the Republic, and the commoners <note>original: "plebs"</note> willingly abstain from command.

<margin>Care must be taken lest they notice.</margin>
The common people in the **Roman Republic** very nearly noticed this "art" or trick. For this reason, the **Tribunes of the Plebs** <note>Elected officials who protected the interests of the commoners.</note> say in **Livy**, Book 4: *“There is surely fraud in this matter, and Sempronius has employed more art than good faith at the assemblies.”* <note>Livy (Titus Livius) was the premier historian of early Rome. This refers to the manipulation of election procedures to favor the elite.</note> Furthermore, it is not permitted for those who administer the Republic to withdraw themselves from the assemblies with impunity. For such behavior is characteristic of <term>dynastōn</term> <note>original: "δυνάςων"; meaning "dynasts" or "despots" who rule by force.</note> rather than <term>aristōn</term> <note>original: "ἀρίϛων"; meaning "the best men" or "aristocrats" who rule by merit.</note>. By this name, **Sulla** is called by **Valerius Maximus** <note>A 1st-century author of a collection of historical anecdotes.</note> in Book 7 as the "Lord of the Field." <note>Referring to the Campus Martius, where elections were held; Sulla dominated the political space through intimidation.</note>

<margin>Why Tarquinius did not appear at the Latin assembly he called, and with what success.</margin>
Therefore **Tarquinius** <note>Tarquinius Superbus, the legendary last King of Rome, known for his tyranny.</note>, when he had called an assembly for the **Latins**, did not show up himself; in my judgment, he did this so that it might serve as an example of his domination and prerogative over the Latins. **Turnus Herdonius**, noticing this deceptive pride, urged the Latins to go home, since Tarquinius did not present himself; they should not observe the day of the council any more than the man who had called it was observing it. **Cicero** also notes the same thing regarding **Mark Antony** in his *Philippics*: *“Antony,”* he says, *“issued an edict that the Senate should be present in large numbers, but he himself was not present.”* For in a free Republic, the laws of the assemblies bind all those who preside over the Republic: which seems to be the reason, among others, that **Caesar** [punished] the **Treveri**, because... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence, referring to Julius Caesar's campaigns against the Treveri, a Gallic tribe.</note>

## CHAPTER IV.

### *That it should be permitted for the commoners <note>original: "plebi"</note> to resign from a Magistracy: but for a Patrician, it should not be permitted. A sophism of the Romans against Appius Claudius. A magistracy is not the supreme power: and yet there are great struggles over it in a Republic.*

<margin>The office of magistrate should be granted to the worthy even if they are unwilling, and the reasons why.</margin>
It is the opinion of **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose *Politics* defined Western government theory.</note> and all political thinkers that the office of magistrate should not only be granted to those who desire it, but also to those who do not, provided they are worthy. This is for two primary reasons: First, because this refusal is often deceptive <note>original: "fucosa"</note>, just as **Tacitus** <note>Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), Roman historian.</note> described regarding **Augustus** <note>The first Roman Emperor (r. 27 BC – 14 AD).</note>, that under the appearance of one refusing, he most ardently desired it. <note>original: "specie recusantis flagrantissimè cupiisse."</note> Second, because the safety of the common State <note>original: "Reipubl."</note> demands it. Furthermore, those who reject honors usually feel the weight of their difficulty and burdens, and for this very reason, they ought to be chosen or retained. **Galba** <note>Roman Emperor (r. 68–69 AD).</note> observed this, of whom **Tranquillus** <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus (c. 69–122 AD), author of *The Twelve Caesars*.</note> says: *“It was thought,”* he says, *“that he would limit Senatorial and equestrian offices to a two-year period, and would not give them except to those who were reluctant and refusing.”* <note>original: "non daturus nisi invitis ac recusantibus."</note>

<margin>In an aristocratic Republic, the commoners were granted the license to resign from a Magistracy.</margin>
Contrary to this rule, in an aristocratic Republic <note>original: "optimatum Republica"</note>, the license to resign from a Magistracy was granted to the commoners. For when magistrates are chosen from the commoners, according to **Livy** <note>Titus Livius (64 BC – 17 AD), the great historian of Rome.</note> in Book 4, power is not merely shared with the lowest classes in a common way, but the supreme command <note>original: "summum Imperium"</note> is utterly snatched away from the leading men and given to the commoners. The same author says in Book 7: *“With the Dictator remaining obstinate, it was better to remove the entire consulship from the Republic than to make it common to both the fathers [patricians] and the plebs.”* <note>original: "consulatum... promiscuum patribus ac plebi facere."</note> Wherefore, when three Tribunes with consular power were created from the commoners, the same Livy says in Book 5: *“not only was command shared with the common people, but...”*

...almost lost the supreme power. <note>original: "summum Imperium"</note> Otherwise, with this freedom to resign, the commoners <note>original: "plebs"</note>—and especially those who are poor—very often abstain from the magistracy, as it is usually joined with heavy financial burdens.

<margin>A penalty should be imposed on the nobles who resign.</margin>
<margin>A trick <note>original: "sophisma"</note> of the Romans against Appius Claudius.</margin>
On the contrary, so that the nobles <note>original: "optimates"</note> may maintain the Republic, a penalty is imposed on those who resign from a magistracy. It is clear to anyone that doing this serves to preserve the present state of the Republic. To this, I refer that Roman trick against **Appius Claudius** <note>A leading Roman official (decemvir) who attempted to seize permanent power around 450 BC.</note>, who was seeking an extension of his term in the Decemvirate <note>A commission of ten men established to write the first Roman law codes.</note>. Thus, the Senators <note>original: "Patres"</note> assigned him the duty of holding the elections. This was a craftiness, says **Livy** <note>Titus Livius (64 BC – 17 AD), the primary historian of early Rome.</note> in Book 3, so that he could not nominate himself—something which no one had ever done before except for the Tribunes, and even then, it was considered the worst of precedents.

<margin>A magistracy is not the supreme power.</margin>
But you will say that a magistracy is not supreme power. For supreme power is something more exalted, says **Tacitus** <note>The Roman historian (c. 56 – 120 AD) famous for his analysis of power dynamics.</note> in the third book of his *Annals*. However, in a Republic, the greatest attention must be paid to that which creeps in little by little. For, says **Aristotle** <note>Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose *Politics* is a foundational text for this author.</note> in Book 5 of his *Politics*, corruption lies hidden because it does not appear so great at first. And in the same book: the state of the Republic is changed through negligence, he says, when those who hate the present state of the Republic are admitted to positions of power. And **Demosthenes** <note>The famous Athenian orator (384–322 BC).</note> in his fourth *Philippic*: Just as in private life, so also in a Republic, daily idleness and sluggishness do not appear in each individual thing immediately as it is neglected, but in the total sum of affairs. And yet, there have always been the greatest contests over obtaining a magistracy; so much so that, as **Livy** testifies in Book 2, the Republic is distracted and torn apart through the magistracies, and the question is more about whose hand power is in, rather than the safety of the state.

## CHAPTER V.

### The Exemption of the Commoners from Jurisdiction. The commoners only desire that their own interests be respected.

<margin>The commoners are not to be admitted to jurisdiction.</margin>
<margin>A comparison of the Magistrate and Jurisdiction.</margin>
<margin>The Emperors also seized jurisdiction.</margin>
The logic regarding jurisdiction is the same. For a magistrate is one who presides by deliberating or—as **Cujacius** <note>Jacques Cujas (1522–1590), a renowned French legal scholar of the Renaissance known for applying humanistic methods to Roman law.</note> defines it—by administering the law <note>original: "juridicundo"</note> and maintaining a continuous jurisdiction. Therefore, whoever is a magistrate holds jurisdiction; but the reverse is not true. For supreme power <note>original: "summum imperium"</note> does not reside within jurisdiction alone. Nevertheless, the power of the person pronouncing the law, as **Ulpian** <note>Domitius Ulpianus (c. 170–223 AD), one of the most influential Roman jurists; his writings form a large part of the later Justinian Code.</note> says, is most extensive. Thus, the Roman Patricians <note>The hereditary aristocratic class of ancient Rome.</note> were unwilling to grant the common people <note>original: "plebi"</note> access to the consulship <note>The highest elected political office of the Roman Republic.</note>, unless in turn they obtained from the commoners the creation of one Praetor <note>A high-ranking Roman official primarily responsible for the administration of justice.</note> from among the "fathers" <note>The Senators or Patricians.</note> to declare the law in the city. See **Livy** <note>Titus Livius (64 BC – 17 AD), the primary historian of early Rome.</note>, *Book 6*. Indeed, even the Emperor **Tiberius** <note>The second Roman Emperor (r. 14–37 AD), known for his complex and often secretive political style.</note>, who was most skilled in the art of ruling, was not satisfied with the investigations of the "fathers" <note>The Senate.</note> and would sit in on the court trials; many things were decided in his presence against bribery and the entreaties of the powerful. On this, **Tacitus** <note>Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56 – 120 AD), the Roman historian famous for his critical analysis of the Emperors.</note> says: *But while truth was being served, liberty was being corrupted*; that is, while Tiberius devoted his efforts to the administration of justice, he occupied the power of the Roman people. It has been noted by others that "truth" is used here in place of "justice." Clearly, the Emperors, not content with the right of Rule itself, seized also the legal investigations and jurisdiction for themselves, as can be seen in **Suetonius’** <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus (c. 69 – 122 AD), a Roman biographer of the first twelve emperors.</note> *Nero*, *Chapter 15*.

Therefore, the Patricians who hold the power do not easily admit the common people to jurisdictions. To do this without danger, they pass a law by which patricians and the wealthy are punished unless they pronounce the law when summoned—and indeed punished severely—whereas the commoners are not punished, or at least only lightly. Such was once the law of **Charondas** <note>A celebrated lawgiver of Sicily (c. 7th century BC) known for his strict laws and his requirement that citizens take part in the legal process.</note>. By this deception, only the patricians...

# Arnold Clapmarius, Book I.

Through which they maintain judicial control, with the commoners excluded.
<margin>A trick by which the common people are kept away from judicial power.</margin>
Therefore, in certain places, as **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), the Greek philosopher whose *Politics* provides the foundation for Clapmarius's analysis of statecraft.</note> testifies, they publish the names of those eligible for jury duty. When this is done, whoever withdraws himself from the Courts falls into the heaviest penalties. To remain safe from these penalties, the commoner <note>original: "plebejus"</note> does not easily offer his name to be recorded among the judicial order, and thus he remains away with impunity. Whence it happens that the **Patricians** <note>The hereditary aristocrats of Rome.</note> and the wealthy obtain the highest leadership of the Republic even against their will. For this is the "power of the few" <note>An oligarchy.</note>, as Aristotle defines it in Book 4 of his *Politics*, Chapter 5.

<margin>The nature of the common people: they only want their own interests respected, and they let the rest pass.</margin>
Moreover, such is the nature of the common people: they only wish for their own account to be taken; once this is obtained, they let everything else pass. The Roman commoners had seized the right of creating magistrates; regarding this, **Livy** <note>Titus Livius (64 BC–17 AD), the primary Roman historian used here to provide empirical evidence for political theories.</note> says in Book 4: *To most, there was no doubt that they would elect the most seditious [troublemakers] from among the common people.* But indeed, the outcome of those elections taught that spirits are of one kind during the struggle for liberty and dignity, and of another kind once the contests are set aside and judgment is uncorrupted. For the people elected only Patricians as **Tribunes**, content with the fact that *consideration had been given to the commoners.* <note>The "sophism" here is that once the people won the *right* to be elected, they were satisfied and chose to elect the traditional elites anyway.</note>

So too at Rome there was a massive struggle over the **Agrarian law** <note>Laws regarding the distribution of public land to the poor, a source of constant social friction in the Roman Republic.</note>. Finally, the opinion of **Fabius** <note>Marcus Fabius Vibulanus, a Roman consul.</note> was that, under the leadership and auspices of **Titus Quinctius**, a colony could be settled on a portion of the land captured from the **Volscians** the previous year near **Antium** <note>The original text says "Aretium" (modern Arezzo), but historical context and Livy’s text (4.11) confirm this refers to Antium, a coastal city.</note>, which was a convenient and maritime city. In this way, without the complaints of the current owners, the common people would go onto the lands, and the city would be in harmony. Therefore, they were ordered to give their names, those who wished to receive land; at that point, Livy writes: *As often happens, abundance immediately created a sense of distaste, and so very few gave their names.*

## CHAPTER VI.

*That the common people are permitted not to have arms. The Law of Arms. The crime of taking up arms. The possession of arms. The Armory of the Romans. The Arsenal of the Venetians.*

<margin>Nor is it permitted for the common people to have arms.</margin>
The Right of Arms, *as I stated in the first book, is not a private right, but a public one.* Regarding this, see the *Single Book of the Code, on the Use of Arms* <note>original: "lib. unic. C. ut arm. us." — referring to the Codex Justinianus, Book 11, Title 47</note>. *And in New Constitution 17, it is not permitted to carry arms unless one is a soldier.* Understand "arms" to mean all kinds, especially those forged machines which ought to be forbidden to private citizens: such as today are **Bombards**, **Culverins**, **Salamanders**, **Basilisks**, larger **Muskets**, **Crocodiles**, and perforated bows, or **Arquebuses** <note>These terms refer to various types of early modern artillery and firearms. "Basilisks" and "Culverins" were heavy cannons named after mythical beasts.</note>, which are used for the demolition of walls.

<margin>To whom the possession of arms most often belongs.</margin>
*The possession of these arms belongs to him who holds the supreme power in the Republic. Thus Aristotle in Book 2 of his Politics, Chapter 8 says: <gloss>For those who possess the arms are also masters of whether the constitution remains or not.</gloss> <note>original: "ἐν ἔχοντες ὅπλα ζινοντες θεῶν δ' ἔδοτοι τὲ τὸ ὅπλα νεκτημένων" — the Greek in the original text is somewhat garbled, but refers to Aristotle's observation that political power follows the possession of weapons.</note> Those who do not have arms are the slaves of those who do. And in Book 3, Chapter 5: In a Republic, that part is the most powerful in which the strength of war consists, and those who are in possession of arms.* For this reason, a peasant is prohibited from carrying arms, or a lance, or a sword, according to *Title 27 of the second book of Feudal Law, concerning the preservation of peace.* Because in *private matters, the Romans were especially scrupulous.* Indeed, even in a rebellion of slaves, they did not wish to arm the common people, because of the "doubtful mind" <note>An idiom suggesting the commoners were fickle or untrustworthy.</note> of the commoners. *Yet they do give arms,* says **Livy** <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> in Book 3, *but not to the general public.* Hence **Minucius** accuses **Melius** of taking up arms. *Weapons,* says Livy in Book 4, *were being collected in the house of Melius, and he was holding meetings at home, and had entered into unmistakable plans to seize the kingdom.*

<margin>To take up arms by one's own authority is a capital offense.</margin>
*For those who take up arms by private authority are judged to be enemies of the Republic.* Hence **Tacitus** <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), Roman historian and politician.</note> says in Book 1 of his *Annals*, that an

<margin>The laying down of arms is a sign of submission.</margin>
...army. And in the *Annals, Book 5* <note>original: "5. Annal." — Tacitus, Annals 6.3 (Clapmarius cites it as book 5)</note>, he writes: *But he did not object to arms, nor to a desire for revolution, but rather he cast his grandson’s youthful loves and lack of modesty as a reproach.* In this way, when enemies are brought under one's power, they are ordered to lay down their arms. *Livy, Book 4: After the general was surrendered, he ordered the arms to be laid down.* And in *Book 5*, the ambassadors of the Falerii said of their own accord: *“Send men,” they say, “who may receive our arms, our hostages, and our city through its open gates.”* And *Caesar, in Book 2 of the Gallic War: Once the hostages were handed over and all weapons collected from the town, he received them into surrender.* And *Tacitus in the Histories says: They were publicly deprived of their arms as a penalty.* And *Gunther, Book 7* <note>Gunther of Pairis, a 12th-century Cistercian monk and poet</note>:

> Leaving both arms and full fortresses to the victor,
> He is miserably driven, stripped bare, to the enemy city.

<margin>It is fitting for the patricians to be equipped with an armory.</margin>
In an Aristocratic Republic <note>original: "Republica optimatum"</note>, therefore, it is necessary for the nobles to have arms, and they should be punished if they do not; however, the **common people** (*plebs*) may go without arms without penalty. Indeed, it is fitting for the **patricians** <term>patricians: the hereditary land-owning elite of Rome</term> to be supplied with an armory, such as existed in Rome. Cicero mentions this in his speech *For Rabirius*, and it was located on the Caelian Hill in the second region, as can be seen in the *Register of Dignities* <note>original: "Notitia utriusque Imperii" — a famous document of the late Roman Empire's administrative structure</note>. Such also is the highly equipped Armory of the Venetians, which they call the **Arsenal** <note>The Venetian Arsenal was the largest industrial complex in Europe before the Industrial Revolution, responsible for the city's naval supremacy.</note>. And yet, under the Emperors, the use of arms was granted to illustrious men whose loyalty had been thoroughly tested, as seen in the *Final Law of the Code on the Provost of the Sacred Bedchamber* <note>original: "l. ult. C. de præp. sac. cubic." — refering to the Codex Justinianus</note>. This was permitted because it seemed to fulfill their own desires while appearing to harm no one, as the Emperor Anastasius says in that same place. Furthermore, in the title *On maintaining peace and its violation* in the *Second Book of Feuds* <note>original: "27. Feud. lib. 2." — referring to the Libri Feudorum, a collection of feudal law</note>: A knight may carry arms to the Count’s palace if he has been requested to do so by the Count.

### CHAPTER VII.

*That it is permitted for the common people to abstain from military training, and in passing and with a distinction: whether it is expedient for citizens to be trained in arms. The arts of the patricians and Princes. The Roman and Turkish cavalry. The trickery of M. Rutilius and Germanicus in quelling a sedition.*

---

<margin>Whether it is beneficial for citizens to be trained in arms is debated.</margin>It is a matter of controversy among political thinkers whether it is beneficial for citizens to be trained in arms; great men disagree on this point. It is clear to me that if citizens are by nature fierce and impatient of being ruled, once they are equipped with weapons and ready for action, they easily turn to rebellion and find a way to seize power. For this reason, the Cretans, while they allowed many things to their slaves, forbade them only the use and possession of weapons.

<margin>In an Aristocracy, it is expedient to train those who hold the highest ranks.</margin>In an <term>Aristocracy</term><note>A form of government where power is held by the nobility or a small, privileged ruling class.</note>, certainly, those who hold the primary positions in the Republic ought to be trained in arms, with a heavy penalty imposed if they fail to do so; but the commoners are allowed to abstain from arms without punishment. Hence it happens that the former learn the military art and easily keep the common people away from the government by force of steel; the latter, however, grow sluggish through leisure and luxury. For this reason, the **Patricians** <term>Patricians: the hereditary land-owning elite of ancient Rome</term> in the Roman Republic were instructed in military science, and especially in the equestrian art <note>The skills of the cavalry or knights</note>. Thus, Consul Valerius said to the Knights: *“Go, young men, surpass the infantry in courage, as you surpass them in honor and rank.”* <note>original: "Agite, inquit, Iuvenes, præstate virtute peditem, ut honore atque ordine præstatis." — Livy, History of Rome, 2.20</note>. And the famous Perseus, in that same Livy, calls the Roman Knights the *“Princes of Youth, the Seedbed of the Senate”*; from there, he says, the Consuls are chosen for the first rank, and from there the Generals are created. Indeed, the entire dignity of the Roman military consisted in the cavalry, just as it does today in the Turkish military <note>The author refers to the Ottoman Empire's Sipahi or elite cavalry units</note>; as Scipio excellently argues on this matter...

<margin>And in a Monarchy, regarding the children of Kings.</margin>
And this principle applies not only in an <term>Aristocracy</term><note>A government ruled by a small elite class.</note>, but also in a **Principate** <note>A form of monarchy, specifically referring here to the early Roman Empire.</note> regarding the children of Kings. It was with this plan that **Caesar Octavian** trained himself for command and taught himself everything that seemed fitting for one who was to occupy the supreme Power. This is noted by **Dion** in Book 45. <note>Cassius Dio, a Roman historian who wrote in Greek.</note> **Tacitus** also writes concerning **Drusus**, the son of **Tiberius**: *Not long after,* he says, *Drusus was sent to Illyricum, so that he might become accustomed to military service and gain the favor of the army; at the same time, Tiberius believed the young man, who was growing unruly with the luxury of the city, was better kept in the camps, and that he himself was safer with both his sons in command of the legions.* <note>original: "Ne multo post Drusus in Illyricum missus est..." from Tacitus's Annals.</note> For military science ought certainly to be the specific domain of the patricians and the nobility.

<margin>Military science ought to be the specific domain of patricians and nobles.</margin>
This is what **Tacitus** reports concerning **Agricola**: that in his early youth he burned with a passion for **Philosophy** beyond what was permitted for Romans and Senators, had his mother's prudence not restrained his fired and glowing mind. Tacitus adds: *His first rudiments of camp life were in Britain, etc.* <note>original: "Prima castrorum rudimenta in Britannia." Gnaeus Julius Agricola was a Roman general responsible for much of the conquest of Britain.</note> For, having left Philosophy behind, he immediately devoted his efforts to military science.

<margin>Likewise civil science and history.</margin>
To these, add **civil science** <note>The study of politics and governance.</note>, the study of **oratory**, and **histories**; through these arts, the patricians easily excel the common people. And yet, I do not know why that famous **Marius** <note>Gaius Marius, a Roman general and statesman known for being a "new man" without noble ancestry.</note> also pleases me regarding war, of whom **Sallust** writes in the *Jugurthine War*: *I have not learned letters; it pleased me little to learn them, since they were of no profit to their teachers toward virtue. But I have learned those things which are by far the best for the Republic: to strike the enemy, to manage garrisons, to fear nothing except a shameful reputation, to endure winter and summer alike, to rest on the ground, and to tolerate want and labor at the same time; with these...* <note>original: "Nõ didici literas... hac". Marius is portrayed as a rugged soldier contrasting himself with the overly-educated, soft nobility.</note>

Seditious soldiers must be separated by strategic skill.

...and by doing other things, our ancestors brought glory to the Republic. These things he [the author] says concerning **Marius**, despite him being a "new man" <note>original: "homine novo." In ancient Rome, a *novus homo* was the first person in a family to serve in the Senate or be elected Consul, lacking the prestige of noble ancestors.</note>. And indeed, it usually happens this way, says **Aristotle** in the *Politics*, Book 5, Chapter 9: The children of governors devote their efforts to luxuries, while those of the poorer classes devote theirs to the Gymnasiums and military exercises. Thus, the latter are both more willing and more capable of attempting revolutions. Furthermore, the trickery of **Marcus Rutilius**, the Roman **Consul**, is not unlike this. When the Roman soldiers had secretly entered into a conspiracy to seize **Capua**, he purged the army by discharging the rowdy men; claiming to some that their term of service was complete; to others that they were now burdened by age or lacked sufficient strength; some were sent on leaves of absence, first individually, then even entire <term>cohorts</term><note>A standard tactical unit of the Roman legion, usually consisting of about 480 men.</note>. Under the pretense of military needs, as they were sent here and there, a large part was sent away; this multitude was then detained by the other **Consul** in **Rome** and the **Praetor**, who invented one delay after another. By this granted leave of departure, the soldiers—unaware of the trickery—were broken. Thus it was said that the "sinews of the conspiracy" <note>original: "nervos conjurationis"</note> had been cut out by the skill of the **Consul**. In the same way, **Germanicus** sent seditious veterans into **Rhaetia**, under the guise of defending the province; but in reality, so that they might be torn away from the camps that were still in a state of fury, no less by the harshness of the remedy than by the memory of their crime. **Tacitus** says the same in the first book of his *Histories*: Armies separated by long distances are the healthiest thing for a state.

For this reason, they stood by and courted six of the tribunes, persuading, warning, promising, and pretending that all hope was placed in the aid of the **Tribunate**. On this point, **Livy** writes: *It is a noble thing for the tribunes and their power to be used not for harassing the Senate or stirring up discord between the social classes, but to show that there is more strength in the tribunate for resisting wicked colleagues.* This use of the **intercession** <note>The *intercessio* was the legal power of a Tribune to veto the actions of other magistrates or even his own colleagues.</note> frequently broke the insolence of the common people. As **Livy** says in Book 6: *The tribunician power now breaks its own force by its own act of interceding.*

The building of **winter quarters** <note>original: "Hybernaculorum." Usually, Roman armies returned home for the winter; permanent winter camps kept them in the field.</note> served the same purpose, as it dissolved the power of the Tribunes. In this way, the common people were deprived of the opportunity to exercise their liberty and to elect magistrates, as noted in **Livy**, Book 5. Under this same pretext, war was often prepared. **Livy** writes in Book 2: *They decree that they should hold a levy as strictly as possible, because the common people grow unruly in times of leisure.* <note>original: "ocio lascivire plebem."</note> 

Hence, the **Tribunes of the plebs** complained so loudly about the sending away of the youth to the **Veliternian** war. These same Romans, when they had angered the common people by punishing their rebellions, threw the **division of lands** before them as a distraction. **Livy** says in Book 4: *It was the most suitable time to throw the division of the **Volanian** land as a soothing balm to their minds; by which act they would lessen the desire for the **Agrarian Law**, which—because the public land was possessed through injustice—was driving the Patricians out.*

### CHAPTER IX.

*How to infatuate the common people with religion; to publicly testify and protect the commoners from injuries; to pretend that certain magistrates are harmful; and to avoid doing everything in too aristocratic a fashion, but rather to act by diversion.* <note>The original Greek phrase "ἐκ παραγωγῆς" (ek paragoges) means to lead someone aside or distract them from the main issue.</note>

<margin>
Eventually, the Roman elites turned all matters toward religion so they could keep the commoners away from the magistracy.
</margin>

When the leading men of Rome had tried everything in vain to prevent the commoners from holding high office, they finally turned every matter toward religion. Indeed, human minds are struck by religion as if by a **thyrsus** <note>A staff associated with the god Bacchus, used here as a metaphor for something that induces a religious frenzy or trance.</note>. Therefore, when it was said at the assemblies that things done by **auspices** <term>Auspices: A religious rite where priests observed the flight of birds to determine if the gods approved of a political action</term> seemed unworthy to the Gods if honors were made common and the distinctions of families were blurred, the effect was immediate. The common people, astounded by religion, elected only Patricians as **Military Tribunes with Consular Power**. <note>A high office that replaced the Consulship for several years, which the commoners fought to be eligible for.</note> On this point, **Livy** says in Book 5: *The Fathers acted not with force, but with prayers, and among those prayers was much mention of the Gods; this was most effective for the religious party.* This is a "secret" <term>Arcanum: A hidden or secret strategy of government</term> which the Patricians used to, as it were, drive the commoners out of their minds. And so, when a Consul who was a commoner was killed—as if this were a sacrificial offering to expiate a sin—the indignant [Patricians]...

### Arnold Clapmarius, Book II

...they would go on, they said, and create consuls from the common people, transferring the **auspices** <term>Auspices: A religious practice where officials looked for signs from the gods, such as the flight of birds, to approve or block public actions.</term> to where it would be a sin. The Gods themselves had vindicated their own divine power and their auspices; for as soon as these were touched by someone who had neither the legal nor divine right to do so, the destruction of the army along with its leader served as a lesson. This was done so that, in the future, elections would not be held while the rights of the families were in such turmoil. **Livy**, in Book 7, notes that in this "secret of state," one thing is being done while another is pretended. against the **common people** <term>Plebs: The general body of free Roman citizens who were not Patricians.</term>, in which one thing is visibly simulated, but another is actually done. <header>Arnold Clapmarius, Book II.</header>

<margin>*Other strategies in which there is no, or at least very little, pretense.*</margin>
...one thing is pretended to be done. But indeed, **Labeo** <term>Labeo: Marcus Antistius Labeo, a famous Roman jurist known for his expertise in both law and grammar.</term> challenged the definition of deceit, arguing that it is possible to outmaneuver someone even without active pretense. The same logic applies to this teaching. For there are certain secrets in which one thing is done and another is pretended; but there are also hidden strategies in which there is no pretense, or at least very little, such as the following.

<margin>*When youth are educated according to the nature of the Republic.*</margin>
First, when the youth are educated according to the form of the government. According to the testimony of **Aristotle** <term>Aristotle: The Greek philosopher whose "Politics" argued that education must be tailored to the specific constitution of the state to ensure its survival.</term>, this is the most effective way to preserve the current state of the Republic; and so **Tacitus** <term>Tacitus: A Roman historian who chronicled the loss of Roman liberty under the early emperors.</term> places this among the foundations of the Roman Principate. For once those who had lived while the Republic was still standing and free had passed away, no one was left who had tasted the sweetness of liberty. Thus Tacitus says, *how few were left who had actually seen the Republic?* <note>original: "quotusquisque reliquus qui Rempublicam vidisset"</note> For youths in an Aristocracy are shaped one way, those of the common people another, and the children of Kings and Princes yet another; that is, the youth must be educated differently in a kingdom, differently under the rule of the nobility, and differently under the rule of the people. This is a point of little dispute. <margin>*Why Brutus executed his own children.*</margin> Indeed, it seems to me that this is what drove **Brutus** <term>Brutus: Lucius Junius Brutus, a founder of the Roman Republic, who executed his sons for conspiring to bring back the exiled Tarquin kings.</term> to execute his own children after liberty had been secured, for they had been born and raised under a monarchy.

<margin>*Laws are adapted to the current state of affairs.*</margin>
Next, laws must be shaped to fit the current state of the government. For some laws, as the Philosopher <note>Referring to Aristotle.</note> testifies, are suitable for a kingdom, others for a Democracy, and others for an Aristocracy. This is why Tacitus says of **Augustus**: in the third book of his *Annals*, *having abolished many old ways, he gave laws by which the Republic might enjoy peace and a Prince.* <note>original: "eum, multis abolitis, dedisse jura, queis pace & principe uteretur Respublica"</note> From this it is clear that since the Empire of today differs greatly from that old Roman one, certain laws of the ancient Roman Republic are not at all suitable for today; such as those concerning the state's power

### On the Secrets of State. Chapter 10.

<margin>Certain ancient laws of the Roman Republic do not suit today's state and why.</margin>
...authority of the Prince, regarding dowries, successions, and other things of that sort: which certain very foolish legal experts nonetheless try to twist, indiscriminately and by force <note>original: "veluti obtorto collo," literally "as if with a twisted neck," a Latin idiom for dragging something into a place where it does not belong</note>, to suit the current State.

<margin>The State is called back to its principles.</margin>
Third: a State must often be reduced back to its founding principles. The most sharp-witted **Machiavelli** <term>Machiavelli: Niccolò Machiavelli, whose "Discourses on Livy" argued that for a republic to survive, it must be periodically "brought back toward its beginnings" to purge corruption.</term> noted that there is no better art than this for preserving the status quo. For it is the nature of States that they easily attract flaws of their own accord, whether through the passage of time or through the carelessness and negligence of those who administer the government. If this corruption creeps further and is not cut away, the State easily transforms into a different kind of government altogether. For, as the **Poet** <note>The author likely refers to a common Maxim or a classical poet like Horace or Lucan</note> sings:

> *If it departs but a little from the top, it verges toward the bottom.*

<margin>The common people must be yielded to as little as possible.</margin>
For this reason, in an Aristocracy, the leading men shall take care not to easily yield to the common people. As the elder Fathers say in **Livy**, Book 3: *just as the young patricians are too fierce, so they would prefer—if limits had to be exceeded—that spirit and boldness remain with their own side rather than with their adversaries.* <note>original: "ut nimis feroces juvenes patricios esse; ita malle si modus excedendus esset, suis quam adversariis superesse animos"</note>

<margin>The origin of the five-year renewal of the State among the Florentines.</margin>
Furthermore, if they have departed in any way from their own laws, they should "resolve" the State like **chemists** <term>Chemists: Here referring to alchemists or early scientists who broke substances down to their essential elements to purify them.</term>. According to Machiavelli, this was the nature of the five-year renewal <note>original: "redintegratio"</note> of the State among the Florentines. **Frederick Barbarossa** <term>Frederick Barbarossa: The Holy Roman Emperor (reigned 1155–1190) who attempted to re-establish imperial rights over the Italian city-states.</term> did the same in the cities of Italy, of whom **Gunther** <note>Gunther of Pairis, author of the epic poem "Ligurinus" about Frederick I.</note> writes in Book 8:

> *But the laws of the ancients and the royal edicts,*
> *Suppressed by a long judicial silence, are quiet; those which Charles once,*
> *And our Otho published, the treasury recognizes few traces*
> *Of its own law on Italian shores.*
> *Consult together: which laws do you wish me either to bring forth*
> *As new, or to renew those that have suffered the decay of age?*

But above all, the people ought to be taught that money...

The same author states: **Caesar** entered into a partnership with **Pompey** and **Crassus** <note>The First Triumvirate, an informal political alliance that bypassed the Senate's authority.</note>, so that nothing should be done in the Republic that displeased any of the three. In this matter, **Brutus** also rightly rebuked **Cicero**, because by exalting the young **Octavius** <note>The future Emperor Augustus; Cicero initially supported him to counter Mark Antony, but Octavius eventually seized total power.</note> with excessive honors, he had armed him against the Republic. But if now someone has grown too great in power, he should be sent away to war, though under the appearance of honor, and quickly recalled—either under the pretense of lightening his burdens or by offering him city honors—and this should not be done except when he is present. Just as the Emperor **Tiberius** offered the consulship to **Germanicus** <note>A popular and successful Roman general. Tiberius feared his influence and used the consulship—a prestigious but largely ceremonial city office by that time—to recall him from his loyal legions in Germany.</note>, the duties of which he was to perform in person, so that he might draw him away from his course of victories. Therefore, Germanicus did not hesitate further, although he understood that these things were being fabricated and that he, through envy, was being pulled away from the glory he had already earned.

<margin>
To commit
the supreme
