especially
military,
to no one
for long.
</margin>

This strategy is primarily used in an **Aristocracy** <term>Aristocratia: Rule by the "best" or the nobility, who must guard against any one of their peers becoming a king.</term>, in which the supreme command—and especially military command—must not be assigned to anyone for a long duration. For this reason, it was forbidden among the Romans to hold the **Dictatorship** <term>Dictatura: In the Roman Republic, a temporary office with absolute authority, intended only for emergencies.</term> for more than six months, as witnessed by **Pomponius**. **Marcus Tullius [Cicero]** repeatedly and sternly expressed this in a letter to **Atticus** concerning Caesar. For what is more shameless? <note>original Latin: "tenuisti provinciam per decem annos..."</note> *You have held a province for ten years, a command given to you not by the Senate, but by yourself, through violence and factionalism; the time has passed, not of the law, but of your own lust. Yet, suppose it was by law: it is decreed that a successor be appointed; you block it and say, "Have consideration for me"; no, you have consideration for us! Should he hold an army longer than the people ordered, against the will of the Senate?* **C. Marius** <note>A Roman general who held an unprecedented seven consulships, contributing to the eventual collapse of Republican norms.</note> also criticizes this natural pride of the nobility and their desire to linger in power, as recorded in the historian **Paterculus**. All the more reason to take care that no one holds the same office twice; **Aristotle** warned of this in his *Politics*, as did **Marcus Rutilius** <note>C. Marcius Rutilus Censorinus, who famously complained when the people tried to elect him Censor for a second time, arguing it was dangerous to the Republic.</note>.

### Book II of Arnold Clapmarius

<margin>
No one should be granted the same power twice.
</margin>

**Censorinus**, having been elected **censor** <note>A powerful Roman official responsible for the census and public morality.</note> for a second time, called the people to an assembly. He scolded them with the gravest speech possible for conferring that power upon him twice, when their ancestors—judging it to be too great—had decided its duration should be strictly limited. Consequently, on his own recommendation, as **Plutarch** <note>A Greek biographer and philosopher.</note> records, a law was passed that no one should be allowed to seek that magistracy a second time. Similarly, in **Athens**, no one could serve as a **presiding officer** <note>original: "ἐπιστάτης" (epistates); the chairman of the public assembly.</note> twice, according to **Pollux** in Book 8. The Decree of the Senate regarding the election of **military tribunes** <note>Officers of the Roman army who also had political duties.</note> pertains to this same principle: *that no consideration should be given to anyone who was currently a tribune of the plebs that year, nor should any tribune of the plebs be re-elected for the following year.*

<margin>
To break the power of one who has grown too influential, and to do so through indirect means.
</margin>
<margin>
By presenting certain reasons, so that he may fall by his own weight.
</margin>

However, it sometimes happens that one individual in the Republic grows excessively powerful, either through their own achievements or through the negligence of their colleagues. In such cases, their strength must be broken. But this should be done through indirect means <note>original: "per ambages"; literally "by windings" or circuitous paths.</note> and a certain roundabout way; for if he is cast down too abruptly, he may resort to desperate measures—extremities that are most dangerous to the Republic. **Pericles** advised this, as **Valerius** <note>Valerius Maximus, a collector of historical anecdotes.</note> testifies in Book 7, Chapter 2: that youths of high nobility and excitable spirit should be restrained early. Yet, once they have been nourished by excessive favor and lavish indulgence, it is difficult to prevent them from holding power: *for it would be foolish and useless to oppose the very strength that you yourself have fostered.* Therefore, arguments must be presented to him through which he might collapse by his own weight, and the flame and "path of envy," as **Livy** <note>Titus Livius, the primary historian of early Rome.</note> calls it, must be suggested. Just as **Manlius** says in the same author: *"Why do we not attack him through the common people? It is safer to attack him by means of the people themselves, so that he may fall, burdened by his own strength."* Thus **Maecenas**, according to **Paterculus** <note>Velleius Paterculus, a Roman historian.</note>, observed the plans of a headstrong young man <note>This refers to the conspiracy of Lepidus the Younger against Augustus, which Maecenas thwarted.</note> through total quiet and dissimulation, and with miraculous speed, and with no...

# On the Secrets of Empire. Chapter 12.

...[disturbance], whether of circumstances or of men, and having suppressed Lepidus, he extinguished the fire of a new or resurrected civil war. 

<margin>
Alexander's cunning in this matter.

**Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great, King of Macedon.</note> was also skilled in this kind of cunning: he invited **Philotas** <note>A high-ranking officer later executed for conspiracy.</note> to a final banquet. The King maintained the composure to not only dine with him but even to converse familiarly with the man he had already condemned. **Tiberius** <note>The second Roman Emperor, known for his secretive nature.</note> acted similarly; when **Libo** was reported for aspiring to the throne, Tiberius honored him with the praetorship <note>A high-ranking judicial office in Rome.</note> and invited him to social gatherings. He showed no change in his expression and was not agitated in his speech; though he had the power to stop him, he preferred to monitor every word and deed the man made.

### CHAPTER XII.

*To foster factions, but to take care they do not erupt; or to dissolve them through art. A **political task** <note>original Greek: "Πολιτικὸν opus"</note>. A **political consideration** <note>original Greek: "Πολιτικὸν σκέμμα"</note>. That two from one family should not be in the Senate at the same time. That great commands should not be continued within one family.*

<margin>
Whether it is beneficial for factions to exist in a Republic.
</margin>
It was the opinion of **Cato** <note>Cato the Elder, a Roman statesman known for his traditionalism.</note> and other very wise men that it is advantageous for the Republic for there to be factions and discord among great and powerful men. I will not disparage their view. However, **Livy** <note>A Roman historian who wrote a monumental history of Rome.</note> says that discord between the social classes is the poison of the Republic.

<margin>
The harmony of the Patricians is the pillar of the Republic.
</margin>
Furthermore, the rule of a few <note>An oligarchy or aristocracy.</note>—as **Aristotle** testifies in Book 5, Chapter 6 of his *Politics*—does not easily collapse from within if it is harmonious; this should be an oracle <note>An undisputed truth or divine guidance.</note> for the aristocrats. For this reason, **Fabius**, **Tiberius Gracchus**, and others set aside their private hatreds for the sake of public benefit.

<margin>
Factions must be artfully dissolved.
</margin>
But if factions now creep in among the leading citizens, these must be artfully and prudently dissolved. Unless this is done, such rivalry eventually erupts, causing one side or the other—strengthened by victory and driven wild by the lust for power—to seize total rule and dominance for themselves alone.

# On the Secrets of Empire. Chapter 13.

<margin>Establish heavy penalties for those who fabricate a crime against another.

Beware lest the common people suffer from scarcity.

The grain supply should be sufficient for the common people.</margin>

When anger is suppressed, everyone begins to see themselves as a judge and a master of life and death over the actions of an enemy. For it is one thing to slander, another to collude <note>The Latin *prævaricari* refers to an advocate who acts in collusion with the opposing side.</note>, and quite another to accuse. This is taught by Jacques Cujas <note>original: "Cujacius," a famous 16th-century French legal scholar.</note> in his observations, books 4 and 10. See also the two most prudent and popular writers on this matter, Niccolò Machiavelli and Scipione Ammirato. And yet, Aristotle rightly warns that in a popular state, a heavy penalty ought to be established for those who have attempted to fabricate a crime against someone. 

In particular, those who rule in a popular Republic must take care that the common people do not suffer from scarcity <note>Latin: *penuria*, referring here to food shortages.</note>, lest they be forced to seek help from the wealthy and submit themselves to them. For the Roman leading men used the opportunity of the <term>annona</term> <note>The state-controlled grain supply or distribution in ancient Rome.</note> in this way to dissolve the <term>tribunician power</term> <note>The power of the Tribunes, who were elected to protect the interests of the common people.</note>. Finally, effort must be made so that the wealthy and over-powerful are "drained" <note>original: "emungantur," literally "to have the nose wiped," a metaphor for being relieved of excess wealth.</note> through duties, tributes, and other hidden but legitimate channels, so that power, supreme authority, and majesty always remain in the hands of the people.

# Book II of Arnold Clapmarius

<margin>
Remedies against those striving for new regimes.
</margin>
...long for a kingdom; while those who are in a kingdom long for liberty. Many are satisfied with no form of government, and no type of Republic. Those who have barely experienced one thing today desire another tomorrow, only to overthrow it again the day after. Even the Jews themselves could not help but regret their recovered liberty. <note>original: "Exod. 16." A reference to the biblical account of the Israelites complaining about their hardships in the desert after being freed from Egypt.</note>

<margin>
Such measures are:
1. Binding the people by oath that no one shall reign.
2. Plundering royal goods.
3. Destroying houses.
4. Confirming actions by law.
5. Abolishing the images of tyrants and those striving for kingship.
6. Damning their memory.
</margin>
Against such tendencies, secret strategies for stabilizing liberty have also been discovered. Such is the example of Brutus <note>Lucius Junius Brutus, the legendary founder of the Roman Republic.</note>, who first of all—lest the people, though greedy for their new liberty, might later be swayed by prayers or royal gifts—bound them by an oath that they would allow no one to reign in Rome. He also gave the royal goods to the common people to be plundered, so that by touching the royal loot, they would lose all hope of peace with the kings forever. <note>original: "Livius lib. 2." Reference to Titus Livius (Livy), a Roman historian.</note> The same author in Book 4 writes: "Nor was it enough for the crime to be expiated by his blood, unless the roofs and walls, within which so much madness had been conceived, were scattered; and the goods, tainted by being used as the price for buying a kingdom, were confiscated." He therefore ordered the <term>quaestors</term> <note>Roman officials responsible for the treasury and financial affairs.</note> to sell those goods and return the money to the public treasury. He then ordered the house to be demolished immediately, so that the vacant area would serve as a monument to crushed and wicked hope. This practice even remained under the Emperors. Thus, in Book 2, Title 53, *On Keeping the Peace*: <note>original: "De pac. ten." Likely a reference to medieval legal codes like the *Constitutiones Feudorum*.</note> *Let his goods be confiscated, and his house destroyed.* This is certainly a fine method for strengthening a common people who are otherwise inconsistent and more fickle than the wind.

For this reason the Aedui <note>A powerful Gallic tribe allied with Rome.</note>, as Caesar reports in Book 1 of the *Gallic War*, confirmed their departure against the Gauls by law. For the same reason, no one in the Roman Republic was allowed to keep an image of a tyrant. Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose, the 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note> writes in Book 1 of *On Duties*: "If someone possesses the image of a tyrant, is he not subject to condemnation?" Thus, the memory of tyrants and of those who had aimed at kingship was condemned. <note>This refers to the Roman practice of *damnatio memoriae*, where the names of traitors or disgraced emperors were erased from monuments and their statues destroyed.</note>

<margin>Not to allow high commands to be long-lasting.</margin>
However, that duration and extension of high commands is particularly dangerous in a popular Republic. As Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> says in Book 4: *“It is a great safeguard of liberty if you do not allow great commands to be long-lasting, and if a limit of time is imposed on those whose authority cannot be limited in scope.”* <note>original: "Libertatis magna custodia est, si magna imperia diuturna esse non finas, & temporis modus imponatur, quibus iuris non potest." <margin>Turning away seditions and civil wars as they give birth to a kingdom.</margin>
This strategy is not strictly a "sophism" <note>In this context, a *sophisma* refers to a political maneuver or "trick" used to maintain power.</note>. It is, however, a hidden and necessary method for preserving a Democracy, others of which you may see in Aristotle's *Politics*. Just as it is necessary, above all in this type of Republic, to beware of seditions and civil wars, which can hardly be settled unless the power is handed over to a single person. Tacitus relates this regarding Augustus: that he took the Republic, exhausted by civil discords, under his command with the title of "Princeps" <note>original: "nomine Principis." Augustus avoided the title "King," instead using "First Citizen" to mask his absolute power.</note>. Therefore, a certain writer...

## CHAPTER XV.

->*Royal secrets, or Secrets of State used against the common people. Devising a pretext and a title for a seized Empire; seeking a justification. The Royal Law, or the Law of Empire. <margin>Secrets of State against the common people.</margin>
Thus far, we have discussed the secrets of Aristocracies and Democracies. As for the royal secrets, however, which Cornelius Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian known for his dark and analytical view of imperial power.</note> calls the *Secrets of State* (*Arcana Imperii*), you would seek them in vain within the works of Aristotle. Therefore, I believe I will perform a worthwhile service if I also extract certain things from other writers—things that remain hidden and are hardly expressed even by the authors themselves. I do this both because no one has done so until now, and because it is of the greatest use in a Principate <note>A term for a monarchy where the ruler is technically the "first citizen" (Princeps).</note>. For it is equally difficult—and I do not know if it is not actually harder—to compel and accustom a people born to liberty (the name of which, as Jovius <note>Paolo Giovio, an Italian historian and physician.</note> says, is most sweet) to the laws of a kingdom. Consequently, those who laid the strong foundations of a kingdom by stripping the common people of their liberty required even greater prudence.

For most kingdoms are occupied by force and war, and sometimes through crimes. Afterward, setting all other things aside, they show these off magnificently—as if they were mysterious puzzles <note>original: "ἀνιγμοῖς"</note>—so that, as Xiphilinus <note>An 11th-century Byzantine monk who summarized the Roman history of Cassius Dio.</note> says, *they may seem to hold nothing by way of a gift* <note>original: "μηδὲν δόσεώς τινος ἔχειν δοκῶσιν"</note>; that is, so that they may appear to hold everything by the consent of the people. Just as in private contracts a "color" <note>A legal term for a plausible pretext or justification used to make an action seem valid.</note> is sought, as Julian says in the seventh book of the *Digest* concerning the Macedonian Decree of the Senate. For this reason, I am quite certain that the "Royal Law" <note>The *Lex Regia*, a law that supposedly transferred all the power of the Roman people to the Emperor.</note>—which is said to have been passed regarding the Emperor's power, and by which the people conceded to him and for his benefit all their command and power—did not exist before the reign of Vespasian. Or, if it did exist, it was either begged for or extorted by force, whatever others may think.

<margin>Examples of those who occupy empire by force.</margin>
For example, Sulla, relying on his army and the legions he brought into the city, ordered himself to be created Dictator for five years under the Valerian Law. When the Senate hesitated, Cornelius the Centurion, the leader of the embassy, threw back his cloak and, showing the hilt of his sword, did not hesitate to say in the Senate house: *“This will do it, if you do not.”* Thus says Tranquillus <note>Suetonius, a Roman biographer known for his "Lives of the Caesars."</note> in his biography of Augustus. Regarding the "Donation of Constantine" <note>A famous forged Roman imperial decree by which the emperor Constantine the Great supposedly transferred authority over Rome and the western part of the Roman Empire to the Pope.</note>, no one is so dull as to not feel the same way: and recently, besides the most learned Hotman <note>François Hotman (1524–1590), a French legal scholar and humanist.</note>, Gentillet <note>Innocent Gentillet (c. 1535–1588), a French lawyer famous for his "Anti-Machiavel."</note> showed this eruditely in his *Apology*. Furthermore, Pope Paul III himself responded candidly and simply <note>original: "καὶ ἀφελῶς"</note> to one who asked about the "Law of the Papacy" and the title to so many principalities: 

> "Oh," he said, "you scholarly man, ignorant of all things, who asks for the right of empire, which we have already possessed for so many years against the force of all men, and defend by the sword."

<margin>
The pretext of the Turks in occupying Rome; the Venetians' Dominion over the sea.
</margin>
Suleiman <note>Suleiman the Magnificent, Sultan of the Ottoman Empire.</note> confessed to the same fraud; claiming that Rome belongs to the Ottomans for the reason that it was alienated by Constantine to the total prejudice of his successors. The Venetians certainly publicly professed that they hold dominion of the sea by no other title than war and victory: as is clear from the witty and candid response sent to the Pope.

### CHAPTER XVI.

->*Accismus, or hesitation in accepting power. He always deliberates on another course. One who pushes himself forward should be suspected. The foolish refusal of Blasius.*<-

<margin>
To undertake empires as if unwillingly, even when they are eagerly sought and conferred.
</margin>
The same method for deluding the common people is used whenever those to whom empires and dignities are entrusted so fashion and compose themselves that they seem to do unwillingly that which they actually love. The Greeks elegantly called this *accismus* <note>original: "ἀκκισμὸν"; a rhetorical term for a feigned refusal of something one actually desires.</note>, named after that woman Acco, who most carefully refused the very things she craved. 

<margin>
The use of Accismus.
</margin>
There is a twofold use for this tactic. First, through this refusal, the true opinions of others are drawn out; as Tacitus reports of the Emperor Tiberius, stating that he introduced a sense of hesitation specifically to look into the secret intentions of the leading men. 

<margin>
By this, the public is kindled.
</margin>
Secondly, by this delay, the common people are kindled more and more to bring about the very thing the ruler intends.

# On the Secrets of Empire. Chapter 16.

<margin>
*The use of this tactic is noted.*
</margin>
Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> mentions this in Book 6. He says that when the elections for creating the Tribunes of the Plebs <note>Officials elected to protect the interests of the common people in ancient Rome.</note> were announced, Licinius and Sextius behaved in such a way that by refusing everything, they most sharply incited the common people toward that which they were actually seeking through their dissimulation: wanting their own honors to be continued twofold.

<margin>
*On Augustus's expertise in this matter.*
</margin>
Augustus <note>The first Roman Emperor.</note> was exceptionally skilled in this art; Tacitus writes in the first book of his *Annals* that Augustus, under the appearance of someone refusing power, actually desired it most passionately. Tacitus says the same of Tiberius <note>The second Roman Emperor.</note>: *He was ambiguous about ruling.* And Suetonius <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, biographer of the first twelve Roman emperors.</note> writes: At last, as if compelled, and complaining that a wretched and burdensome slavery was being enjoined upon him, he accepted the empire; yet he did so only in a way that gave hope that he would one day lay it down. The Emperor Otho also beautifully feigned such hesitation 
<margin>
*And of the Emperor Otho.*
</margin>
when he was made leader: according to the same Suetonius, he acted as if he had been snatched from the public and compelled by force to take up and wield the Empire, and then went to the palace by the common will of all. Hence the judge <note>original: "arbiter," likely referring to Petronius Arbiter, a Roman courtier.</note> said:

> I do not want to hold at once that which I desire,
> Nor does a victory already prepared for me please me.

<margin>
*The impulse of feigned refusal.*
</margin>
It is read that Ivan the Terrible <note>original: "Ioannes Basilides," the first Tsar of Russia.</note>, the Duke of Moscow, used the same art. Such a person is called an <term>ironist <note>original Greek: "είρων" (eirôn). In classical Greek thought, the "eirôn" is a character who downplays their own abilities or intentions to deceive others.</note></term> by Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle.</note>. For so he says in his *Characters*: Whatever the dissembler does, he keeps it secret, and says he is still deliberating. For this reason, it is even cautioned by law that magistrates should not appoint those as guardians who want to thrust themselves forward, or who give money to be appointed. It was promulgated that such men are subject to punishment in the *Digest* <note>The *Digest* is a major part of the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the collection of Roman laws compiled under Justinian I.</note> under the section on "Guardians and Curators" (Law 21) and the section on "Proxies" (Law 25). A proxy who asserts his own proxy-ship is not to be tolerated: for by this very act he is suspect, as he thrusts his labor upon an unwilling party. Hence the Emperor Alexander <note>Alexander Severus (reigned 222–235 AD).</note> was accustomed to say that those who are unwilling, not those who are campaigning for office, should be placed in the Republic. And for this very reason, the first Emperors feigned this kind of <term>accismus <note>A rhetorical term for a feigned refusal of something that is actually desired.</note></term>.

A great difficulty concerning this tactic.

There is, however, a great difficulty regarding this matter. For such hesitation, as long as it does not appear to be a ruse, has its own dignity and use; but when it breaks out and becomes obvious, it is foolish and ridiculous. Such are those who, when they most greedily desire something, refuse it in such a way that their lust and greed are apparent even to the blind. Tacitus <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus, the Roman historian known for his analysis of power dynamics.</note> notes this in the case of Blaesus. This Blaesus, when he was being chosen as Proconsul of Africa, *responded with the appearance of one refusing; but he was not heard with the same firmness, nor with the consensus of those flattering him: from then on, what was covered by the hidden gains of many was made plain* <note>original: "respondit specie recusantis; sed neq; eadem asseveratione & consensu adulantium auditus est: exin promptum quod multorum intimis quæstibus tegebatur." ### CHAPTER XVII.

->*Removing leisure from the common people. Distinguishing the defiant from the submissive. Opponents <note>original: "Ἀντίτεχνοι" (Antitechnoi) — literally "rivals in an art," here meaning political antagonists.</note> as the defiant ones. Private individuals who are excessively exalted. <margin>
Keeping the common people occupied with war and other business.
</margin>
Just as in a kingdom, and in other Republics, the common people <note>original: "plebs"</note> must be kept away from high command and the exercise of arms; so, on the other hand, it is sometimes expedient for the State to send the common people, and all those who hate the current state of the Republic, into war. This is a strategy that the greatest Emperors and Princes have frequently observed. If there is no need for war, then the common people must be exhausted by other means, just like that Herod <note>Herod the Great, King of Judea.</note>, of whom Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the Jewish-Roman historian.</note> says in Book 15, Chapter 13: *he guarded against conspiracies and riots by taking away the leisure of the common people and always exhausting them with labors* <note>original: "eum cavisse conjurationes ac turbas, quod otium abstulerit plebi, eumque semper laboribus fatigaverit."</note>. Aristotle hints at the same in Book 6 of his *Politics*. Hence Livy says in Book 6: *Fear, then, the Fathers* <note>original: "Patres" — referring to the Roman Senators.</note>

He says: *To wicked minds and those agitating for more than is fitting for a citizen, not being in command is like being in slavery*; later Emperors called them *impious and enemies of Majesty*. # On the Secrets of Empire. Chapter 18.

<margin>
*The creation of a magistrate.*
*Reasons for this secret.*

*2. The extension of commands threatens the current State.*
*3. The power of bestowing favors upon many wins authority for the Prince.*

[...proposed that] they should be held for a five-year period, and that the prince should nominate twelve candidates for each year. Regarding this, Tacitus says in Book 2 of the *Annals*: *There was no doubt that this proposal penetrated deeper, and that the Secrets of State were being tested.* <note>original: "Arcana Imperii" — a central concept in this work, referring to the hidden strategies used by rulers to maintain power.</note> This is a royal secret used against the patricians <note>The hereditary aristocrats of Rome.</note>. First, because the creation of a magistrate belongs to the Emperor. Second, because the extension of commands <note>term: *prorogatio* — the legal extension of a magistrate's term of office beyond its original limit.</note> was a threat to the current State, as there was a danger that the Roman Republic might be restored to its former condition by this method. Thus, Tacitus later adds: *Men grow proud even with an annual appointment; what if they held office for five years? Likewise, offenses are barely avoided on a year-by-year basis, even though the hope of a near opportunity consoles those who are rejected; how much hatred would come from those who are cast aside for more than five years?* Third, the prince’s ability to bestow favors upon many people was being snatched away, even though a prince—and especially a new one—needs nothing more than the favor and goodwill of the citizens.

How great the power and authority is of one who has the opportunity to give gifts and gratify citizens in a Republic can be seen in Aristotle, Book 2 of the *Politics*, Chapter 7; Cassiodorus also suggests this. *Therefore,* he says, *antiquity desired the dignity of the provinces to be refreshed by annual succession, so that no one would become insolent through long-lasting power, and so that many might find the joy of advancement.* For this reason, Aristotle criticizes the Spartan <note>original: "Laconicam" — referring to Laconia, the region of Sparta.</note> Republic, because in it the magistrates remained in office for a long time and with the greatest command. For this same reason, Augustus, so that more people could take part in administering the State, devised new offices. The same reasoning applies to why, when the Tribunes of the plebs <note>The representatives of the common people in Rome.</note> proposed that they be allowed to host games at their own expense...

# Arnold Clapmarius, Book II.

He did this because the Republic could have shifted back toward its former state through such "private popularity" <note>The author suggests that if individuals were allowed to give gifts to the public, they would win a personal following that threatened the Emperor's central authority.</note>.

<margin>*Hence Augustus's establishment of the five-year lottery for provincial appointments.*</margin>
Moreover, Augustus acted with equal parts cunning and wisdom regarding the following: under the old Republic, when a Roman consul was allotted a province, he would depart for that province with full Command <note>term: *Imperium* — the supreme executive and military power held by high-ranking Roman magistrates.</note> immediately after laying down his consulship. Augustus was the first to decree that after resigning his office, the magistrate should remain in the city for five years before departing for a province. In this way, consuls as well as Praetors <note>Magistrates primarily responsible for the administration of justice.</note> went to the provinces not at random, but according to the order in which they had held those offices in the city. His plan was surely this: that during that five-year interval, they might set aside the pride and ferocity of spirit they had absorbed from holding a powerful annual office, and "wear down" those ambitions through the quiet of a private life.

<margin>*That great Commands should be entrusted to those of the toga rather than to military men.*</margin>
This was the same reason why—though previously the Praetorian Prefects <note>The commanders of the Emperor’s personal bodyguard, who eventually became the most powerful administrative and judicial officials in the Empire.</note> (whose office was the most important and, as Zosimus <note>A 5th-century Greek historian who wrote about the Roman Empire.</note> testifies, next only to the throne) were chosen from the military—legal science later claimed this position for itself. It seemed unsafe to grant such immense power to men skilled in military matters, even those of humble birth. Thus, through the efforts of Ulpian, Papinian, and other Jurisconsults <note>term: *ICtorum* — an abbreviation for *Iurisconsultorum*, professional legal experts whose opinions were authoritative.</note>, it was ensured that this most distinguished office was managed by the "art of the toga" <note>The toga was the garment of peace; the "art of the toga" refers to civil administration and law, as opposed to "the art of war."</note> rather than by military force. For this reason, Pomponius calls these legal experts "Leading Men," and Spartianus, writing about Julian <note>Referring to the Emperor Didius Julianus, who was a famous jurist before taking the throne.</note>, says that a nobleman is made even more noble by the study of Law. Furthermore, as for that proposal by Asinius Gallus: although it seemed to pose a danger to the current regime, Tiberius nevertheless delayed it as if it were actually an increase of his own power, and in a speech that appeared favorable...

### CHAPTER XIX.

->Why Tiberius continued the terms of<-
->Magistrates and Jurisdictions. Two kinds of<-

<margin>The reasons are explained why Tiberius, contrary to the previous secret of state, continued the commands of officials.</margin>
I have previously stated that it is a secret of State <note>term: *Arcanum Imperii* — literally a "secret of empire," referring to the hidden political strategies or "tricks of the trade" used by rulers to maintain their grip on power.</note> that commands <note>term: *Imperia* — the supreme executive and military power held by high-ranking Roman officials.</note> should not be extended, especially in a sovereignty that has been recently seized. For this reason, Julius Caesar and Augustus made all magistracies annual. But indeed, as Tacitus says in the second book of his *Annals*, it was the custom of Tiberius *to extend commands, and to keep most men at the head of the same armies or judicial districts until the end of their lives.* And in Book 4 of the *Annals*: *The Emperor [Tiberius] entrusted his affairs to every highly distinguished man, and even to some unknown men based on their reputation; and once they were appointed, they were kept in place without any limit, so that many grew old in the same duties.* Various reasons for this practice are recounted, which rightly deserve investigation. Cassius Dio <note>A Roman historian of Greek origin who wrote a massive history of Rome.</note> testifies that Tiberius, when asked about this, replied that leeches rest after they have drunk much blood, but the bites of fresh ones are the sharpest <note>Tiberius’s cynical metaphor suggests that long-serving officials, having already enriched themselves, are less "hungry" for bribes and plunder than new ones.</note>. Others thought this was done by Tiberius out of a weariness of taking on new cares. For, as the poet Horace says:

> Kings are said to press many cups upon,
> And to torture with unmixed wine, the one whom they labor 
> To see through, to know if he is worthy of friendship.

Hence the Emperor Alexander Severus said that he who wishes to create a Senator ought to be a great man. Some said it pertained to the imperial majesty that those things which had once been decided [should remain...]

### ARNOLD CLAPMARIUS, BOOK II.

...so they were kept as if for eternity. Some believed this was done out of envy, so that more people would not enjoy the honors of office. There were others who thought that, just as his nature was cunning, so his judgment was anxious; for he did not seek out eminent virtues, and yet he hated vices. He feared danger to himself from the best men, and public disgrace from the worst. For from the latter, there is danger to the Republic; from the former, danger to the Prince. These are the ones whom the Greeks call <term>phthonoumenous</term> <note>original Greek: φθονουμένους — those who are the objects of envy or political suspicion.</note>, whom the jurist Ulpian calls persons notable for their shameful conduct, and whom Cicero calls the scandalous herds of desperate men. And yet, as Sallust says, the "best" men are more suspected by kings than the "worst"; for the virtue of another is always terrifying to them. Tacitus provides the reason in the third book of his *Annals*: *for the best of mortals desire the highest things.* These are the views of others.

<margin>Two types of men existed in Rome.</margin>
Furthermore, as I have stated, there were two kinds of men in Rome, just as Athenaeus testifies there were in Athens. Some favored the domination of the Princes, whom Gunterus calls "the faithful"; today we might say "Dear Loyalists" <note>original German: *Liebe Getrewe*</note>. Others were still mindful of their former liberty, desiring the Republic to be restored to its previous state. The Germans distinguish these as the "Good Imperialists" <note>original German: *gut Keyserisch* — those loyal to the Emperor.</note> and the "Good City-partisans" <note>original German: *gut Stättisch* — those favoring the independence of cities or republican liberty.</note>.

<margin>To what sort of people commands were given and extended by Tiberius.</margin>
To these latter men, Tiberius did not give <term>imperia</term> <note>term: *imperia* — supreme executive or military authority.</note> or legal jurisdictions, much less did he extend their terms; rather, he kept a close watch, both publicly and privately, on their lives, plans, and speeches. This was especially true for those whose virtue was well-attested, such as Asinius, Aruntius, Haterius, Piso, and Scaurus. Indeed, Aristotle expressly advises in the last chapter of the third book of his *Politics* that Princes should keep those people around them who are not only friends to the ruler himself, but also to the Empire—those who do not wish the current state of affairs to be overturned. Therefore, Tiberius gave and continued the terms of those men who were endowed with only mediocre virtues:

It categorizes Roman society into two factions: those loyal to the Emperor and those yearning for the old Republic.</summary>

->### ON THE SECRETS OF EMPIRE. CHAPTER 19.<-

...of those. Such men were Sabinus, Capito, and, under the Emperor Claudius, Vitellius; on whose statue was this inscription: *Of unshakeable loyalty toward the Prince.* <note>original Latin: "Pietatis immobilis erga Principem."</note> For this reason, the Emperor not only extended Poppaeus Sabinus's command over the province of Moesia, but even added others, Achaia and Macedonia. These he would have given to others—whose dispositions he did not yet know or held in suspicion—only with great anxiety and peril.

So too did Jovian <note>Jovian was a Roman Emperor who reigned for only eight months (363–364 AD).</note>, as reported by Ammianus Marcellinus in his 25th book. To secure his position at the beginning of his reign, he ordered Maliarchas, one of his close associates then active in Italy, to succeed Jovinus as the Master of Arms <note>original Latin: "armorum Magistro" — a high-ranking military office in the late Roman Empire.</note> throughout the Gallic provinces. Jovian had looked ahead with natural pragmatism: he wanted a commander of higher merit (and therefore a source of suspicion) to be removed from the center of power, so that a man of lesser ambition, promoted to higher things, might support his master's still-wavering status with great zeal.

For this same reason, Maecenas persuaded Augustus that he should choose the Prefect of the Praetorian Guard only from the <term>equestrian order</term> <note>The equestrians or "knights" were the lower of the two aristocratic classes in Rome, often used by Emperors for sensitive posts because they lacked the political pedigree of the senators.</note>, lest someone relying on the nobility of his family should attempt something against the Prince himself.

Furthermore, Sabinus had his provincial command extended not because of any exceptional skill, as Tacitus says in his *Annals*, but *because he was equal to the business at hand, and not above it.* <note>original Latin: "quod par negotiis, neque supra erat."</note> Such men are truly the best courtiers, 
<margin>Character of the good Courtier.</margin>
and are therefore dear to Princes. Indeed, according to the same author, *industry and vigilance are no less harmful among such men whenever they are used as a pretense for seizing the throne.* <note>original Latin: "industria ac vigilantia haud minus noxiæ sunt, quoties parando regno finguntur."</note> In this regard, Tacitus praises his father-in-law <note>Gnaeus Julius Agricola, the subject of Tacitus's famous biography.</note>. *He did not seek fame,* he says, *through his own speeches, but because he seemed equal to the task.* And elsewhere: *nothing was staged for show.* Velleius Paterculus says of Piso: *he was very like someone in active leisure.* <note>original Latin: "actu, inquit, otioso simillimus."</note> For all others, that very greatness of reputation is their undoing.

<margin>Whether a Prince may be created outside of Rome.</margin>

It contributes greatly to the preservation of a kingdom that at any time there should be an heir to the Empire, and a certain, designated heir. This is primarily for the following reason: a princedom or kingdom, upon the death of a King without an heir, is easily pulled into factions and changed into another form of Republic. This has been testified to by Aristotle, and examples are readily found in the cases of Alexander the Great, Filippo Maria <note>Filippo Maria Visconti (1388–1447), the last Duke of Milan of the Visconti line, whose death without a legitimate heir led to the short-lived Ambrosian Republic.</note>, Queen Joanna of Naples <note>Joanna II (1371–1435), whose various adoptions of heirs led to civil wars between the houses of Anjou and Aragon.</note>, and others. Regarding Alexander, Justin <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian.</note> writes: *Alexander,* he says, *when asked whom he would make heir to the Empire, replied: "the most worthy."* By this statement, it was as if he had sounded a trumpet-blast of war among his friends, or cast an apple of discord among them; thus, all rose up in rivalry and sought the silent favor of the soldiers through the ambition of the common people. And Curtius <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, historian of Alexander.</note> says in his tenth book: *Without a certain heir of the king, and without an heir of the kingdom, everyone will drag the public power toward themselves.* I take this to be a <term>royal secret</term> <note>original Latin: "arcano regio"</note> against the nobles of the realm. For where the successor is uncertain, the Republic easily relapses into its former state <note>Clapmar suggests that without a clear heir, the "secret" is that power tends to return to the people or the aristocracy, dissolving the monarchy.</note>.

# On the Secrets of Empire. Chapter 22.

<sig>E 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: also,</meta>

<margin>Sovereignty does not tolerate a partner. <note>original Latin: "Principatus non patitur consortem."</note> Let there be one ruler, one king. <note>original Greek: "Εἷς κοίρανος ἔσω, εἷς βασιλεύς." A famous quote from Homer’s Iliad (2.204) advocating for monarchy over divided leadership.</note></margin>
Cornelius Nepos <note>A Roman biographer and historian (c. 110–24 BC).</note> provides the reason: *For the state,* he says, *cannot be well managed by the commands of many.* Just as this holds true in military matters, so too is it most beneficial in every administration of great affairs, as Livy <note>Titus Livius, the premier Roman historian of the Augustan age.</note> testifies. And yet, those words of Livy in Book 3 cannot be applied to this situation: in the Roman army, when there had been two Consuls of equal power, the supreme command—by the concession of Agrippa <note>Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, a general and close advisor to Augustus who famously yielded authority for the sake of efficiency.</note>—remained with his colleague. He who was preferred responded courteously to the submissiveness of the one who yielded by sharing both plans and honors, thus making his unequal partner an equal. Sovereignty, however, does not tolerate a partner; and as Seneca <note>A Stoic philosopher and advisor to Emperor Nero.</note> beautifully put it: *Neither kingdoms nor wedding torches know how to bear a partner.* <note>original Latin: "Nec regna socium ferre, nec tædæ sciunt." From Seneca's tragedy *Thyestes*.</note> On this account, Nero rightly excluded a woman—even though she was his mother <note>Agrippina the Younger, who attempted to exert significant control over Nero's early reign.</note>—from public business. And it is only right that the Prince alone should act and administer, or at least oversee, all those things pertaining to the majesty of the realm; nor should he easily allow another to occupy the principal position. Such was the error of Bibulus <note>Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus, Julius Caesar's conservative colleague in the consulship of 59 BC.</note>, who, wanting to obstruct the actions of Julius Caesar, kept himself at home for the greater part of the year. By doing so, while he wished to increase the resentment against his colleague, he instead increased Caesar's power.

<margin>It is a virtue to call the prudent into council.</margin>
Nevertheless, it is the duty of a good prince to call wise men into his council. Micipsa <note>King of Numidia in North Africa (reigned 148–118 BC).</note> advises this in Sallust <note>A Roman historian known for his accounts of the Catilinarian conspiracy and the Jugurthine War.</note>: *It is not armies nor treasures that are the safeguards of a kingdom, but friends.* And the Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian <note>Theodosius II and Valentinian III, Roman Emperors of the 5th century.</note> stated excellently in Book 8 of the Code on Laws: *We well recognize that whatever has been ordained with your counsel redounds to the happiness of our Empire and to our own glory.* And as Pliny <note>Pliny the Younger, a Roman lawyer and author known for his many letters describing life under the Empire.</note> says in Book 3 of his Letters: *All things are indeed under the judgment of one man, who alone has undertaken the cares and labors of all for the common benefit; yet, by a certain healthy balance, to us* <note>The text continues on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page argues that for a state to be stable, supreme power must rest with a single individual rather than being divided, though a wise ruler should still seek counsel from prudent advisors.</summary>

### Arnold Clapmarius. Book II.

...also, like streams, flow down from that most kind fountain; we ourselves can draw from them and, as it were, provide for absent friends.

<margin>The division of principalities is most dangerous. <note>original Latin: "Divisio principatuum perniciosissima."</note></margin>
But we must also take care that sovereignty is not easily torn apart; instead, the entire power of the Empire, all **royal rights** <term>regalia|The specific rights, honors, and powers belonging exclusively to a monarch, such as coining money or collecting certain taxes.</term>, and all **fiefs** <term>feuda|Feudal lands or estates held on condition of allegiance and service to a lord.</term> and public revenues should rest with one person. Otherwise, from such a partition, both the empire and the subjects themselves suffer harm. Lambert of Hersfeld <note>An 11th-century German historian and monk, often cited by his Latin name "Scaffnaburgensis."</note> gives the reason: *Lest,* he says, *with the province divided among many, the renown of that family should fade through the poverty of the household.* There are far too many examples of this in the kingdoms of **France**, **Poland**, and others. Indeed, our ancestors acted laudably, as Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD) whose work *Germania* describes the customs of the ancient Germanic tribes.</note> reports in his *On the Customs of the Germans*, when they granted all estates and manorial rights to one heir, ordering the rest to depart with only a small sum of money. This practice still holds in the kingdom of **France** according to the **Salic Law** <note>A code of law established by the Salian Franks; it is most famous for excluding women from land inheritance and royal succession to keep power centralized.</note>, and in other illustrious families of Germany, which **Aristotle** also hints at and approves of in various places. For this reason, I would wish even more for someone to compare, examine, expand upon, and illuminate Aristotle’s *Politics* alongside other writers and historians, and even with **Civil Law**. This would be a vast field for exercising industry and talent, and one which I have decided to traverse—though at a very slow pace. To that end, in the future, I have not only devoted all my effort to those refined writings of the jurisconsults <note>Legal experts; the Latin "ICtorum" is an abbreviation for *Iurisconsultorum*.</note>, but even to those rough thickets of **Bartolus** and **Baldus**. <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato and Baldus de Ubaldis were the most influential medieval legal commentators, known for their dense, complex, and sometimes "thorny" style of analysis.</note>

# On the Secrets of Empire. Chapter 23.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

*Supporting the property qualifications of Senators. Observing excessive wealth and excessive poverty in a great man. Not elevating new and foreign men too much. Moderate governance.*

<margin>Take care that senators are not oppressed by great poverty, and enrich the poor.</margin>
Above all else in a principality, especially a new one, every effort must be made to remove those things that seem to lead the State back to its former condition <note>original: "pristinum statum," referring to the restoration of the old Republic.</note>. Among these, the most important is to take care that great men and senators are not oppressed by poverty. Because this condition is most bitter, it calls to the minds of great men the memory of the former Republic and solicits—even inflames—their spirits to recover it. For this reason, Tacitus <note>A Roman historian known for his analysis of power and tyranny.</note> praises Tiberius—otherwise a most greedy prince—for supporting the wealth requirements <term>census|The minimum amount of property or wealth required to maintain one’s status as a member of the Senate.</term> of the Senators. 

And in the 13th book of his *Annals*, he says that when Nero was consul for the third time, Valerius Messala entered the consulship as well. Few of the elderly then remembered that his great-grandfather, the orator Corvinus, had been the colleague of the deified Augustus (Nero's great-great-grandfather) in that same office. But the honor of this noble family was increased by the gift of five hundred thousand sesterces <note>A significant sum of Roman currency.</note> annually, with which Messala might support his blameless poverty. The Prince also established an annual sum for Aurelius Cotta and Auterius Antoninus, even though they had squandered their ancestral wealth through luxury.

# On the Secrets of Empire. Chapter 23.

<margin>
The purpose and effect of the secrets of empire.
</margin>
But these are generally the secrets of empire, which take care that the Republic <term>Respublica|the state or "Commonwealth"</term> is not changed, or does not flow into another form; most of these secrets are based on simulation, fiction, and <term>irony|original Greek: εἰρωνεία (eironeia); here meaning political dissimulation or acting with a hidden motive</term>. For example, Tiberius assisted the <term>census|the minimum property qualification required for a Roman to hold the rank of Senator</term> of the Senators, not because he was led by love toward them, nor driven by a desire for generosity, but so that he might take away from men endowed with great spirit the opportunity to plot something against himself and the present Republic. <margin>

matters which are called "secrets of the State"—and properly "secrets of Empire" and <term>sophisms|σοφίσματα (sophismata); in this context, political maneuvers or clever tactics used to maintain the status quo</term>—which preserve the present form of the State, let what has been said so far suffice. There now follow those secrets of the State which are called **Secrets of Ruling**. These differ from the former secrets in two ways: first, because the former are like the defenses of the State itself, whereas these are the ramparts and fortifications of those who actually hold power; and second, because most of the former are based on pretense and simulation, while only a few of these are. This distinction is very clear, and others have learnedly observed it in the works of <term>Tacitus|Publius Cornelius Tacitus, a Roman historian known for his analysis of the psychological and political "secrets" of the emperors</term>. This proverb emphasizes that political wisdom must benefit the ruler personally, not just the abstract state.</note>

# ON THE SECRETS OF RULING. CHAPTER I.

<margin>They are defined.</margin>
For these **Secrets of Ruling** are the most private, hidden, and concealed plans or methods, introduced not only for preserving the original state of affairs, but also—and primarily—for the security of those who hold the leadership in the State <term>Respublica|The Commonwealth or "public affair"</term>, whether they be one person or many. They are specifically directed against those who strive to wrest power away from the Princes, unless they are prevented. As Attius says, 
> *Many are unjust and unfaithful to a kingdom; few are good.* <note>original: "Multi iniqui atque infideles regno, pauci sunt boni." Lucius Accius (or Attius) was a Roman tragic poet.</note>
Against such people, Emperors and any leaders of cities in a State have rightly devised certain secret plans, both for the sake of protecting themselves and also for the purpose of enchanting the common people <term>plebs|The common citizens, as distinguished from the nobility</term>. As Seneca says,
> *Many have taught others how to deceive while they themselves fear being deceived.* <note>original: "Multi fallere docuerunt, dum timent falli." From Seneca the Younger's Moral Letters.</note>

<margin>The affinity between the Secrets of Empire and of Ruling.</margin>
And yet, these secrets of ruling and the **Secrets of Empire** are very closely bounded and joined together. For it is impossible for the State to be safe if the prince or the leading men of the State are not safe, and vice versa. Therefore, that famous Emperor <note>Likely referring to a Roman Emperor like Marcus Aurelius or a similar figure emphasizing the union of leader and state.</note> excellently denied that he could be safe if the State were not safe, and swore that he would not depart from its embrace except in death. But where the Prince suffers, who is the head of the State, there all the members must grow weak and be worn out. Jovius <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), an Italian physician, historian, and biographer.</note> also understands both of these secrets when he says in the last book of his *Histories*:
> *Francis, when dying, shared with his son Henry the secrets for protecting the kingdom, and by which arts especially he might earn the devotion of the subject peoples.* <note>original: "Franciscus moriens Henrico filio arcana tuendo regno communicavit, & quibus maxime artibus subjectarum gentium studium promereretur." Referring to King Francis I of France and his successor Henry II.</note>

Furthermore, I establish as many secrets of ruling as there are secrets of Empire. For they are either secrets of **Monarchical** ruling, or secrets of **Aristocratic** ruling, or secrets of **Democratic** <note>original: "Popularis"</note> ruling. These ensure that the commoners are safe; those ensure that the patricians are secure from the snares of others; those ensure [that]

### Arnold Clapmarius, Book III.

...so that the King, or Prince, may be safe and inviolable.

<margin>
*The Difference between the Secrets of Ruling and the Rights of Sovereignty.*
</margin>
From all these points, it is clear that those who confuse these **secrets of ruling** with those things called the **rights of sovereignty** <term>jura imperii|The fundamental legal powers that constitute a state's authority</term> possess very little understanding of these matters; for they differ in many ways. *First*, the rights of sovereignty, as previously stated, are one and the same, and do not vary according to the variety of Republics. However, the secrets of ruling are of one kind in a Kingdom, another in an Aristocracy, another in a Democracy, and still others in other forms of State. *Second*, the secrets of ruling can be delegated to others, whereas the rights of sovereignty certainly cannot. *Third*, the rights of sovereignty are in the open, and it is lawful for them to be known and understood by everyone; but the secrets of ruling are hidden and concealed counsels, to which that line of the Poet applies: *hence a faithful silence for the sacred rites*. <note>original: "hinc fida silentia sacris." A quote from Virgil's Aeneid (3.112), often used to describe political or religious secrecy.</note> *Fourth*, the rights of sovereignty are majestic and full of majesty (whence they are also called the **rights of majesty**) while the secrets of ruling are much more humble. One who acts against the latter does not so much openly harm or diminish majesty as they slowly and secretly creep toward power. Such a person is called fierce, stubborn, or a "good citizen" <note>Here, "civilis" implies someone acting with the strategic modesty of a private citizen while seeking power.</note>; the other is a defendant of majesty, a public enemy <term>perduellis|Specifically a traitor or an enemy who carries out internal war against the state</term>, as in that old song of Gaius Martius in Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian. The "song" refers to a prophetic or ritualistic verse.</note>, which the most learned *Scaliger* <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a preeminent scholar of the Renaissance known for his work in historical chronology and textual correction.</note> restored to its original brilliance:

> *Children of Romulus, if you wish to expel the public enemies,*
> *And the plague-sore, which from nations far-off and foreign*
> *Has come.* <meta>catchword: (narum</meta>

*Lastly*, the secrets of ruling, just like the secrets of state <term>arcana imperii|The broader category of state secrets</term>, are like the bulwarks of the rights of sovereignty, not the right of sovereignty itself. All these things become clearer through examples of both and by comparing them with one another.

He concludes that these secrets act as a protective "bulwark" or fortification for the state's legal authority.</summary>

### CHAPTER II.

->Mastery, *Lordship* <note>original German: "Herrschafft"</note>. Legitimate and just Tyranny. Tyrannical Mastery. Liberty. The measure of liberty. Dissolute license. The terms for Mastery. Ruling names. Emperor, King, Lord, Caesar, Lord <note>original Greek: "κύριος" (kyrios)</note> & Potentate <note>original Greek: "δυνάστης" (dynastes)</note>. <margin>What mastery is:</margin>
Before we approach this doctrine concerning the secrets of mastery, it must first be established what mastery actually is—that which the Greeks call sovereign rule <note>original Greek: "κυρίαν ἀρχὴν" (kyrian archēn)</note>, the Italians *Lordship* <note>original Italian: "Signoria"</note>, the Germans *Lordship* <note>original German: "Herrschafft"</note>, and the French *Highness* <note>original: "Alteße" (Altesse)</note>. This term "mastery" is one that men of a more severe or rigid character find difficult to stomach. It is, however, that supreme force of commanding; and it properly belongs to those who newly occupy or hold power by force and the law of war, or, as the jurist Pomponius says, "by the kingly hand" <term>manu regia|A legal concept referring to the direct, forceful acquisition of power, often contrasted with peaceful succession</term>. During such a time, few things are handled by force (as Tacitus says regarding the beginning of the reign of Augustus), so that there may be peace for the rest.

<margin>How far it is a just tyranny.</margin>
For mastery is joined with a certain violence and pride, and it is nearly indistinguishable from tyranny; indeed, at my own risk, you might call it a "legitimate and just tyranny." Hence, in an ancient glossary, it is said: "he masters" <note>original: "dominatur"</note> means "he acts as a lord" <note>original Greek: "δεσποτεύει" (despoteuei)</note> or "he acts as a tyrant" <note>original Greek: "τυραννεῖ" (tyrannei)</note>. And Virgil says in the 6th book of the *Aeneid*: *From here our race shall master long-lived Alba.* <note>referring to the Roman ancestors ruling the city of Alba Longa</note>. In the sacred wisdom <note>referring to the Bible, specifically Proverbs 29:2</note>, the translators have maintained: *when the just master the people, they rejoice; and when the impious master them, the people groan.* Yet, it is opposed to that tyranny which Apuleius calls "tyrannical mastery." Concerning this, I accept the word of Sallust: *later, when the royal power—which in the beginning had served to preserve liberty and increase the Republic—turned into a haughty mas-*

...and turns it into mastery: and that saying of Curtius in Book 6: *they fight for liberty, these for mastery* <note>original Latin: "illi pro libertate hi pro dominatione pugnant"</note>. This is the reason why the wisest Roman Princes loathed the title of "Lord" <note>original Latin: "Domini vocabulum"</note>. For it implied a master-like and violent rule over slaves, as Suetonius testifies regarding Augustus and Tiberius, Pliny regarding Trajan, and Giovio regarding Giuliano de' Medici. Hence that line of the Poet: *You hold the name of Lord, he that of Prince.* <note>The "Prince" (Princeps) was a title meant to imply "First Citizen," avoiding the baggage of kingship or slave-mastery.</note> This is also clear from that verse of Martial:

<margin>How mastery does not take away liberty from citizens.</margin>

And yet mastery, or the Principate <term>Principatus|The early period of the Roman Empire where the ruler was officially styled as 'First Citizen' (Princeps) rather than an absolute monarch</term>, does not in the least take liberty away from citizens. It was famously said of the Emperor Nerva that he joined the Principate and liberty together. And this liberty is a middle ground between abrupt slavery, such as exists under tyrants, and dissolute license, or corrupted liberty. Tacitus beautifully calls this the "measure of liberty" <note>original Latin: "modum libertatis"</note> in Book 4 of his *Histories*: *just as for the worst princes mastery without measure (understand: tyranny) is pleasing, so for even the best, a measure of liberty is pleasing.* Regarding this, Gunther writes in Book 3:

<margin>What true liberty is.</margin>

> *What greater liberty could happen to you,*
> *Than to serve your king?* and in Book 8:
> *The greatest liberty for us,*
> *Is to obey so mild a man.*

Cicero understands the same thing: *Let nothing,* he says, *be sprinkled by me [with harshness], yet let nothing be common or dissolute.* For excessive liberty is not liberty, but a certain loose and overflowing license: such as was among the Parthians of old, as Tacitus testifies in Book 2 of the *Annals*. <header>On the Secrets of Mastery. Chapter 2. 113</header>

...and indeed, they were more without a master than in a state of liberty. Sallust says of the Aborigines <note>The earliest inhabitants of central Italy, ancestors of the Romans</note>: *a rustic race of men, without laws, without command, free and unconstrained* <note>original Latin: "genus hominum agreste, sine legibus, sine Imperio, liberum atque solutum"</note>. Livy, in Book 5, severely criticizes this kind of "liberty": *since that is finally what liberty is at Rome: not to respect the Senate, nor the magistrates, nor the laws, nor the customs of the ancestors, nor the institutions of the fathers, nor the discipline of military service.*

<margin>What mastery is. In what kind of state mastery is necessary.</margin>
Mastery <term>Dominatio|A form of rule that is more absolute or forceful than the standard republican governance</term> is, therefore, nothing other than legitimate command, but a little more forceful. Yet it is necessary, especially in a Republic that is newly occupied, or one full of the most seditious and fierce citizens. Anyone who wishes to govern such a state by the "royal way" <note>meaning the standard, mild, or constitutional path</note> will act preposterously and will, as the saying goes, nourish a snake in his bosom. Whether you call these the "secrets of mastery," or "secrets of the principates," or by any other name, it is the same. For those *terms of mastery*, as Tacitus calls them, or *masterful names* as Horace calls them—such as Emperor, Lord, Caesar, King, Prince, *Lord and Power* <note>original Greek: Κύριος καὶ δυνάμεως (Kyrios kai dynameos)</note>, and many others—seem to me to have been one and the same; except that a veil was pulled over the people’s eyes <note>original Latin: "glaucoma obducta fuit populo," literally "a cataract was drawn over the people"</note>. Tacitus speaks of this openly and truly regarding Vitellius: *He sent ahead into the city an edict,* he says, *by which he deferred the title of Augustus and did not accept that of Caesar, although he diminished nothing of his power.* Nor is there any reason for Pliny to argue the contrary, since even those terms of mastery are used indiscriminately by writers. Hence Justinian speaks of the *royal sentiment* <note>original Latin: "regalis sensus"</note> and Tacitus of the *instruments of rule* <note>original Latin: "instrumenta regni"</note>. In Book 14 of the *Annals*, regarding a situation where the opinion was that it portended a change of king, Vespasian is called by that same Tacitus the *Lord of things*; and Suetonius says of Galba: *that a prince and lord of things would one day arise from Spain.*

<margin>
Why the Roman Princes loathed the title of "Lord."

...and he turned [the word] into mastery: and that passage from Curtius, Book 6: *those men fought for liberty, while these fought for mastery* <note>original Latin: "illi pro libertate hi pro dominatione pugnabant"</note>. This is the reason why the most venerable Roman Princes loathed the term "Lord" <term>Dominus|A title implying the absolute ownership of a master over a slave, which the early Emperors avoided to appear as "First Citizens" rather than kings</term>. For it suggested a master's rule and an unyielding power, as Suetonius testifies concerning Augustus and Tiberius, Pliny concerning Trajan, and [Paulus] Jovius <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), a Renaissance historian</note> concerning Giuliano de' Medici. Hence the line of the poet: *You hold the title of Lord, he that of Prince.* This is also clear from that verse of Martial:

> *You know you were born of a slave, and you flatteringly admit it*
> *When you call your father "Lord," Sosiabane.*
> <note>Martial, Epigrams 9.10. To call a father "Lord" was seen as a sign of servility or low birth.</note>

<margin>
How mastery does not take away the citizens' liberty.
</margin>
And yet, mastery, or the principate, by no means takes away liberty from the citizens. It was famously observed of the Emperor Nerva that he joined together the principate and liberty. This liberty is a middle ground between abrupt servitude—such as exists under tyrants—and dissolute license, or corrupted liberty. Tacitus, in Book 4 of his *Histories*, beautifully calls this a "measure of liberty": *just as for the worst princes mastery without limit (by which he means tyranny) is pleasing, so for the best princes, a measure of liberty is pleasing.* Regarding this, Gunther [Ligurinus] <note>A 12th-century poet who wrote the 'Ligurinus,' an epic on Frederick Barbarossa</note> writes in Book 3:

<margin>
What true liberty is.
</margin>
> *What greater liberty could come to you,*
> *Than to serve your king?*
> and in Book 8:
> *The greatest liberty for us,*
> *Is to obey so peaceful a man.*

Cicero understands this same thing: *Nothing I do*, he says, *is harsh, yet neither is anything populist or dissolute.* For excessive liberty is not liberty, but a certain unbridled and overflowing license: such as once existed among the Parthians, as Tacitus testifies in Book 2 of the *Annals*. Unsure, surely, of unbridled...

<page-num>113</page-num>
<header>Concerning the Secrets of Mastery. Chapter 2.</header>
<meta>catchword: CA-</meta>

...certainly, and more accurately described as being without a master than being in a state of liberty. Sallust says of the Aborigines <note>The earliest mythical inhabitants of Italy</note>: *a wild race of men, without laws, without authority, free and unrestrained.* <note>original Latin: "genus hominum agreste, sine legibus, sine Imperio, liberum atque solutum"</note> Livy, in his fifth book, severely criticizes this kind of liberty: *since that is what liberty has finally come to at Rome; to respect neither the Senate, nor the magistrates, nor the laws, nor the customs of the ancestors, nor the institutions of the fathers, nor the discipline of the military.*

<margin>What mastery is.</margin>
Mastery is, therefore, nothing other than lawful authority, but exercised somewhat more forcefully. 
<margin>In what kind of Republic mastery is needed.</margin>
This is nonetheless necessary, especially in a state that has been newly occupied, or one full of the most seditious and fierce citizens. Anyone who wishes to govern such a people by the "royal road" <note>meaning a standard or gentle path of governance</note> will act preposterously and, as the saying goes, will nourish a serpent in his bosom. Whether you call these the "secrets of mastery," or the "secrets of princedoms," or by any other name, it is all the same. For those *terms of mastery*, as Tacitus calls them, or as Horace calls them *masterly names*, such as General <note>original Latin: "Imperator"</note>, Lord <note>original Latin: "Dominus"</note>, Caesar, King, Prince, Lord <note>original Greek: "Κύριος" (Kyrios)</note> and Ruler <note>original Greek: "δυνάμεως" (dynameos)</note>, and many others, seem to me to have been one and the same thing; except that a "cataract" <note>a metaphor for a medical condition or blindfold used to obscure vision</note> was drawn over the eyes of the people. Tacitus says this openly and truly concerning Vitellius: *He sent an edict ahead to the city, by which he deferred the title of Augustus and did not accept that of Caesar, though he subtracted nothing from his power.* Nor is there any reason for Pliny to say otherwise, since even those terms of mastery are used interchangeably by writers. Hence Justinian speaks of a *royal sentiment* <note>original Latin: "regalis sensus"</note> and Tacitus speaks of the *instruments of kingship*. In the 14th book of the *Annals*, where there is an opinion that a change of king was portended, Vespasian is called by that same Tacitus the "Lord of affairs"; and Suetonius says in his life of Galba: *that a prince and master of affairs would someday arise from Spain.*

<summary>This page defines 'Mastery' as a more forceful but still lawful form of authority necessary for stabilizing rebellious or newly conquered states. It also explains how Roman Emperors used various titles (like Prince or Caesar) to hide the reality of their absolute power from the public.</summary>

### CHAPTER III.

->The Royal Secrets of Mastery. That Senators<-
->or illustrious Knights are not permitted to enter<-
->Egypt. Egypt is the lock of the land and<-
->the sea. The craftsmanship and labor of the<-
->Egyptians are fearsome to Roman Princes.<-

<margin>Where the secrets of mastery originated.</margin>
<margin>What the royal secrets of mastery are.</margin>
<margin>The law of Augustus is such a secret: that it was not permitted to enter Alexandria, the lock of land and sea.</margin>
<margin>The cause of that law.</margin>
Hence, therefore, the secrets of mastery were born. First, indeed, there are those of royal mastery: certain hidden strategies pertaining to the security of the King or Prince against those who lust for power—not so much out of hatred for the kingdom, but out of hatred for the King himself, as was once a common saying regarding Cassius <note>Gaius Cassius Longinus, one of the lead assassins of Julius Caesar</note>. These secrets are especially necessary in a kingdom because, as Livy truly says in his 37th book, the majesty of Kings *is more difficult to pull down from the highest peak to the middle, than it is to be cast headlong from the middle to the very bottom.* <note>original Latin: "difficilius summo fastigio ad medium detrahitur, quam à mediis ad ima præcipitatur"</note> Augustus prevented this danger by passing a law that forbade any Senator from entering Alexandria. For Tacitus says in the second book of his *Annals*: *Augustus, among other Secrets of Mastery, set Egypt apart, forbidding Senators or illustrious Roman Knights to enter without permission, lest whoever occupied that province—the lock of land and sea—might pressure Italy with famine, even with a small garrison against massive armies.* <note>original Latin: "Augustus... seposuit Ægyptum, ne fame urgeret Italiam, quisquis eam provinciam claustraque terræ ac maris... insedisset." Egypt was the "breadbasket" of Rome; controlling its grain supply meant controlling the city of Rome's survival.</note> This is the testimony of Tacitus. I also believe this was the reason that Gallienus <note>A Roman Emperor in the 3rd century AD</note>, when he wished to grant proconsular power in Egypt to Theodotus, was stopped with this saying: *it is not proper for the consular fasces to enter Alexandria.* <note>The "fasces" were bundles of rods and axes symbolizing high Roman judicial authority. The saying implies that formal Roman political power was intentionally kept out of the city to maintain the Emperor's personal control.</note> I find another reason as well: lest if any Roman entered a province that was turbulent and naturally seditious, he might be led by the company of that people toward the same rebellious path his own nature was already taking him. This is why Tiberius [reproved] Germanicus <note>Germanicus was a popular general and the adopted son of Emperor Tiberius; his unauthorized visit to Egypt in 19 AD caused great political tension.</note>, when he had set out for Egypt...

<header>On the Secrets of Mastery, Chapter 3. 115</header>

...whether for the purpose of studying its ancient history or for the care of the province, <note>The text continues from the previous page, describing the actions of Germanicus, a popular Roman general.</note> [Tiberius] rebuked him most sharply because, contrary to the institutions of Augustus and without the Prince’s permission, he had entered Alexandria. He complained most severely about this matter in the Senate. This incident is believed to have been the cause of Germanicus's death. *Suetonius, Life of Tiberius.* <note>Suetonius was a Roman historian who wrote biographies of the first twelve emperors.</note> Doubtless, Augustus had protected himself in this way because he did not want any senator to go to a place from which a danger to his mastery could be created.

With this same strategy, when Vespasian was about to seize the Roman Empire, he assigned various provinces to others, but he himself occupied the "barriers of Egypt." *Tacitus, Histories, Book 3.* <note>Tacitus notes that by controlling Egypt, Vespasian could starve Rome into submission.</note> And for this reason, the victorious Julius Caesar previously left the kingdom of Egypt to Cleopatra and her younger brother; he feared making it a province, lest if it ever obtained a more forceful governor, it might provide the material for a revolution. <note>original Latin: "novarum rerum materia," literally "material for new things," a common Roman idiom for political upheaval.</note>

To this also pertains that passage from Tacitus in the third book of the *Histories*: *He added, he said, strategy to power; since Egypt held the locks of the grain supply <note>original: "annonae," the state-controlled grain distribution essential for feeding Rome.</note> and the revenues of the most wealthy provinces, the army of Vitellius could be forced into surrender through the lack of pay and grain.* 

Hence Diocletian, according to the testimony of Suidas, <note>The Suda (or Suidas) is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> held the Egyptians especially suspect and punished them in various ways because of the excessive cleverness <note>original: "artificia," referring to their technical and alchemical skills.</note> they possessed. He even sought out and burned the ancient writings concerning the smelting of gold and silver—a terrible example, certainly, but done with the intention that the Egyptians, if enriched by those means, might not easily rebel. For the same reason, Egyptians were not permitted to be citizens of another city, as Josephus <note>A first-century Jewish-Roman historian.</note> testifies in his work *Against Apion*.

<margin>
A law that illustrious men may not travel abroad without the Prince's order, nor go to the armies.
</margin>
The Roman Princes so thoroughly looked after their own mastery that it was not even permitted for a senator or an illustrious man to depart abroad without the command or permission of the Prince; much less was it allowed to travel to the armies. This was because such travel appeared to be the easiest opportunity for winning over the affections of the soldiers. Regarding Caesar, Suetonius <note>Suetonius was a Roman historian famous for his biographies of the first twelve emperors.</note> says: *He enacted that no citizen over the age of twenty and under forty, unless serving in the military or on a magistrate's staff, should be absent from Italy for more than three continuous years; nor should any son of a Senator travel abroad except as a companion or staff member of a Magistrate.* Regarding Augustus, Dio Cassius <note>A Roman consul and historian who wrote in Greek.</note> states more explicitly in Book 52: <note>original Greek: "προεῖπε πᾶσι τοῖς βουλεύσι, μὴ ἐκδημεῖν ἔξω τῆς Ἰταλίας, ἄν μὴ αὐτός τινι κελεύση"</note> *He proclaimed to all Senators that none of them should travel outside Italy without his order.* Indeed, it was not only forbidden to go outside Italy, but even to go outside of Rome itself, according to Suidas <note>The Suda (or Suidas) is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient world.</note>. This is a **secret of mastery** <note>original: "arcanum dominationis"</note> specific to royal power, and it contributes greatly to the security of Princes—especially those who have recently seized power and have not yet taken root. For such rulers can be cast out and driven from their kingdom with the slightest shock.

<margin>
A Senator was nevertheless permitted to travel for private business; he would simply request a single "free embassy."
</margin>
Furthermore, in a free Republic <note>Referring to the era before the Emperors, when Rome was governed by the Senate and the people.</note>, it was permitted for a Senator to travel even for private business; he would simply request a single **free embassy** <term>libera legatio: a legal status allowing a senator to travel on private business while enjoying the privileges and expenses of an official diplomat</term>, so that he might go and be away with greater dignity.
