->*Nor was my gemstone signet ever proven by a deceptive seal*<-
->*To have placed lying marks upon the wooden tablets.*<-

Indeed, this is not only wicked, but also dangerous to the Prince himself, because he who uses the same script or handwriting as the Prince can make the Prince appear suspect and hated in strange ways among the subjects; and he can open a path for himself to the Empire. The Emperor Titus himself—since he could imitate any handwriting—confessed that he could have often been the greatest forger. Suetonius <note>The Roman biographer, often referred to by his cognomen Tranquillus.</note> mentions this in his *Life of Titus*.

With this strategy in mind, Augustus is said to have labored at nothing so much as ensuring that those whom he had destined as heirs to the empire should imitate his own handwriting, as the same Suetonius reports in his *Life of Augustus*. The legates of the Greek Emperor Manuel <note>Manuel I Komnenos, 12th-century Byzantine Emperor.</note> imitated this fraud: concerning which Gunther <note>Gunther of Pairis, author of the epic poem *Ligurinus*.</note> writes in his fifth book:

->*under the false image of the king with an impressed seal.*<-

<page-num>120</page-num>
<header>Arnold Clapmarius. Book III.</header>

...otherwise called the *daily acts* <note>original: *diurna acta*, the daily gazette or official public records of Rome</note>, were issued; about which Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet of the 1st and 2nd centuries AD.</note> says:
> *Those things will be done in the open, and they will desire to be recorded in the official acts.*

<margin>What kind of public acts there were, and concerning what matters.</margin>
In the acts of the senate were contained the acts, or public records, concerning Sanctuaries, concerning the gods received into the Republic, concerning treaties entered into, and concerning embassies sent and received. Indeed, they contained all those things that were said or done in the senate concerning any matter whatever, about which Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian and politician.</note> says: *The appearance of that day was grand, when the senate looked into the favors of their ancestors, the pacts of their allies, the decrees of those who were powerful before Roman might, and the religion of the deities themselves.* These records, while the Republic stood, were preserved in the record office <note>original: *tabulario*</note>, as Livy <note>The author of a monumental history of Rome.</note> testifies in Book 45.

<margin>That public acts should not be in the possession of anyone other than the prince, or in the archive.</margin>
Afterward, they were allowed to be in the possession of no one except the Prince or his prefect. Whence Tacitus [writes] in the 13th book of his *Annals*: *The Prince transferred the care of the public records from the quaestors to the prefects.* <note>The quaestors were lower-ranking officials; the prefects were direct appointees of the Emperor, showing a shift toward centralized control.</note> Therefore, for a private citizen to keep record-keepers <note>original: *actuarios*</note> was treated as a crime; and I categorize this as a secret of rule <term>arcanum dominationis: a political technique used by a ruler to maintain exclusive power</term>. Tacitus, in Book 15 of his *Annals*, writes regarding the accusation of Junius Torquatus: *He ordered,* he says, *the accusers to charge that he kept noblemen whom he called "Secretaries of Correspondence," "Secretaries of Petitions," and "Secretaries of Accounts"—titles of the highest concern and premeditation, etc.* <note>By using these titles, Torquatus was accused of setting up a "shadow government" that mimicked the Emperor's own bureaucracy.</note> For what else are these "titles of highest concern" than public record-keepers and census officials? Suetonius <note>A Roman historian known for his biographies of the Twelve Caesars.</note> reports almost the same thing regarding Pomposianus, who was killed by Domitian *because it was commonly rumored he possessed an imperial horoscope, and he carried around a map of the world on parchment and speeches of kings and generals from Livy; and because he had given his slaves the names of Mago and Hannibal.* <note>Possessing these items and using these names was seen as a sign of "imperial" ambition, which was a death sentence under a paranoid Emperor.</note>

<margin>Public acts are called by various names;</margin>
Furthermore, I find these acts called by various names. In civil law, they are pre-eminently <note>original: *κατ' ἐξοχήν*</note> called *Acts*; as in Law 45 "On Res Judicata." In the old glossary they are called *Gesta* [Deeds]; as also in Law 31...

The Code <note>original: *C.*, referring to the *Codex Justinianus*</note> on donations, and the Digest <note>original: *D.*, the *Digesta*, a collection of legal rulings</note> on proofs, Book 10, call these "public monuments." Similarly, Livy <note>A famous Roman historian</note> calls them at times "public records," "public commentaries," or "public tablets." Polybius <note>A Greek historian of the Hellenistic period</note> refers to them as *records* <note>original Greek: ὑπομνήματα</note>; Tacitus <note>A Roman senator and historian</note> as the "acts of the fathers"; Ammianus <note>A 4th-century Roman soldier and historian</note> as "public volumes"; Dio <note>Cassius Dio, a Roman historian of Greek origin</note> as *public writings* <note>original Greek: δημόσια γράμματα</note>; and Vopiscus <note>One of the credited authors of the *Augustan History*</note> as "public registers" or "public instruments." In the *Eastern Responses* <note>Legal opinions from the Eastern Roman Empire</note>, they are called *papers of the secrets* <note>original: οἱ τ' ὑφ' ἡμᾶς σεκρέτων χάρτοι, *secreta cartæ*</note>.

Those who had the care of these acts were called "guardians of the law" <note>original Greek: νομοφύλακες</note> among the Athenians; later they were called <term>Quaestors</term> <note>officials in charge of the treasury and archives</note> or <term>Chartophylacii</term> <note>keepers of the records</note>, and today they are known as Chancellors, or Prefects of the Court and Archive. However, the care of these matters is neglected in our time, to the great detriment of the State. Cicero <note>The famous Roman orator and statesman</note> once complained about this in his speeches against Rullus, as did Plutarch <note>A Greek-Roman biographer</note> in his life of Cato the Younger. For this reason, I highly praise that decree of the Senate found in the writings of Capitolinus <note>One of the authors of the *Augustan History*</note>:

> *That no scribes, no public slaves, and no tax officials should be present at those proceedings: the Senators themselves should record them, and the Senators should fulfill all the duties of the tax officials and scribes, lest anything should happen to be leaked.*

### Arnold Clapmarius. Book III.

...otherwise the daily gazette <note>original: *diurna acta*, a sort of daily public record in ancient Rome</note> were issued: about which Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet</note> wrote:
> *These things will be done in the open, and they will desire to record them in the acts.*

<margin>
What the public acts were, and concerning what matters.
</margin>
In the acts of the senate were contained the acts, or public records, concerning Sanctuaries, the adoption of Gods, the Republic, treaties entered into, and embassies sent and received: indeed, all those things that were said or done in the senate concerning any matter. About these, Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian and senator</note> says: *Magnificent was the sight of that day, when no one looked into the favors of our ancestors, the treaties of our allies, the decrees of those who were powerful before the Roman might, and the religious rites of the deities themselves.* These were certainly kept in the public records office <note>original: *tabulario*</note> while the Republic stood, as Livy testifies in Book 4.

<margin>
That public acts should not be in the possession of anyone but the prince, and should remain in the archive.
</margin>
Afterwards, no one was permitted to hold them except the Prince or his prefect. Thus Tacitus in the 13th book of his *Annals*: *The Prince transferred the care of the public records from the quaestors to the prefects.* Consequently, for a private citizen to employ record-keepers <note>original: *actuarios*</note> was treated as a crime; and I therefore categorize this as a secret of rule <note>original: *arcano dominationis*, a technique used by rulers to maintain power</note>.

<margin>
That no one should have private secretaries, or public tax officers, or nobles to handle correspondence.
</margin>
Tacitus, in Book 15 of his *Annals*, writes regarding the accusation of Junius Torquatus: *I ordered*, he says, *the accusers to charge him with having nobles whom he called his "secretaries for correspondence," "petitions," and "accounts"; titles intended as a very careful rehearsal for imperial power, etc.* For what else are these titles of "extreme care" but record-keepers and public tax officials? Suetonius reports nearly the same regarding Pomposianus, noting that he was killed by the Emperor Domitian *because it was commonly said he possessed an imperial horoscope, and carried about a map of the world on parchment, along with the speeches of kings and generals from Titus Livy; and because he had given his slaves the names of Mago and Hannibal.* <note>Mago and Hannibal were famous Carthaginian generals; giving slaves these names was seen as a sign of royal or military ambition.</note>

<margin>
Public acts are called by various names;
</margin>
Furthermore, I find these acts are called by various names. In civil law, they are called "Acts" <term>preeminently</term> <note>original Greek: κατ’ ἐξοχὴν</note>; as in Law 45 regarding court judgments. In the old glossary, they are called "Deeds" <note>original: *Gesta*</note>; as also in Law 3.

<header>On the Secrets of Rule. Chapter 5.</header>

In the Code concerning Donations, law 10; and in the Digest concerning proofs, they are called **public monuments** <note>original: *monumenta publica*; in this context, "monuments" refers to enduring written records or archives</note>. Similarly, Livy <note>A Roman historian</note> calls them sometimes **public monuments**, sometimes **public commentaries**, and sometimes **public tables**; Polybius calls them **memoirs** <note>original: *ὑπομνήματα* / *hypomnemata*</note>; Tacitus calls them **acts of the fathers** <note>referring to the records of the Senate</note>; Ammianus calls them **public volumes**; Cassius Dio calls them **public writings** <note>original: *δημόσια γράμματα* / *demosia grammata*</note>; Vopiscus calls them **public registers** or **public instruments**; and in the Eastern Responses <note>legal opinions from the Byzantine East</note> they are called **the secret papers under us** <note>original: *οἱ ὑφ᾽ ἡμᾶς σεκρέτων χάρτοι*, or *secreta cartæ*</note>. Those who had the care of these acts were called **guardians of the law** <note>original: *νομοφύλακες* / *nomophylakes*</note> among the Athenians; later, 
<margin>Also those who have care of these records.</margin>
they were called **Quaestors**, **Keepers of the Charts** <note>original: *Chartophylacii*</note>, and today they are called **Chancellors**, or **Prefects of the Court and Archive**. Yet the care of these things is neglected in our time to the great detriment of the State. Cicero once complained of this in his speech against Rullus, as did Plutarch in his life of Cato of Utica. For this reason, I highly praise that **Decree of the Senate** <note>original: *Senatusconsultum*</note> kept at the Capitol: that no scribes, no public slaves, and no tax officials should be involved in those acts. Instead, the Senators themselves were to receive them, and Senators were to fulfill all the duties of tax officials and scribes, lest anything should by chance be betrayed.

### Arnold Clapmarius, Book III.

...to govern the Republic, and Emperors were adopted into their names. Certainly, many occupied the empire with the help of these men. For Tacitus writes thus concerning Augustus: *When he had enticed the soldiers with gifts, the people with grain, and everyone with the sweetness of peace, he began to rise up gradually.* And Aurelianus says the same regarding *the soldiers chosen through gifts, etc.* For this reason, those who became princes rightly took note of—and indeed pursued with hatred—those who were influential through the favor of the soldiers, for relying on such favor they could very easily stir up revolutions. Thus Aurelianus notes in his work on Octavius:

<margin>
Lest anyone should court the favor of the soldiers.
</margin>

He also vehemently censured his uncle, who, by calling the soldiers "fellow-soldiers" <note>original: *commilitones*; a term implying equality that Augustus and later Emperors often avoided to maintain distance and authority</note> in a new and flattering manner, had softened the authority of the Prince while striving to be more beloved. On this account, according to Tacitus in the third book of his *Annals*, Piso was accused because he had sought the favor of the soldiers through ambition; likewise, because he had corrupted the common soldiers through license and injuries to the allies to such an extent that he was called the "father of the legions."

<margin>
Lest anyone other than the Prince determine the pay for the soldiers.
</margin>

Tiberius took it even more poorly regarding Junius Gallio, who had proposed that the Praetorians <note>the elite unit of the Imperial Roman army that served as personal bodyguards to the emperors</note>, with their pay increased, should acquire the right of sitting in the fourteen rows <note>the rows in the theater reserved for the Equestrian order or knights, a sign of high social status</note>; and so Tiberius rebuked him vehemently through letters: *What did he have to do with the soldiers, whom it was proper to receive neither the orders of the Emperor nor rewards, except from the Emperor?* First, he mentions "orders": for it was a **secret of rule** <note>original: *arcanum dominationis*; a political technique or "trick" used by a ruler to maintain power</note> that no one should address the Praetorians except the prince.

<margin>
Lest anyone address the Praetorians.
</margin>

Julian certainly did not want this, as Ammianus Marcellinus testifies, lest he should seem to have affected that which Augustus believed was owed to himself alone. Thus Herodian writes regarding Commodus: *During the days in which they were occupied with the funeral of the father, it seemed right to the friends to lead the youth to the camp, so that he might speak to the soldiers and, having given them money (as is the custom for those succeeding to the throne), he might act with great- [spirit]* <note>original Greek: ἐν ὅσαις περὶ τὴν κηδείαν τοῦ πατρὸς τὸν υἱὸν ἀπησχόλουν, ἔδοξε τοῖς φίλοις προσαγαγεῖν τὸ μειράκιον εἰς τὸ στρατόπεδον· ὡς διαλεχθείη τε τοῖς στρατιώταις καὶ χρήματα δωρησάμενον. (ὡς ἔθος ἐστὶ τοῖς βασιλείαν διαδεχομένοις) μεγαλο-</note>

### On the Secrets of Ruling. Chapter 6.

*...by a wise distribution, he might win over the army:* <note>original Greek: φρονὶ ἐπιδόσει οἰκειώσηται τὸ στράτευμα</note> *that is, so that the* <margin>Lest soldiers receive rewards from anyone but the Prince.</margin> *soldiers do not receive rewards from anyone except the Prince. Once the funeral of* Marcus <note>Marcus Aurelius, Roman Emperor from 161–180 AD</note> *was celebrated, it seemed best to his friends to bring* Commodus *to the army, so that he might address the soldiers with rewards and (as is the custom for new Emperors) bind their minds to him by distributing money. Therefore* Tacitus *mentions "rewards," the right over which belonged solely to the Prince. For this reason, those mutinous soldiers in* Tacitus, *Book 1 of the* Annals, *say: it is clearly a new thing that the Emperor refers only the soldiers' benefits to the senate; therefore, the same senate should be consulted whenever punishments or battles are declared. Are rewards to be under a master, but punishments without any judgment? Therefore* Philotas <note>a general under Alexander the Great who was executed for conspiracy</note> *says in his defense in* Curtius, *book six: "And which of you has been corrupted by gifts? Which leader, which prefect have I cultivated too excessively?" And this is what* Verus *warns* Marcus Antoninus <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>: *that he should not have such a man among his active commanders* <term>præcinctos|literally "those girt for battle," referring to officers in active service</term> *whom the soldiers listen to gladly and see gladly. To this also belongs the example of* Absalom, *who, about to wrest the Empire from his father, first won over the hearts of all the soldiers to himself. Silanus was accused of the same crime, because he was too lavish with distributions and sought the support of the soldiers through corruption.* <margin>Excessive dependencies are suspected.</margin> *For this reason, the law "contra"* <note>original: *l. contra. C. de re mil.*; a reference to the Justinian Code regarding military affairs</note> *seems to me to have been passed: that soldiers may not be transferred from their units* <term>numeris|standard military units or cohorts</term> *to other units without the Prince's command. Thus, it is added at the end of the law: "unless the Imperial Majesty has ordered this to be done for the sake of public utility." For all dependencies* <note>original: *clientelæ*; the Roman system of patronage where a powerful man provides protection in exchange for political or military loyalty</note> *and excessive friendships are suspected by Princes. This is what the Philosopher* <note>Aristotle</note> *warned in Book 5 of the* Politics, *chapter 8: that caution is needed lest anyone become too powerful through the support of friends; rather, dependencies of this kind ought to be abolished.*

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on military loyalty to the physical security of the state. It examines the "right of fortification" as a sovereign power, continuing the author's exploration of "secrets of statecraft" (arcana dominationis) that a ruler must guard to prevent challenges to their authority.</meta>

### Arnold Clapmarius, Book III.

### CHAPTER VII.

*That no one should fortify a city of their own accord. The law of Romulus regarding the right to fortify. The jumping over walls; the destruction of walls, and in passing, certain matters concerning the use of ramparts.*

<margin>City walls are considered sacred according to the law of Romulus.</margin>
That law of Romulus—that city walls are considered sacred—seems to me to suggest a very great secret of statecraft <note>original: *arcanum dominationis*; Clapmarius uses this term to describe the hidden techniques or "tricks" rulers use to maintain power</note>. Certainly, by jumping over the wall, Remus seemed to wish to take the power from his brother, or at least to show that his authority was diminished. Therefore the Poet <note>Ovid</note> says in the 4th book of the *Fasti*:

> "Let no one cross either the walls or the trench made by the plow;
> deliver whoever dares such things to death."

For that act is hostile and abominable, as the jurist Pomponius says in the second law of the *Digest* <note>the *Digest* was a vast collection of Roman legal opinions compiled under Emperor Justinian</note> regarding the division of things.

<margin>No one is permitted to build a citadel or surround a city with walls.</margin>
For this reason, the right of fortification belonged to no one, except to him whom the Prince <note>the Sovereign or Emperor</note> had granted it. Tacitus says in the 5th book of his *Histories*: "The Jews, having purchased the right of fortification, built walls in peacetime as if for war." And Ulpian <note>a famous Roman jurist</note> says in law 9 of the *Digest* regarding the division of things: "It is not permitted to repair municipal walls without the authority of the Prince or the governor, nor to join or build anything upon them." Therefore, buildings so joined to the walls that an ambush might be feared from them ought to be demolished and razed, according to the law "Buildings" in the *Code* <note>the *Codex Justinianus*, another part of Roman Law</note> concerning public works. It is certainly a secret of statecraft <note>original: *arcanum dominationis*</note> that no one be allowed to build a citadel or surround a city with walls. Wherefore, when Marsus, the governor of Syria, had informed Claudius Caesar that Agrippa <note>Herod Agrippa I, King of Judea</note> had begun a wall of immense size around Jerusalem <note>original: *Hierofolyma*</note>, Claudius—suspecting revolution and discord—sent a message to Agrippa regarding the new work. Once this was done, Agrippa immediately ceased the work, as Josephus writes in book 19 of his *Antiquities*, chapter 7.

<meta>catchword: And</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the legal and political "secret" that the right to build or repair city walls belongs solely to the sovereign. It uses Roman law and historical examples, such as Romulus and Agrippa, to show how private fortifications are viewed as a threat to state security.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the sovereign control over fortifications. While the previous page established that the right to build walls belongs solely to the Prince, this page explores the inverse: the Prince's right to destroy walls as a form of political punishment and the strategic regulations regarding how close a neighbor may build a stronghold to an existing city.</meta>

# On the Secrets of Statecraft. Chapter 7.

<margin>
Rebels punished by the demolition of their walls.
</margin>

And quite often, rebels were punished by the demolition of their walls. Suetonius writes in his life of *Galba*: "He punished certain cities of the Spanish and Gallic provinces <note>original: *Hispaniarum Galliarumque*</note> that had been slower to join his cause by destroying their walls." And Guntherus <note>Gunther of Pairis, a 12th-century Cistercian monk and poet who wrote the *Ligurinus*, an epic about Frederick Barbarossa</note> says of the people of Piacenza:

> And grace was returned to the guilty on such a condition,
> that with the towers leveled, the whole city should mourn,
> its walls torn down into ruinous heaps;
> and the wide trenches they had begun to dig out of fear of the king,
> they should fill back up with mounds of earth.

Nor was it permitted to build others elsewhere. The same author writes in Book 4:

> Tortona <note>original: *Terdona*, an Italian city</note> raises her ancient citadels, though we forbid it,
> and dares to repair the forbidden ruins.

And in the same place:

> Lest the people continue to enclose the city,
> they were ordered to cease work on the wall they had begun.

<margin>
Many cities were granted the privilege that no neighbor may build a castle within one or two miles.
</margin>

Indeed, even today, according to the testimony of Gail <note>Andreas Gail, a 16th-century legal scholar known as the "Papinian of Germany"</note>, many cities have obtained a privilege from the Emperors so that it is not legal for neighbors to build a castle <note>original: *castrum*</note> within one or two miles of the city, because this increases the power and strength of the neighbors while bringing danger and fear to the cities themselves. Curtius <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, a Roman historian of Alexander the Great</note> records this regarding the King of the Scythians in Book 7: that he ordered a city which the Macedonians had founded on the riverbank to be demolished by a military force, as it felt like a yoke placed upon their necks <note>original: *suis impositam cervicibus*, literally "placed upon their own necks," an idiom for a nearby threat or burden of servitude</note>. This is the primary argument used by those who disparage fortifications, both modern and ancient. Yet they are of the greatest use; and the Romans frequently placed their entire safety within them, as can be seen in that passage from Livy's Book 32: "Do you see, Aulus Cornelius, that peak above the enemy? That is the citadel <note>original: *arx*</note> of our hope and safety, if we seize it quickly, since the Samnites <note>an ancient Italic people and rivals of early Rome</note> in their blindness have left it unguarded." And Tacitus calls Cremona a "bulwark" <note>original: *propugnaculum*</note>...

Nor is Augustus, after receiving news of the defeat of Varus <note>original: *clade Vari*; the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 AD, where three Roman legions were annihilated by Germanic tribes</note>, said to have been so terribly frightened for any other reason—to the point that he struck his head against the wall—than that there was no defensive bulwark between Germany and Italy which could have slowed the onslaught and incursions of the Germans. ## CHAPTER VIII.

->*That no one should build a citadel or build too magnificently. That no one should erect or ascend a military platform. That no one should sit on a shield. Giving the signal to the Praetorian Guard. The golden ring. The golden statue of Fortune.*<-

<margin>
That no one should build magnificently.
</margin>
It also seems to be a secret of Royal rule <term>arcanum dominationis</term><note>Clapmarius uses this term to describe the hidden "tricks of the trade" or methods used by rulers to maintain their absolute power</note> that no one should build too magnificently. Such magnificence in private citizens is usually viewed with suspicion by Princes. Tacitus says in the third book of his *Annals* concerning Piso: "Among the incitements to envy was a house looming over the Forum decorated for a festival; there were banquets and feasts, and because of the busyness of the location, nothing was hidden." Likewise in Book 15 of the *Annals*, Nero orders his men to preempt the attempts of the Consul <note>Atticus Vestinus, suspected of joining the Pisonian conspiracy</note>; to occupy his house as if it were a citadel, and to suppress his chosen youth, because Vestinus had a house looming over the Forum and handsome slaves of his own age <note>who could be used as a private militia</note>. ## CHAPTER IX.

->*That Consuls should not scatter money. That no one should hang royal curtains. Imperial garments. Purple, the Purple Inscription. Insignia of Empire. <margin>Other similar examples are gathered together.</margin>
I would like to collect in this chapter, in a somewhat hurried fashion and out of chronological order <note>original Greek: *kai hysteron proteron*, literally "the last first"</note>, several other examples of this matter. <margin>That Consuls should not scatter money.</margin> For that decree of Marcian <note>Emperor Marcian, reigned 450–457 AD</note>, stating that Consuls should not scatter money <note>original: *C. de Coss. & non sparg. ab his pec.*; referring to the Justinian Code section on the Consular games</note>, is nothing other than a safeguard for Royal dominance. This is clear from what was said before; however, Justinian softened this law, and Leo <note>Emperor Leo VI the Wise</note> completely abolished it in his *Novel 94* <term>Novel</term><note>From the Latin *Novellae Constitutiones*, these were "new laws" issued to update the existing legal code</note>.

<margin>That no one should keep private prisons.</margin>
There was almost the same reason for the Decree providing that no one should keep private prisons. This was because doing so displayed a certain appearance of Imperial power. Similarly, there is the Decree of Honorius and Theodosius: <margin>Setting titles on estates or hanging royal curtains.</margin> that no private citizen should place titles <note>Identifying placards or inscriptions</note> upon their own or others' estates, or hang royal curtains <note>original: *regia vela*; these were ceremonial draperies or awnings that signaled the presence of the Emperor or his specific protection</note>. <margin>Or seizing the property of others in the name of the treasury.</margin> Although that law primarily acts to prevent anyone from seizing the lands of others in the name of the imperial treasury <term>fiscus</term><note>The private or state treasury of the Roman Emperor</note>, it also looks toward this goal: that no one might creep toward the empire by this means. For it belongs to the Royal Majesty, as the Emperor says in Book 1 of the Code, that only our own houses and patrimonies should be distinguished by the inscription of titles. The Decree of Valentinian regarding garments of all-silk and gold is of the same sort <note>Referring to laws restricting the use of expensive materials to the imperial family</note>.

### On the Secrets of Governance. Chapter 9.

<margin>That no one should wear garments of gold, silk, or all-purple except the Prince.</margin>
Let no one wear garments of gold except the Prince; let no one dye fleeces with the sacred murex <note>The *murex* is the sea snail used to produce the prestigious Tyrian purple dye</note>; let no one use silk or all-purple garments, such as those the Prince uses. These, as the Emperor Theodosius <note>Theodosius II, who ruled the Eastern Roman Empire in the 5th century</note> says in Law 4 of the Code under the same title <note>original: *l. 4. C. eod.* referring to the *Codex Justinianus*</note>, are dedicated solely to the Prince and his household. For this reason, the sale of purple was repeatedly prohibited by countless imperial decrees <note>original: *purpuræ nundinæ*</note>. From this, those who greeted the Emperors were said to "adore the sacred purple" <note>original: *sacram purpuram adorare*; a ritual of deep respect for the office</note>. Furthermore, it was not permitted to dye purple artificially or dip it in an imitation color; this was accepted for the sake of public reputation, and so that it would not be easy for rebels to dress a Usurper <note>original: *Tyrannum*, often used to mean a pretender to the throne</note> in the purple of imperial majesty, whether real or imitation. This is evident from Marcellinus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus, a 4th-century Roman historian</note> and the Code. On this account, the law forbids certain things from being exported to barbarians, lest they, enticed by the sweetness of the produce, launch an attack on the Roman Prince. This was the primary reason for the Gauls' arrival in Italy, according to Livy <note>Titus Livius, the famed Roman historian who wrote *Ab Urbe Condita*</note>.

<margin>The purple signature; which belonged to the Emperor alone.</margin>
<margin>The entire last book of the Code is full of the secrets of governance.</margin>
I notice the same Secret in the Purple Signature <note>original: *Inscriptione Purpurea*, referring to the use of sacred red/purple ink</note>, which was for the Emperor alone, as found in the Code. There, the Emperor Leo says: "Let it be legal or permitted for no one to possess this composition of sacred ink <note>original: *sacri incausti*</note>, nor to hope for it from anyone else. Namely, whoever attempts this with a tyrannical spirit shall be punished with the death penalty, following the confiscation of all goods." Thus he spoke. Indeed, almost the entire last book of the Code <note>The *Codex Justinianus*, the foundation of Roman law</note> seems to me to contain nothing but these secrets of governance, provided there are people to unpack them; yet these are interpreted quite differently by most commentators.

For those insignia of Empire, or as Dio <note>Cassius Dio, a Roman historian of Greek origin</note> calls them, "the [emblems of authority]" <note>original Greek: τῆς [ἀρχῆς ἐπίσημα] — the catchword *τῆς* refers to the start of the phrase on the next page</note>...

# Arnold Clapmarius, Book III.

<margin>
The insignia of empire are attributed to the Sovereign alone.
</margin>

Why should you not include the *insignia* <note>original: *τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐπίσημα*, meaning the distinctive marks of rule</note> here as well? For these were the marks of empire granted to the Sovereign alone. Thus Vitellius, when he intended to designate his son alone as heir to the Empire, surrounded him with all the emblems of imperial fortune. Tacitus mentions this in the *Histories*, Book 2. Tacitus notes these same insignia in the *Annals*, Book 1: *There were,* he says, *the night watches, weapons, and the rest of the court; soldiers accompanied him into the forum, and soldiers into the senate house.* And Herodian says regarding Gordian: *All the sovereign's procession followed him—whatever soldiers were present, and city youths of tall stature, in the likeness of those who accompany the Emperor in Rome; likewise the laurel staff, the symbol by which Sovereigns are distinguished from private citizens. Furthermore, fire was carried before him according to custom, etc.* To these were added the diadem, the crown, the scepter, and the throne <note>original: *sella*, literally "seat" or "chair of state"</note>.

<margin>
Also the diadem, crown, scepter, and throne.
</margin>

Hence Virgil <note>The author uses Virgil’s family name, Maro</note> writes:

> Both the throne of the kingdom and the *trabea* <note>a ceremonial toga worn by kings and consuls</note>, the insignia of our people.

To occupy this throne was a capital crime. Curtius reports the same regarding the throne of the kings of Persia in Book 8. Likewise the cross. Jerome says quite vividly: *How the image of the Savior's cross <note>original: *patibuli*, meaning the gibbet or cross</note> decorates the purples of Kings and the burning jewels of their diadems?* I remember reading that the Roman Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> later held this exclusive right. In these insignia, a certain great majesty was usually placed.

<margin>
He who holds the insignia holds the empire.
</margin>

Therefore, the Flemish urged the English to seize the insignia of France; by doing this, they thought they could be freed from the oath sworn to the French King <note>This refers to Jean Froissart's account of the Hundred Years' War, where the Flemish convinced Edward III of England to claim the French coat of arms to justify their support for him</note>. *Froissart*. For he who holds the insignia, holds the empire; nor was there ever any separation between the insignia and the empire, as Cujacius <note>Jacques Cujas, a renowned 16th-century legal scholar</note> writes in *Observations*, Book 20, Chapter 37.

# On the Secrets of Statecraft. Chapter 10.

### C H A P T E R X.

*That no mention should be made of an heir when two are contending for the Empire and the Prince is still living. The Princes of Youth, Augusti, Caesars, Minor Kings, Kings of the Romans, the Dauphin, the Infante. The political blunder <note>original Greek: Σολοικισμὸς (solecism), here meaning a tactical error or absurdity</note> of Galba, Chosroes, and others in the naming of an heir.*

---

<margin>That the successor should not be in doubt.</margin>
It is in the interest of the State, within a sovereignty, that the successor should not be in doubt <note>original: *ne successor in incerto sit*</note>, to speak with Tacitus. For indeed, it is also beneficial for the Prince himself, partly so that he may rely on more fortifications <note>original: *munimentis*, referring to political supports or safeguards</note>, and partly so that the hopes of others may be restrained. This is also what Pliny says in Book 2, Epistle 2: "I would prefer to become a father at this time, when I would be both secure and happy"; and he offers this prayer to Pædo Augustus:

> And let there grow up for you Youths twice worthy of Caesar,
> And let them hand down the race of Caesar forever.

<margin>The prudence of Augustus in this matter.</margin>
Augustus, a most wise Prince, in order to retain the sovereignty <note>original: *dominationem*</note> he had seized amidst so many waves of factions and conspiracies and to transmit it to posterity, brought his grandsons Gaius and Lucius into the family of the Caesars, having "purchased" them from their father by bronze and scale <note>original: *per æs & libram*, a formal Roman legal ritual for adoption where a symbolic sale took place using a copper coin and a balance scale</note>. When they died, he again adopted Agrippa Postumus and Tiberius by a law of the assembly <note>original: *curiata lege*, a law passed by the ancient Roman *Comitia Curiata* to formalize adoptions</note>, but on the condition that Tiberius first adopt Germanicus.

<margin>Likewise that of Tiberius.</margin>
Tiberius followed these footsteps, as he did many others, and even brought Drusus close to the supreme power <note>original: *summæ rei*, referring to the highest affairs of state</note>, lest, if a successor were sought outside the Augustan house, the memory of Augustus and the name of the Caesars should be turned into a mockery. There are three hundred examples from other Princes and Kings; among which this recent and illustrious one is found in Charles IV <note>Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1346–1378), who famously promulgated the Golden Bull to clarify imperial succession</note>.

Arn. Clapmarius, Book III.

...who while still alive obtained that his son should be created **King of the Romans**, that is, the heir to the Empire.

<margin>The **King of the Romans** today is he who is the heir to the Empire.</margin>
For those who were formerly called the **Princes of Youth**, or as Zonaras translates it, <note>original Greek: πρόκριτοι τῆς νεότητος</note> "the chosen among the youth," or "successors to the rule" <note>original Greek: διάδοχοι τῆς ἀρχῆς</note> as it appears in Dio; or "heirs and partners in the Empire" in Suetonius; or "Augusti and Caesars" in Ammianus and Spartianus; or as found in the *old glossary*, "Little Kings" <note>original Latin: *Regulli* or *Reguli*—the glossary states that a *Regullus* is the "son of a king"</note>—these are now what we call the **Kings of the Romans**. This is in the same manner as the **Dauphins** in France, the **Infantes** in Spain, and the **Princes of Scotland**.

<margin>If two have hope for the Empire, neither should be named.</margin>
While these things hold true as a general rule, if there should be two or more who have hope of attaining the Empire, it is better to name neither of them, *so that you may live without danger*, as *Law 77, paragraph 24 of the Digest on Legacies (Book 2)* says regarding this same matter. For once one is named, the hope of the other is cut off, and from that desperation, recklessness and audacity are fueled. Under the Emperor Tiberius, there were Germanicus and Drusus. Drusus was the son of the Prince and was strong in his father's love; Germanicus, however, was the step-grandson of Augustus, adopted by Tiberius at the command of the very man who had granted him the Empire <note>Augustus forced Tiberius to adopt Germanicus to ensure the succession remained within his own bloodline</note>. To this was added the immense favor of the people for Germanicus, stemming from the estrangement they felt toward his uncle, and finally the glory of his military achievements. Indeed, he even surpassed Drusus in the nobility of his mother's lineage, claiming Mark Antony as his grandfather and Augustus as his great-uncle. By contrast, it was felt that Drusus’s great-grandfather, the Roman knight Pomponius Atticus, seemed to diminish the dignity of the ancestral portraits of the Claudian house, as Tacitus records.

<margin>That no mention of an heir be made while the Prince is still living.</margin>
During that time, as part of the "smoke" <note>original: *fumo*, referring to a strategic facade or "smokescreen" used to obscure the true workings of power</note> of the secrets of statecraft, no mention of an heir was made while the Prince was still living. Thus, Tacitus says of Tiberius, *that he suspended his judgment.*

### Concerning the Secrets of Rule. Chapter 11.

...with everything prepared, he awaited the King's arrival, yielding the title of the captured city, as is proper. Hence Tacitus says of Tiberius: *He was tormented by the military glory of Germanicus.* <note>original: "Bellica Germanici gloria angebatur." Germanicus was a popular Roman general and the nephew of Emperor Tiberius; his successes in Germany made the Emperor deeply insecure.</note> And elsewhere regarding Otho: *Otho was elated and drew the glory to himself, as if he himself were successful in war and had expanded the Republic through his generals and his armies.* <note>original: "Lato Ottone, & gloriam in se trahente..." Otho was a short-lived Emperor during the "Year of the Four Emperors" (69 AD).</note>

<margin>
The reasoning behind the secret.
</margin>
For when the authors of deeds <note>meaning the generals or subordinates actually carrying out the work</note> draw the fame of those actions to themselves, they overwhelm the majesty and reputation of the Prince, and through this military glory, they easily strive for the Empire.

<margin>
The boasting of Silius is noted.
</margin>
Therefore, it is a **secret of royal rule** that no one besides the Prince should take the fame and glory of an achievement for himself. Thus, regarding that Silius <note>Gaius Silius, a general under Tiberius</note> who had commanded vast armies for seven years: when he boasted excessively that his soldiers had remained obedient while others fell into sedition, and that Tiberius's power would not have lasted if those legions too had desired revolution, Tacitus says: *Caesar felt his own fortune was being destroyed by these claims, and that he was unequal to such great merit.* <note>Essentially, the general's claim that the Emperor owed him his throne was an unpardonable insult to the Emperor’s supreme authority.</note> How much more prudent was Maecenas <note>A close advisor to Augustus</note>, of whom Pedo <note>Albinovanus Pedo, a Roman poet</note> wrote:

> It was a greater thing to have been able to achieve triumphs, yet not desire them; 
> It was a greater thing to have abstained from great honors.

<margin>
Likewise, the prudence of Agricola.
</margin>
And that famous Agricola <note>Gnaeus Julius Agricola, the general responsible for much of the Roman conquest of Britain</note>, as Tacitus testifies, never exulted in his deeds for his own fame, but as a servant, he credited his success to the author and Commander. <summary>This page explores a "secret of rule" (arcanum dominationis) regarding military glory: a ruler must ensure that subordinates do not claim credit for victories, as such fame can be used to challenge the throne. Historical examples from the Roman Empire illustrate how boasting by generals led to imperial resentment or downfall.</summary>

<header>Arnold Clapmarius, Book III.</header>

...that the deed was enough. And regarding Albert, Count of Tyrol, Guntherus <note>Gunther of Pairis (c. 1150–1220), a Cistercian monk and poet known for his epic on the deeds of Frederick Barbarossa.</note> wrote beautifully:

> *While others think great things of it, he himself*
> *Neglects it, and measures the deed with modest honor:*

The Emperor Constantius also looked to this principle; according to Ammianus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus, a 4th-century Roman soldier and historian.</note> in Book 16, he testified through edicts that he had both fought and conquered, even when he had not been present for the actions. In this same way, Domitian celebrated false triumphs—a manner although ridiculous and inept, yet done with the hope of preserving his authority. This was nonetheless a serious crime, and was once called the **crime of the false battle** <note>original: "crimen falsæ pugnæ." This refers to the legal and moral offense of a leader fabricating a military victory to gain political standing or a "Triumph" (a formal victory parade).</note>.

<margin>Domitian's false triumphs.</margin>
Regarding Domitian's false triumph and the genuine victory of Agricola <note>Gnaeus Julius Agricola, the Roman general responsible for much of the conquest of Britain.</note>, Tacitus writes:

> *He was conscious,* he said, *that his recent false triumph over Germany had been an object of derision—having bought people through trade whose dress and hair were styled to look like captives—but now a true and great victory, with so many thousands of the enemy slain, was being celebrated with immense fame. This was most terrifying to him: that the name of a private citizen should be raised above that of the Prince. In vain had the pursuits of the forum and the glory of civil arts been driven into silence, if someone else occupied military glory; for while other things could somehow be more easily ignored, the virtue of a good leader was an Imperial quality.* <note>original: "ducis boni Imperatoriam virtutem esse." Tacitus is highlighting the Emperor's jealousy: if a general is a better soldier than the Emperor, the Emperor's unique status is threatened.</note>

So he said. For military glory is, or ought to be, the exclusive property of the supreme Prince.

# On the Secrets of Rule. Chapter 12. 137

<margin>To venerate the images and names of Emperors on standards.</margin>
Images, statues, and temples were established for the Emperors. From this practice came the signs, names, and likenesses of them on military standards and shields. For this reason, when Vitellius’s rule was in danger, Tacitus writes in Book 3 of the *Histories* that the leaders of the Cassii <note>The soldiers of the Cassian faction or a specific military unit supporting the rebellion.</note> removed the name and images of Vitellius. This same honor was later given to Christ, to which Prudentius <note>Aurelius Prudentius Clemens (c. 348–413 AD), a Roman Christian poet.</note> referred:

> *Christ, woven into purple with jeweled gold,*
> *Marked the labarum; the name of Christ* <note>original: "labarum." The military standard used by Constantine the Great, featuring the Chi-Rho symbol.</note>
> *He had inscribed as the emblems of the shields.*

<margin>Those acting against this were accused of a crime.</margin>
Hence, whoever was said to have venerated the image of another more than that of the Prince was made a defendant for defiance, or indeed for the **crime of treason** <term>læsæ majestatis (lèse-majesté): an offense against the dignity or majesty of the ruler or the state.</term>. This crime was leveled against Marcellus because his statue was positioned higher than that of Caesar. Likewise, Lucius Ennius was accused of the same treason because he had converted a likeness of the Prince into silver for common use. And when the Roman people surrounded the Senate house carrying images of Agrippina and Nero, Tiberius complained that nothing remained except for them to take up the sword and choose as their Leaders and Emperors those whose images they had followed as standards. For images of generals were also seen on standards. Yet Tiberius gave gifts to the Syrian Legions because they alone had venerated no image of Sejanus <note>Lucius Aelius Sejanus, the ambitious commander of the Praetorian Guard under Tiberius.</note> among their military signs.

<margin>Vows and rituals for the safety of the Prince alone.</margin>
Thus, when the Priests <note>original: "Pontifices," members of the highest council of Roman priests.</note> undertook vows for the safety of the Prince and also commended Nero and Drusus to the same gods, Tiberius was impatiently pained that young men were being made equal to his old age, and he pardoned them for this only with great reluctance. I refer to this as a **secret of rule** <note>original: "arcanum dominationis."</note>: that vows were to be conceived for the health of the Prince alone, according to Book 1 of the Code on the Offering of Vows.

# Arnold Clapmarius, Book III. 138

Pliny says in his *Panegyric*, *“It is the single vow of all”* [referring to the] *Right of the Prince* <note>original: "Ius Principis." From Pliny the Younger's speech praising Emperor Trajan.</note>; and also because by this reasoning, the majesty of the Emperor was equaled by the dignity of others.

<margin>To be called Eternal, Venerable, and Holy Emperors.</margin>
Moreover, the Emperors primarily strove not only to be strong and be thought of as such, but also to be **holy and venerable**, because nothing moves the minds of the common people more than religion. As Curtius <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, a Roman historian who wrote a history of Alexander the Great.</note> testifies concerning the Persians in Book 8: *“The Persians wisely worship their kings among the Gods. For they believe it to be the safeguard of the majesty of the empire and its safety.”* From this comes that saying of Paul, *“I say, you are Gods.”* <note>original: "Dico Dii estis." Clapmarius attributes this to the Apostle Paul, though it is a famous quote from Psalm 82:6, often used in political treatises to discuss the divine authority of rulers.</note> By this name, the Roman Emperors, even the Christian ones, called themselves **eternal, holy, and divine**, as in the *Code on Armories, Law 2*: <note>original: "l. 2. C. de Fabric." Refers to the Codex Justinianus, the collection of Roman laws compiled under Emperor Justinian.</note> *“Let those who work in the armories adore our eternity”*; and frequently elsewhere. <margin>Ammianus mocks this exaggeration.</margin> However, Ammianus Marcellinus <note>A 4th-century Roman soldier and historian known for his critical view of imperial excesses.</note> not undeservedly mocks this exaggeration <term>hyperbole: an intentional exaggeration used for rhetorical effect</term>, and others detest it. Hence, whoever swore falsely by the Roman Prince was beaten with clubs. <note>original: "l. si duo §. ult. D. de jurejur." A reference to the Digest of Roman law regarding perjury.</note> Tiberius, according to Tacitus, said: *“An oath sworn by the Prince should be judged just as if one had deceived Jupiter.”*

<margin>To have private rites and to prohibit others from having them.</margin>
For this reason also, it was permitted to almost no one except the Prince to hold private religious rites or to create new Gods, as I gather from Suetonius. And Callisthenes says in Curtius, Book 8: *“Can it be that you and I, Cleo, have made Gods?”* And Aemilius Probus <note>A name historically associated with the biographer Cornelius Nepos.</note> says of Alcibiades: *“He was also splashed with infamy because he was said to hold religious mysteries in his own house, which was a crime according to the custom of the Athenians; and it was judged that this pertained not to religion, but to conspiracy.”* Therefore, the Princes alone worshipped **Fortune** in their household shrine <term>Lararium: a private shrine in a Roman home dedicated to the Lares, the guardian spirits of the household.</term>; as if she were a native inhabitant and the founder of the Roman Empire. By a similar reasoning, it was permitted to no one [else]...

## CHAPTER XIII.

->That no one may practice the magic art. Mathematicians.<-

<margin>The ultimate reason for this secret of state.</margin>
For many have competed for the Empire on this pretext alone: that they believed it was owed to them by fate. Such was Lentulus <note>Publius Cornelius Lentulus Sura, a Roman politician involved in the Catiline conspiracy.</note>, who prophesied that the kingdom was destined for his family based on the <term>Sibylline verses</term> <note>A collection of oracular utterances traditionally consulted by the Roman state in times of crisis.</note>. And concerning a certain Telephus, Suetonius <note>Roman historian and biographer of the first twelve Caesars.</note> writes in his life of *Augustus*: *“Finally,” he says, “Telephus, as if the rule were owed to him by fate, attacked both Augustus and the Senate”*; to omit countless others.

<margin>The art of divination, as being dangerous in the principate, is prohibited.</margin>
This circumstance drove the Emperors to declare the art of divination damnable, according to Law 6 of the *Code on Malefactors* <note>original: "l. 6. C. de mal." Refers to the section *De Maleficis et Mathematicis* in the Codex Justinianus.</note>. In older times, it was prohibited by the <term>interdiction of fire and water</term> <note>A legal formula for Roman banishment, effectively stripping a person of citizenship and property.</note>, as is clear from the fragments of Ulpian <note>One of the great Roman legal authorities.</note>; later it was punished by the death penalty: *“Since it strikes at Majesty itself when it is harmed,”* as Law 7 of the same Code says. Moreover, those who predicted the future were called <term>Mathematicians</term> <note>In the Roman world, "mathematicus" often referred specifically to astrologers and casters of horoscopes, rather than students of geometry or arithmetic.</note>; hence Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet.</note> says: *“Your horoscope is known to the Mathematicians.”* <note>original: "Nota Mathematicis genesis tua."</note>

<margin>The distinction between Mathematics and those who profess it excessively, and which or who are the genuine ones.</margin>
For I do not mean that true and genuine Mathematics, which, as <term>Diocletian</term> <note>Roman Emperor from 284 to 305 AD.</note> testifies, it is in the public interest to learn and practice, or which...

### CHAPTER XIV.

*To fortify oneself with guards; to be armed and armored. The excessive security of Caesar, and the lack of discernment* <note>original Greek: "ἡ ἀπαιδευσία" (hē apaideusia), meaning a lack of education, refinement, or practical judgment.</note> *in dismissing the Praetorian soldiers. The guard of the royal body.*

<margin>
The Prince must fortify himself against the plots of men.
</margin>
Just as the right to bear arms is by no means appropriate for a private citizen; so, conversely, a Prince must fortify himself with arms against the plots of factious men. For, as Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> says in Book 2: *Majesty is poorly protected by arms without strength.* Therefore, Romulus kept three hundred armed men for the protection of his person—whom he called the <term>Celeres</term> <note>The "Swift Ones," a personal bodyguard of 300 men established by the legendary founder of Rome.</note>—not only in war, but also in peace. Livia similarly and diligently warned Augustus to establish the most exquisite guard for his body. And Maecenas said to the same: *I advise,* he said, *that you take two of the most excellent knights to command the guard, so that there are those who carry out the protection of your person.*

### Arnold Clapmarius, Book III.

<margin>
This is not tyrannical.
</margin>

<margin>
The difference between legitimate dominion and tyranny.
</margin>

I do not listen to those who think that this <note>Referring to the use of armed guards and state secrets.</note> is something more than tyrannical. Indeed, the use of these <term>secrets of state</term> <note>original: "arcanorum," referring to the *arcana imperii* or hidden techniques of power.</note>, even by Aristotle’s testimony, is not meant so much for a tranquil and peaceful Republic as for one that is turbulent and seditious. There is a great difference between legitimate dominion and tyranny. The latter looks only to its own advantage; the former looks to both its own and that of its citizens. The latter is seized through crimes; the former may be held by force, but it is the force and right of war. The latter is fortified by arms for the destruction of its citizens; the former for its own support and protection.

<margin>
The guarding of the royal person is necessary, as is recommended by various examples.
</margin>

For this reason, Augustus acted rightly when he went into the Senate house protected by a breastplate under his clothes and girded with a sword. Tiberius acted rightly when he stationed guards at the funeral of Augustus, even though he was mocked for it by the people. Following their example, Cosimo de' Medici <note>Cosimo I de' Medici (1519–1574), the first Grand Duke of Tuscany, who consolidated power in Florence.</note>, having taken command of the Florentine state, never entered the senate unless he was armed and accompanied by a military troop. Even Masinissa <note>A King of Numidia (c. 238–148 BCE) known for his long reign and alliance with Rome.</note>, trusting men very little, hedged his safety with a pack of dogs, according to the writer Valerius Maximus. For what other cause, by fortune, was there for the so unexpected and hasty death of Gaius Julius Caesar, other than that he neglected his watches and dismissed the Praetorian soldiers <note>The elite bodyguard of the Roman emperors.</note>, who are the strongest strength of a royal person? 

Therefore, while Caesar mocked Sulla <note>Lucius Cornelius Sulla (138–78 BCE), the Roman dictator who unexpectedly resigned his power.</note>—saying that Sulla "did not know his political ABCs" <note>original: "literas nescivisse." Caesar famously joked that Sulla couldn't "spell" dictatorship because he gave it up.</note> because he had resigned his Dictatorship—Caesar himself is much more to be scolded. For Caesar, though he did *not* resign his Dictatorship, nevertheless dismissed his guards. *For a Principate sought by arms, as Pansa and Hirtius <note>Gaius Pansa and Aulus Hirtius, consuls and supporters of Caesar who warned him of conspiracies.</note> warned him in the writings of Paterculus <note>Velleius Paterculus, a Roman historian.</note>, had to be maintained by arms.* For this reason, the English writer Henry Savile <note>Sir Henry Savile (1549–1622), a scholar and translator of Tacitus, whose political commentaries were widely read.</note> deservedly calls Caesar a "solecism" <note>A grammatical error or absurdity; here, a metaphor for a political blunder.</note> and the worst possible grammarian. Truly the Tragic poet says in *Hercules Furens*...

<margin>
Political illiteracy <note>original: "ἀπαιδευσία" (apaideusia), meaning a lack of education or ignorance.</note> of Julius Caesar in dismissing his bodyguard.
</margin>

<meta>catchword: Quod</meta>

<summary>Clapmarius distinguishes between protective "dominion" and destructive "tyranny," arguing that a ruler must maintain armed guards for safety. He cites historical examples like Augustus and Cosimo de' Medici, concluding that Julius Caesar's assassination was a result of his "political illiteracy" in dismissing his guards.</summary>

<header>On the Secrets of Rule. Chapter 14.</header>
<meta>catchword: to be endured.</meta>

> A drawn sword protects
> what you know you hold against the will of your citizens.
<note>original: "Quod civibus tenere te invitis scias, / Strictus tuetur ensis." This quote is from the Roman tragedy *Octavia*, traditionally attributed to Seneca.</note>

For this reason, Augustus and Tiberius used a Germanic guard, Galba used the *Recalled Veterans* <term>Evocati</term> <note>Soldiers who had finished their service but re-enlisted voluntarily at the commander's invitation.</note>, Caligula used the Batavians <note>A Germanic tribe from the Rhine delta known for their loyalty and elite status as imperial bodyguards.</note>, Antoninus used Germanic cavalry, and others used various other units; by doing so, they both rendered themselves safe from the crimes of their citizens and struck terror into wicked men. For this same reason, the most ancient kings—as seen in the writings of Xenophon and Justin—kept tasters around them, who would mix or pre-taste the drink because of the danger of poison. This custom is still in use by Kings today. Furthermore, the historian Suetonius calls the stationing of soldiers the *force of Rule* <note>original: "vim Dominationis"</note>. By the stationing of soldiers, he says, that is, *having assumed the force and appearance of Rule*; and Naevius calls them *guards of the royal body*.

### CHAPTER XV.

*Not leaving the seat of Empire, that is, the head of affairs; and a discussion of the reasons why Tiberius, Antoninus, Justinian, King Charles of France, and Murad <note>Refers to the Ottoman Sultan, likely Murad II or III.</note> did not depart from the city: it is characteristic of Imperial Majesty to act with precision. The imprudence of the Gauls in deserting Milan.*

Rome, as has been said, was the seat of the Roman Empire and the head of affairs <note>original: "caput rerum," a common Latin idiom for the capital city or the center of power.</note>. Concerning which, the famous Romulus says in the first book of Livy: *Go, announce to the Romans that the heavenly gods so will it, that my Rome be the head of the world.* <note>original: "Abi nuncia, inquit, Romanis, cælestes ita velle, ut mea Roma caput orbis terrarum sit."</note> Therefore, the Roman Princes did not easily desert that Seat. Regarding the Emperor Augustus, Suetonius writes: *He did not leave the city for long.* Elsewhere he says: *For two continuous years after obtaining the Empire, he did not set foot outside the gate.* Tiberius did the same.

<meta>This page continues Chapter 15 of Book III, examining the "Secrets of Rule" regarding why a ruler should remain at the seat of power. It specifically analyzes the case of Emperor Tiberius during the military mutinies in Illyricum and Germany.</meta>

<header>Arnold Clapmarius, Book III.</header>
<meta>catchword: for the most part</meta>

Tiberius... For when a sedition broke out in Illyricum <note>A Roman province in the western Balkans. The mutiny occurred in 14 AD upon the death of Augustus.</note>, the common people began to blame Tiberius, saying that he himself ought to go and confront them with his Imperial majesty; but Tiberius remained unmoved and fixed in his resolve against these rumors: he would not abandon the "head" <note>The capital city, Rome.</note>, nor would he put himself and the State at risk. You may refer this repeatedly—at my own peril—to the *Secrets of Rule* <note>original: "arcana Dominationis"</note>.

<margin>Reasons that detained Tiberius.</margin>
Indeed, these reasons were not for nothing; on the contrary, they were most weighty. Although Tiberius devised a different pretext by extolling the greatness of the Empire, his true reasons were as follows: *First*, because the city was the head of affairs, from which government spreads to all things, as Tacitus says in the second book of the *Annals*. *It is not fitting*, he says elsewhere, *for Princes to abandon the city from which government of all things proceeds simply because one or two cities are in turmoil.* <note>original: "Neque decorum... Principibus si una alterave civitas turbet, omissa urbe, unde in omnia regimen, &c."</note> *Secondly*, lest he cast himself and the State into danger. For the "little fox" <note>A metaphorical reference to Tiberius's legendary cunning and cautious nature.</note> preferred to maintain his grip on the seat of Empire rather than leave, thereby making the State—and thus his own Rule—vulnerable to the plots of conspirators in his absence. *Thirdly*, because if he had gone, he would have had to satisfy either both armies (the one in Illyricum as well as the one in Germany), or neither, or only one of them. If he satisfied both, it would have been contrary to the safety of the State, which was unequal to such heavy financial burdens. If he satisfied neither, he feared they would both attempt violence against him and extract by necessity what they could not obtain voluntarily. Thus, Tacitus says in the first book of the *Annals*: *Severity is dangerous and bribery is shameful, whether nothing or everything is granted to the soldier when the State is in a state of uncertainty.* <note>original: "Periculosa severitas, flagitiosa largitio, seu nihil militi, seu omnia concederentur, in ancipiti Republ."</note> If he satisfied only one, and thus preferred that army over the other, there was a danger that those passed over would be incensed by the insult. *Fourthly*, it was therefore more advisable for his sons to be sent while the Imperial majesty remained intact, for which there is greater reverence from a distance; and as Caesar says: *for the most part, all things...* <note>The text cuts off here, leading into a common Roman sentiment that distance lends enchantment or fear to authority.</note>

<summary>This page analyzes Tiberius’s strategic decision to stay in Rome during provincial mutinies, framing it as a "secret of rule" designed to maintain central authority and avoid being manipulated or assassinated by the military.</summary>

### On the Secrets of Rule. Chapter 15.

...for the most part, those things which are out of sight disturb the minds of men more intensely; and as Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> writes in his 35th book: "The constant sight of great men makes them less respected, as it creates a sense of over-familiarity." <note>original: "continuus aspectus minus verendos magnos homines ipsa satietate facit"</note> Fifth. Ambassadors were permitted to act with ambiguity, to offer the judgment of the Senate as a pretext, and even to refer certain matters back to the Emperor; <margin>It belongs to the Imperial majesty to act decisively.</margin> but it is the duty of the Imperial majesty to act decisively in all things, and to the point. This means, as Alciatus <note>Andrea Alciato (1492–1550), a famous Italian jurist.</note> interprets it, acting without any "plastering" or wrapping up of one’s speech; or, as Cicero writes in the eighth book of his letters to Atticus, acting without any exception. Therefore, Tacitus <note>The Roman historian.</note> says of Drusus <note>Son of Tiberius.</note> that he put forward the judgment of the Senate and of his father as a shield for his actions. Sixth. If the soldiers were to resist Germanicus and Drusus, they could be softened or broken; but if they resisted the Emperor himself—that is, if the Imperial majesty were violated—what remedy could they hope for?

<margin>They followed these examples.</margin> Antoninus, Justinian, that Charles, the King of France <note>Charles V, known as "the Wise."</note>, Murad <note>original: "Ammurates." Likely Murad II, the Ottoman Sultan.</note>, and others practiced the same. <margin>The withdrawal of Princes.</margin> Antoninus <note>Refers here to Marcus Aurelius.</note> asserted the reason that the presence of the Prince’s entourage would be too heavy a burden for the provincial subjects; but in my judgment, the reason recorded by Capitolinus <note>Julius Capitolinus, one of the authors of the *Historia Augusta*.</note> is truer: that while the Emperor was away, the seat of the Empire might be seized by conspirators.

Therefore Murad, that Emperor of the Turks, dared to boast that while sitting in Constantinople, he accomplished greater things than any of his ancestors had in the battle line itself. And Tiberius used to say that his ambassadors provided the loyalty and courage, while he himself remained at the head of strategy. The reason for this, however, was none other than that Constantinople was the seat of the Empire, and full of Christian enemies most hostile to the Turkish name.

<margin>Specifically regarding Charles, King of France.</margin> Thus Charles the Frenchman waged war with Edward, King of England <note>Edward III.</note>, through his brothers, lest if things went unsuccessfully—as is the fortune of war—while the King was absent, the Parisians would stage a revolt after their own fashion. And yet Edward is said to have remarked that he never had to deal with any enemy who took up arms less...

### CHAPTER XVI.

->*Restraining the Empire within its boundaries. Fear, in place of counsel and prudence. The limits of the Roman Empire under Augustus. The difficulty of retaining an Empire in remote regions. The necessity of long rest for a sick Republic. The hidden cause of the Catilinarian conspiracy.*<-

<margin>
*The happiness of a Republic should be established on the prudence of commanding and obeying, not on size.*
</margin>
The happiness of a Republic, as the most illustrious writer of Roman history <note>Likely referring to Sallust, who often discussed the decline of Roman morals and the "health" of the state.</note> testifies, does not consist in its size, but in the highest prudence of commanding and obeying. To me, this seems like an oracle, especially in a Republic that is turbulent and suffering from many internal discords. A wise architect certainly does not build too many stories or heavy structures above, nor does he raise a house higher than the foundation can bear. Therefore, once the Emperor Augustus had secured the 
<margin>
*The source of Augustus’s plan to restrain the empire within its boundaries.*
</margin>
Empire, he formed a plan to restrain it within its current boundaries, as Tacitus <note>Cornelius Tacitus, the Roman historian.</note> and Dio <note>Cassius Dio, a Roman historian of Greek origin.</note> report. This passage seems to me to savor of a great "secret of rule" <term>arcanum dominationis</term>. For Augustus did not do this out of envy—as was the case with Hadrian <note>Emperor Hadrian (reigned 117–138 AD) famously withdrew from several of his predecessor Trajan's eastern conquests.</note>—nor out of some specific fear, dread, or even laziness, as the common people perhaps believed. Rather, he acted out of the highest prudence, lest—as Dio testifies—if he wished to expand the borders of the empire, he would find it more difficult to protect and more easily lose what had already been gained. # On the Secrets of Rule. Chapter 16.

<sig>G 2</sig>

...army, if, along with **Scipio Ammirato** <note>Scipione Ammirato (1531–1601) was an Italian historian often called "the new Tacitus" for his political commentaries.</note>, you interpret fear as prudence—or, as **Tacitus** calls it elsewhere, "counsel." For example, in his *Life of Agricola*, he says: *And the long neglect of Britain even in peace was called a "counsel" by the Divine Augustus, and by Tiberius especially*—or, as **Lipsius** <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606) was a preeminent Flemish scholar whose editions of Tacitus were standard for the era.</note> reads it, a *precept* <note>original: "præceptum"</note>—*and in other places fear is taken for prudence.* Hence **Petronius Arbiter** <note>A Roman courtier and author during the reign of Nero.</note> says: *As much as each person fears, so much does he flee.* For fear makes men safe. **Thucydides** <note>The famous Greek historian of the Peloponnesian War.</note> writes: *Mutual fear is the only reliable basis for an alliance.* <note>original Greek: "τὸ δ' ἀντίπαλον δέος, μόνον πιστὸν ἐς ξυμμαχίαν"</note> And **Tacitus** notes in his *Germania*: *Germany is separated from the Dacians by mutual fear, or by mountains.* So says **Ligurinus** <note>Gunther of Pairis, a 12th-century poet whose epic "Ligurinus" celebrated the deeds of Frederick Barbarossa.</note>:

> Indeed fear urges them on, and dangers make them brave.

<margin>Reasons for this policy.</margin>
And indeed, there are other reasons for this policy of restraint. First, because the fortune and the gamble of war are changeable, and so too is the fortune of virtue itself. Hence **Seneca** <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero.</note> writes in his play *Hercules Furens*: *After many labors, virtue is accustomed to slacken.* For this reason, the famous **Corbulo** <note>Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, a highly successful Roman general under Claudius and Nero who eventually fell victim to the Emperor's jealousy.</note> did not wish to push his luck beyond danger after so many years of earned glory.

<margin>The limits of the Roman Empire.</margin>
Secondly, it was because the Roman Empire was already laboring under its own massive weight. Its boundaries were the Euphrates to the East, the cataracts of the Nile and the deserts of Africa to the South, Mount Atlas to the West, and the Danube and Rhine to the North, which presented a great difficulty for retention. Therefore, **Tacitus** writes in the first book of the *Annals*: *The Empire was enclosed by the Ocean or distant rivers; the legions, provinces, and fleets were all connected to one another.* All of these measures pertained to the security of the Prince.

<margin>The difficulty of retaining remote territories.</margin>
Regarding this matter, there is a fine speech by the **Venetians** found in **Guicciardini’s** <note>Francesco Guicciardini (1483–1540), a Florentine statesman and one of the major political writers of the Italian Renaissance.</note> third book of his *History*. They argued that while the city of Pisa was indeed very convenient for the Venetians, they could only reach it through the territory and ports of others; thus, it could be preserved only with great difficulty and expense against the attacks of the Florentines...

<margin>The political policy of Augustus. <note>original Greek: "πολιτικὴ αἵρεσις"</note></margin>
> When the Roman state was frequently brought to the brink of ultimate disaster by civil wars, I settled and strengthened it. Then, having subdued the Thracians and Scythians, I did not devise one war after another, but concentrated on the description of the Law and the correction of those things which had been corrupted by the civil wars; and so forth.

It was surely in the interest of the Republic, which was sick and wounded, to rest, lest—as **Florus** <note>Lucius Annaeus Florus, a 2nd-century Roman historian.</note> says—*the wounds might be torn open by the very act of healing.* For this reason, a wise writer also praised **Tiberius** <note>The second Roman Emperor, known for his cautious foreign policy.</note> for being *uninterested in extending the Empire.*

## CHAPTER XVII.

->*That no one may kill a Prince, even an enemy, with impunity.*<-
->*That the acts of prior Princes be preserved, even those of Tyrants.*<-
->*That a Prince should not easily be put to death.*<-

<margin>Royal blood is not to be shed easily. A famous saying of **Lorenzo de' Medici** <note>The Florentine statesman known as "the Magnificent" (1449–1492).</note>.</margin>
The safety of the Prince himself, as well as the reverence of the citizens toward their rulers, is based on this: that no person of royal or princely blood should be easily killed. Indeed, even the murder of a Prince, however much he may be an enemy, should not remain unpunished. As the great Lorenzo de' Medici said, he did not wish to permit the idea to take root in the minds of men that it is lawful to spill royal or princely blood. For a Prince who kills another Prince sets an example for his own murder and leaves his own side exposed. Therefore, **Holy David** <note>The biblical King David, who famously refused to strike down King Saul, the "Lord's anointed."</note> said: *I killed him,* he says, *who brought the news of Saul’s death and expected a reward; how much more so should wicked men be punished who have killed a righteous man in his own house and sleeping in his bed?* <note>A reference to 2 Samuel 4, where David executes those who murdered his rival Ish-bosheth.</note> With the same wisdom, Augustus punished the assassins of...

### Arnold Clapmarius, Book III.

<margin>
*The Senate is indeed immortal; but no less subject to the conspiracies of wicked citizens.*
</margin>
...for the sake of [wicked] citizens, there is a need for arts of this kind. For although the Senate, as that Emperor used to say, is immortal, while a Prince is mortal; the former is no less subject to the injuries of wicked citizens than the latter, unless it actively opposes them. Examples of conspiracies against the senate and the <term>Patricians: The hereditary noble families who held exclusive right to high office in early Rome.</term> are obvious. Such was that famous plot of **Catiline**, who had planned to slaughter the entire senate, except for the children of **Pompey**. For the perpetration of this crime, a single night of the **Saturnalia** <note>A Roman festival in December where social norms were inverted and slaves were temporarily "equal" to masters, providing a perfect distraction for a coup.</note> was appointed.

<margin>
*What the secrets of Aristocratic rule are.*
</margin>
Therefore, just as the secrets of royal rule are hidden plans devised for the safety of the Prince; so the <term>Aristocratic Secrets: (Arcana Aristocratica) Strategies and hidden political maneuvers used by a ruling elite to maintain their collective power and prevent a revolution.</term> of rule are the intimate and hidden plans pertaining to the safety of the Nobles, or Patricians, in a Republic.

<margin>
*Many of these agree with the royal secrets.*
</margin>
There are many of these which are common with the royal secrets. Such as the rule that no briberies or secret gatherings should occur. For these, as **Livy** <note>Titus Livius (64 BC – 17 AD), the primary historian of the Roman Republic.</note> testifies, are invitations to recklessness among the common people. Concerning secret gatherings, the same Livy says in Book 2: *Then indeed the common people began to hold nocturnal meetings, some on the Esquiline Hill and others on the Aventine, so that they would not be thrown into confusion by sudden decisions in the forum, and might not act entirely by rashness and chance. The consuls, judging this matter to be ruinous (as indeed it was), reported it to the Senators.*

<margin>
*Such is the rule against briberies and gatherings.*
</margin>
Concerning Bribery, the same Livy says in the same book: *The Senators felt a public anxiety that the consuls were building up wealth through bribery that was dangerous to liberty.* And a little later: *Those lands would bring slavery to those who received them.* To which those words of **Marcus Tullius Cicero** to **Atticus** in Book 2, Letter 17, fit beautifully: *There is nothing that should not be feared; admittedly, he is preparing a tyranny.* <note>original: ὁμολογουμένως τυραννίδα συσκευάζεται (homologoumenōs tyrannida syskeuazetai). Cicero used Greek to keep his political criticisms private in his letters.</note> *For what do that sudden joining of family ties, the Campanian land, and the outpouring of money signify?*

<summary>Clapmarius defines "Aristocratic Secrets" as the protective measures a ruling elite uses to prevent their overthrow, drawing parallels to the safety of Kings. He highlights historical examples from Rome, such as Catiline's conspiracy and the Senate's fear of public bribery and secret nocturnal assemblies.</summary>
