### On the Secrets of Rule, Chapter 18.

If these were the worst examples, they would still be too much of an evil. But it is the nature of the matter that these cannot be the extreme limit. For how could these things please them in themselves? They would never have come to this point unless they were preparing a path for other destructive goals. Thus, in **Livy** <note>Titus Livius, a Roman historian</note>’s fourth book, the Senators <note>referred to here as "the Fathers"</note> rebuke the Consuls because they allowed the bribes and secret gatherings of **Spurius Maelius** <note>A wealthy Roman accused of seeking to become king by distributing grain during a famine.</note> to take place in a private house.

<margin>*That no one should build in a fortified place.*</margin>
<margin>*That no patrician should live on the Citadel or the Capitol.*</margin>
Furthermore, none of the **Patricians** <note>The hereditary noble class of ancient Rome.</note> should build too splendidly. Livy writes in his second book: *Valerius, the Consul, came under suspicion of seeking the kingship because he was building on the summit of the Velia* <note>A ridge in Rome near the Forum.</note>. *He would have been impregnable in such a high and fortified place; therefore, he immediately moved the building materials down from the Velia, and his house was built at the bottom of the slope.* From this, a law was brought to the people *that no patrician should live on the Citadel or the Capitol.*

I will not even mention how the magnificence of these buildings grates upon the minds of the poor and invites rebellion. **Catiline** says in **Sallust**: *What mortal with a man’s spirit can endure that they have a surplus of riches, which they pour out in building over the sea and leveling mountains, while we lack the family means for even the necessities of life? That they build two or more houses, while we have no family hearth anywhere?* **Horace** likewise rebukes: *Wealth built up high, and masses of stone cast into the deep.* And **Petronius**: *They build with gold, and send their dwellings to the stars, yet they are driven out from the water by rocks.* <note>Referring to the Roman trend of building villas on artificial islands or piers jutting into the sea.</note>

<margin>*That Senators and patricians be considered holy.*</margin>
Above all, however, it serves the safety of the patricians that the senators and patricians be regarded as holy and inviolable. For this reason, among the Romans, the **Auspices** <note>The religious practice of interpreting the will of the gods from the flight of birds or other natural signs; it was a powerful political tool.</note> belonged to the Patricians alone. Livy asks in book 6: *In whose hands, therefore, are the auspices according to the custom of our ancestors?*

<meta>The catchword "Nempe" (Certainly/To be sure) indicates the start of the answer to the rhetorical question posed at the end of the page.</meta>

It also emphasizes that the nobility's safety is bolstered by their exclusive control over religious authority, such as the Roman auspices.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "Aristocratic Secrets"—the strategies used by a ruling elite to maintain power. ### Arnold Clapmarius, Book III.

<margin>
To punish most severely any injuries done to a Patrician or Senator. That a Patrician should not easily be put to death. Against whom specifically these "secrets" in an Aristocracy should be used.
</margin>
Namely, the power remains in the hands of the **Fathers** <note>original: "Patres" — the Senators</note>. And in Book 23 [of Livy's History], it is noted that a private citizen could not follow the **auspices** <note>term: auspices — the practice of interpreting omens from birds to determine the gods' approval for state actions; this was a religious monopoly held by the ruling class</note>, nor could any public action be taken without them; only in foreign service could someone newly conceive of such things.

For this reason, it was considered a great crime to strike a man of the Senatorial order or to inflict any injury upon him. As **Arnobius** <note>An early Christian apologist and rhetorician</note> says in his fourth book: *To humiliate a magistrate, or to pursue a Senator with insults, is most dangerous according to their own decrees and carries the heaviest penalties.*

By a similar logic, **Patricians** <note>The hereditary noble class</note> should not be easily subjected to capital punishment. When the **Decemviri** <note>term: Decemviri — a ten-man commission established to codify Roman law; they eventually became tyrannical</note> were about to lay down their power, they begged and warned the Fathers to guard them against the envy of the masses; they urged them not to accustom the **plebeians** <note>The common people</note> to the execution of the Fathers by spilling noble blood (Livy, Book 3).

Secret strategies of this kind must be used in an Aristocratic Republic against those who would rather "pollute" themselves with the blood of the Nobility than bear their rule with a calm mind.

## C H A P T E R   X I X.

->The creation and power of the Dictator. That the Patricians alone should carry swords. The breastplate of Cicero as Roman Consul. Lictores. Fasces.<-

<margin>
The creation of the Dictator, which represented his majesty.
</margin>
Above all, the creation of the Roman **Dictator** <note>In Rome, a temporary emergency magistrate with absolute power</note>—following the passage of the law of **appeal** <note>term: provocatio — the right of a Roman citizen to appeal a magistrate's death sentence to the assembly of the people</note>—seems to capture the very essence of a "secret" of Aristocratic rule. **Appius Claudius** <note>A Roman politician known for his harsh, anti-plebeian views</note> testifies to this in Livy’s second book. A Consul who was truly always <note>original: "ἀεὶ" — Greek for "always"</note> hostile to the commoners, he said: *This evil has grown so much because of the right of appeal. Come, let us create a Dictator, from whom there is no appeal; then this madness, which sets everything on fire, will fall silent. Let anyone then dare to strike my **lictor** <note>term: lictor — an officer attending a magistrate, carrying the "fasces" (rods and axes) to carry out punishments</note>, knowing that the right over his back and his life belongs solely to that one man [the Dictator].* Indeed, had the Roman Fathers not employed this strategy, they would have been almost—if not entirely—unable to withstand the violence and ferocity of the common people.

<summary>This page discusses the legal and religious "secrets" used by the Roman elite to protect themselves, focusing on the sanctity of the Senatorial class and the use of the Dictatorship to bypass the commoners' right of legal appeal.</summary>

# Concerning the Secrets of Government, Chapter 19.
### G 6
<meta>catchword: res.</meta>

<margin>The nature of the Dictator’s majesty.</margin>
For the Dictator possessed great force and power; so much so that it was strictly forbidden to appeal his decisions, especially when he was appointed according to the highest law. Thus, Livy says in Book 8: <note>original: "Dictatoris... edictum pro numine semper observatum"</note> *The Dictator’s edict was always obeyed as if it were the will of a god.* And the Tribunes in Book 6 say that *the Dictatorial lightning bolt was created against them.* In the same place: *Neither the tribunes of the people, nor the common people themselves, dared to raise their eyes or even mutter against the Dictatorial power.* Nor was he created only in times of war, but also in peace. Livy writes in Book 7: *This year had Marcus Fabius as Dictator, not out of any fear of war, but so that the Licinian law might not be observed in the consular elections.* <note>The Licinian law was a piece of legislation intended to open the consulship to plebeians; the aristocracy used a Dictator to bypass these democratic rules.</note>

<margin>That the Dictatorship should not be long-lasting, and why.</margin>
Furthermore, it was a healthy practice in a free Republic that such great force and majesty lasted for only six months, lest someone, relying on long-term power, might overthrow the Republic. For it often happens that a **Principate** <note>term: Principate — a form of government where power is concentrated in a single leader, marking the transition from a Republic to an Empire</note> follows a Dictatorship of this kind. As can also be seen in that passage from **Tacitus**, *Annals*, Book 11: <note>original: "Exhaustis, quas Dictator Caesar lege Cassia, & Princeps Augustus lege Senia sublegêre"</note> *With the patrician families exhausted, whom the Dictator Caesar replaced by the Cassian law and the Prince Augustus by the Senian law, etc.*

<margin>That the Patricians should walk about armed.</margin>
To this also belongs the practice that, in this Republic, the **patricians** <note>the hereditary noble class</note> should be protected and go about with swords and weapons. Although this is considered of little importance, it nonetheless wonderfully deters the common people and increases the force and authority of the patricians. Hence **Cicero**, although he boasted to Atticus that he was protected by the strongest goodwill of men, nevertheless as **Consul** <note>one of the two annually elected chief magistrates who jointly ruled the Republic</note> went up to the Field of Mars with a broad and conspicuous **breastplate** <note>term: lorica — a piece of defensive armor, specifically a breastplate</note>. By this action, he ensured his own safety, but stirred up the greatest hatred against Catiline and Antony.

<margin>The Consuls with their lictors and fasces.</margin>
For this reason, the Consuls <note>original: "Coss." — abbreviation for Consules</note> used to walk with **lictors** and **fasces**. Therefore, a "secret of rule" was tested when Livy says: *The lictors were violated...* <note>The text breaks off here as the sentence continues on the next page.</note>
<term>lictors</term> — attendants who walked before high-ranking Roman magistrates, carrying the fasces as symbols of their power to punish or execute.
<term>fasces</term> — a bundle of wooden rods tied together around an axe; it represented the magistrate’s authority to administer corporal and capital punishment.

## CHAPTER XX.

### *That Senators, Consuls, or Patricians should not desert the City, or withdraw from it. That peace should not be sought from anywhere else but Rome.*

<margin>
That the Patricians should not easily abandon their ancestral seat.
</margin>
<margin>
This error of Pompey and the Senate was noted by Cicero.
</margin>
It also concerns the safety of the **Patricians** <note>the hereditary noble class of Rome</note> that they do not easily abandon their ancestral seat. Concerning this, Cicero most severely accused Pompey—and indeed the entire Roman Senate—because they departed Rome when Caesar was approaching with his army, doing so "not at all in an aristocratic manner" <note>original Greek: οὐ πάν' ἀριστοκρατικῶς</note>. "I was not surprised," he says in Book 8, Letter 1 to Atticus, "that he who had abandoned the head itself would not spare the remaining members." And in Book 7, Letter 11: "By all that is holy, what do you think of Pompey’s plan? I ask this because he left the city; for I am at a loss <note>original Greek: ἀπορῶ</note>, as nothing then was more absurd. Would you leave the city? You would have done the same, then, if the Gauls were coming." He continues, "The Republic is not found in the walls, but in the altars and hearths." Themistocles <note>an Athenian general</note> did the same, for a single city could not withstand the flood of all the Barbarians <note>referring to the Persian invasion of Greece</note>. But Pericles did not do the same, almost fifty years later, when he held nothing but the walls. Our ancestors once, when the rest of the city was captured, nevertheless held the citadel. And a little later: "There is much complaint among the people that the city is without Magistrates, without a Senate." <margin>Petronius.</margin> In this matter, Petronius also criticizes Pompey:

->You know not, Great One, how to guard<-
->the Roman citadels; seek rather the walls of Epidaurus.<-

How much more bravely in the past, when the Roman **plebeians** <note>the common citizens</note> wanted to migrate to the city of Veii, did the **Optimates** <note>term: Optimates — the "Best Men," a conservative political faction supporting the Senate's authority</note> struggle against it. They declared they would sooner die in the sight of the Roman people than leave Rome to move to Veii.

It uses the historical example of Pompey fleeing Rome during Caesar's civil war to illustrate how abandoning the "head" of the state demoralizes the body politic.</summary>

# On the Secrets of Rule, Chapter 20.

<margin>
The reason for this secret: the absence of the Senators gives wicked citizens the audacity to plot revolutions.
</margin>
Add to this that when the "Fathers" <note>term: Patres (Fathers) — a common term for the members of the Roman Senate</note> are absent, wicked citizens easily plot revolutions. *Livy, in Book 3, regarding Terentillus* <note>Gaius Terentilius Harsa, a Tribune who proposed limiting the power of the Consuls</note>, who took advantage of the timing and plotted because the Republic was vulnerable. *He, it says, thinking that the absence of the Consuls gave an opening for the actions of the Tribunes, spent several days attacking the pride of the Fathers;* And later: *The Fathers feared that they might receive a yoke while the Consuls were absent.* Therefore, in these civil struggles, the patricians—and especially those who hold command—should not easily depart from the City. An example of this is the exile of Caeso, a most fierce defender of the patricians. When the Tribunes, as if victors, *says Livy in Book 3, after the Fathers were struck down by Caeso’s exile, believed the law was almost passed, and as far as the older Fathers were concerned, they had yielded possession of the Republic.*

<margin>
Peace should not be sought from anywhere else but the city of Rome.
</margin>
Furthermore, for this reason, peace was not sought from anywhere else but from the city of Rome: both so that it would not be extorted from an army that had been put at risk, and so that no one outside Rome could make peace at the risk of both the Republic and the senators themselves. This is clear from the Caudine and Numantine treaties <note>historical reference: these were famous military disasters where Roman generals made unauthorized peace deals that the Senate later rejected, arguing that only the central government in Rome had the authority to make peace</note>, which are discussed elsewhere.

That Patricians should not contract marriages with commoners.
</margin>
In this Aristocratic Republic—one in which certain specific and distinguished families hold power—it is fitting to rely on the same means of preservation: that the Patricians do not mix with the blood of commoners <note>original: plebejis</note>. This is partly because this mixing and kinship takes away, or at least diminishes, the nobility and reputation of the Patricians; and partly...

# Arnold Clapmarius, Book III.

...also, because the commoners <note>term: plebeji (plebeians) — the general body of free Roman citizens who were not members of the hereditary nobility (patricians)</note>, motivated by this kinship and being counted in the census, strive to become participants in the Republic. For this reason, it was provided in the Laws of the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman law, dating to c. 450 BCE</note>: *Patricians shall not join in marriage with the plebeians.* This cause led to the greatest dissensions in the Roman Republic. For *these marriages* (the words are Livy’s) <note>Titus Livius, a Roman historian who wrote a monumental history of Rome</note> *bring about a mixing of the clans, and a disturbance of both public and private auspices* <note>term: auspicia (auspices) — religious rites used to interpret the will of the gods before taking public action</note>, *so that nothing remains pure, nothing uncontaminated; once every distinction is removed, no one will know himself or his own kin. For what other power do promiscuous marriages have, except that the couplings of the commoners and the "Fathers" are made common, almost in the manner of wild beasts? Thus, whoever is born would be ignorant of whose blood he is, or what sacred rites he belongs to, being half-plebeian and not even at peace with himself.* These are the words of Livy.

<margin>The reason for this secret.</margin>
This is certainly a "secret" <note>term: arcanum (secret) — here referring to a political tactic or "trick of the trade" used by a ruling class to maintain its grip on power</note> of Aristocratic rule. For once the commoners have obtained these family connections, they also attain everything that belongs to the Patricians, such as magistracies, priesthoods, ranks, military commands, and triumphs. By this method, the Roman Patricians made themselves wonderfully indebted to the plebeians.

<margin>A remedy so that impoverished Patricians do not seek kinships with plebeians.</margin>
But you might say: in this way, some noble families occasionally fall into poverty. Why then do they not receive from the public treasury as much as is needed for the dignity of the family? Augustus <note>The first Roman Emperor</note> used this kind of generosity toward Marcus Hortalus, the grandson of Hortensius, so that (as the imperial writer says) *a most distinguished family would not be extinguished.* Unless this is done, there is a danger that more men like Catiline <note>Lucius Sergius Catilina, a Roman senator who led a famous conspiracy to overthrow the government after losing his status and wealth</note> will burst out into speech, such as that found in Sallust <note>A Roman historian and politician</note>: *After the Republic fell under the legal jurisdiction and power of a few men, Kings and local rulers were always their subjects and taxpayers, etc. All the rest of us—energetic, good, noble and ignoble—have been a mere rabble without influence,*

<meta>catchword: influence [tia],</meta>

<summary>This page argues that forbidding intermarriage between nobles and commoners is a "secret of rule" designed to protect the religious and political monopoly of the aristocracy. It also suggests that the state should financially support impoverished nobles to prevent them from becoming revolutionary leaders like Catiline.</summary>

# Arnold Clapmarius, Book III.

<page-num>159</page-num>
<header>On the Secrets of Rule, Chapter 21.</header>

...[poverty], without authority, subject to those whom, if the Republic were strong, we would be a source of dread.

<margin>That new families should be substituted for those that have become extinct.</margin>
Therefore, it is all the more necessary that as the oldest families die out, new ones are chosen to take their place. This was frequently done in Rome, both to prevent the highest affairs of the Republic from falling into the hands of too few as time passed, and also to ensure the power of the Patricians <note>term: Patricii (Patricians) — the hereditary noble class of ancient Rome</note> themselves was not diminished. If this practice is useful in a principate <note>term: principatus — a system where one person holds primary power but maintains the outward forms of a republic</note>, how much more does it apply to a Republic where specific families hold the leadership. Regarding the Emperor Claudius, Tacitus writes in Book 11 of his *Annals*: *In those same days, Caesar [Claudius] enrolled the oldest families and those with distinguished parents into the number of the Patricians.* Only a few remained of the families that Romulus had called "of the greater clans" <note>term: majorum gentium — the original noble families established at Rome's founding</note> and L. Brutus "of the lesser clans" <note>term: minorum gentium — newer noble families added to the Senate after the expulsion of the kings</note>; even those raised up by the Dictator Caesar under the Cassian Law and by the Prince Augustus under the Saenian Law had been exhausted. Long ago, that famous King Romulus, after the destruction of Alba Longa, chose the Tullii, Servilii, and Quintii for the Senate so that this part of the Republic might also grow. With the same intention, Gaius [Caligula]—as Dio witnesses in Book 59—gave the *laticlavium* <note>term: laticlavium — the "broad stripe" of purple worn on the tunic, which signaled the wearer's rank as a Senator</note> to certain Knights <note>term: Equites (Knights) — the wealthy social class just below the senatorial nobility</note>, which is to say, the hope of senatorial dignity.

### CHAPTER XXII.

->*That no language other than the native tongue should be used.*<-
->*The crime of a foreign speech. The dignity of the German language. Demagogues. Tribunes of the people.*<-

<margin>That the native language should be sacredly observed.</margin>
To preserve the authority of the Republic, it is also of the greatest importance that the native language <note>term: lingua vernacula — the local mother tongue of a specific people</note> be sacredly observed and utilized. Valerius Maximus writes in Book 2, Chapter 2: *One can see how much the ancient magistrates maintained their own majesty and that of the Roman people from this fact: that among other indicators of dignity to be upheld, there was also this—*

<meta>catchword: also</meta>

<summary>This page argues that an aristocracy must replenish its ranks with new families to avoid shrinking into a weak oligarchy and introduces the concept that maintaining a native language is vital for state authority.</summary>

<margin>
The observance of the Latin language among the Romans.
</margin>
They also maintained [the language] with great perseverance, so that they never gave responses to the Greeks except in Latin. Indeed, even when the Greeks’ own fluency—in which they are very strong—was stripped away, they were forced to speak through an interpreter. This was done not only in our city <note>Rome</note>, but even in Greece and Asia, so that the honor of the Latin voice would be spread more venerable among all nations. Nor did the Romans lack a love for learning, but they believed that in every matter the *pallium* <note>term: pallium — a Greek-style cloak associated with scholars and philosophers</note> ought to be subject to the *toga* <note>term: toga — the characteristic garment of Roman citizens, symbolizing civic and political authority</note>: judging it unworthy for the weight and authority of the empire to be sacrificed to the allurements and sweetness of literature. This is what he says. And Phavorinus <note>A 2nd-century philosopher and advisor to Emperor Hadrian</note> used to say that an Emperor could grant Roman citizenship to Barbarians, but he could not grant it to Barbarian words and names; *Since these [words] receive their force and property from the natural usage of the citizens, which, as stated in Law 2 of the Digest regarding usage, cannot be changed by the authority of the Senate.* <note>original: "Quippe quae à naturali civium usu, qui ut est in l. 2. D. de usu. autoritate Senatus immutari nequit, vim atque proprietatem accipiunt."</note> Regarding this matter, Alexander the Great accused Philotas <note>A Macedonian general executed by Alexander for conspiracy</note> while he stood on trial for using a foreign tongue. *Do you not see that Philotas is seized even by a hatred of his native speech? He alone is disgusted to speak it: but let him speak however he pleases, provided you remember that he is equally distant from our customs and our language.* <note>original: "Ecquid videtis odio etiam sermonis patrii Philotam teneri? Solus quippe fastidit eum dicere: sed dicat sane utcunque cordi est: dum memineritis aeque illum à nostro more atque sermone abhorrere."</note> In the same 
<margin>
The Turkish language among the Turks.
</margin>
way, the Turkish Emperors <note>The Sultans of the Ottoman Empire</note> display the majesty of their rule, so that they will not listen to the ambassadors of foreign Princes, nor respond to them, in any language other than their own. To this point also belongs 
<margin>
The German language in the Imperial Chamber.
</margin>
the constitution of the Empire <note>The Holy Roman Empire</note>, which mandates that lawsuits in the Chamber <note>term: Camera Imperii — the Reichskammergericht, the highest judicial body of the Holy Roman Empire</note> may not be pleaded in any language other than German. Of this language—whatever slanders Arias Montanus <note>Benito Arias Montano (1527–1598), a Spanish scholar and polyglot</note> may throw—the majesty is so great, and the dignity so high, that it can compete with almost all others, not only in elegance, but also in the refined phrasing of its words and the grand sweep and structure of its sentences.

<margin>That talkative and maliciously eloquent men should not creep into the Republic.</margin>
Therefore, one must take greater care that talkative and maliciously eloquent men do not creep into the Republic. Indeed, like war-trumpets <note>original: "litui"</note>, they rouse and inflame the minds of the common people against the patricians <note>the ruling aristocratic class</note>. Such were formerly the Demagogues <note>term: Demagogi — popular leaders in Athens who often swayed the crowds through emotion rather than reason</note> among the Athenians, and the Tribunes of the Plebs <note>officials elected to protect the interests of the commoners</note> among the Romans. Today, certain men from the sacred order <note>the clergy</note>—to the shame of our religion—occupy their place, such as that man Rokycana <note>Jan Rokycana (c. 1396–1471), a Hussite archbishop and political leader in Bohemia</note>, by whose sermons and drunken rants George of Kunštát and Poděbrady <note>King of Bohemia (r. 1458–1471)</note> invaded the Kingdom of Bohemia. It is all the more praiseworthy that some states suppress the loquacity and ambition of such men to such an extent that they are permitted to speak publicly about almost nothing else except the corruption of morals and the salvation of souls.

### CHAPTER XXIV.

->*Certain other ways of obtaining fame and reputation, and shared counsels. The stupendous greatness of soul of the Romans; Outward physical majesty; A great spirit in adverse circumstances.*<-

---

<margin>A primary secret: the zeal for protecting fame and reputation. It is shown that the Romans excelled above other nations in this. Shown by examples of the Senate, Caesar, and Germanicus.</margin>
Indeed, that zeal for fame and reputation—as they call it—is a most powerful force in preserving any Republic. In this matter, the Romans were more skilled than all other nations and most worthy of our admiration. For example, consider the decree passed by the Roman Senate that the eight thousand captives who survived the disaster at Cannae <note>A catastrophic defeat by Hannibal in 216 BC where the Romans refused to ransom their own captured soldiers to maintain a standard of "victory or death"</note> should not be ransomed at any price. Of the same character is that saying of Caesar: *it is not the custom of the Roman people to accept any terms from an armed man.* <note>original: "non esse consuetudinem populi Romani, ullam accipere ab homine armato conditionem"</note> Likewise, there is that voice of a great spirit: *that crossing the Rhine by boat was consistent with neither his own dignity nor that of the Roman people.* <note>Refers to Julius Caesar’s decision to build a massive bridge across the Rhine in 55 BC simply to prove Roman engineering and resolve to the Germanic tribes</note> Therefore, he built a bridge. Just as the greatness of soul of the Romans in accepting gifts frequently threw neighboring nations into a stupor: such as the case of Germanicus <note>A popular Roman general and nephew of Emperor Tiberius</note>, who, while the Gauls, Italians, and Spaniards were offering weapons, horses, and gold, praised their zeal, but took only the weapons and horses for the war, while assisting the soldiers with his own money.

<margin>In which deed he vividly expressed the "greatness of soul" of the Philosopher.</margin>
By this deed, he vividly expressed that "magnanimity" <note>Greatness of soul; a key virtue in classical ethics</note> of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>. First, he took the horses and weapons, but rejected the gold. *For it is characteristic of the magnanimous man,* says Aristotle in the *Ethics*, Book 4, Chapter 3, *to take things that are not so much useful and profitable as they are excellent, elegant, and worthy of a Commander.* Clearly, horses and weapons were fitting for a Commander, while gold was for someone of the common people. Next, because he praised their zeal and accepted the gifts almost as if with a sense of reserve <note>original: "pudore"; here meaning a noble restraint or modesty</note>. This is also a trait of a magnanimous man, according to Aristot-

<margin>The Prince is armed by the majesty of his physical appearance.</margin>
And indeed, sometimes the august appearance and majesty of the body itself arms the Prince; by which many have been deterred and stunned, and have even abstained from the slaughter they had intended. Just as it has been handed down to memory regarding Augustus. When a certain soldier turned his face away from him and was asked by Augustus why he did so, he replied: *Because, Caesar, I cannot bear the lightning of your eyes.* <note>original: "Quia Cæsar, fulmen tuorum oculorum ferre non possum."</note> Thus, nothing preserves the safety of Princes more, and nothing more quickly crushes the plots of conspirators, than a reputation and majesty kept intact and "under roof." <note>The Latin "sarta tecta" is a legal metaphor meaning "well-repaired" or "in good order."</note> As Tacitus prudently notes in the 4th book of his *Annals*: *For the rest of mortals, their plans consist in what they judge to be to their advantage; the lot of Princes is different, for whom the highest affairs must be directed toward their reputation.* <note>original: "Cæteris mortalium in eo stare consilia, quid sibi conducere arbitrentur: Principum diversam esse sortem, quibus præcipua rerum ad famam dirigenda."</note>

<margin>An example of greatness of soul in a Leader of the Germans.</margin>
Such greatness also shone in that leader and Prince of the ancient Germans who, having been routed by Catualda, fled to the Romans and wrote to Tiberius: *not as a fugitive or a suppliant, but from the memory of my former fortune.* <note>original: "non ut profugus aut supplex, sed ex memoria veteris fortunæ." Refers to Maroboduus, King of the Marcomanni, who maintained his dignity even in exile.</note> For in ruined circumstances, a great spirit often devises its own fortune and borrows from audacity.

<margin>Regarding Conon.</margin>
There was the same gravity in Conon <note>An Athenian general during the Peloponnesian and Corinthian Wars</note>, who refused to "adore" <note>perform ritual prostration</note> the King to whom he had been sent as an envoy. This was what they called <term>προσκυνεῖν</term> <note>Proskynesis: The Persian custom of bowing or prostrating before a superior, which Greeks viewed as degrading and fit only for gods.</note> according to the testimony of Aemilius Probus <note>Often identified with the biographer Cornelius Nepos</note>; he refused lest he burn a mark of shame upon his own city, which had previously been accustomed to command other nations.

<margin>Sluggishness of mind opens the Prince to attack.</margin>
Truly, that sluggishness and lethargy of the mind opens the side of Princes to attack, such as the stupor that existed in the Emperor Vitellius when his Empire was in peril. Of whom Tacitus says in the 3rd book of his *Histories*: *Such sluggishness...* <note>Vitellius was famously criticized for his gluttony and indecision during the civil wars of 69 AD.</note>

### CHAPTER XXV.

### The strongest defenses of rule: piety and divine worship; mercy; the absence of injury; and mild governance. The force of Fate in the downfall of Princes and Republics.

<margin>
The mercy and piety of those who rule surpass all preceding secret counsels.
</margin>
Furthermore, the mercy of those who rule, along with piety and divine worship, surpasses all these <term>arcana</term> <note>The "secrets" or hidden strategies of statecraft that the author has been cataloging.</note>, as stated in an old prophecy of C. Martius <note>Gnaeus Marcius, a legendary Roman seer whose prophecies were consulted by the Senate</note>, the ancient seer:
> If you do these things, you will always rightly rejoice,
> and thus your Republic will become better.
> For that God will strike down your enemies to a man,
> who now peacefully feed upon your fields and lands.
<note>original: "Hac si faxitis, recte gaudebitis semper... Nam is Dius vestros perduelles stinguet ad unum..."</note>

For where citizens are burdened too heavily by taxes and other payments, it is inevitable that conspiracies against the life of the Prince will be formed. This is what Galba <note>The Roman Emperor Servius Sulpicius Galba</note> advised Piso: *Consider,* he said, *what you either did not want or did want under another Prince.* <note>original: "Cogita, inquit, quid aut nolueris sub alio Principe, aut volueris." A reminder that a ruler should treat subjects as he himself would wish to be treated.</note> And the famous Maecenas <note>A powerful advisor to the first Roman Emperor, Augustus</note>, as recorded in Dio <note>The historian Cassius Dio</note>, says: *In no matter will you slip, if you freely do those very things which you would want another to do if you were subject to his command.* <note>original: "Nulla in re laberis, si ea ipsa libenter feceris, quæ velles alium facere, si ejus imperio subjectus esses."</note> 

<margin>
Likewise, no one should be recklessly harmed.
</margin>
Therefore, no one should be recklessly harmed; instead, the <term>auspicium</term> <note>A Roman term for the formal beginning or "omened start" of an undertaking.</note> of rule ought to begin with mercy, as Livia <note>Livia Drusilla, the influential wife of Augustus</note> rightly advised Augustus. In which matter, it is prudent—

->The inauguration of rule must be made from mercy.<-

# ARNOLD CLAPMAR

### BOOK FOUR.
### CHAPTER I.

<margin>Which concerns the Right of Sovereignty <note>original: "Iure dominationis"</note>.</margin>
*The difference between public and private law. In the former, force and the welfare of the people hold more sway than equity. Human law. The law of war. Commercial dealings in war. The supreme law of military jurisdiction is money. How other laws yield to the Right of Sovereignty.*

<margin>
Public laws should not be decided indiscriminately from private law. The difference between the two types of law.
</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing floral and leaf motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>
Those who weigh and decide public affairs—which concern kingdoms and peoples—indiscriminately based on civil and private law, seem to me to act quite wrongly; and this for two reasons in particular. The first of these is the difference and the dignity of the matter itself. The safety of one or two individuals depends on private cases; but on public cases depends the safety of the people, of Republics, and indeed of several kingdoms. In comparison to public business, private matters are of minimal consideration; for, as a most serious writer <note>Likely referring to the Roman historian Sallust or Tacitus, who often lamented how private interests interfered with the state.</note> testifies, private affairs have always hindered and will continue to hinder public business. Hence the Poet <note>Horace, a Roman lyric poet.</note> wrote in *The Art of Poetry*:

> This was wisdom in times past,
> To separate public things from private, and sacred from profane.
> <note>original: "Fuit haec sapientia quondam, / Publica privatis secernere, sacra profanis."</note>

I do not diminish the zeal of those who [write] about the law of war, treaties, embassies, the magistrate, and supreme power <term>imperium</term> <note>The legal authority to command, particularly in a military or judicial capacity.</note>, not only from histories...

> But not so that the gentle should combine with the savage; not so that
> Serpents should be paired with birds, or lambs with tigers.
<note>original: "Scimus & hanc veniam, (canit Poeta) petimusque, damusque vicissim: Sed non ut placidis coëant immitia; non ut Serpentes avibus geminentur, tigribus agni." These lines are from Horace's *Art of Poetry*. The author uses them to argue that while some flexibility is allowed in law, one cannot unnaturally mix the rules of private life with the harsh necessities of ruling a state.</note>

<margin>That in public affairs little account is taken of private law.</margin>
Furthermore, in public matters, small—indeed, almost no—account is taken of private law. This is because these matters are ruled by privileges, treaties, the force of arms, soldiers, and money. Add to this the obscurity of private matters, which, as Cicero testifies in the second book *On the Orator* <note>original: "2. de Orator."</note>, are often much more obscure than public ones. Likewise, what Ulpian <note>A prominent Roman jurist.</note> calls "judicial subtlety" <note>original: "judicialis illa subtilitas"</note> is least applicable to public business.

<margin>And in many ways, for the sake of the kingdom, civil law is set aside.</margin>
Hence it has happened that for the sake of the kingdom <note>original: "regni caußá"</note>, civil law has been set aside in many ways, according to that maxim: **Let the welfare of the people be the supreme law.** <note>original: "salus populi summa lex esto." A fundamental principle of Roman law stating that the safety of the state overrides individual legal rights.</note> Nor is this without reason or example. For since neither the law of nature, nor the law of nations—or as Tacitus calls it, "human law"—nor civil law could be adapted to all times due to their narrowness, it follows that when wars broke out, civil law was set aside;

<margin>For what reason.</margin>
this was done both because of the pride and stubbornness of the citizens, and also because of the ferocity of the soldiers. Thus, a new Law was established, which is called the **law of war**. <note>original: "Ius belli"</note>

<margin>The law of war.</margin>
Just as Camillus says in the fifth book of Livy: "There are laws of peace, just as there are laws of war, and we have learned to wage them no less justly than bravely." <note>original: "Sunt, inquit, pacis, ita & belli jura, justéque ea non minus, quam fortiter gerere didicimus."</note> Tacitus writes in the third book of the *Histories*: "The commercial dealings of war were cut off by the murder of Sabinus." And the Poet <note>Likely the Roman poet Claudian.</note> says:

> But at least you should have killed the captive by the law of war.
<note>original: "At belli saltem captivam lege necasses."</note>

Hence Curtius says in the ninth book of his *History of Alexander*: "To such an extent does war change even the laws of nature into their opposite." For this reason, military laws are more severe than those of civilians. <note>original: "paganorum." In the legal language of the time, *paganus* referred to a private citizen or "civilian" as opposed to a soldier.</note>

<meta>catchword: l. 5. §.</meta>

It distinguishes between the "judicial subtlety" of private law and the practical, often harsh necessities of public governance during times of conflict.</summary>

<page-num>170</page-num>

<header>Arnold Clapmarius, Book IV.</header>

<margin>*The military laws regarding civilians are harsh.*</margin>
<note>original: "Iura militaria paganorũ atrocia." In Roman legal contexts, "pagani" refers to civilians or non-soldiers, rather than "pagans" in the religious sense.</note> 
See the Digest <note>A massive collection of Roman legal opinions compiled under Emperor Justinian.</note>, Book 49, Title 16, Law 5, Section 1: "On Military Affairs." During such times, the calamity of war very often introduces things that are unjust, as Justinian says in the Code <note>The "Codex Justinianus," a collection of imperial laws.</note>, in the single law under the title "On the removal of lapses." Indeed, military commanders often look not so much for what is right and fair in their inquiries as they do at the greatness of the sums of money—which, as *Mucianus* <note>A Roman general and ally of Emperor Vespasian.</note> used to say, are the sinews of war <note>original: "bellorum nervi."</note>. These practices, however, are abolished once peace is restored, as noted in the aforementioned law in the Code. And so, those things are practiced which are contrary to civil law; and they occur, as *Tacitus* says in the first book of the *Annals*, by way of a good precedent rather than by a granted right.

<margin>*Examples in civil law of things introduced against reason.*</margin>
There are many examples of this within civil law itself, as the commentators testify regarding Law 1 of the Digest "On the Office of the Proconsul." *Julian* <note>Salvius Julianus, a prominent Roman jurist.</note> also says in Law 51 of the Digest "On the Aquilian Law": *Many things have been accepted into civil law against the logic of argument, for the sake of the common good, and this can be proven by countless instances.* Seneca also maintains in his *Letters* that the formal responses of legal experts hold weight even if a reason is not provided. As *Ulpian* <note>Another famous Roman jurist.</note> says: "although this is extremely hard, yet the law is so written." <note>original: "id perquam durum est, tamen lex scripta est." This is a famous legal maxim (Digest 40.9.12.1) emphasizing that the written law must be followed even if it produces a harsh result in a specific case.</note>

<margin>*The diversity of laws and their origins.*</margin>
Just as, therefore, the law of nature is corrected by the law of nations, the law of nations by military law, military law by the law of embassy, and the law of embassy by civil law:

<margin>*All laws yield to the law of sovereignty.*</margin>
so this civil law is in turn corrected, and allows a bridle <note>original: "frænum."</note> to be placed upon it, by that law which I call the Law of the Realm or of Sovereignty <note>original: "jure, quod appello Regni sive dominationis." This is Clapmarius’s central thesis: that there is a "higher" law used by rulers that supersedes ordinary civil law.</note>. *Cicero* describes the nature of this when he says in his speech *In Defense of Rabirius Posthumus*: *These are the commands of Kings: take heed and obey the word; if you complain beyond what is asked, take note; and those threats: "If I find you here by the second light of day, you shall die."*

It cites Roman jurists and authors like Tacitus and Cicero to justify the idea that legal reason must sometimes yield to the harsh realities of power and state survival.</summary>

<header>On the Right of Sovereignty, Chapter 2.</header>

## C H A P T E R  II.

*The Right of Sovereignty is named in four ways: The force of power, the force of the kingdom, the force of the Empire, and the force of the Prince. Also called the correction of legal justice <note>original Greek: ἐπανόρθωμα νομίμου δικαίου</note>, reason of state <note>original Italian: ragion di stato</note>, royal exceptions, extraordinary rights, dispensations, and the definition of this right. The care of the public good before God and men. The sayings of great heroes.*

---

<margin>The Right of Sovereignty is called by various names.</margin>
<margin>By the Latins.</margin>
<margin>By Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>By the Italians.</margin>
<margin>By legal experts.</margin>
This Right of Sovereignty is known by many names. Cicero, in his *Letter to his brother Quintus*, calls it *the force of power* <note>original: "vim potestatis"</note>. He says, *“So that, with the Empire and the force of power and the rods of office <note>The "fasces," bundles of rods symbolizing a Roman magistrate's power.</note> set aside, you may join the tax-collectors with the Greeks through grace and authority.”* Curtius <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, a Roman historian.</note> sometimes calls it *the Right of the kingdom* <note>original: "Ius regni"</note>. Attius <note>A Roman tragic poet.</note> calls it *the force of the Empire* <note>original: "vim Imperii"</note>: *“Nor,”* he says, *“shall the wild hearts of men grow cold, until they have thoroughly felt the force of the Empire.”* Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian known for his analysis of power.</note> occasionally calls it *the force of the Prince* <note>original: "vim Principis"</note>, while others call it simply that which is permitted by the right of the kingdom. Aristotle calls it *political justice* <note>original Greek: δίκαιον πολιτικόν</note>; also *dynastic power* <note>original Greek: δυναςευτικῶ</note> in the second book of his *Politics*, chapter 8. In the fifth book of the *Politics*, he calls it the *correction of legal justice* <note>original Greek: ἐπανόρθωμα νομίμου δικαίου</note>, and elsewhere *absolute monarchy* <note>original Greek: παμβασιλείαν</note>. The Italians call it *the reason of dominion, of lordship, of kingdom, or of Empire* <note>original: "Ragione di dominio, di Signoria, di regno, d' Imperio"</note>; and most elegantly of all, *reason of state* <note>original Italian: "ragionamento di stato." This is the famous concept that the state's survival justifies actions that would otherwise be illegal or immoral.</note>. Legal experts <note>term: jurisconsults</note> call it now *royal exceptions*, now *restrictions*, now *extraordinary rights* <note>original: "jura exorbitantia"</note>—so called because they deviate from the "orbit," that is, the broad and common path of law—now *dispensations*, now a *limiting disposition*, and now *limiting laws*; that is, those things which depart from the common rules of Law and derogate from the statutes. To Cicero, "to limit" means this, as he writes in his *Letter to Appius Pulcher*: *“The following year will limit something from your generous and beneficial nature.”*

<margin>No one except the Prince is allowed to decide regarding this right.</margin>
Likewise, these are Rights regarding which no one, except the Prince <note>In this context, "Prince" refers generally to any sovereign ruler or head of state.</note>, is permitted to decide. For such a right is of a kind than which nothing is more lofty or more august in this human society...

It highlights how this supreme power, though called by many names, represents the ruler's authority to bypass common laws for the sake of the state.</summary>

...can be conceived in society, according to that law which is the Prince of all others, and which is called the command of the immortal God. For the earthly Prince is, as it were, a deputy and a beneficiary of this divine Ruler. Hence Horace, in Book 1, *Ode* 1:

> Dreaded kings rule over their own flocks, 
> But over the kings themselves is the empire of Jove. <note>original: "Regum timendorum in proprios greges, / Reges in ipsos imperium est Iovis." Jove or Jupiter refers to the supreme deity.</note>

And Gunther says in Book 6:

> ->This power looks upon no head above its own,<-
> ->Except for the King of the heavens.<- <note>original: "Nullum caput ista super / Aspicit, excepto cælorum rege, potestas." From the *Ligurinus*, an epic poem by Gunther of Pairis.</note>

---

<margin>The Right of Sovereignty is defined.</margin>
Therefore, I define it thus: it is a certain supreme right or privilege, introduced for the public good against common or ordinary law; yet it is not alien to divine law; and it is a right that acts as a kind of "legitimate tyranny" <note>This term suggests a power that is absolute like a tyranny but used for legal and moral ends.</note>. Or, as Alciatus <note>Andrea Alciato (1492–1550), a famous Italian jurist who founded the school of legal humanism.</note> defines it, it is a certain relaxation or correction of common law.

<margin>The definition is explained.</margin>
It can be called a "privilege" because, although that term usually refers to private individuals, it can be applied here. For just as privileges in civil law are corrections of the law regarding the benefit of one or another person, so the Rights of Sovereignty are corrections of the laws

<margin>Specifically why it is stated that this right was introduced for the public good.</margin>
regarding the safety and benefit of the many; that is, of both the Prince and the citizens. I add "for the sake of the public good" <note>original: "bono publico"</note> because a sacred and ancient account of this must be maintained; to this principle, all laws and even the Prince himself must yield. Just as the Emperor Otto <note>The Roman Emperor Otho, who committed suicide in 69 AD to prevent further civil war.</note> chose death rather than suffer so many Roman youths and so many excellent armies to be laid low again and torn from the Republic, as Tacitus reports. He certainly did not want, as Suetonius <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, a Roman historian who wrote *The Twelve Caesars*.</note> writes, to assert his sovereignty at such great risk to things and men. This is also the reason given for why King Charles <note>Likely referring to Charles of Anjou or a similar medieval monarch.</note> was defeated in battle by Montfort <note>Simon de Montfort, a leader in the Baron's War or the Albigensian Crusade.</note>; (which most people, according to Froissart <note>Jean Froissart, a major medieval chronicler of the Hundred Years' War.</note>, believed happened because of a...

<meta>catchword: pact (original: pacto)</meta>

He illustrates this self-sacrificing duty of the Prince through the examples of Emperor Otto and historical figures who prioritized the state over their own power.</summary>

...made by a pact,) because a war could not have been ended by any other means. But why should I deal only with mortals? Look, if you please, at the actions and counsels of the highest and immortal God; <margin>How one may depart from private law for this reason is shown from sacred matters.</margin> are they not the same? What? Did He not give His only and most innocent Son to death for the sake of the public good—that is, for the salvation of the human race—according to that saying of Caiaphas in John, chapter 8 <note>Though the text cites Chapter 8, this famous phrase is found in John 11:50 and 18:14: "It is expedient that one man should die for the people."</note>: *It is expedient for one man to die for the people*. Concerning this example, however, and others of that kind, because they are more mystical <note>original: <term>μυστικώτερα</term> (mystikōtera). This refers to things that are hidden, sacred, or beyond ordinary understanding.</note> by right and beyond human comprehension, they must be considered reverently and soberly.

<margin>The saying of a great hero is noted.</margin>
Just as with that saying of Moses: *Rather erase me from the book of life, and forgive the people their sin*. Which voice, in this our age, a most warlike and incomparable King <note>Likely a reference to Henry IV of France (1553–1610), who was famous for his pragmatism and devotion to the state's survival.</note> is said to have uttered: that for the salvation of the people, he would even go to the underworld. A great utterance, immortal gods! Neither easily measured by our own character, nor easily imitated. Rightly says Nonius Pedo <note>A Roman poet of the Augustan age.</note>:

> *The same things do not befit the common people and the heights of affairs.* <note>original: "Non eadem, vulgusq, decent, & culmina rerum." This suggests that leaders must follow a different moral or legal code than ordinary citizens.</note>

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>The rights of dominion differ from the secrets of state.</margin>
-> *In what way the rights of dominion differ from the secrets of state. The separation of honor and utility. What difference there is between the right of dominion and the right of command. Law placed in the hand; Laws by the law of the hand <note>original: <term>ἐν χειρὸς νόμῳ</term> (en cheiros nomō). A Greek idiom referring to power exercised by force or direct action.</note>; to govern with the hand; to act with the hand; to extend with the hand; to hand over the provinces <note>original: <term>ἐγχειρίζειν τὰς ἐπαρχίας</term> (encheirizein tas eparchias).</note>.* <-

Most people refer these rights of dominion so much to the "secrets of republics" <note>The hidden strategies of statecraft, often called *arcana imperii*.</note> that they confuse them with the "secrets of state." While they judge correctly in the first part, they wander into error in the second. Truly, these rights of dominion are hidden counsels and the privileges for the safety of Princes...

...and for the preservation of public affairs; yet these are not what we have called the secrets of state <term>arcana dominationis</term>. <margin>Most of these things are against common law, not "secrets."</margin> *First*, for the rights of sovereignty <term>jura Dominationis</term> are those which are permitted by the law of the realm; many of these are contrary to common law and present a certain appearance of inequity and injustice—such as punishing one who has not been condemned, or invading the kingdoms of others. However, they are done for the interest and safety of the Prince and the state. And these things—namely, honor and the safety of the state—are sometimes separated, even against the will of any good man in the Republic. As in that passage of Tacitus concerning the Emperor Galba: 
> *There was added a saying of Galba’s, honorable for the state but dangerous for himself: that he chose his soldiers, he did not buy them.* <note>original: "accessit Galbæ vox, pro Republ. honesta, ipsi anceps; legi à se militem, non emi." From Tacitus, *Histories* 1.5. Galba was famously frugal and refused to pay the bribes/bonuses to the soldiers that had become customary, leading to his downfall.</note>

For in this matter, it is not so much the law as public utility <term>utilitas publica</term> that is considered. Concerning which Livy says in Book 3: 
> *Neither did it set a limit for each man's own [right], but rather by the hope of strength; and whatever you intended had to be held by force.* <note>original: "Neque suum cuiq; ejus modum faciebat, sed virium spe; & manu obtinendum erat, quod intenderes." From Livy, *History of Rome* 3.39, describing the lawless behavior of the Decemvirs.</note>

But the secrets of state <term>arcana dominationis</term> are not done against common law; and even if they were, they do not have this appearance of injustice. Second, the secrets of state are properly and for the most part concerned with the actions of others; such as that no one is allowed to address the guards <note>original: <term>praetorianos</term> (the Praetorian Guard)</note> publicly, or to enter a fortified castle. <margin>The rights of sovereignty concern the actions of the Prince. The secrets of state concern the actions of the citizens.</margin> Indeed, the rights of sovereignty concern the actions of the Prince. These are the things permitted to the Prince and those who hold leadership in the state; whereas the secrets of state are those things not permitted to others. For example, it is a secret of state that no Senator or illustrious man should grow in too much favor with the soldiers; it is a right of sovereignty to break that same man and "clip his wings," lest he cause any disturbance. Indeed, I have no doubt that these things ought to be distinguished and subtly discerned in this way.

<header>Concerning the Rights of Sovereignty, Chapter 3.</header>

<margin>
Whether the rights of sovereignty are included under the right of empire, and the difference between the two.
</margin>

...of sovereignty <term>dominationis</term> are included under the right, which is called, of Empire <term>jus Imperii</term>. This is indeed not an absurd view; however, they are included in such a way that the right of sovereignty is born and proceeds from the right of empire. For we have said that the right of Empire, or Majesty <term>Majestas</term>, consists primarily in two things: both that the Prince be free from the laws <note>original: "legibus solutus." A fundamental legal concept in early modern political thought, suggesting the ruler is not bound by civil laws but remains under divine and natural law.</note>, and that he impose laws on others. Thus, this right of sovereignty is a certain restriction of those laws from which he is free, and a limitation of them: for he is not free from all laws. Next, the right of Empire contains nothing unjust, but is joined with every highest form of equity. Furthermore, the use of the right of Empire is properly in a peaceful and tranquil Republic; but truly the right of sovereignty is for a violent and seditious one, in which the right is placed in the hand—"by the law of the hand" <note>original Greek: τῇ ἐν χειρὸς νόμῳ (*tē en cheiros nomō*). This refers to the idea of "might makes right" or the necessity of using force when legal systems fail.</note>—as the Greeks say. 

Hence Pomponius says "to govern all things by hand." And Tacitus in his *Life of Agricola* "to act by hand," and Livy "to hold out by hand"; the Greeks elegantly say "to place the provinces into the hands" <note>original Greek: ἐγχειρίζειν τὰς ἐπαρχίας (*encheirizein tas eparchias*)</note>. During such times, many things are done—and ought to be done—contrary to Common Law <term>jus commune</term>, as Aristotle himself testifies in his *Politics*. Hence Livy writes in Book 2: "Internal discord and external war brought it about that there was a need for this magistracy" <note>Livy is referring to the creation of the office of Dictator in the Roman Republic, an emergency role granted absolute power for a short term.</note>, not to mention now that the rights of Empire are general, while the rights of sovereignty are special and must be considered in context for the specific form of the Republic. Indeed, it pleases me to distinguish all these things in this way, lest it be like a "disorderly mob" <note>original Greek: ἄτροπος ὄχλος (*atropos ochlos*). He uses this metaphor to describe a confused heap of legal concepts that lack proper categorization.</note> of ideas.

## CHAPTER IV.

->*Why these rights of sovereignty are so heavily criticized, and whether deservedly? Injustice is compensated by the public good; and the limits or boundaries of this Law are set by religion and faith: likewise, how many kinds of these rights there are.*<-

---

<margin>
Whether the rights of sovereignty are to be condemned. They are defended out of necessity because most Republics are turbulent.
</margin>

Therefore, those who so greatly detest and condemn these rights are acting in vain and are overly superstitious. Nicephorus says truly and correctly:
> *Those who place all their thoughts in the knowledge of God alone, for them the mountains and caves are suitable; but he who, along with virtue and piety, has also learned the civil way of life and gained knowledge of various matters, he is truly fit to lead the people toward what is best.* <note>original Latin translation of Nicephorus Gregoras, a 14th-century Byzantine historian and philosopher.</note>

And first of all, the world is so arranged that you will very rarely—indeed, never—find any Platonic Republic <term>Politia Platonica</term> <note>A reference to the idealized, perfect state described in Plato's *Republic*. Clapmarius argues that rulers cannot act as if they live in a perfect world.</note>; on the contrary, most states are turbulent, or at least less than orderly, in which trying to act exactly and perfectly in every detail is the height of madness. Cato, a wise and serious man as he was, nevertheless defended the treasury <term>aerarium</term> and the taxes <term>vectigalia</term> too stubbornly. By opposing almost all the tax-collectors <note>original: "publicanis." These were private contractors who collected taxes for Rome, often through predatory means.</note>, he alienated the Knights <term>Equites</term> from the Senate, and among many allies, he made the Republic discordant—indeed, "two-headed." <note>original: "bicipitem Rempublicam." This refers to the political rift Cato the Younger caused between the senatorial class and the wealthy equestrian class, which weakened the state.</note> Cicero himself complains of this many times. Likewise, Pompey—according to Tacitus—having been made censor, while he investigated the morals of the common people too severely and introduced remedies more heavy than the crimes themselves, lost by arms that which he defended by arms. Rather, diseases of this kind must be treated for the sake of the Republic's health. Tacitus notes this beautifully regarding the Emperor Galba, who, while he strove to be too observant of honor—and [ruined] himself...

<meta>The text cuts off here, with the catchword "Rem-" suggesting the next page continues with "Rempublicam" (the Republic).</meta>

<summary>Clapmarius argues that "Rights of Sovereignty" are necessary tools for a ruler because real-world states are messy and turbulent, unlike Plato's ideal Republic. He uses Roman historical figures like Cato and Pompey to show how rigid adherence to morality can sometimes damage the state more than the vices they seek to cure.</summary>

...greatly afflicted the Republic: and so he adds that other matters were not according to this form.

<margin>From utility, namely that the inequity of this right is compensated by the public good.</margin>
Next, that appearance of inequity, which those foolish critics sniff out but are unable to swallow or digest, is in reality not inequity at all—and even if it were, it is compensated by the public good. Why is it that these critics pursue only the inequities and disadvantages of laws, while ignoring the underlying right and utility? To me, indeed, it shall be an eternal law that a rule is just if its inequities are outweighed by its utility. And there is that golden—not to say divine—saying of Cornelius Tacitus <note>original: "Habet aliquid ex iniquo omne magnum exemplum, quod contra singulos utilitate publica rependitur."</note>:
> *Every great precedent has some element of injustice in it, which is repaid against individuals for the sake of the public utility.*

<margin>Consider that all laws are good which are beneficial in the sum total.</margin>
And that saying of Plutarch:
> *You may sometimes depart from Justice in small matters if you wish to keep it safe in great ones.*

And that of the Emperor Nerva:
> *It is equally bad to have a Prince under whom everything is permitted, as one under whom nothing is.*

And the words of Cato:
> *No law is sufficiently convenient; the only question is whether it benefits the greater part and serves the whole.*

<margin>That these rights do not contradict divine law.</margin>
Finally, these rights do not in the least contradict divine law; otherwise, they would not be rights <term>jura</term> at all, but outrages <term>flagitia</term>. For just as the laws of war, the laws of the treasury <term>fiscus</term>, and the laws of the Republic’s embassies have their own fixed boundaries—beyond which, if they wander, they are no longer rights but the height of injustice—so too it is here. For example, if the treasury were to seize everything, if violence were done to nature, or if traps were laid under the guise of an embassy or the Republic, the law of nations and divine law would be violated. In the same way, the Rights of Sovereignty <term>Iura dominationis</term> have their own certain limits. If they rush beyond these bounds and fly into the territory and <margin>But let them have their certain limits.</margin> possession of vices, they are no longer rights, but crimes—or, as Tacitus calls them, the outrages of sovereignty. Such a case, among others, is that described by Ammianus Marcellinus in Book 14:
> *Whatever satisfied Caesar’s implacability was weighed as if it were right and law.*

<summary>Clapmarius argues that minor injustices in the law are justified by their benefit to the public good and identifies the "Rights of Sovereignty" as legitimate only when they remain within the bounds of divine law and moral limits.</summary>

### CHAPTER V.

### The Rights of Royal Sovereignty: what they are and of what kind. The Opening and the Right of Asylums.

<margin>
The rights of royal sovereignty are noted. To open asylums.
</margin>
First, then, the rights of royal sovereignty are those actions permitted to a Prince contrary to ordinary law, both for the sake of preserving and increasing the Commonwealth, and for his own personal security.

<margin>
Three types of men were formerly accustomed to flee to these.
</margin>
In reviewing these, the first that presents itself to me is the opening of Asylums <term>Asylum: a sacred place of refuge where fugitives or debtors were immune from seizure</term>, in which, as Plutarch reports, men of all ranks were received; neither was the slave returned to his master, nor the debtor to his creditors, nor the criminal to the magistrates. For these three types of men used to flee to Asylums. This is also noted by Tacitus in the 3rd book of the *Annals*: *The temples were being filled with the worst of slaves; with their help, those burdened by debt were received against their creditors, and those suspected of capital crimes were sheltered.* <note>original: "Complebantur templa pessimis servitiorum, eorum subsidio obarati adversum creditores, suspectique capitalium criminum receptabantur."</note> In this matter, Romulus <note>The legendary founder of Rome</note> is severely criticized. # On the Law of Sovereignty, Chapter 8.

The historian <note>Tacitus, the Roman senator and historian whose *Annals* are the primary source for this period.</note> especially praises this in Agrippina: that she brought with her the grandson of Germanicus <note>This refers to the future Emperor Nero, whom Agrippina brought into the household of Claudius.</note>, a youth altogether worthy of imperial fortune, of noble stock and from the Claudian family, who might unite their descendants; this was done lest a woman of proven fertility carry the unsullied glory of the Caesars into another house. Therefore, her reasoning prevailed. But you will ask, by what right? Nay, by the very best right—that is, by this law of kingship, or rather, the **law of sovereignty**. <margin>Hence the marriage of Emperor Claudius to his brother’s daughter.</margin> For first, Agrippina was from the Augustan house; if she were to marry anyone else, there was a danger that her husband might plot against the Empire of Claudius, relying on this marriage to the Emperor’s niece. For a woman is, as Pliny says in his *Letters*, *sometimes a plague to the human race*. <note>original: "interdum pestis generis humani"</note> For this very reason, Rufus Crispinus was driven into exile, being hated by Nero because he had once held Poppaea <note>Poppaea Sabina, who later became Nero’s wife.</note> in marriage. Tacitus, in Book 5 of the *Annals* <note>Clapmarius likely means Book 12 for the marriage of Claudius, or is citing a specific edition's numbering.</note>, notes that Afinius was also suspected by Tiberius of plotting things greater than a private citizen should, because he had married Vipsania, the daughter of Marcus Agrippa and formerly the wife of Tiberius. Secondly, it was considered a sacrilege <term>nefas</term> <note>A term denoting something that is not only illegal but a violation of divine or natural order.</note> for the splendor of the Augustan house to be transferred to another family. This would have brought a certain disdain and contempt upon the Caesars. Tacitus witnesses this in Book 5 of the *Annals*, stating that the Roman Republic was in mourning because Julia, the daughter of Drusus and formerly the wife of Nero <note>Nero Caesar, the eldest son of Germanicus, not the later Emperor Nero.</note>, had "married down" <note>original: "denupserat"</note> into the house of Rubellius Blandus, whose grandfather many remembered as a mere Roman knight from Tibur. Add to this that she was of proven fertility—or, to speak with Varro, she was not yet "past childbearing." <note>Clapmarius plays on the Latin words *experta* (proven) and *exparta* (having finished bearing children).</note> Furthermore, it was expedient both for the State and for the Prince himself that heirs be born. <header>Arnold Clapmarius, Book IV.</header>

For although this may be the case, the Romans, with respect to their own sect—as Galen <note>A famous Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire whose writings often touched on social customs.</note> records somewhere—and thus for the sake of their own religion, deserved an excuse in these matters as in others.

<margin>It is contrary to neither civil nor international law.</margin>
For it is not contrary to Civil Law <note>The *Ius Civile*, the law specific to Roman citizens.</note>, as Cujacius <note>Jacques Cujas, a 16th-century legal scholar known for studying Roman law through a humanist lens.</note> correctly conveys from the fragments of Ulpian <note>A high-ranking Roman jurist whose writings make up a large part of the Digest.</note> in Book 13 of his *Observations*; much less is it contrary to the Law of Nations <note>The *Ius Gentium*, or laws considered common to all mankind.</note>. But indeed, says the wise writer <note>Likely Tacitus, whom the author cited on the previous page.</note>, *marriages to brothers' daughters are new to us, but customary for other nations*. <note>original: "nova nobis in fratrum filias conjugia, sed aliis gentibus solennia"</note> And even if it were greatly against civil law, Claudius opposed this law—of which he himself was the fountain and head—with the "public good"; a concept that was broad in scope, and at that time encompassed almost the entire known world. Moreover, elsewhere in civil law itself, a departure from the general rule is made due to the "excellence of the person" (Law 2 of the Code <note>The *Codex Justinianus*, the collection of laws compiled under Emperor Justinian.</note> on the reading of sentences from a petition); just as more privileges are granted to illustrious persons than to those of lower rank (Law 17 of the Code on dignities). I will say nothing now of the dispensations of the Popes on this matter, as can be seen in the *Book of Taxes of the Apostolic Penitentiary* <note>A reference to the *Taxae Sacrae Poenitentiariae*, a list of fees for ecclesiastical pardons or legal exceptions.</note>. But truly, as for what some cite regarding Ptolemy of Alexandria or Heraclius <note>A Byzantine Emperor who controversially married his niece, Martina.</note>, they speak in vain. For these men sought marriages of this kind merely to satisfy their lust, not to preserve public tranquility.

<margin>Why later princes prohibited them.</margin>
Therefore, later Emperors prohibited these marriages by establishing a penalty, so that today it is generally not permitted to marry any woman within the third degree of kinship <note>Under Roman and Canon law, an uncle and niece are considered to be in the third degree of consanguinity.</note> (Law 17 of the Code on marriages and the final law of the Code on incestuous marriages). Nor do I approve of that which was taken as a precedent by a special decree of the Senate <note>The *Senatus Consultum* passed specifically to legalise Claudius's marriage to Agrippina.</note>. For, as the Jurist says in Law 14 of the Code on Laws: 
> *What has been accepted against the reason of the law is not to be extended to its consequences.* <note>original: "Quod contra rationem juris receptum est, non est producendum ad consequentias"</note>

Although I think it was done for this reason: so the Emperor would not seem to be committing incest, and thus the people would not despise the rule of a "profane" Prince. This, Seneca reproached...

### C H A P T E R I X.

->*That a woman of the imperial house should not marry at her own whim. The care of marriages among Princes. The path to Empire through marriages.*<-

<margin>Princes must take great care regarding marriages.</margin>
<margin>Marriages should not be free for the imperial family.</margin>
The marriages of great Princes are of the greatest concern, and ought to be so, because wars both arise from them and, in turn, cease because of them—just as Froissart charmingly remarked, that the wars of great leaders have comic endings. <note>In the classical sense, a "comic ending" refers to a story that concludes with a wedding and the restoration of order, as opposed to a tragedy.</note> This is the reason why, although marriages should otherwise be free, this rule is changed for imperial women. For indeed Agrippina, the widow of Germanicus, was a woman most greedy for power; when she had complained somewhat too freely, Tiberius took her hand and said in a Greek verse: *“If you are not queen, little child, do you think you are being wronged?”* <note>original: "εἰ μὴ, inquit, τεκνίον, ὑβρίζεσθαι δοκεῖς;" The Greek implies that unless she is ruling as an autocrat, she feels insulted.</note> For so Canter <note>Theodore or Willem Canter, 16th-century humanist scholars.</note> conjectures those were his words, which Suetonius <note>A Roman historian known for his biographies of the first twelve Caesars.</note> records as a threat...

->C H A P T E R XI.<-

<margin>To purge the State of those whose virtue is too conspicuous.</margin>
Doctors say that through bloodletting and purging, a great deal of even "good blood" is ejected and scraped away. The same reasoning applies to the Republic, in which individuals are sometimes found whose virtue is so prominent that they easily attract the devotion of the common people, even against their own will; from such people, the State must be purged. ...must be used. Thus our sharp historian <note>original: "acer Historicus noster." And yet, by some fate I know not, those who return from such removals often obtain the Empire. <term>Tiberius</term> certainly removed himself as far as possible from the public eye so that, by avoiding the weariness of constant presence, he might protect his authority through absence, and even increase it if the Republic should ever need him—as <term>Suetonius Tranquillus</term> <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus (c. 69–122 AD), Roman historian and author of *The Twelve Caesars*.</note> says in his life of Tiberius. > ->*He will rule with much blood*<-
> ->*Whoever comes to the kingdom from exile.*<- <note>original: "Regnabit sanguine multo Ad regnum quisquis venit ab exilio."</note>

For in a crime that is manifest and notorious, according to the legal commentators, it is not necessary to observe the usual order of trial; in such cases, punishment ought to be swift. <note>original: "l. 2. C. Quan. lic. un. sine iud. &c."</note> For such is the condition of Princes, as Hadrian <note>Roman Emperor Publius Aelius Hadrianus (r. 117–138 CE).</note> said shrewdly but truly: *“Those accused of aspiring to the throne are never believed unless they have been killed.”* Therefore, a remedy must be sought immediately, and not after the cause is already lost. <note>original: "post vulneratam causam." Literally "after the case has been wounded."</note> Generally, in all matters, that which a person fears another will do is treated as a fact in order to prevent it from happening.

<margin>
Prudence is required in public punishments and care, and also in detention in prison.

Tacitus writes in the second book of his *Annals*: <note>referring to the historian Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD).</note> *Tiberius did not dare to punish him openly, but ordered him to be killed in a secret part of the palace and the body to be removed in secret.* <note>original: "Nec Tiberius pœnam eius palam ausus, in secreta palatii parte interfici iussit, corpusque clam auferri." It seemed to him that both outcomes were dangerous: for the Pope to remain in prison, or for him to be released. <note>Refers to the aftermath of the Sack of Rome in 1527, when Pope Clement VII was held captive by Charles V's troops.</note> For care must be taken lest a man, having been changed from a captive into a free enemy, might do great harm through the schemes of his supporters.

<margin>
One can be condemned even without being accused.
</margin>
Finally, it matters little whether a person has been formally accused or not; for even a <term>suspected guardian</term> <note>original: "tutor suspectus." In Roman law, a guardian could be removed from their position if suspected of fraud or negligence, even before a crime was proven.</note> can be removed without a formal accusation for the benefit of the ward, if the facts of the matter are completely obvious to the judge. <note>original: "l. 3. D. de susp. tut. & curat." Refers to the Digest of Justinian, Book 26, Title 10.</note> Nor do I think that the saying of Marcus <note>Marcus Aurelius, Roman Emperor (reigned 161–180 AD).</note> found in the writings of Volcatius <note>Volcatius Gallicanus, one of the authors of the *Augustan History*.</note> applies here: *“We cannot make a man a defendant whom no one accuses.”* <note>original: "Non possumus reum facere, quem nullus accusat."</note> For this is a certain privilege which sets aside Common Law, and which is deservedly granted to the Prince as a public person, both for the sake of the Prince himself and for the Republic.
