<page-num>198</page-num>
<header>Arnold Clapmarius, Book IV.</header>
<meta>catchword: Therefore</meta>

...to act cruelly in many matters, so that peace may exist for the rest. And Gunther <note>Gunther of Pairis (c. 1150–1220), a Cistercian monk and author of the epic poem *Ligaurinus*.</note> elegantly writes in Book 1:

> *A King’s patience often does more harm*
> *Than his rigor. The latter harms a few, but the former incites*
> *everyone,*
> *As long as they hope to carry out their crimes with impunity.*

Nor does this hold true only in war (where it is customary, as Polybius <note>Polybius (c. 200–118 BC), a Greek historian who emphasized the pragmatic and often brutal realities of Roman military success.</note> testifies, *to exercise cruelty for the sake of terror*) but also in the Republic. For this reason, a sharp writer from Tuscany <note>A reference to Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527). This likely refers to his critiques of Florentine policy in *The Prince* or the *Discourses*.</note> mocks the Florentines because, when they had brought the rebelling people of Arezzo back under their power, they acted too leniently with them. *As if indeed*, he says, *the whole city could not have been destroyed without dishonor to the Florentines, etc.* Therefore Caesar <note>Julius Caesar, specifically referring to his actions at the siege of Uxellodunum during the Gallic Wars.</note>, thinking that the rest should be deterred by the example of punishment, cut off the hands of all who had carried arms, but granted them their lives, so that the punishment of the wicked might be more visible. For an end is not easily put to war unless these measures are sometimes used to break persistence.

<margin>Not only in time of war, but also in time of peace, and why.</margin>
But these things, I say, pertain to the <term>jus belli</term> <note>The law or right of war.</note>. Yet even in time of peace, and especially when seditions are spreading, there is a use for this severity. Thus that writer of Mimes <note>Likely referring to Publilius Syrus, a Latin writer of sententious maxims.</note> said: *Whoever spares the wicked harms the good.* <note>original: "Bonis nocet, quicunque parcit improbis."</note> For this reason, Pompeo Colonna <note>Pompeo Colonna (1479–1532), a powerful Italian cardinal and politician who served as Viceroy of Naples.</note> ordered the hand of a very honorable Neapolitan Knight to be cut off when, following a quarrel, he drew his sword toward the head of his opponent in the halls of the house without causing a wound. When the foremost of his friends begged for a reprieve from the punishment, he responded that unless he did so, audacity—which seemed innate to the minds of the Neapolitans—would be nourished and increased, and there would be no shortage of those who would not hesitate to bring a blade into his own bedchamber and unsheathe it for slaughter. Truly, Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus (c. 340–402 AD), a Roman statesman and orator known for his traditionalist views.</note> correctly wrote in a certain Letter: *As much severity must be added to the laws as crimes have increased.* <note>original: "Tantum legibus severitatis addendum est, quantum flagitia creverunt."</note>

<summary>This page argues that strictness and even calculated cruelty are necessary tools of statecraft to prevent widespread lawlessness. Using historical examples from Caesar and the Medici-era Florentines, Clapmarius suggests that punishing a few severely preserves the safety of the many.</summary>

For this reason, the same Colonna <note>Prospero Colonna (1452–1523), a celebrated Italian condottiero (mercenary captain) who served both the Papacy and the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, when he was proclaimed by a Spaniard through a herald—with the ignominious blast of a trumpet—to have refused a duel, ordered the man to be slaughtered on the spot. And when the ambassador of the King of Spain complained about this matter to Pope Julius <note>Pope Julius II (reigned 1503–1513), known as the "Warrior Pope" for his military campaigns.</note>, the Pope replied nothing else than that it was done most rightly; for his personal attendants <note>original: "servi à pedibus," literally "slaves at the feet," referring to household servants or lackeys.</note>, to avenge such an injury, had crushed Spanish insolence with Roman pride.
*Thus says Giovio.* <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), an influential historian and physician who recorded the lives of famous men.</note>

<margin>To punish those aware of a conspiracy against the prince.</margin>
With the same severity, those who are aware of a conspiracy against the Prince are also punished (*Law 5 of the Code on the Julian Law of Majesty*) <note>The *Lex Julia Majestatis* was the Roman law governing high treason. Under certain conditions, even failing to report a plot was a capital offense.</note> so that plots may be uncovered more quickly. *For the various reasons for this, see Curtius, book 6.* <note>Referring to the Roman historian Quintus Curtius Rufus, who wrote a history of Alexander the Great.</note> But it also applies to those things which strike the mind of anyone. It is so dangerous to fall into such times and, as it were, "nights," as Philotas <note>A general under Alexander the Great who was executed for failing to report a conspiracy, despite claiming he did not believe the threat was credible.</note> used to say: *If, when we inform, we are hated, and when we are silent, we are suspected, what ought we to do?* And although normally, by reason of consent alone, no one is bound to punishment (*Law 18 of the Digest, On Punishments*), but only when an act has followed (*Law 225 of the Digest, On the Significance of Words*).

<margin>What kind of intent is punished in place of the deed.</margin>
However, it is different in the crime against the Prince, in which the intent is punished (*the aforementioned Law 5 of the Code on the Julian Law of Majesty*). But understand "intent" in such a way—as Cujacius <note>Jacques Cujas (1522–1590), a prominent French legal scholar and expert in Roman law.</note> rightly teaches regarding the said law of the Digest—that an "initiation of the deed" is joined to it; that is, a faction or a conspiracy. For the sole and naked intent cannot be punished. And thus I understand those words of Gunther, Book 8:

->*Whatever he had dared to commit against the*<-
->*August Kings,*<-
->*Or even had meditated,*<-

And that line of the Poet: <note>This is a quote from the Roman satirist Juvenal, *Satires* 13.208–209.</note>

->*And he who thinks of any silent crime within himself,*<-
->*Bears the guilt of the deed, etc.*<-

The founders of the law, according to the testimony of Cujas <note>Jacques Cujas (1522–1590), a preeminent French legal scholar who revitalized the study of Roman law.</note>, do not approve of this at all. Likewise, Velleius Paterculus <note>A Roman historian (c. 19 BC – c. 31 AD).</note> in book 2 barely approves of that sentiment: *So much did those men look at the will to sin rather than the degree; they judged actions by the intent, and assessed what was committed, not to what extent.* <note>original: "Adeò illi viri magis voluntatem peccandi intuebantur, quam modum..."</note> Some of these legal principles, which display a certain cruelty, are balanced by public safety; and rightly so, they were established for the safety of the Prince to deter the wicked attempts of desperate men.

### CHAPTER XIV.

*Imperial Pardon. Harmful Vengeance. Why one should not inquire into every crime or every perpetrator. A place for repentance.*

<margin>To absolve the guilty.</margin>
Sometimes the guilty are also acquitted by this right. For, as Claudian <note>A late Roman poet (c. 370–404 AD).</note> says:
> *It is a beautiful thing to forgive one who is already wretched,*
> *and it is a form of punishment to have seen a man begging for mercy.*

And Tacitus in the *Agricola*: *To know everything, but not to pursue everything; to grant pardon to small sins, severity to great ones; and to be content not always with punishment, but more often with repentance.* This is also what Germanicus <note>A popular Roman general and nephew of Emperor Tiberius.</note> judged in the *Annals*: *Time should still be granted, if, following a recent example, they might look out for their own interests.*

<margin>To take care, however, lest subjects be provoked by excessive punishments.</margin>
This also contributes to the security of the Prince, so that subjects are not provoked by excessive punishments. This was the reason for imperial pardons <note>original: "imperialium abolitionum." In Roman law, an *abolitio* was a formal stay of proceedings or a wiping away of a criminal charge.</note>, which were issued either at the start of a reign or on account of a festival day, as the legal expert says in *Law 8 of the Digest, regarding the Turpilian Decree of the Senate.* It was even observed that whenever the Prince entered the city, no execution was to be carried out on anyone, as Tranquillus <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, the biographer of the Roman Emperors.</note> mentions in his life of Augustus.

But you will say that in this way, crimes go unpunished.

# On the Law of Rule. Chapter 14.
<sig>I 5</sig>
<meta>catchword: CAn-</meta>

...to proceed. For my part, I will always approve of that saying of Thrasea <note>Publius Clodius Thrasea Paetus (died 66 AD), a Roman Senator known for his principled opposition to the Emperor Nero.</note>: *Not everything that a guilty defendant deserves to suffer should be decreed under an excellent Prince.* <note>original: "Non quicquid nocens reus pati meretur, id egregio sub Principe statuendum est."</note> And in Seneca’s *Hercules Furens*, Amphitryon says: "Let silent evils pass away thus":

> Hercules: *Am I to be unavenged?*
> Amphitryon: *Vengeance has often been harmful.*

<margin>Lest unorganized disturbances revive.</margin>
To such an extent are crimes sometimes increased more and more by overly harsh remedies and punishments. This especially has a place in conspiracies, as Tacitus <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), the primary historian of the early Roman Empire.</note> says regarding the Emperor Tiberius: *Although many from the Prince's household, along with knights and Senators, were said to have sustained the conspiracy with their resources and aided it with their advice, no inquiry was made.* <note>original: "...sustentasse opibus, juvisse consiliis dicerentur, haud quaesitum."</note> Similarly, Theodosius <note>Theodosius I (the Great), who ruled 379–395 AD.</note>, forecasting the future with his military knowledge, forbade investigations into conspirators, lest, by spreading fear through many people, the unorganized disturbances of the provinces might be revived. And Trajan <note>Roman Emperor (r. 98–117 AD) known for his moderate administration.</note> wrote back to Pliny in the tenth book of his *Epistles*: *Christians are not to be hunted down; but if they are brought forward and proven guilty, they are to be punished.*

However, one who offends again and, as the saying goes, "returns to his vomit" <note>The Latin "ad nauseam redit" literally means "returns to the point of sickness/nausea," alluding to the biblical proverb about a dog returning to its vomit to describe a habitual sinner.</note>, does not enjoy the Prince’s general pardon. <note>Cited from the Code of Justinian, Book 3, "On the episcopal hearing."</note> Indeed, when Frederick I <note>Frederick Barbarossa (1122–1190), Holy Roman Emperor.</note> was at his inauguration, a certain minister—who had fallen from favor because of some great crime—threw himself at the Emperor's feet. He believed that the Emperor’s heart would be softened by the joy of the day's celebration; nevertheless, Frederick refused him, saying that he was punishing him not out of hatred, but out of a love for justice.

# CHAPTER XV.

## Regarding the punishment of the children and relatives of conspirators, lest they follow their parents' examples as they grow. On venting rage against the names of the condemned. Extreme measures. On punishing hostages.

<margin>Punishing the offspring of conspirators.</margin>
While all these measures may seem to be joined with some level of inequity, that which follows seems especially unjust: the fact that the offspring of conspirators are sometimes punished just as severely as the perpetrator, even when they are entirely innocent. According to the standard rules of law, a crime or a father's punishment can inflict no stain upon the son. For every person is subject to the consequences of their own deed, and no one is made the successor to another's crime. <note>original: "l.26. D. de pœnis: & peccata suos debent tenere autores. l.22. C. eodem." These refer to the *Digest* and the *Codex*, parts of the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the foundational body of Roman law which established that guilt should be individual rather than hereditary.</note>

However, this practice is carried out partly so that parents, moved by love for their children, might refrain from the slaughter of Princes, and partly because the examples of a father's crime—regarded here as a hereditary trait—are feared in the children, as the Emperors Arcadius and Honorius <note>Arcadius (r. 383–408) and Honorius (r. 393–423) were the sons of Theodosius I and ruled the Eastern and Western Roman Empires, respectively.</note> state. Tertullian <note>An early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD) from Carthage.</note> also wrote:

> *The authors of crimes, lest the wicked deed grow further,*
> *He extinguished, along with the offspring following the sins of the fathers.*

And Cicero says in his *Eleventh Letter to Brutus*: *Therefore, when we ask that we grant mercy to his children, nothing is offered to prevent the ultimate punishments from being undergone by us if (which may Jupiter avert as an omen) the father of the boys should win. Nor indeed does it escape me how bitter it is for the crimes of parents to be paid for by the punishments of children; but it was excellently arranged by the laws that the love for one's children should make parents more devoted to the Republic.* <note>Cicero is discussing the children of Lepidus, a Roman general and politician who had been declared a public enemy.</note> And so

<summary>This chapter examines the "justified" injustice of punishing the innocent children of conspirators to deter treason and prevent hereditary vendettas. It contrasts the ideal of individual legal responsibility with the state's perceived need for collective security.</summary>

It is Lepidus who is cruel to his own children, not the man who judges Lepidus an enemy. <note>original: "Lepidus crudelis in liberos, non is qui Lepidum hostem judicat." Marcus Aemilius Lepidus was a member of the Second Triumvirate; when he was declared a public enemy, his children lost their rights. The author argues the guilt lies with the father for committing the crime, not the state for the punishment.</note> Above all, this rule was established because of the thirst for paternal revenge with which children burn. It is not unlike the curse that Dido <note>The mythical Queen of Carthage in Virgil’s *Aeneid*, who swore eternal enmity between her people and the descendants of the Trojan Aeneas (the Romans).</note> calls down:

> *May some avenger arise from our bones,*
> *Who will pursue the Dardanian colonists with fire and sword.*
> <note>original: "Exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor, / Qui face Dardanios ferroque sequare colonos." Aeneid, Book 4, lines 625-626.</note>

<margin>A closer look at fairness.</margin>
But so it is—and it is unjust. Who denies it? Yet, through this terror, potential assassins of rulers <term>tyrannicides<gloss>those who kill a ruler they deem a tyrant</gloss></term> are more quickly restrained from shedding royal blood. And yet, parents are hardly held back even by these punishments, as seen in so many examples of conspiracies. Therefore, Tacitus writes in Book 5 of his *Annals* concerning the children of Sejanus: *It was decided thereafter that measures should be taken against the remaining children of Sejanus.* <note>Sejanus was the powerful prefect of the Praetorian Guard under Emperor Tiberius; after his fall, his innocent children were brutally executed to prevent any future uprising in his name.</note> And Ammianus Marcellinus writes: *Intercepted by the imperial upheaval, they all perished to a man, including their offspring who were still small, so that they might not grow up to follow the examples of their parents; they were destroyed by a similar fate.* <note>original: "Intercepti imperiali motu interiêre omnes ad unum... ne ad parentum exempla subcresceret."</note> This practice even had a place regarding the children of enemies. Tacitus says: *Mutianus ordered the son of Vitellius to be killed, claiming that discord would remain unless he extinguished the seeds of war.* <note>Vitellius was a short-lived Emperor in 69 AD; Mutianus, a general for the rival Vespasian, ordered the execution of Vitellius's young son to ensure the new regime's stability.</note> Hence Seneca writes in his play *Hercules*: *Sons are the avengers of a father's kingdom.*

So it is among the Venetians: when a Duke <note>The Doge of Venice, the supreme authority of the Republic.</note> dies, his administration is examined and drawn into a formal inquiry; if it was found to be somewhat unjust or too fierce, rage is vented upon the dead man and his relatives. <note>This refers to the *Sindicato*, a Venetian legal process where a deceased Doge's conduct was audited, and his heirs could be fined for his wrongdoings.</note>

Furthermore, rage was vented not only against the sons, but the entire memory of the person was condemned, as mentioned above. Hence Guntherus <note>Likely Gunther of Pairis, a 12th-century Cistercian monk and poet who wrote the *Ligurinus*, an epic about Frederick Barbarossa.</note> writes:

> *And he condemns the fierce spirits and the cruel names of the guilty,*
> *And angry parents hated the children.*

And Seneca in the play *Octavia*:

> *The fierce Tyrant rages against the name*
> *Of the mother; he desires her memory to be buried.*
> <note>original: "Sævit in nomen ferus / Matris Tyrannus, obrui meritum cupit." This refers to Nero's attempts to erase the memory of his mother, Agrippina, after her murder.</note>

> *The fear of death destroys statues and honors*
> *Throughout the whole world.*
> <note>original: "Simulacra, titulos destruit mortis metus, Totum per orbem." A sentiment often found in Roman tragedy, suggesting that the terror of execution wipes away a man's legacy.</note>

And as Curtius writes: *Nothing, he said, among all his rash and ill-considered actions, had moved the King more than the honorable mention of Parmenio.* <note>original: "Nihil... ex omnibus inconsulto ac temere actis, Regem magis moverat quam Parmenionis cum honore mentio illata." Referring to Alexander the Great’s regret or sensitivity regarding his execution of the veteran general Parmenio.</note>

<margin>Other Emperors have bound the children of conspirators to themselves through acts of kindness.</margin>
However, many Emperors were so far from punishing the children of conspirators that they instead bound them to their service through many favors. Alexander, in the eighth book of Curtius, says: *I have long since abolished that custom of killing innocent relatives and parents along with the guilty, and I declare that all of them shall remain in the same state of honor they previously held.* The Emperor Verus used to say much the same: *No one kills his own successor.* <note>original: "nemo successorem suum occidit." A political maxim suggesting that executing a rival is often futile, as destiny or the state will always produce a replacement.</note> This is why Diocletian not only spared the children of Cassius <note>Avidius Cassius, who rebelled against Marcus Aurelius; the text here attributes the mercy to Diocletian, though historically it is often associated with the Antonine era.</note> but even bestowed honors upon them. In matters of this kind, the most extreme plans are often the best. For they must either be put to death, or they must be softened with many rewards. There is no third way. This is slightly different from what Amphitryon says to Hercules in the works of Seneca:

> *Decide, whatever you decide, knowing that*
> *your cause*
> *And your reputation stand on a narrow and perilous edge:*
> *You either live, or you fall.*
> <note>original: "Sic statue, quicquid statuis... Aut vivis, aut occidis." From Seneca’s play *Hercules Furens*.</note>

It was with this strategy that Suleiman, the Emperor of the Turks, sought to lure the famous pirate Hayreddin Barbarossa to his side with the most splendid and precious rewards. He even offered him the office of <term>Grand Admiral<gloss>Architalassus</gloss></term>, so that he might conquer with favors the man he could not defeat in war, and ensure he could no longer inflict damage upon the Ottoman state.

<margin>The punishment of hostages.</margin>
By this same law, hostages are punished, even if they are personally innocent—including women, whom we read were delivered as hostages by both the Romans and the Germans.

## CHAPTER XVI.

### Taking property from citizens for the sake of the Commonwealth. These rights are to be measured not so much by the fullness of power as by common utility. Surrendering the people’s property to the enemy, conducting censuses, and imposing taxes. The census, or tax assessments <note>original: "Losungen," referring to a specific form of municipal tax or contribution in early modern German states.</note>, is the soul of Commonwealths.

<margin>Taking goods from citizens.</margin>
Public utility, says the Emperor <note>Referring to the Code of Justinian, Book 12, Title 62, Law 3.</note>, must be preferred over private contracts. Although that was said in that context with a different intent, it can nonetheless be applied here. For whenever it is in the interest of the Commonwealth for private property to be designated for public use, then citizens and subjects must step away from their rights; and if they are unwilling, they may be compelled by the Prince, certainly by this Right of Rule <term>Right of Rule: "Ius dominationis," the sovereign legal authority that allows a state to override individual interests for the preservation of the whole.</term>. This certainly seems unjust, even miserable, yet it is granted in favor of the Commonwealth; as the Roman Consul Levinus says in Livy’s 26th book: 
> When the Commonwealth is safe, it easily keeps private property safe; by losing public interests, you preserve nothing of your own. <note>original: "Respublica incolumis, & privatas res facile salvas præstat, publica perdendo, tua ne quicquam serves."</note>

Regarding times of war, the matter is clear. Jovius <note>Paolo Giovio, a 16th-century historian.</note> writes: The French, when Milan was besieged by the Emperor, following the advice of the Venetian Gritti, burned the suburban buildings—a necessary but miserable measure—so that the Emperor could not use them to pitch camp, nor approach the walls more closely and safely under the cover of roofs. Vercingetorix says the same in Caesar’s 7th book on the Gallic War: *for the sake of safety, the comforts of family property must be neglected*; <note>original: "salutis causa rei familiaris commoda negligenda esse"</note> thus he persuades the Gauls to calmly destroy their own grain and burn their buildings, seeing that through this loss of family property, they might achieve perpetual rule and liberty.

But does this also apply outside of war? Indeed it does, quite seriously, when public utility demands it. However, outside of war—which is the more merciful opinion—this should hardly happen unless [the cost is] repaid and to some extent <note>The sentence continues onto the next page.</note>

For while the Prince possesses all things, he does so not through **Ownership**, as Seneca says, but through **Command**. <term>Ownership vs. Command: Seneca’s distinction between "dominium" (private legal ownership) and "imperium" (sovereign political authority over a territory).</term> And as the poet Ligurinus writes in his third book:

<margin>The rights of rule are to be measured by the health of the Republic, not by the fullness of power.</margin>
And yet, concerning that which some claim—that it is lawful for a Prince to take away someone’s property without any cause—I do not attribute this to the **Right of Rule** so much as to the **Shame of Rule**, as Cornelius Tacitus calls it. This opinion has flowed from no other source than flattery and the desire to earn favor; nothing more disgraceful can be said of a priest of justice <note>A metaphor for a judge or legal scholar who "serves" the law as if in a temple.</note>. For these matters, and others of this kind, are to be measured not so much by the "fullness of power" as by public health and utility. *As if, indeed,* says Sallust, *doing injury were the essence of using command.* And that remark about the Emperor Titus in Suetonius is praiseworthy: *he abstained from the property of others as much as any man ever did.*

<margin>Whether it is lawful for a Prince to surrender the goods of citizens to an enemy for the sake of peace.</margin>
But is it lawful for a Prince, by the Right of Rule or of War, to surrender the goods of citizens that have been plundered on both sides once a treaty is struck? Certainly so, especially if peace cannot be achieved otherwise; and thus citizens are forever excluded from any legal action to recover them. For the claim made in the legal "gloss" <note>Standard medieval legal commentaries on Roman law.</note>—that the settlements made by masters do not prejudice the rights of subjects—does not apply to those who command according to their own will and, as Curtius says, in the "royal manner"; but rather to those whose Rule is restricted by various conditions. But this is no minor matter <note>original Greek: "ὁδ᾽ οὐ πάρεργον."</note>. A wise Prince will act in these matters soberly and circumspectly, because, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> teaches in the 5th book of his *Politics*, chapter 6: *conspiracies are set in motion by the taking of property.*

<margin>Conducting a census.</margin>
And these are nearly all the rights of royal sovereignty, to which you may add others of a similar kind. For that method of conducting a **census**, by which the resources of the citizens are not only made known but also recorded in the census tables—and from which, accordingly, taxes and tributes are paid and the republic is thereby enriched—requires, in my opinion, no excuse. For since an Empire can in no way be maintained without taxes, citizens ought to be of a calm mind when they redeem their perpetual peace and leisure with some portion of their fruits <note>That is, their income or agricultural produce.</note>, as Cicero writes to his brother Quintus. And a census of this kind, which we call *Lofungen* <note>original: "Lofungen." An archaic German term for a wealth tax or contribution, common in the Free Imperial Cities of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, is the soul of great Republics. Wherefore Livy not undeservedly calls it a most healthy thing for a great future Empire. And the Emperor Claudius calls it an arduous task: *How arduous this task is,* he says, *we are learning right now by a very great experiment, even though nothing further is sought than that our resources be publicly known.* <note>This refers to a speech by the Emperor Claudius, preserved in part by Tacitus, regarding the difficulty of assessing the wealth of the Roman provinces for taxation and social ranking.</note>

<margin>Certain specific prohibitions regarding alliances with Princes.</margin>
There is a certain prohibition against any of the nobles of a Prince or King taking a daughter of that ruler as a wife. For if such a man is supported and bolstered by this marital dignity, he easily takes on a desire for absolute rule. This is clear from the preceding sections; however, it should be referred more to the secrets of rule <term>arcana dominationis; political techniques used to maintain power</term> than to formal legal rights.

For it is a matter of great danger for a man born with the status of a Prince to live in a free Republic, just as Seneca says, *it always cost much to be born a God* <note>original: "semper magno constitit nasci Deum." From Seneca’s *Apocolocyntosis*, implying that divine or royal status carries a heavy price or burden, often leading to arrogance or political friction.</note>. And so I believe that in an Aristocratic Republic, one must beware of those who derive their origin from Kings.

<margin>Dangerous to be born a prince in a Republic.</margin>
This very matter spurred Caesar to invade the Republic, as is clear from his funeral oration for his aunt Julia <note>Julia was the wife of Gaius Marius and the aunt of Julius Caesar. In his eulogy, Caesar emphasized her—and thus his own—descent from both the early Roman kings and the goddess Venus.</note>:

> *In her lineage there is both the sanctity of kings, who have the most power among men, and the ceremony of the Gods, in whose power the Kings themselves remain.* <note>original: "Est in genere & sanctitas regum, qui plurimum inter homines pollent, & ceremonia Deorum, quorum ipsi in potestate sunt Reges." Quoted from Suetonius' *Life of Julius Caesar*.</note>

<margin>The expulsion from the Republic of those who grow too much in status.</margin>
Such people, and whoever increases too much through this or other kinds of honors, can be ejected from a free Republic, and indeed by this "right of rule." For this reason Scipio Africanus willingly and deservedly left the city. For, as Livy testifies, *it was dangerous, especially in a free Republic, for one man to be the head and summit of the Empire: for the city, mistress of the world, to hide under the shadow of Scipio, and for his nod to be taken as the decrees of the fathers [the Senate], etc.* <note>Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus, the general who defeated Hannibal, eventually went into self-imposed exile after being accused of corruption by political rivals who feared his immense popularity and influence.</note>

<margin>Hence the Ostracism of the Athenians and Ephesians.</margin>
The Ostracism <term>a democratic process where citizens voted to exile a prominent individual for ten years to prevent tyranny</term> of the Athenians and Ephesians serves this same purpose: *Let no one among us excel alone, but if anyone should stand out, let him be in another place and among other people.* Under this name, the Romans expelled all the Tarquins from the Roman state, lest they have any appearance of sedition through family ties <note>original: "per gentilitatem."</note>, as Varro says in Nonius; just as Brutus bravely and excellently said to the Consul Tarquinius <note>This refers to Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, the co-consul with Brutus, who was forced to resign and go into exile simply because he shared the name of the recently expelled kings.</note>: "Remove this fear," he said, "of your own will. We remember, we admit, you ejected the kings, [now] release... <note>The sentence continues on the next page.</note>

<margin>Punishment of individual household members for the death of a single master.</margin>

As Cassius says, *it is compensated for against individuals by the public utility.* <note>original: "contra singulos utilitate publica rependitur." A legal principle suggesting that individual hardship is justified by the collective good.</note> For I am not ashamed to repeat this opinion so often, for which Marcus Tullius Cicero provides the reasoning in his speech for Cluentius: *Our ancestors decreed,* he says, *that if a military crime were committed by many, punishment would be inflicted on some by drawing lots, so that fear might reach everyone, while the punishment reached only a few.* <note>original: "Cluentiana." Referring to Cicero's speech *Pro Cluentio*.</note> For the soldier who did not hold his position, or who feared the attack and force of the enemy, can later become a better citizen, a good man, and a useful member of society. Therefore, lest he commit a fault in war out of fear of the enemy, a greater fear of death and execution was established by our ancestors; however, so that not too many would suffer the death penalty, that drawing of lots <term>sortitio; the Roman practice of decimation, where a small portion of a group was chosen by lot for punishment to deter the whole</term> was arranged. Thus says Cicero.

---

### C H A P T E R XVIII.

->Prohibiting the children of the proscribed from the rights of their rank; and a brief demonstration of the difference between these Aristocratic rights and Royal rights.<-

<margin>Excluding the children of the proscribed from public honors.</margin>
Sulla <note>Lucius Cornelius Sulla, the Roman dictator known for his "proscriptions" or state-sanctioned killings of political enemies.</note>, having expelled and proscribed a great many Senators and Roman knights, passed a law prohibiting the children of the proscribed from the right of seeking public honors; at the same time, the sons of Senators (to use the words of Velleius) were forced to bear the burdens of their rank while losing its rights. It is asked: was this done rightly? Certainly, Velleius Paterculus <note>a Roman historian</note> judged it to be a most unworthy act. To me, however, it seems he acted both by the right of rule and for the safety and tranquility of the current Republic. Just as Cicero says in his first *Philippic*: *Not because I approve of it, but because I believe the greatest consideration must be given to leisure and peace.* <note>original: "Non quod probem; sed quod rationem habendam esse censeo maxime otii & pacis."</note> And Quintilian <note>a famous Roman teacher of rhetoric</note> in his eleventh book, chapter one, says: *In many cases,* he says, *the harshness of a speech must be softened with another tone, as Cicero did regarding the children of the proscribed.*

<meta>catchword: What [Quid]</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the legal and political justification for collective punishments, such as military decimation and the exclusion of the children of political enemies (the proscribed) from public office, arguing these harsh measures are necessary for state stability.</summary>
<keywords>Cicero, Sulla, proscription, decimation, military discipline, public utility, Aristocratic rights, political exclusion, Roman law</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how Aristocratic Republics maintain stability through the exclusion of potential enemies. It follows the previous page's introduction to Chapter 18, which established the harsh legal precedent of punishing the children of political enemies to ensure the safety of the state.</meta>

<page-num>211</page-num>
<header>Of the Law of Domination, Chapter 18.</header>

For what is more cruel than for children born to honorable parents and ancestors to be removed from the service of the Republic? Therefore, that most skilled master of guiding the human mind <note>Quintilian, the renowned Roman educator and rhetorician</note> admits that such a thing is harsh; yet he argues that the stability of the state is so bound to the laws of Sulla <note>Lucius Cornelius Sulla (138–78 BC), a Roman dictator who consolidated power through 'proscriptions,' or state-sanctioned killings of political rivals</note> that if these laws were dissolved, the state itself could not stand. Thus, it so happens that he seemed to be acting, in part, for the sake of those very people he was arguing against. Quintilian expresses this excellently. For they <note>the children of the proscribed</note> lost the rights of their social rank for this reason: so they would not have the power to throw the Republic into chaos out of a desire for revenge. The same logic applied to the sons of Brutus <note>The sons of Lucius Junius Brutus, who were executed for plotting to restore the monarchy after the Roman Republic was founded</note>, whom it was necessary to remove from the scene once liberty had been secured. On this point, see Machiavelli <note>Niccolò Machiavelli, who discusses the necessity of "killing the sons of Brutus" to maintain a new state in his *Discourses on Livy*</note>.

<margin>This is proven to be appropriate for Aristocratic rule.</margin>
Strictly speaking, it is clear that this practice fits an Aristocratic government <term>Aristocracy; a system where power is held by the nobility or a small elite class</term> because, once the supreme power later passed to a single ruler, these individuals were restored to their honors. Suetonius writes this of Caesar: *He admitted even the children of the proscribed to public offices.* <note>original: "Admisit ad honores & proscriptorum liberos."</note> For this reason, Cicero calls it a law of the circumstances, rather than a law of the man. In the same way, when Alexander <note>Alexander the Great</note> wrote letters to Greece upon his return from India, decreeing that exiles from all cities—except those convicted of murder—should be restored to their homes, great unrest arose. This was because many had been driven from their homelands not by the law, but by the political factions of the Princes; these same Princes feared that if those men were recalled, they would become more powerful within the Republic. <note>Ref: Justin, Book 13. Marcus Junianus Justinus was a Roman historian who epitomized the works of Pompeius Trogus.</note>

<margin>These laws must be adapted to Republics in their own way.</margin>
For not all of these laws are suitable for all Republics indiscriminately, nor for all times; rather, they must be adapted to each state in their own specific way.

It argues that while such measures seem cruel, they prevent civil unrest caused by revenge, noting that Monarchy often relaxes these rules to consolidate personal power.</summary>

<margin>The admission of brothels.</margin>
Furthermore, I believe that the establishment of brothels <note>original: "lupanaria"</note> can be justified by this same legal logic. These are permitted here and there in large Republics due to human lust, specifically so that the violation of honorable women might be averted. This is consistent with what a Jurisconsult <note>A professional legal expert in Rome</note> wittily remarked in the Digest <note>A collection of Roman legal rulings; specifically Book 27, Title 'De hereditatis petitione'</note>, stating that brothels are sometimes maintained even on the estates of honorable men. Catullus <note>Gaius Valerius Catullus, a Roman poet</note> also alludes to this: *She gave us a home and a mistress.* For this reason, when the Emperor Nero fell in love with the freedwoman Acte and grew to loathe his wife Octavia—a noble woman of proven virtue—not even the Emperor’s stricter friends opposed the affair. For they feared, as Tacitus <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus, the Roman historian</note> says, *that he might break out into the violation of illustrious women if he were prohibited from satisfying that lust.* Moreover, this practice was profitable to the treasury and the public purse. Under the Emperor Severus, such brothels, as well as the pimps themselves, paid a tax on the profits of prostitution. This revenue was returned to the treasury to be used for the repair of public buildings, such as the amphitheater, the circus, and others.

<margin>Other examples of similar concessions in the policy of Moses, specifically regarding reason.</margin>
Similar to this is the law found in Deuteronomy 23: *You may charge interest to a foreigner, but to your brother you shall not.* This was granted to the Jews because of their "hardness of heart" <note>The idea that strict laws must sometimes be relaxed or adapted for a people who are morally stubborn or difficult to govern</note>. There is also the word of Christ to the Pharisees in the 19th chapter of Matthew: *Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, permitted you to divorce your wives; but from the beginning it was not so.* Of the same nature is the Valerian Law <note>The *Lex Valeria*, which allowed any citizen to kill a man attempting to set himself up as a king or tyrant without a trial</note>, which permitted the killing of a tyrant first and the judging of the case afterward; this was allowed because of the

D.De injust. rup. irr. teftam." — This refers to a specific section of the Roman Digest concerning wills and public safety</note>. This *Spurius Maelius*, because he had reached for kingship in a free Republic, and had failed to obey the summons of the Dictator to plead his case—and had instead incited the crowd by crying out for their protection—was struck down in public by the Master of the Horse.

<margin>Why the injustice of great examples is compensated.</margin>
But again, you will say: "This was truly unjust, for he was neither heard nor condemned." Yet, the truth is that a public trial could not be conducted against him without the risk of an uprising <note>original: "seditionis periculo"</note>; and perhaps, due to the favor of his political faction, he would have escaped the charge. I need not repeat that this appearance of injustice is covered and compensated for by public utility. For as in all political actions, so especially in this matter, the words of that most elegant poet <note>Lucretius, from his work *On the Nature of Things*</note> hold true:

->From the very fountain of delights<-
> Something bitter rises, which stings 
> even among the flowers themselves;

To these, many other points can be added, and many can be illustrated by examples. To me, as *Pliny* <note>Pliny the Younger, a Roman author and lawyer</note> says in his *Letters*, the selection of these matters was more difficult than the discovery of them.

In such a state, many things are permitted for the sake of the safety of the individual, and these are also fitting for a contemporary Democratic Republic.

...actions are performed for the sake of preserving the Republic, even if they are somewhat unjust. I will refrain from repeating these examples, however, because it is easy for anyone to take them from what was previously said and adapt them to this specific category of statecraft.

<margin>The killing of Timoleon's brother is categorized here.</margin>
Yet, I cannot restrain myself from mentioning here that famous act of kin-killing <note>original: "parricidium". While "parricide" usually refers to killing a parent, in Latin it also denoted the murder of any close relative or a heinous crime against the state.</note> committed by Timoleon. His brother, Timophanes <note>original: "Timophoontem"</note>, was plotting to seize power as a tyrant and was even threatening many great men in the Republic with the most extreme punishments. After Timoleon warned him to stop—to no avail—he immediately ordered him to be run through with a sword, and indeed, within the very walls of his home. Because Timoleon later regretted this deed and consequently withdrew from public affairs, Teleclides rebuked him harshly:
> *If,* he said, *you conduct yourself excellently in the upcoming struggle, we shall judge that you killed a tyrant; but if not, we shall judge that you killed a brother.*

Truly, he did not do this driven by hatred for his brother, but impelled by an incredible love for his fatherland. He acted not so much by private authority as by public authority, for he was among the leaders of the Senate. In fact, Roman law is so far from punishing those who kill parents or children who have become enemies of the state <note>original: "hostes patriae"</note>, that such individuals were instead granted rewards, as is found in the law <note>original: "l. 25. D. De relig. & sumpt. fun." This refers to a section of the Digest of Justinian concerning funeral expenses and religious duties, where the state's safety overrides normal family obligations.</note>.

<margin>The act of Manlius, who killed his treasonous sons.</margin>
Therefore, to me, Timoleon is no more a murderer of kin than that famous Manlius <note>Titus Manlius Torquatus, a Roman consul who executed his son for engaging the enemy against orders, prioritizing military discipline over family.</note> who ordered his treasonous sons to be killed, or Servilius Ahala, who struck down Maelius when he was accused of seeking kingship. Indeed, Plutarch <note>The famous Greek biographer and philosopher.</note> vividly describes the grief that Timoleon felt over his brother's death:
> *To such an extent,* he says, *do the judgments of men waver, and are swept sideways by any praise or blame. Just as those gluttons seized by great hunger swallow down food but feel nausea once they are full, so we lose heart once our deeds are finished.*

Thus Plutarch wrote regarding Timoleon. And I do not know...

<margin>
Whether

...whether Nero can in any way be excused for the murder of his mother <note>Agrippina the Younger, who was killed by her son Nero in 59 AD</note>. For as I consider the whole history, many crimes and signs of a power-grab come to light: for instance, that among other things, she <note>Agrippina</note> courteously received Nero's tribunes and centurions; that she held the names and virtues of the nobility in honor; that she sought a leader and invaded other factions and similar secrets of sovereignty <term>arcana dominationis: the hidden or "dirty" maneuvers used by rulers to maintain control</term>. Indeed, even Burrus and Seneca themselves, as Cornelius Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian who chronicled the corruption of the early Empire</note> testifies, believed matters had descended to such a point that unless she were dealt with first, Nero would have to perish. This is the very thing that the character Octavia <note>Nero’s wife</note> criticizes in Seneca’s play:

> *Let him extinguish me too, lest he fall by our hand.*

Nevertheless, the act is still an atrocious thing, and utterly alien to natural affection and piety. No one would easily swear to the slaughter of their own kin unless they had declared war on all their own feelings. Justin <note>A Roman historian of the 2nd century</note> rightly says in Book 16: *In parricide <note>original: "parricidio"; here meaning the murder of a close relative</note>, no cause can be considered just enough to serve as a defense for the crime.*

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter 20 and 21 regarding the limits of sovereign power. ### Arnold Clapmarius, Book IV.

...is the head of these, and it is right that all members of the Republic yield and lower their symbols of authority <term>fasces: bundles of rods and axes that symbolized a Roman magistrate's power to punish or execute</term> before it.

<margin>Nay, indeed they yield to divine law.</margin>
<margin>Religion is the limit of human majesty and power.</margin>
Nevertheless, this majesty has its own boundaries, such as religion, decency, and good faith. For these, like victorious goddesses, cast a bridle upon human power and restrain it, lest it go further than divine law permits. As the Poet <note>The Roman poet Horace, *Odes* 3.6.5</note> says: *You rule because you carry yourself as lesser than the Gods.* <note>original: "Diis te minorem quod geris, imperas"</note> Therefore, in the Roman Republic, when the Senate was consulted regarding the petition of the Campanians, even though that city <note>Capua, the capital of Campania</note> seemed to a great part of the Senate to be the largest and most opulent in Italy, with the most fertile land, and close to the sea for a variety of provisions—a literal granary for the Roman people—nevertheless, good faith was held more ancient and important than such great utility, as Livy <note>Titus Livius, the famous Roman historian</note> excellently records in Book 7. And as that Praetor of the Achaeans boldly said: *We revere you, Romans, and if you wish it, we even fear you; but we revere and fear the immortal Gods more.* <note>original: "Veremur, inquit, vos, Romani, & si ita vultis etiam timemus, sed plus veremur & timemus Deos immortales."</note> *Livy, Book 39.*

<margin>In which nothing should be changed without a probable cause.</margin>
For this reason, those are rightly punished under this law who, without any probable cause—whether driven by ambition or led by a desire for novelty—rashly change something in religion. They thrust forward new questions that have not yet been decided despite many consultations, torturing the souls of curious men and mixing heaven and earth <note>a classical idiom meaning to cause total chaos or upheaval</note>. This insolence must be restrained in those who, to use the words of my favorite author Tacitus, *slip into ambition under the guise of religion.* <note>original: "religionis specie in ambitionem delabuntur"</note> Provision was made for this in the Digest, Book 2, *On Extraordinary Crimes*.

<margin>It should not, however, be used as a pretext.</margin>
Religion is indeed pure and incorruptible in itself, like a young maiden; yet it is so infected and obscured by so many dyes and types of white lead <note>referring to "cerussa," a toxic lead-based cosmetic used to whiten the skin; here a metaphor for hypocrisy</note> that, whatever is actually being done, religion alone is used as a pretext. Hence Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus, a Roman poet and philosopher</note> wrote:

->*How often in the past*<-
->*Has religion brought forth wicked and impious deeds.*<-
<note>original: "Quod sæpius olim / Relligio peperit scelerosa atq; impia facta." From *On the Nature of Things*, Book 1.</note>

<summary>Clapmarius argues that sovereign power (Majesty) is not absolute but must be constrained by religion and moral integrity. He warns against those who use religious reform as a cover for political ambition or to cause social instability.</summary>

## On the Right of Sovereignty, Chapter 21.

And **Tacitus** writes in the *Annals*, Book 1: *Loyalty toward a parent and the needs of the Republic were taken up [as pretexts].* <note>original: "Pietatem erga parentem & tempora Reipubl. sumpta." Tacitus is describing how Augustus used the excuse of avenging his adoptive father, Julius Caesar, to seize power.</note> Even the famous **Sinon** <note>OCR reads "Simon"; Sinon was the Greek spy who convinced the Trojans to bring the Wooden Horse into their city.</note> uses this same appearance of piety in the Poet’s <note>Virgil's</note> *Aeneid*, Book 2:

> They were warned to set up this statue in place of the Palladium,
> For the offended deity, to atone for the grim sacrilege.
> <note>original: "Hanc pro Palladio, moniti, pro numine laeso / Effigiem statuere, nefas quae triste piaret."</note>

<margin>Religion cannot be thrust upon an unwilling people.</margin>
In truth, the lust for power almost always adopts this cloak; however, religion cannot be thrust upon an unwilling people, much less can they be forced to believe what they do not in fact believe. For as **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author from Carthage</note> truly says: *This contributes to the reputation of irreligion: to take away the freedom of religion and forbid the choice of divinity; so that I am not allowed to worship whom I wish, but am forced to worship whom I do not wish.* <note>original: "Hoc ad irreligiositatis elogium concurrit, adimere libertatem Religionis, & interdicere opinionem divinitatis; ut non liceat mihi colere quem velim, sed cogar colere, quem nolim."</note> And **Curtius**, though a secular writer, says in Book 8: *as if minds could be commanded just as easily as tongues.* <note>original: "tanquam perinde animis imperari possit, ac linguis."</note>

<margin>Religion is not the cause of seditions in itself.</margin>
Regarding the claim that seditions <term>sedition: conduct or speech inciting people to rebel against the authority of a state</term> arise from this difference of religions: why then do they not punish those who disturb the Republic, while sparing those who labor day and night for the peace of the Republic and weary the immortal God with prayers for the public safety? For it is not religion—this one or that—that is the cause of sedition, but rather the mindless and corrupt spirit of the most depraved men.

<margin>The evils of Republics do not come from religion.</margin>
Therefore **Orosius** <note>A 5th-century Christian historian</note> says: *The evils of republics are not born from religion, but have always existed throughout the entire world.* <note>original: "Rerumpublicarum mala non nasci ex religione, sed fuisse semper in universo terrarum orbe."</note> I am pleased to conclude this chapter with a most beautiful and truly Christian sentiment by **Scipione Ammirati** <note>An Italian historian and political theorist</note> in his commentary on Tacitus. *And because,* he says, *religion is a greater thing, as we have said, than the **reason of state** <term>reason of state: the principle that the interests and security of the state take precedence over all other considerations, including morality</term>, and its accounts are settled differently from those of men, and there is no proportion between temporal and eternal things: it is necessary, in such circumstances, to look first to religion and see if it opposes you; because in such a case, it is necessary to accommodate the reason of state to religion, and not...*

**Arnold Clapmarius, Book IV**

...from religion to the **reason of state** <note>original: "ragione di stato." This Italian phrase refers to the justification for a ruler to act outside of normal law or morality to preserve the safety of the state.</note>. And many more things on this subject are discussed by that truly wise and eloquent writer.

### CHAPTER XXII

*Similar examples, taken from both sacred writings and civil law. The sacrilege of Frederick Barbarossa. The non-legitimate and non-ordinary method. How a Prince confirms those things which were not done by right.*

<margin>Other things established against natural equity are recounted.</margin>
Indeed, many other things—found in both sacred scripture and civil law—have been established against **natural equity** <note>the universal sense of fairness</note> and ordinary or common law, out of respect for the public good or other specific circumstances. I would like to recount several of these here. <margin>On account of the public good: the example from the Bible of David asking the Priests for the Showbread.</margin> In ancient times, it was a sin for anyone except the Priests and Levites to eat the **Bread of the Presence** <note>original: "panes propositionis," the twelve loaves of bread placed in the Jewish Temple; see 1 Samuel 21</note>; yet when David was in danger of starvation, he did not fear to ask the Priests for it, nor did the Priests refuse him. Our Savior used this same argument against the Pharisees when some of His followers, forced by hunger on the Sabbath, plucked ears of grain and ate the rubbed seeds. <margin>The "Bronze-Beard" [Frederick Barbarossa] invading sacred places.</margin> Following their example, **Frederick Barbarossa** <note>Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1155–1190), nicknamed "Aenobarbus" or Bronze-Beard</note>, when he was hard-pressed by a lack of supplies, seized goods from sacred places. Later, however, he compensated those Bishoprics with distinguished and even more generous gifts, as **Otto of Freising** <note>A 12th-century bishop and historian</note> records. Regarding this matter, **Gunther** <note>Gunther of Pairis, author of the poem "Ligurinus"</note> writes in Book 2:

> *Indeed, it is the mark of a good mind to acknowledge a fault,*
> *Even where no fault exists.*

<margin>From Canon Law.</margin>
According to these principles, I believe the Law 9 of the Digest on the **Julian Law regarding Embezzlement** <note>original: "l. 9. D. Ad L. Iul. pecul." Refers to Roman laws against stealing public or sacred property</note> should be interpreted. Likewise, in **Canon Law** <note>the law of the Church</note>, when an enemy is approaching, it is permissible to fortify a house of God or a sacred tower and use it as a defensive stronghold.

What else? Is it not accepted, contrary to laws and natural reason, that a son—even if he is not the heir—may be held liable for a principal debt, and a wife is considered to have a secondary claim in a pledge? <note>original: "l.4.C. De primipil."</note> So it is in the Law of Deposits. <margin>Learn more examples.</margin> Natural law (or the law of nations) and civil law often fight against each other.

> "If," says Tryphoninus <note>Claudius Tryphoninus, a Roman jurist of the early 3rd century AD</note>, "we look at natural law and the law of nations, things must be restored to the one who gave them; if we look at civil law and the order of the laws, they must instead be handed over to the public treasury."

Thus it is established by law that no one should "speak the law" for themselves <note>that is, take the law into their own hands</note>. Yet if a judge does not make himself available, nothing prevents one from avenging a suffered injury by one's own authority. Similarly, a **suspect guardian** <note>a legal guardian suspected of embezzling or mismanaging a ward's assets</note> is removed, even if he does not hesitate to give an account of his bad management once the guardianship has ended. In the same way, **minors** <term>impuberes: children under the age of puberty who were normally legally incapable of marriage</term> are forbidden to be joined in marriage. Yet this is permitted when the benefit of peace encourages it <note>often referring to political marriages between royal families to end wars</note>. Of the same note are the laws regarding Treason and acts done to defraud creditors. 

By this same reasoning, a judge sentences a notorious robber to death, even though the criminal does not fall under his specific jurisdiction. A similar example to this is found in Tacitus, Book 1 of the *Annals*. Menius, the Prefect of the Camp, had ordered two mutinous soldiers to be punished with death, contrary to military law. <margin>
The circumstances must be taken into account here.
</margin>
I will now pass over other circumstances, which **Aulus Gellius** <note>a 2nd-century Roman author known for his work *Attic Nights*</note> calls "appendices and critical moments." These include the frequency of minor offenses, stubbornness, place, time, and other factors of that kind. In respect to these, the law itself has often been either restricted or expanded, not only by philosophers but even by the lawgivers themselves. **St. Augustine** says of this: *“The Emperor has the power to pass other laws; not rashly, but for a just cause and the safety of the Republic; and thus even to confirm things that were not done according to the law.”* Hence even in civil law, principal contracts are held as just and legitimate, even if they were not made according to the strict letter of the law. <margin>Absolute rule is a middle ground between legitimate government and tyranny.</margin>
**E**XCEPTIONAL is the nature of a supreme and vast Empire, such that it is sometimes of great importance to depart from the path of equity, as is established from the preceding book. Nevertheless, one must not deflect so far that the matter descends into Tyranny. For **Absolute Rule** <term>Dominatio: a form of rule where the sovereign has near-total control, distinct from both a balanced 'Imperium' and a lawless 'Tyrannis'</term> is a certain middle ground between civil **Government** <term>Imperium: legitimate, legal authority</term> and **Tyranny**. If this rule, by abandoning the former, verges toward Tyranny, it is no longer Rule, nor Law, nor Government, but the highest injustice and extreme tyranny; and as **Tacitus** <note>a Roman historian known for his analysis of power dynamics</note> calls it in the 14th book of his *Annals*: a **Shameful Crime of Rule**. <note>original: "Flagitium Dominationis"</note> Regarding the times of the Emperor Claudius, Tacitus writes that through indirect attacks, he transferred all the shameful crimes of that rule onto his mother. Just as elsewhere he speaks of the "shameful crimes of military service"...

<meta>catchword: bloody-</meta>

In Italy, this is called *the bad reason of state* <note>original Italian: "la cattiva ragione di stato," a term used to describe the immoral application of political necessity</note>. And indeed, you would correctly record those laws of absolute rule among the "odious" ones, from which, according to the legal interpreters, one should not depart at all; but rather, these are the ones which are accepted stubbornly and to the letter. Otherwise, they would not be a limitation or an exception, but a transgression—or, as Aristotle elegantly calls flawed Republics, a certain *perversion* <note>original Greek: παρέκβασις (parekbasis), meaning a deviation from a proper constitutional form</note>. Instead, these are foul and barbaric methods, and crimes committed for the sake of preserving and increasing power—or, as we speak today in a single word, Machiavellian counsels.

<margin>These are today called Machiavellian counsels. How a Prince ought to avoid them.</margin>
These are the things that Princes, as much as possible, ought to avoid. With a wisdom truly beyond her sex, the famous Livia said to Augustus: *It is necessary for you to do nothing by way of injury; but also to not even appear to do so. For while it is enough for private individuals to commit no crime, Princes are not even permitted to be under suspicion.* And as Theseus says in Seneca's *The Mad Hercules*:

> Our crimes are punished in a greater measure. <note>original Latin: "Scelera taxantur modo majore nostra," implying that the misdeeds of rulers carry heavier consequences or are judged more severely than those of commoners.</note>

And yet, such acts are often covered by the name of "law." Hence Tacitus writes: *For what others call crimes, this man calls remedies; while using false names, he calls cruelty "severity," greed "parsimony," and your punishments and insults he calls "discipline."*

<margin>Various names for these outrages.</margin>
Furthermore, Tacitus elsewhere calls outrages of this kind the *force of the Prince* (in the 5th book of his *Annals*): *But those ready for revenge were hindered by the force of the prince.* Elsewhere, he calls it the *force of Absolute Rule* <term>Dominatio: rule characterized by the master-slave dynamic rather than the citizen-magistrate relationship</term>. Just as Paterculus writes in his 2nd book: *Marullus almost experienced the force of Absolute Rule.* Cicero, in the 1st book of *On Duties*, calls them *clever and malicious interpretations of the law.* The writer of the *Dialogue on Oratory* calls it a *bloodthirsty sentence.* Ammianus describes it as *law shaded by contrived lies*; likewise, *bloody law*; and likewise, a *bloody will*. He opposes this to civil and just government in his 15th book: *Civil and just government,* he says, *having been converted into mere will.*

<summary>Clapmarius defines "Machiavellian counsels" as the point where statecraft becomes "bloody law" or "the force of the prince." He argues that rulers must avoid even the appearance of these "odious" crimes, which are often disguised with the false names of legal necessity.</summary>

### On the Crimes of Absolute Rule. Chapter 1.

...bloody [rule], which the Germans express through **dangerous laws** <note>original German: "gefährliche Rechten"</note>.

<margin>
Irrelevant sayings of various authors.

Of this same sort <note>original Latin: "cujus farinae," literally "of this flour"</note> is that saying of Caesar: *that for the sake of a kingdom, one must be a criminal*. And that of Euphemus in Thucydides: *For a man who is a tyrant, or a city that holds an empire, nothing is irrational if it is advantageous* <note>original Greek: Ἀνδρὶ τυράννῳ ἢ πόλει ἀρχὴν ἐχούσῃ, οὐδὲν ἄλλογον, ὅτι ξυμφέρον</note>. To a Prince, nothing is unjust if it is profitable. And there is the saying of Eteocles in Euripides: *for the sake of a kingdom, the law must be violated*. And Seneca's: *Where only honorable things are permitted to the ruler, his reign is precarious*; and that of Tacitus regarding Agrippina: *Nothing at home was immodest, unless it served her power*. And Lepidus in Sallust: *Nothing is glorious unless it is safe; and everything done to retain rule is honorable*. And finally, that of Lucian:

->*The entire power of the scepters perishes, if it begins*<-
->*to depend on what is just.*<-

<margin>
The rights of rule differ from the crimes of rule to such an extent that they are almost opposites.
</margin>
Therefore, the "rights of rule" <term>jura dominationis; legal prerogatives used for the state's benefit</term> differ from the "crimes of rule" <term>flagitia dominationis; immoral acts committed by tyrants</term>; indeed, they are, as it were, opposites. First, because in these crimes, only private utility is considered, whereas in those rights, both private and public utility are considered. These crimes are done for the sake of fulfilling cruelty and lust; those rights are for the sake of preserving public tranquility. Finally, in those rights, account is taken of the divine will, honor, faith, and modesty; in these crimes, all such things are injured and trampled underfoot.

<margin>
It is shown, however, in what way they agree. They are called the secrets of the house.
</margin>
Yet both are hidden and secret methods <term>rationes; the underlying logic or "reasons" of state</term> for strengthening and increasing empire. For this reason, it should seem less strange to anyone that these crimes are referred by me to the "secrets of Republics" <note>Clapmarius's central concept is "Arcana Imperii," or the hidden secrets of power</note>. I add that Tacitus himself, in the first book of the *Annals*, calls them *secrets of the house* <note>original Latin: "arcana domus"</note>, or as I might say in our modern fashion, *secrets of the Court* <note>original Latin: "arcana Aula"</note>. For "House" is used to mean "Court," just as "Rule" <note>dominatio</note> is used for "Empire" <note>imperium</note>; as Tacitus says, *a stepmother heavy upon the house of the Caesars*. This terminology we also retain today, such as the **House of Austria** or the **House of Saxony**. Thus elsewhere, Tacitus calls the lusts of the imperial house the *secrets of the nights*.

### CHAPTER II.

*How the secrets of the house differ from the crimes of absolute rule. Masters of rule. Masters of the people. A partner in secrets. The arbiter of secrets, removing rivals of the empire: maintaining a combined household or court with the state.*

<margin>How the secrets of the house and the crimes of rule differ from one another.</margin>
The "secrets of the house" <term>arcana domus; private or familial schemes used by a ruling dynasty</term> are understood by Cornelius Tacitus only in a negative sense. These are not the "rights of the court," nor those "palatine laws and rights" so frequently mentioned by writers on German affairs; rather, they are mere "crimes of absolute rule" <term>dominationis flagitia; immoral acts used to maintain a tyrant's grip on power</term>. Yet they differ from one another in this specific way: the "secrets of the house" are properly hidden and serve as domestic or private plans. That is, they are the secret arts and courtly crimes committed within the Imperial household to preserve power, through which any who seem to oppose or crave the current rule are crushed by any means necessary. These acts are almost always committed against brothers, blood relatives, and others joined by close family ties. Regarding this, consider the words of Tacitus in the 12th book of the *Annals*: *Nothing in the home was immodest, unless it served her power* <note>original Latin: "Nihil domi impudicum, nisi dominatione expediret." Tacitus is here referring to the ruthless ambition of Agrippina the Younger.</note>. On the other hand, the "crimes of absolute rule" are more general in nature and concern the entire method of governing the state.

<margin>Illustrated with examples from the Turkish house.</margin>
For example, in the Turkish house <note>The Ottoman Empire was frequently used by Renaissance and Baroque political theorists as the ultimate example of "oriental despotism" and ruthless family politics.</note>, those perpetual "parricides" <term>parricidia; the systematic execution of a new Sultan's brothers to prevent civil war</term> appear to be "secrets of the house." However, the "crimes of Turkish rule" go beyond the palace walls; they are the violent and wicked methods of ruling the subjects themselves. Because of this, Tacitus calls those who were skilled in these matters "Masters of Absolute Rule" <note>original Latin: "dominationis magistros"</note>—whom the common people today call "Machiavellians." In the same way, when discussing a popular Republic, the historian Livy calls the Tribunes "masters of the common people." Those who were privy to such things were called "partners in secrets." Tacitus says, "Sallustius was a partner in secrets" <note>referring to Sallustius Crispus, the grand-nephew of the historian Sallust and a key advisor to the emperors Augustus and Tiberius</note>; and Suetonius says of Otho...

### C A P V T III.

*The crimes of royal rule. Incest, illegal marriages. Committing adultery for the sake of the kingdom. Divorces; Papal dispensations: acting in the royal manner, without fear of the laws. Royal words.*

<margin>
There are as many crimes of rule as there are rights of rule. Namely: royal, aristocratic, and popular. The crimes of royal rule.
</margin>
I have previously categorized the **Rights of Rule** <term>Jura Dominationis; the specific legal powers that define a government's authority</term> as threefold; now I establish just as many **crimes** <term>flagitia; shameful acts or abuses of power</term>. Specifically, there are the crimes of Royal Rule, Aristocratic Rule, and Popular Rule. For, as **Marcus Tullius [Cicero]** says, *there is even a tyranny within a populace.*

But first let us look at the crimes of kings. Such are the acts of those who contract **incestuous marriages**, or who perform **divorces** at their own whim, both for the sake of increasing their power and for the exercise of lust. I believe it was for this reason that **Absalom** <note>The son of King David who rebelled against him; see 2 Samuel 16:22.</note> lay with his father's concubines—that is, the royal concubines; and it is what **Suetonius** records concerning **Augustus**. He says: *Augustus practiced adultery, not out of lust,*

...[not by] custom, but by a deliberated plan, so that he might more easily seek out the secret plans of his adversaries through their respective wives. <margin>Incestuous marriages and divorces carried out to increase power and indulge lust.</margin> And there is that passage from **Tacitus** <note>Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), a Roman historian known for his dark portrayal of the early emperors.</note> concerning the same man: *A wife was also taken away from Nero, and the priests were consulted in mockery as to whether she could be legally married while a child had been conceived but not yet born.* <note>original: "Abducta Neroni & uxor..." — This refers to Nero taking Poppaea Sabina as his wife while she was pregnant, a violation of traditional Roman religious law.</note> And regarding **Tiberius**: *He burned with such untamable crimes and lusts that, in a royal manner, he defiled free-born youth with sexual outrages.* And later: *Then, for the first time, previously unknown names were invented—the <term>sellarii</term> <note>From the Latin "sella" (chair/stool); refers to those who performed sexual acts on tiered benches.</note> and the <term>spintriae</term> <note>A term for those who invented new and "monstrous" forms of intercourse.</note>—named for the filthiness of the place and the variety of their endurance. <margin>Papal dispensations contrary to Divine Law.</margin> To this category belong almost all the dispensations of the Popes that conflict with Divine Law, and especially those of **Martin V** <note>Pope Martin V (reigned 1417–1431). The author here reflects Protestant-leaning legal critiques common in the 17th century.</note>, such as allowing a man to carnally know his mother or a kinswoman with impunity, or to have a sister in marriage. Or that a monk might be permitted to have a wife for a time, and once a child has been fathered, he might then—as a "father accomplished" with ears lowered—return to his monk's cowl. On these matters, see the work of **Hotman** <note>François Hotman (1524–1590), a French legal scholar and Huguenot who wrote "Brutum Fulmen" (The Thundering Bolt) against the authority of the Pope.</note> in his *Brutum Fulmen*. Those who undergo divorces according to their own lusts commit this same crime of power. <margin>Crimes are quickly imitated.</margin> How much more modest was the Emperor **Henry III**! <note>Henry III (1017–1056), Holy Roman Emperor. ### CHAPTER IV.

-> *Atheism. To set sail in matters of faith. To plunder sacred things: and through satire. Did the Romans interpret religion according to the occasion? Superstition is superior to Atheism.* <-

<margin>To twist and regard religion for the sake of the kingdom.</margin>

Among the Romans—who were otherwise Pagans—there was a great reverence for religion; indeed, I do not know if it was ever greater anywhere else. **Valerius Maximus** <note>A Roman author of the 1st century AD known for his collection of historical anecdotes.</note> says: *They always considered that all things should be placed after religion: even in those matters where they wished the highest dignity of majesty to be seen.* For this reason, they did not hesitate to make the Empire serve sacred rites; they believed that the future governance of human affairs would go well and consistently only if they had faithfully served the divine power.

Therefore, they are falsely accused of neglecting religion or of having interpreted their religion merely to suit the occasion. **Machiavelli** <note>Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527), the political philosopher who argued in his "Discourses on Livy" that the Romans used religion primarily as a tool for social control and military discipline.</note> charges them with this irreligiousness and strives to prove it. And in this, he is im- <note>The text breaks here; the next page likely begins with "pious" (impius), meaning "impiously" or "wickedly."</note>

# Chapter 4: On the Crimes of Dominion

<margin>
That no nation was more steadfast in religion than the Romans is shown through examples.
</margin>

...is pious, and in that regard he is false. Indeed, no nation was ever more steadfast in religion than the Romans. For this reason, they never referred matters of human affairs to the Senate without first examining the sacred rites. **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC) was a prolific Roman scholar and writer known as "the most learned of the Romans."</note> says: *No matter should be referred to the Senate concerning human affairs before those concerning the divine;* and **Livy** <note>Titus Livius (59 BC–AD 17) wrote a monumental history of Rome, "Ab Urbe Condita."</note> in his sixth book: *The Consuls consulted the Senate on no matter before they consulted them on religious affairs.* Much less did **Papirius** <note>Lucius Papirius Cursor was a Roman general known for his strict adherence to military discipline and religious ritual during the Samnite Wars.</note> interpret the augury according to his own whim, but rather exactly as the **chicken-keeper** <note>original: *pullarius* — a religious official who observed the feeding habits of sacred chickens to determine if the gods favored a planned action.</note> had reported it. For he who attends a sacred omen, if he reports anything false, takes the religious burden of the lie upon himself. 

Thus, that passage in **Livy** concerning the son of Papirius—*born before the doctrine that spurns the gods* <note>original: "ante doctrinam Deos spernentem nato." This refers to a later era of Roman history where skepticism became more common.</note>—should not be understood as referring to the General, who interpreted the **sacred dance** <note>original: *tripudium* — a favorable omen occurring when the sacred chickens ate so hungrily that bits of food fell from their mouths to the ground.</note> just as it had been reported to him; but rather in respect to the chicken-keeper. Because the keeper had lied, he was stationed among the front ranks where, after a spear was rashly thrown, he fell before the standards and thus atoned for his own crime. So too was **Gabinius** <note>Aulus Gabinius was a Roman statesman who was later tried and exiled for accepting a massive bribe to restore the Egyptian King Ptolemy XII to his throne without Senate approval.</note> condemned, as **Dio** <note>Cassius Dio (c. 155–235 AD) was a Roman consul and historian who wrote in Greek.</note> records in Book 39, because he had restored **Ptolemy** to his kingdom with a Roman army against religious protocol and the Decree of the Senate. On this point, **Ammirato** <note>Scipione Ammirato (1531–1601) was an Italian historian who wrote "Discourses on Tacitus" as a direct rebuttal to the perceived "godless" pragmatism of Machiavelli.</note> rightly argues against **Machiavelli** <note>Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527), the author of "The Prince," often criticized by later writers for suggesting that rulers should use religion merely as a tool for control.</note>, a politician of great sharpness and judgment, but of a less healthy and pious mind.

<margin>
By whose example this crime of our nation must be [judged].
</margin>

Since these things are so, it is a shame of our nation to twist religion toward this or that opinion according to the whim of each individual, and even to hold it in total disregard for the sake of the kingdom. For those speeches of great Heroes—that a kingdom is worth a single error, and others of that kind—are not easily to be snatched up as examples. To be sure, I do not deny that in civil matters it is permissible to "round the cape" <note>original: *promontorium flectere* — a nautical metaphor meaning to change one's course or tactics to suit the prevailing winds of politics.</note> and, as **Ulpian** <note>Domitius Ulpianus (c. 170–223 AD) was one of the Great Jurists whose work forms the basis of Roman Law.</note> says, to act in one way and then another; indeed, I consider it worthy of praise. But whether this is permissible indiscriminately, and for everyone, in matters of religion and...
