### Arnold Clapmarius, Book V.

...regarding our faith, to be honest, I have not yet fully explored it. This is especially true because the condition of great Princes is such that they lead others by their own example. I know and approve of that saying by a great and pious Theologian: *The wounds of the Church should be handled gently; however, they must be handled so gently that they do not collect pus and become inflamed due to too soft or superficial care.*

<margin>That the sacred objects of enemies should not be plundered under the pretext of the law of war or the rights of the kingdom.</margin>
It is also a shameful thing for those who dare to plunder and devastate the sacred objects of their enemies, using what they call the **right of the kingdom** <term>jus regni — the legal authority of a sovereign</term> or the **right of war** <term>jus belli — the legal justifications for conduct during armed conflict</term> as a generic excuse. As **Guntherus** <note>Likely Gunther of Pairis (c. 1150–1220), a Cistercian monk whose epic poem *Ligurinus* recounts the deeds of Frederick Barbarossa.</note> writes in his sixth book concerning the Pope's Cardinals:

> *To despoil divine houses, to carry off sacred vessels,*
> *To strip the crosses of their coverings, to tear gold from the books,*
> *To scrape together everything they can with their cruel*
> *Claws and carry off what they have gathered, etc.*

But this is not a "right"; it is the height of impiety. In this regard—by the immortal gods!—how much more humane were the Romans and other nations than we are. **Livy** <note>Titus Livius (59 BC–AD 17), the preeminent historian of Rome.</note> writes in Book 1: *Nevertheless, the temples of the Gods were spared, for so the King’s edict had commanded.* And elsewhere: *An edict was issued that the sacred gold should be left alone.* 

<margin>The piety of Suleiman is praised in this regard.</margin>
In the same way, **Suleiman** <note>Suleiman the Magnificent (r. 1520–1566), the tenth Sultan of the Ottoman Empire, known for his legal reforms and military conquests.</note>, the most excellent Emperor of the Turks, abstained in all his conquests from touching even the sacred objects of his enemies—which were considered "profane" according to his own religion.

<margin>Caesar is also noted.</margin>
Two reasons for this practice occur to me. The first is that he might enjoy the safety of his own sacred rites as a reciprocal benefit, applying the same law during the destruction of cities. The second is that through such piety, he might make himself a figure of veneration both to his own people and to the enemy; being a prudent man, he achieved this. For he was a Prince of such a character that he could be compared to any of the ancients. Therefore, **Caesar** <note>Julius Caesar (100–44 BC).</note>, wishing to win praise for himself and stir up hatred toward **Pompey** <note>Pompey the Great (106–48 BC), Caesar's rival in the Roman Civil War.</note>...

<margin>
A clever argument of the speaker to stir up hatred against Pompey.

<margin>
Objection of modern soldiers.
</margin>
But, our modern soldiers <term>Stratiotae — a term used here for professional soldiers or mercenaries</term> say that this seems too superstitious. To them, I would like to respond with the words of that great man, **Julius Caesar Scaliger** <note>A celebrated Renaissance scholar (1484–1558) who was considered a standard-bearer for classical learning.</note>, who is to me like one of the ancients:

> *No human work is better for increasing divine worship than superstition. Just as ambition itself is a vice, yet is the mother of the greatest virtues, so too is superstition. By gradually removing something from it, you shape it as if by licking a bear cub <note>original: "quasi ursae catulum lambendo formas" — a reference to the ancient folk belief that bear cubs were born unformed and their mothers licked them into shape.</note>. And those who have drunk from that naked and simple religion from the beginning are shaken by even the smallest argument, grow weak with the lightest friction, and finally become atheists <note>original: ἀθεοὶ (atheoi)</note>.*

We know an almost infinite number of such people. Thus speaks the incomparable Scaliger.

### Arnold Clapmarius, Book V. ###

...he killed them, made vulnerable by their own unpopularity. He killed many openly; others, for whom a public accusation would have been too showy and suspicious, he killed secretly; and others he drove into exile, all for the sake of the kingdom's security. **Livy** <note>Titus Livius (64 BC–17 AD), the Roman historian who chronicled the history of Rome from its founding.</note> records the same of his father: **Tarquinius** <note>Tarquinius Superbus, the seventh and final King of Rome, known for his tyrannical rule.</note> killed the leading men of the senate whom he believed favored a revolution. He did this with the intent of wrongly securing the kingdom, taking a perverse example from his own actions. For he possessed no right to the throne other than sheer force. Indeed, by this very path, many have advanced toward power and protected it once seized. And many today would insist upon that same path, were it not for the immortal God opposing their cruelty and impiety.

<margin>
No greater harvest of this fraudulent malice can be found than in the Papacy.
</margin>
Nowhere was there a greater harvest and abundance of this fraudulent malice than in the Papacy. It is said that **Pope Alexander** <note>Alexander VI (r. 1492–1503), born Rodrigo Borgia, whose papacy became synonymous with corruption and nepotism.</note> devised a plan which, due to its monstrosity, has been called wicked: that all the petty rulers <term>Reguli — minor princes or lords of Italian city-states</term> who were under his command should be killed to a last man. This was largely carried out, resulting in the greatest infamy for the Popes among posterity. Furthermore, having prepared a banquet on the **Vatican Hill**, he had decided to remove several Cardinals by poison. But truly, through a servant's error—or rather by the plan of the just and immortal God—he received the Falernian wine <note>A prestigious wine from ancient Italy, often used in literature to denote luxury.</note> from the poisoned bottles, drank it diluted, and died a foul death. Thus, as Livy says, having seemed to act by fraud, he was destroyed by his own reward <note>original: "sua peremptus mercede"</note>.

<margin>
And in the Turkish Empire.
</margin>
The cruelty of the **Turks** <note>Referring to the Ottoman Empire.</note> is similar toward their brothers, kinsmen, Pashas, and Viziers. And since the current Emperor maintains a great many women, no one doubts that the same will happen, according to the custom of the nation <note>A reference to the Ottoman practice of fratricide or "the Law of Fratricide," where a new Sultan would execute his brothers to prevent civil war.</note>. There are, however, those who think that this is the sole foundation of the Turkish Empire...

### CHAPTER VI.

#### *Avenging private injuries through the power of office. The distinction between the public and private person. The Valerian Law concerning Sulla. The Royal Law concerning the sovereignty of Vespasian.*

<margin>Avenging private enmities through the power of office.</margin>
They must be of no character at all (to say nothing harsher) who, being unable to harm someone as private citizens, avenge themselves through the power of their office and command. This might be tolerable in part, were it not for the fact that they believe they do so by right. But you—do not call "Law" that which is repugnant to honor, to your command, and to your dignity; or that which is contrary to the duty of a good judge, as stated in *Law 19 of the Digest, on the office of the prefect* <note>The *Digest* is a massive compendium of Roman legal opinions compiled under Emperor Justinian in the 6th century.</note>. How much more rightly does **Livy** <note>Titus Livius (64 BC – 17 AD), the premier Roman historian.</note> say in Book 39: *It is not a good example for a man to pursue even his own feuds through the exercise of office.* And in Book 42: *An injury,* he says, *though just, should by no means be pursued by a Roman Consul while in office.* 

There is also a sound speech by the Emperor <note>Emperor Tiberius (r. 14–37 AD), often described by historians as "cunning" or "secretive."</note>, otherwise most cunning, in the case of **Piso** <note>Gnaeus Calpurnius Piso was a Roman statesman accused of poisoning the beloved general Germanicus; the trial was a major political scandal.</note>: *For,* he said, *if a subordinate has cast off the boundaries of his duty and his obedience to the Emperor, and has rejoiced at his death and my grief, I shall hate him and banish him from my house, but I will not avenge private enmities with the power of the Prince:* as **Merserus** <note>Josias Mercier (c. 1560–1626), a French scholar known for his influential commentaries on Roman historians.</note> correctly reads it. And the Emperor **Hadrian** <note>Roman Emperor (r. 117–138 AD) known for his travels and building projects, including Hadrian's Wall.</note>, when he was asked whether he would take vengeance on the enemies he had before he attained the throne...

It cites Roman Law and historians like Livy and Tacitus to emphasize that a "good judge" or leader must separate their private feelings from their public duties.</summary>

<header>Arnold Clapmarius, Book V.</header>

...command, would he not wish to take punishment? He replied that they had truly escaped. And Louis XI <note>The author attributes this famous quote to Louis XI, though it is traditionally ascribed to his successor, Louis XII, who was the Duke of Orléans before ascending the throne.</note> was urged by his advisors to punish those whom he knew to be his enemies when he was still the Duke of Orléans; he responded nobly: *“It is not becoming for the King of France to avenge the injuries of the Duke of Orléans.”* Hence the Poet <note>Virgil, in the *Aeneid*.</note> says: *“Jupiter the King is the same for all.”* 

<margin>The court must be separated from the State.</margin>
Indeed, the court must be distinct from the State, just as one persona is private and another is public. To this end, there is a record of Charles V <note>Charles V (1500–1558), Holy Roman Emperor.</note> which I recall seeing: *“We, Charles the Fifth, send greetings to you, Charles, Archduke of Austria, etc.”* <note>original German: "Wir Carll der fünffte / entbieten dir Carll Ertzhertzogen zu Oesterreich / &c." This formal greeting illustrates the distinction between Charles's public role as Emperor and his private/familial relationship with his kinsman.</note>

<margin>The Valerian Law regarding Sulla’s command was an outrage of tyranny.</margin>
What else, then, was that Valerian Law <note>The *Lex Valeria* (82 BC) granted Sulla the office of dictator with total power.</note> which, according to Plutarch, granted Sulla impunity for all past actions and, for the future, the power of life and death, the confiscation of goods, the establishment of colonies, and the right to take away or grant kingdoms at his whim? What else does it smell of but the outrage of Tyranny? Therefore, Cicero rightly calls it *“the most unjust and the least law-like of all laws.”*

<margin>The law concerning Vespasian’s command is praiseworthy.</margin>
How much more praiseworthy is that law concerning the Command of Vespasian <note>The *Lex de Imperio Vespasiani* (69 AD), a bronze tablet of which still survives, formally conferring powers upon Emperor Vespasian.</note>: *“That whatever he shall deem to be for the utility of the State, and according to the majesty of things divine and human, he shall have the right and power to act and to do.”*

<margin>What things are unlawful for a Prince.</margin>
From this it is clear that those things which are contrary to the majesty of the State, as well as to divine laws, are by no means permitted to the Prince.

# CHAPTER VII.

-> *Sending forth assassins and hired killers. Killing an enemy outside the camp and army; poisoning weapons; raging against women. The Roman art. The murder of the Roman consul Marcellus: the crime of assassination.* <-

<margin>Suborning assassins.</margin>
The impudence and monstrous cruelty of those who kill through treachery the men with whom they cannot compete in virtue is truly remarkable. The interpreters of the law call this shameful act the "crime of assassination" <note>original: "crimen assassinatus." In the early modern period, this was a specific legal category for premeditated murder by hire or treachery, often involving a breach of public trust.</note>. As Euripides beautifully wrote:
> No man of spirit deigns to kill an enemy by stealth. 
<note>original Greek: "οὐδεὶς ἀνὴρ ἔμψυχοϛ ἀξιοῖ λάτρα, κτεῖναι τὸν ἐχθρόν." From the play *Andromache*.</note>
*No one of a noble mind kills an enemy secretly.* And this is what Alexander the Great reproached Darius with: *“You undertake impious wars,”* he said, *“and though you have weapons, you bid for the heads of your enemies; just as you—a King of so great an army—recently wished to buy an assassin for a thousand talents to kill me.”* This is what Valerius <note>Valerius Maximus, a Roman author of historical anecdotes.</note> calls *“not deserving victory, but buying it.”* Such a man was that Caepio <note>Quintus Servilius Caepio, a Roman consul who, in 139 BC, bribed the companions of the Lusitanian leader Viriatus to murder him in his sleep.</note>, who arranged for Viriatus to be killed like a pirate or a thief. Or like that Pope, Leo X, who sent the hitman Cavellanus to kill the Duke of Urbino <note>Feltrius refers to Francesco Maria I della Rovere, the Duke of Urbino, of the house of Montefeltro.</note>, whom he was unable to overcome in war or open combat. For to say nothing of the <margin>Why this is a shameful act.</margin> fact that this is done against the Law of Nations <note>term: "jus gentium" (the law of nations). A set of laws considered common to all mankind, governing interactions between states, including the "rules of war."</note>—which, as Livy says, *“the laws of war and arms ought to be conducted no less justly than bravely”*—the nature of war is such that unless a man defeats the spirits of his enemies by fighting openly and by agreement, <margin>Namely, that he alone achieves victory</margin> he achieves no certain victory.
> There is no greater victory, sings the Poet,
> Than that which subdues enemies who have also confessed it in their hearts.
<note>A quote from the poet Claudian, suggesting that true victory requires the enemy to mentally acknowledge their defeat, which does not happen in a sneak attack or assassination.</note>

...openly defeats the enemy.

<summary>This page argues that assassination and the use of hired killers are "crimes of rule" that violate the Law of Nations and the noble spirit of warfare. Using historical examples like Alexander the Great and the Roman Consul Caepio, it asserts that true victory is only won through open, brave combat rather than treachery.</summary>

Therefore, when Adgandestrius <note>A prince of the Chatti, a Germanic tribe.</note>, the Prince of the Chatti, promised the death of Arminius <note>The Germanic leader who famously defeated the Roman legions at the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest.</note> by letter if poison were sent to accomplish the killing, the Roman Senate gave a most praiseworthy response: *that the Roman people take vengeance on their enemies not by fraud, nor by secret means, but openly and in arms.* <note>original: "non fraude, neque occultis, ſed palam, & armatum populum Romanum hoſtes ſuos ulciſci." Quoted from Tacitus, *Annals* 2.88.</note> This voice was truly worthy of Roman majesty. Whence Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> frequently calls this the *Roman art* <note>original: "artem Romanam." This refers to the Roman ideal of winning through military prowess rather than trickery.</note>. By this same example, Alfonso, that King of Naples, replied to Roberto de Pallenta, who offered to kill the King of Castile: "If I knew that by this means I would occupy the entire world, let alone the kingdom of Castile, I would certainly not commit such a crime." The virtue of Fabricius <note>Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, a Roman consul known for his integrity.</note> against Pyrrhus is well known, of which Cicero says: *A single deserter could have ended that great war and removed a grave adversary of our Empire, but it would have been a great disgrace and a scandal; for since it was a contest of honor, the enemy should have been overcome not by crime, but by virtue.* <note>original: "Magnum... bellum perfuga unus... ſed magnum dedecus & flagitium..." From Cicero’s *De Officiis*.</note> So he said. For regarding what they bring up concerning Mucius <note>Mucius Scaevola, who attempted to assassinate King Porsena.</note>, Judith <note>The biblical heroine who beheaded Holofernes in his sleep.</note>, and Flaminius, it is surely a case of *pigs smelling one way, and puppies another* <note>original: "aliter olent ſues, aliter catuli." An Erasmian proverb meaning that different people or situations are judged by different standards; what is a crime for one might be a heroic necessity for another.</note>. And these things are so common that I am almost ashamed to rehash them...

<margin>To kill an enemy outside the camp and the army.</margin>
<margin>To invert the nature of arms, or to infect them with poison.</margin>
But an enemy is not rightly killed everywhere; such as outside the camp and the army. For this reason, David calls those men "wicked" who had killed a righteous man in his own house and while sleeping in his bed <note>A reference to 2 Samuel 4, where the killers of Ish-bosheth are executed by David for their treachery.</note>. However, something else must be said of Marcellus <note>Marcus Claudius Marcellus, a Roman general in the Second Punic War.</note>, who went out to scout along with his military tribunes, and not without a moderate force of cavalry. Add to this that rivers must not be corrupted <note>i.e., poisoned.</note>, much less should weapons be infected with poison. For the nature of weapons is to wound by cutting or piercing; but when they are infected with poison, their very nature and use are inverted. Indeed, these are properly the monstrous crimes of war, and as Cicero calls them, the crimes of...

<margin>
Breaking faith.
</margin>
I find that almost nothing was established in the Roman Republic that did not take its origin from the cradle of the Empire. Seneca suggests this in Book 19, Epistle [108]. 
<margin>
Among the Romans nothing was more ancient than to keep it sacredly.
</margin>
For since from the first birth of the city—through royal institutions and partly also through Laws—the omens, ceremonies, assemblies, appeals, the council of the fathers <note>The Senate.</note>, the classification of cavalry and infantry, and the entire military system were divinely established, etc. It is clearly of such great importance for Republics that firm and valid foundations be laid. The following was not the least of these: that faith and oaths, having driven away the fear of laws and punishments, should rule the city, as Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> says. And posterity observed this so sacredly that among them nothing was more ancient <note>In Latin, *antiquius* (more ancient) often carries the idiomatic meaning of "more important" or "of higher priority."</note> than faith. 
<margin>
Preserved faith is the pillar of the empire.
</margin>
Which the Emperor also says in Law 20 of the Code on Settlements: *nothing is more suited to human faith than to observe agreed pacts.* <note>original: "nihil fidei humanæ magis convenire, quam servare pacta conventa." From the Codex Justinianus.</note> For as to what is objected against us regarding the Numantine, Caudine, and Paetine treaties <note>Refers to various "shameful" treaties made by Roman generals under duress, which the Roman Senate later refused to honor on legal grounds.</note>, that was not treachery, but rather the law and command of both the people and the Prince.

Vitellius

<margin>And the treachery of others is noted.</margin>
...[Vitellius] circumvented the brother of [Flavian] <note>Flavius Sabinus, the elder brother of the future Emperor Vespasian.</note> against the pledge given, and had him slaughtered by soldiers. He then tried in vain to cast the blame upon the soldiers, even though Sabinus had sent a messenger to him with mandates and an inquiry as to why the pacts were being disturbed, as Tacitus reports in his *Histories*. For this reason, Vitellius was later deservedly reproached; because by the slaughter of Sabinus and the burning of the Capitol, the "commerce of war" <note>original: "belli commercia." A Roman legal concept referring to the customary rights and safety of negotiators and the possibility of a mediated peace.</note> had been severed.

<margin>Of Prosper Columna.</margin>
Thus Prosper Columna <note>A famous Italian condottiero or mercenary leader (1452–1523).</note>, when he had been released from prison on the condition that he promise by a signed bond <term>syngrapha</term> <note>A written contract or promissory note signed by both parties.</note> that he would serve under the royal standards, if within a certain time Francis <note>King Francis I of France.</note> wished to use his services upon providing pay; Prosper, acting beneath his dignity, joined himself again to the Imperialists <note>original: "Caesarianis." Those supporting the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.</note>, as Jovius records. On which account Lautrec <note>Odet de Foix, Vicomte de Lautrec, a French military commander.</note> not undeservedly accused him of treachery, with Prosper excusing himself in vain by claiming the necessity of his imprisonment forced the promise.

<margin>Of Pope Julius II.</margin>
In the same way, Pope Julius II dared to boast—by a most shameful example, by Hercules!—that he entered into treaties and alliances with the French and Germans (whom he himself called "Barbarians") for no other reason than for the sake of deception. All these things were done treacherously, and by no right, much less the "Right of Dominion."

<margin>Of Francis, King of the French.</margin>
I do not know if the same could not be said repeatedly of Francis, who, having agreed that he would either ratify the conditions of peace or return to captivity, did neither. <note>This refers to Francis I's failure to uphold the Treaty of Madrid (1526) after being captured by Charles V at the Battle of Pavia.</note>

How much more correctly did the famous Belisarius <note>The great Byzantine general under Emperor Justinian.</note> say in Procopius:
> *It is a base thing,* he said, *O Theodebert, for all others who have even the slightest virtue at heart, but especially for a Prince, to lie and break faith; moreover, I judge that to violate an oath and pacts even sanctioned in writing is not fitting even for the most abject of men.*

For those "petty perjuries" <note>original: "pejuratiunculae."</note>, as Plautus says, are characteristic of parasites, and not at all of kings. Such is the kind of deceit the Poet touches upon:

<margin>
The crime of dominion: craftiness, and the dissolution of pacts regarding religious liberty.
</margin>

> ->Whereby you disturbed the Trojan race,<-
> ->Against law and faith, by breaking the treaty:<-
<note>original: "quo contra jura fidemque / Iliacam, rupto turbasti foedere gentem." A quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (X.91), where Juno is accused of inciting the breaking of a peace treaty.</note>

That dissolution of pacts regarding the liberty of religion is also nothing other than a "crime of dominion" <note>original: "flagitium dominationis." This refers to an act where a ruler abandons law in favor of raw power.</note>: just as that slow and crafty butchery of minds of which Nazianzenus <note>Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390 AD), a prominent theologian. He is likely referring to the Emperor Julian’s subtle methods of undermining Christianity without outright martyrdom.</note> speaks. "That behavior," he says, "is truly wicked and malignant; for since he could not entice us openly, nor compel us through tyranny, he wished—out of shame—to drape a fox’s skin over a lion’s <note>A classic metaphor for combining brute force with deceptive cunning.</note>, or, if you prefer, to drape the mask of Minos <note>In mythology, Minos was a judge of the underworld; here it implies a mask of false justice or stern legality.</note> over the highest injustice, gently applying force." 

It is pleasing to adorn this chapter with a "crown" <note>A rhetorical flourish or concluding example.</note> concerning the Emperor Claudius. When he was asked to pardon Mithridates <note>Mithridates of Bosporus, a client king who rebelled against Rome.</note>, he hesitated whether it would be better to accept the captive under a pact of safety, or to reclaim him by force of arms. To be sure, the latter was uncertain and difficult; but the former was safe, yet joined with the necessity of keeping one's word <term>fides</term> <note>A central Roman virtue involving trust, reliability, and the keeping of oaths.</note>.

<margin>
*Either faith must not be given, or once given, it must be kept.*
</margin>
For either faith must not be pledged, or once pledged, it must be kept. To those who refuse to grasp this, I only recall to their memory the calamities which for the most part—indeed, always—follow and await the perjured and the treacherous, as if stalking them from behind. Regarding all these matters, see more in the works of Hotman <note>François Hotman (1524–1590), a French legal scholar and writer known for his works on sovereignty and resistance.</note> and others.

## CHAPTER IX.

->*Deceiving under the guise of a parley. Violating the laws of hospitality.*<-

*He circumvents enemies under the guise of friendship and a parley.*

Furthermore, Princes can defend themselves by no law when they circumvent their enemies under the guise of friendship and a parley <note>original: "colloquii." In this manner, the famous [Mark] Antony, against the law of nations, ordered the King of the Armenians <note>Artavasdes II, whom Antony lured to a meeting and then captured in 34 BC.</note> to be killed after enticing him with the appearance of friendship; and Tiberius drove the King of the Cappadocians <note>King Archelaus, who was summoned to Rome by Tiberius in 17 AD and died shortly thereafter in disgrace.</note> to his death after he had been summoned through deceit.

# On the Crimes of Dominion, Chapter 9. 241

<margin>
Among the Turks, there is almost none.
</margin>
Even today, those who emulate Roman military discipline above all others nevertheless return to the character of barbarians—that is, their own natural disposition—in this: that they set little value upon the laws of hospitality and diplomatic conference, and indeed violate them most shamefully. For example, not so long ago, Mahomet <note>Likely Sultan Mehmed II, known as "The Conqueror."</note> summoned Stephen, the King of Bosnia and Rascia, and Mailat, the Voivode of Transylvania, to him under the guise of goodwill, and then ordered them to be flayed alive <note>original: "vivosque excoriari jussit"</note> after seizing Stephen's provinces, as Traduccius records in *The Conquerable Turk*.

<margin>
Whether Caesar is beyond blame in the slaughter of Commius.
</margin>
Regarding Commius <note>A leader of the Atrebates who initially served Caesar but later joined the Gallic rebellion under Vercingetorix.</note>, whom Caesar wished to kill through the pretense of a conference, there is a controversy. For in my judgment, Caesar is not entirely beyond blame, even though Commius, having been reconciled to the Romans so many times, very often rebelled and returned to his old ways <note>original: "ad vomitum rediit," literally "returned to his vomit," a biblical idiom for repeating a folly.</note>. This man’s ferocity and hostility easily provoked Caesar; otherwise, Caesar observed the laws of conference most sacredly. For he said of himself: *Lest it be said that they were circumvented by him through a breach of faith during a conference, etc.* <note>original: "Ne, inquit, dici possit, eos a se per fidem in colloquio circumventos, &c." From Caesar’s *Gallic Wars*.</note>

<margin>
The origin of "amistia" and Commius.
</margin>
Furthermore, that which Caesar himself testifies regarding Commius is memorable: *That he asked for only one thing, that it be granted to his fear <note>original: "timori suo," referring to a state of extreme distrust or "amistia."</note> that he never come into the sight of any Roman.* There was the same "amistia" <note>A term derived from Greek meaning a lack of trust or a state of being "un-mixable," often used to describe deep-seated suspicion following a betrayal.</note> in Pompeo Colonna <note>A powerful Italian cardinal (1479–1532) often at odds with the Papacy.</note>, who, when recalled to Rome by the Pope, could be induced by no pledges or hostages to return to the city. This kind of hesitation and distrust is born from a faith that has been suspected and violated.

### Chapter X.

->The punishments of Eusebius, Herdinus, Dolabella, Vespinus, and others. Providers of dominion, architects of empires. The Notorious. The Eulogy.<-

<margin>To suppress those suspected merely by rumor as enemies of the State without ordinary process.</margin>
It is true that sometimes the safety of the State demands that enemies of the Republic be suppressed "in the blade" <note>original: "in herba," an agricultural metaphor for stopping something before it grows or takes root</note> and without any, as we say, ordinary <term>process</term> <note>Legal "ordinary process" refers to the standard, formal steps of a trial or judicial inquiry.</note>. But indeed, this practice is appropriate not for those who are merely suspected, but for those whose crime is manifest and notorious. For those who hurry defendants to punishment—whether through the treachery of accusers or for some slight reason, and suspected only from rumor, but neither convicted nor condemned—do so not by the right of dominion, nor *properly* <note>original Greek: κυρίως (kyriōs), meaning in a legitimate or authoritative sense</note>, as Aristotle says. Tiberius remarks on this in Tacitus, *Annals*, Book 3: *He was not indeed unaware of what was being spread about Silanus, but one must not decide based on rumor.* <note>C. Junius Silanus was a proconsul of Asia accused of extortion and treason; Tiberius argues here for a degree of judicial restraint against gossip.</note> And elsewhere: *I beg you, do not take the alleged crimes as proven just because the cause is connected to my own grief.*

<margin>Examples of this monstrosity in Marcellinus.</margin>
Mention of this monstrosity <note>original: "immanitatis," referring to the savage disregard for legal norms</note> occurs nowhere more frequently than in the *History* of Ammianus Marcellinus, as in Book 14: *as if license were granted to cruelty, certain people, judged through the clouds of suspicion, were condemned as guilty.* And he speaks of a certain Eusebius <note>Eusebius was a high-ranking official (praepositus sacri cubiculi) under Emperor Constantius II; he was eventually executed under the later Emperor Julian.</note>, who, imploring heaven for justice, was punished with a death sentence, though he had neither confessed nor been proven guilty. And elsewhere: *With an enemy pressing him, or even none at all, this alone being sufficient: that he had been named, reported, or accused.* In the same place, regarding the outrages of Constantius: *And now, with the trumpets of internal destruction sounding; his turbulent nature raged, no longer secretly as before, but twisted away from the consideration of truth; with no one solemnly inquiring into the reliability of the charges or their authors, nor distinguishing the innocent from the company of the guilty, just as*

<meta>The text cuts off here at the catchword "veluti," which will lead into a comparison or simile on the following page.</meta>

<summary>This page argues that while the state may occasionally bypass legal formalities for its own safety, it should only do so when crimes are "notorious" and proven, rather than acting on mere rumor or political suspicion. Clapmarius cites the Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus to illustrate the "monstrosity" of legal systems that condemn the innocent alongside the guilty during times of political turmoil.</summary>

...as if driven out, all justice departed from the courts; with the legal defense of cases falling silent, the executioner became the broker of plunder, and the abduction of persons and the confiscation of goods were carried out everywhere throughout the eastern provinces. <margin>Suetonius.</margin> Suetonius says the same regarding the Emperor Galba: he condemned certain distinguished men of both the senatorial and equestrian orders on the slightest suspicion and without a hearing; so much so that, as Tacitus adds, they perished as if they were innocent. <margin>Curtius.</margin> And Curtius, writing of Alexander the Great in Book 3, notes that he killed many men distinguished in war—the very men who had helped him conquer so many nations—without a trial <note>original: "indicta causa," a legal term meaning "without the case being pleaded" or "without a hearing."</note>. <margin>Livy.</margin> And Livy in Book 1 writes of Herdinius, who was put to death without a trial; and Cicero, in his orations against Verres, records that highly honorable and upright men were made defendants in their absence and were condemned and exiled without a hearing. <margin>The crime is condemned.</margin> Under what guise, you will ask? Doubtless under the pretext of "Dominion" <note>Clapmarius uses "Dominatio" to refer to the absolute, often hidden, power of a ruler used to preserve the state.</note> acting against conspirators. But O the wickedness, O the crime! Is it really necessary for a kingdom to be preserved through such examples of cruelty and injustice? And even if this were so, who among mortals, I ask, will believe a Prince in a matter so doubtful, so suspicious, and so hateful? Truly, as Livia says in Dio Cassius, Book 52: <term>χαλεπώτατα οἱ πολλοὶ πείθονται, ὅτι τις ἄοπλός ὤν, ἐπιβουλεύει τῷ ὡπλισμένῳ</term> <note>original Greek: "The masses are most difficult to convince that someone who is unarmed is plotting against one who is armed."</note>: the common people believe only with the greatest difficulty that an unarmed man is laying snares for one who is armed. <margin>Those who openly teach such crimes to Princes are marked for criticism.</margin> And yet, there are those found who openly teach these types of crimes to Princes. Tacitus says: Vitellius, as the "Masters of Dominion" crept into his confidence, became more arrogant and cruel, and ordered Dolabella to be killed. For this was the name given to those who were skilled in these arts of dominion, just as there were once masters of writing, of the public records, of the <term>Vicesima</term> <note>The *vicesima hereditatium* was a 5% Roman inheritance tax; the "masters" were the specialist administrators of these departments.</note>, and of livestock. By Livy they are also called the "Architects of Empires." Hence Tacitus in the 12th book of his *Annals* calls them <term>provisores ingruentium dominationum</term> <note>original Latin: "Foreseers (or providers) of encroaching tyrannies."</note>. Nero was taught these same arts to the letter...

<header>Arnold Clapmarius, Book V.</header>

<margin>Nero was openly taught [in these ways].</margin>
Take Nero, of whom the same Tacitus writes: *Nero killed Vespinus <note>Likely Atticus Vestinus; the OCR "Vespinum" reflects a common variation in early modern editions of Tacitus.</note>, without any crime, accuser, or informer, having turned to the violence of Dominion* <note>original: "Nero Vespinum, sine ullo crimine & accusatore & indice ad vim Dominationis conversus occidit."</note>. Of the same sort is the response of Emperor Henry IV when he was warned not to hang Reinold, the Count of Burgundy: *The heaven,* he said, *He gave to the Lord of heaven, but the earth He gave to the children of men* <note>original: "Cœlum, inquit, cœli domino, terram autem dedit filiis hominum." A cynical use of Psalm 115:16 to justify earthly tyranny.</note>. Everything was done impiously, unjustly, and wickedly, and thus by this crime of dominion.

<margin>An objection in favor of this crime.</margin>
But those advocates for the "Arts of Dominion" <note>Clapmarius often uses "candidati" to refer to those who study or aspire to the methods of absolute rule.</note> argue in return that many of these victims were actually guilty. Yet I see no reason why they could not have been punished according to the laws and through the ordinary legal process, if they were indeed guilty. Tiberius spoke excellently—and contrary to his usual character—and I would wish this to be like an oracle for Princes: *Power should not be used where the laws can act* <note>original: "non utendum esse imperio, ubi legibus agi possit."</note>. And Livy says of Philopoemen, the leader of the Achaeans: *It was not because he wished them to be saved, but because he did not want them to perish without their case being heard* <note>original: "indicta causa," a technical legal term for a case decided without a defense being presented.</note>. In this regard, Curtius criticizes Alexander in Book 8: *The slaughter of no one excited greater hatred against him among the Greeks than that of a man endowed with the best character and skills, whom he not only killed, but even tortured without his case being heard; a cruelty followed by late repentance.* And as a rule, the Emperors did not wish anyone to be condemned rashly without an accuser: regarding this, see the work of Cujacius <note>Jacques Cujas, a famous 16th-century French legal scholar.</note> *Book 1, observation chapter 33,* and Tertullian. Not even on the basis of notorious reports or the records of officials or peace officers <note><term>Irenarcharum</term>: Ancient Roman police officials tasked with maintaining the peace and capturing criminals.</note>, as is stated in *law 6 of the Code regarding the custody and production of the accused*. Because, as Marcianus says in that same law, *it is well known that not everyone writes such records in good faith.* Therefore, the Pope was right to place the Florentines under interdict <note>A form of ecclesiastical strike where most sacraments are forbidden to a community.</note> because they had thrown Archbishop Salviati <note>Francesco Salviati, who was involved in the Pazzi Conspiracy against the Medici in 1478; he was lynched from the window of the Palazzo Vecchio.</note> from the windows, hanging by a rope, without a hearing.

# CHAPTER XI.

->Waging war without cause, placing Right in arms;<-
->feigning causes for war; pitting others against each other;<-
->and the touch of injustice cast upon the Romans in<-
->the seizure of Cyprus. <term>Forced Service</term><note>original: "Angreia," a Latinization of the Greek "angareia," referring to the state's power to press persons or property into public service, often used here to denote the burdens of war.</note>.<-

<margin>Waging war without cause out of a mere lust for ruling.</margin>
The <term>lust for ruling</term><note>original: "cupiditas dominandi." A central concept in political theory describing the addictive nature of power.</note> among mortals is immense and profound. No one is content with even the greatest empire; today, having occupied a kingdom, tomorrow he pants for others, and does so, as they say, by the "right" of his own kingdom and power. But would you truly call that "right" to me, in which there is not even a shadow of justice? And yet, they believe themselves to be superior to others; of whom the Lyric Poet <note>Referring to the Roman poet Horace in his *Ars Poetica*.</note> says:

> If by chance he represents the honored Achilles,
> Let him deny that laws were made for him, and claim everything through arms.
> <note>original: "Honoratum si forte reponit Achillem, / Iura neget sibi nata, nihil non arroget armis."</note>

And Seneca in *Hercules Furens*, Act 2:

> Right lies in arms; fear oppresses the laws.
> <note>original: "Ius est in armis, opprimit leges timor."</note>

Such is that saying of Tiridates <note>A King of Armenia whose words were recorded by the historian Tacitus.</note>: *In the highest fortune, that which is stronger is more equitable; to keep one's own belongs to a private house, but to fight for what belongs to others is the glory of a king.* And that saying of the Gauls in Livy, Book 5: *That they carry their right in their arms, and all things belong to the brave.* Similar to this is the response of that Bajazet <note>Bajazet I (r. 1389–1402), Sultan of the Ottoman Empire.</note>, the Emperor of the Turks; who, being warned by the ambassadors of Sigismund <note>Sigismund of Luxembourg, then King of Hungary and later Holy Roman Emperor.</note> to stay away from Bulgaria, led the ambassadors into his armory and, smiling, indicated that his "right" was placed there—certainly in his weapons; and that it extended beyond Bulgaria to the ends of the earth. Almost the same is the reasoning of the Popes, so much so that they claim the words of the Prophet for themselves, quite ridiculously and preposterously: *He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth.* <note>original: Psalm 72:8. Clapmarius is criticizing the Papacy for using biblical mandates for spiritual rule to justify earthly territorial expansion.</note> Concerning these, see the books of the *Pontifical Ceremonies*. The Romans indeed, and especially while the Republic stood, hardly any...

...they waged war, unless provoked by injuries, either themselves or their allies and confederates. However, they are not excused by me in all things. Concerning the military occupation of Cyprus—which is to say, its candid seizure—Ammianus Marcellinus <note>A 4th-century Roman soldier and historian known for his objective accounts of the later Roman Empire.</note> always writes: *It does not shame me to say,* he says, *that the Roman people invaded this island more out of greed than justice. They pretend various causes for war.

Pitting others against each other so that you may devour them once they are drained by mutual wars.

Of the same character are those who search for causes for war and, finding none, invent specious pretexts. <note>original: "prophases," from the Greek "prophasis," meaning a false excuse or an alleged reason that hides the true motive.</note> Just like those who set others against each other, so that they might eventually devour those who have been drained by mutual wars. This was an art practiced by that Pope of whom Jovius <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), an Italian physician and historian.</note> writes in his *Life of Colonna*: He nourished the controversy between the Colonna and the Orsini families <note>Two powerful rival noble families in Renaissance Rome whose feuds often destabilized the Papacy.</note> immensely with wondrous pretense: favoring now these, now those, and secretly supplying money and arms to both, so that once they were worn down by mutual disasters, they might finally be destroyed by him without any trouble. And Tacitus <note>The famous Roman historian known for his analysis of power and corruption.</note> writes concerning Drusus in the second book of his *Annals*: *Drusus sought no small glory by enticing the Germans into discords, so that, once Maroboduus was broken, they might be pursued even unto their destruction.* <note>original: "Drusus non mediocre decus quæsivit, inliciens Germanos ad discordias..." Maroboduus was a King of the Marcomanni who became a threat to Rome.</note>

Even in private life there are such pests among men.

## CHAPTER XII.

*Abolishing taxes; alienating the assets of the empire. Taxes pledged as collateral by Charles IV; and in passing <note>original: "en parodō"</note>, can they be reclaimed? Augustus's military treasury. The one-percent tax on goods for sale.*

Deservedly does Ulpian <note>Domitius Ulpianus, a prominent 3rd-century Roman jurist whose writings formed a large part of the Digest of Justinian.</note> call taxes <term>vectigalia</term> <note>Specifically, revenues derived from public lands or customs, though here used for state revenue in general.</note> the "sinews of the State." Tacitus provides the reason in the 4th book of his *Histories*: "For neither can the peace of nations be maintained without arms, nor arms without pay, nor pay without taxes." Cicero also writes in his *Letters to his brother Quintus*: "An empire cannot in any way be maintained without taxes." For by these, the principality is sustained, and enough remains for sudden gifts, necessities, and extraordinary expenses. 

For this reason, when the Emperor Nero wished to abolish all taxes and give that "most beautiful gift to the human race," the Roman Senate taught him otherwise. They said that the "dissolution of the Empire would follow if the fruits by which the State is sustained were diminished." They argued that if <margin>Alienating the assets of the empire.</margin> customs duties were removed, it would naturally follow that the abolition of all other taxes would be demanded. 

Indeed, it is a "crime of rule" <note>Clapmarius uses "flagitium dominationis" to describe actions that seem beneficial but actually undermine the state's survival.</note> specifically where the assets of the Empire are alienated <note>The legal act of transferring ownership or rights of state property to private individuals or foreign powers.</note>. For how can that be worthy of the name of "law" <margin>A Prince cannot alienate the assets of the empire.</margin> which overturns the State? And this is the nearly universal opinion of legal scholars: that the Prince, though he may be all-powerful, cannot alienate the assets of the empire. For these can no more be drained or <sig>L 4</sig> <meta>eviscerated (catchword: evisce-)</meta> than the private inheritances of citizens.

<summary>Clapmarius begins Chapter 12 by arguing that taxation is the essential "sinew" of a state and that rulers commit a grave error (a "crime of rule") when they attempt to abolish taxes or sell off state assets, as this inevitably leads to the empire's collapse.</summary>

<keywords>taxation, state revenue, Ulpian, Tacitus, Nero, alienation of assets, fiscal policy, sovereignty, Roman Law</keywords>

<page-num>248</page-num>
<header>Arnold Clapmarius, Book V.</header>

...ought to be eviscerated <note>original: "eviscerari debent"</note>, to use the Emperor's own word.

<margin>Tolls pledged by Charles IV to the estates of the Empire diminished Imperial power.</margin>
For this reason, those tolls <note>original: "telonia"</note> and taxes <term>vectigalia</term> <note>State revenues, often derived from customs or public lands.</note> that were pledged as collateral by Charles IV <note>Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1346–1378), known for the Golden Bull of 1356.</note> to the Estates of the Empire—as Johannes Nauclerus <note>A German historian and theologian (d. 1510) known for his "Chronicon."</note> testifies—wonderfully diminished the power of the Emperor. Julius Pflug, the Bishop of Naumburg, argued this point forcefully in a certain speech. Yet, I do not know whether a revocation of these pledges would not violently disturb the current state of the Republic. First, because by such a measure, the affairs of the Empire would slide back to their former condition. Secondly, because the remaining Estates would be stripped of nearly all their power—to say nothing of the fact that the equality between the Estates would perish, which Machiavelli <note>Niccolò Machiavelli, the Florentine political philosopher.</note> so greatly approves of and embraces in his book *On the State of Germany*.

<margin>The safety of the Republic is situated almost entirely in its taxes.</margin>
Nor does the opinion of the legal experts <note>original: "ICtorum," an abbreviation for Iurisconsultorum.</note> on this matter escape me, though it is not permitted to harvest their fruit in this place <note>The author means he will not delve into the complex legal arguments of the jurists here.</note>. To me, certainly, the entire safety of the Republic seems to be situated in its taxes. For this reason, Hannibal acted excellently: he not only did not abolish the old taxes, but even added new ones. In doing so, as Æmilius Probus <note>A name often used in the Renaissance to refer to Cornelius Nepos, the Roman biographer.</note> testifies, he ensured not only that there was money to be paid to the Romans according to the treaty, but even that a surplus remained to be placed in the treasury. Conversely, it brought much ill-will upon Pope Leo X, as Jovius <note>Paolo Giovio, a 16th-century historian and biographer.</note> reports, because after contracting heavy debt, he surrendered public taxes to moneylenders. For private wealth can be dispersed, but not public wealth. Just as Nicephorus Botoniates <note>Byzantine Emperor (r. 1078–1081).</note>, upon seizing the empire, abolished everything owed to the treasury in its entirety and instituted "new tablets" <note>original: "novas tabulas," a Roman term for the total cancellation of debts.</note> by a magnificent edict, as is recorded in the *Eastern Constitutions*.

<margin>The military treasury</margin>
The memory of that military treasury <note>original: "ærarium militare," a fund established by Augustus to pay retirement bonuses to veteran soldiers.</note> which Augustus established stirs me at this point.

<page-num>249</page-num>
<header>On the Crimes of Rule, Chapter 13.</header>
<sig>L 5</sig>

<margin>The military treasury was the foundation of Augustus's rule.</margin>
Augustus established a military treasury <note>original: "ærarium militare"</note>, into which was paid the twentieth part <note>A 5% inheritance tax known as the "vicesima hereditatium."</note> of all inheritances, legacies, and gifts made in expectation of death <note>original: "mortis causa"</note>. Exceptions were made for those left to the closest of kin, agnates <term>agnatis</term> <note>Relatives through the male line.</note>, and the poor. To this, he later added the hundredth part <note>A 1% sales tax known as the "centesima rerum venalium."</note> of all goods for sale, specifically those sold by the Roman princes at auction. This arrangement was the very foundation of the Roman Principate. During that time, the annual pay for the soldiers—calculated in our currency—amounted to five million, five hundred sixteen thousand, sixty-two pounds, and ten shillings, according to the reckoning of Savilius <note>Sir Henry Savile (1549–1622), an English scholar and translator of Tacitus.</note>. This sum is thought to be greater than what the Great Turk <note>The Ottoman Sultan, used here as a benchmark for extreme wealth.</note> receives today in two years from all his combined revenues. For this reason, when the people pleaded for relief, Tiberius declared that the military treasury relied upon the support of that one-percent sales tax.

### CHAPTER XIII.

*Immense donations, or rather princely extravagances: and whether they can be retracted by successors. Donations abolished by the Court of Paris.*

<margin>Tiberius's decree—that successors should not ratify benefits from predecessors unless they themselves granted them—and why it is useful.</margin>
There was a decree by the same Tiberius stating that benefits granted by previous Princes should not be considered valid by their successors unless they themselves granted the same favors to the same people. While this rule is of great use regarding granted properties in general, it was especially necessary because of the immense scale of princely donations. For what if Nero had abolished all the taxes of the Empire? Should his successors have been bound by such a ruinous decree? Indeed, the Republic ought not to suffer for the faults committed by a Prince, just as Gunther <note>Gunther of Pairis (c. 1150–1220), a Cistercian monk and poet who wrote "Ligurinus," an epic on the deeds of Frederick Barbarossa.</note> beautifully sings regarding sacred matters in his second book.

<page-num>250</page-num>
<header>Arnold Clapmarius, Book V.</header>

For it is not right that what a pastor has done unjustly should be turned back into a loss for the Church <note>original: "Neque enim quod pastor inique Gesserit, Ecclesiae fas est in damna refundi." A legal principle suggesting that the institution should not suffer for the personal failings of its leader.</note>. This was also a restriction placed upon the Roman Principate; just as Pliny the Younger says in his *Panegyric* concerning the law of the Empire: *“It is worth noting these words, which were undertaken on behalf of our Empire: [that the gods protect you] only if you have ruled the Republic well and for the benefit of all.”* <note>Pliny’s *Panegyricus* was a speech addressed to the Emperor Trajan, emphasizing that the Emperor's power is conditional upon his service to the state.</note>

<margin>Princely extravagances may be retracted not without merit.</margin>
From this, it is clear that princely extravagances of this kind are retracted with good reason. For I do not listen here to those who deny that the concept of "extravagance" can even be applied to a Prince. Lampridius <note>A presumed author of the *Augustan History*.</note> writes beautifully concerning Alexander Severus: *“A day never passed without him doing something gentle, civic, or pious; but he did so in such a way that he did not overturn the treasury.”* Nero, however, had squandered—says the historian <note>Tacitus, in his *Histories*.</note>—two billion, two hundred million sesterces <note>original: "bis & vicies mille sestertium." A staggering sum equivalent to a significant portion of the empire's annual budget.</note>. Therefore, when Galba seized power and found himself in need of money, he ordered that individuals be publicly summoned to return their gifts, with only a tenth part of the previous Emperor's generosity allowed to remain with each recipient. On this, Tacitus says: *“It was most just that it should be recovered from the very source of the scarcity.”* <note>Meaning it was fair to take money back from those who had grown rich off the waste that caused the current financial crisis.</note> And Tiberius rightly says in the second book of the *Annals* by the same author: *“If all the poor began to come here and seek money for their children, the individuals would never be satisfied, and the Republic would fail.”* Furthermore, he rebukes those who break into the treasury; for if it is exhausted by ambition, it must be replenished through crimes. From this follows the situation that Marcus Tullius Cicero deplores: that the incomes of private citizens are most abundant, while the tax revenues are almost nothing. How much more blessed was that Republic of which Horace writes in his second book of *Odes*:

> *For them, private wealth was small,*
> *But the common wealth was great.* <note>original: "Privatus illis census erat brevis, / Commune magnum." From Horace, Carmina 2.15, contrasting the frugality of early Romans with the luxury of his own time.</note>

<margin>The Law of Philip</margin>
For this reason, in France, Philip of Valois <note>Philip VI (r. 1328–1350), the first Valois king of France.</note>, by a law passed, ordered the Prince’s grants to be revoked, unless [they were confirmed] by records...

<header>Arnold Clapmarius, Book V.</header>
<meta>catchword: against,</meta>

Taken from Plato: <note>original Greek: "αἱ γὰρ τῶν τυράννων δεήσεις οἶσθ’ ὅτι μεμιγμέναι ἀνάγκαις"</note> *For you know that the requests of tyrants are mingled with compulsions.* Cicero mentions this same idea in his *Letters to Atticus*. The same is found in that saying of Dio regarding Nero: *No law is more powerful than weapons; for just as each man is most powerful, so he seems to say and do all things with the greatest justice.* Hence Aristotle in the 6th book of his *Politics*, chapter 3, says: <note>original Greek: "ἀεὶ γὰρ ζητῆσι τὸ ἴσον καὶ τὸ δίκαιον οἱ ἥττες, οἱ δ' κρατῶντες, οὐδὲν φροντίζουσι"</note> *The weaker always seek equality and justice, but those who are in control care nothing for it.* Always the more feeble seek what is fair and just, but those who have more power think little of such things. And yet, it is a crime of kingship to exempt others who are polluted by the same offense. To this Juvenal alludes:

> Let Clodius <note>A Roman politician known for his scandalous behavior</note> accuse adulterers, and Catiline <note>A famous conspirator</note> accuse Cethegus.

And that well-worn proverb:

> A Hebrew does nothing against a Hebrew; Catiline does nothing against Cethegus. <note>A contemporary proverb suggesting that criminals or distinct social groups protect their own from the law.</note>

And these are generally the crimes of secret domination. For just as those rights and secrets of domination <term>jura et arcana dominationis: the technical legal and strategic tools used to maintain power</term> have their place in a kingdom or a Princedom, so these "crimes of rule" are usurped by tyrants. Even the smallest of these crimes make Princes hated and expose them to the plots of the citizens. The Tragic poet <note>Seneca the Younger</note> says truly and sharply in the play *Octavia*:

> The people always demand more from the one at the top.

# On the Crimes of Rule, Chapter 18.

...on the contrary, those things which others claim are permissible for Princes, we say refer back to tyranny.

<margin>Aristocratic crimes of rule</margin>
Moreover, there are nearly as many aristocratic crimes, and they almost exactly match those of an **Oligarchy** <note>Rule by a small, often corrupt elite group</note>: and yet, most of the crimes of kings can be applied here as well. Certainly, in the same Roman Republic, the Consuls, Dictators, and Decemvirs held a power that was almost the same as the royal authority of the Triumvirs.

<margin>Royal [crimes]. That Roman Consuls, the Dictator, Decemvirs, and Triumvirs held royal power.</margin>
Regarding the Consuls, Cicero says: *Let there be two with royal power,* <note>original Latin: "Duo regio imperio sunto"</note> and the Poet writes:

->Rome sees nothing higher<-
->than the Consul in his supreme martial power.<-
<note>Original Latin: "Nullum martia summo / Altius Imperio Consule Roma videt." From the poet Claudian.</note>

And the matter is plain before the **Terentillian law** <note>A proposed Roman law intended to document and limit the arbitrary power of the consuls</note>, which was later passed concerning the reduction of Consular power. Concerning the **Decemvirs** <note>A ten-man commission established to codify Roman law</note>, Livy writes: *Then, upon the opinion of Appius Claudius, a decree of the Senate was made that, with the other magistrates being abolished, Decemvirs should be created with consular and royal power, and without the right of appeal.* And in Book 3, he adds: *They had the appearance of ten kings.* Concerning the Dictatorship, Cicero says in the first of his *Philippics*: *He utterly removed the Dictatorship from the Republic, which had already seized the force of royal power.* He likewise calls the rule of **Sulla** <note>A Roman general who seized power as dictator</note> a "Lordship," and Tacitus says in Book 1 of his *Annals*: *Neither Cinna's nor Sulla's lordship lasted long.* Nor is there reason for others to object; it is one thing to be a King, and another to hold royal power. For I know that Cicero himself distinguishes them in the first *Philippic*: *...not only having removed the kingship, which we had endured, but also royal power.* I have chosen to present this here so that it may be understood that aristocratic crimes are almost the same as those that were royal.

# Of the Crimes of Rule, Chapter 18.

<margin>Regarding Lucius Siccius, killed by the decemvirs.</margin>
They forged judgments at home and pronounced them in the forum; if anyone appealed to a colleague, he departed from the one he had approached in such a state that he regretted not having stood by the original decree. And by this crime, the famous Lucius Siccius <note>Lucius Siccius Dentatus, often called the "Roman Achilles" for his bravery; he was murdered by the Decemvirs for his opposition to their rule</note> was killed by the **Decemvirs** <note>original: "Decemviris"; a ten-man commission that seized absolute power in Rome around 450 BCE</note>.

<margin>The daughter of Lucius Virginius.</margin>
The same wickedness belonged to Appius Claudius, who, in order to gain possession of Lucius Virginius's daughter through love, after he noticed everything was walled off by her modesty, turned his mind to cruel and arrogant force, as Livy says. The story is well known and need not be inserted here <note>Referring to the story of Verginia, whose father killed her to protect her from Appius Claudius’s lust, sparking a revolution against the Decemvirs</note>. But those proscriptions were the most shameful of all, about which Velleius Paterculus <note>A Roman historian (c. 19 BCE – 31 CE)</note> writes thus:

<margin>Sulla, with his indiscriminate proscriptions.</margin>
> "Sulla," he said, "was the first to invent the example of proscription; so that in a city where a legal judgment for a petty insult <note>original: "petulantis convicii"</note> is granted even to a worn-out actor, in that same city a bounty was established for the murder of a citizen; and he who killed the most received the greatest reward; nor was the prize for an enemy killed in battle more abundant than for a citizen; and every man became the price for his own death."

These are Paterculus's words. I am almost inclined to also include here the matter of the Fabii <note>The three Fabii brothers were Roman ambassadors who broke the law of nations by attacking the Gauls they were sent to negotiate with</note>, whom the Gauls demanded be handed over to them because they had taken up arms against the **law of nations** <note>original: "jus gentium"; the ancient equivalent of international law</note>. Livy says in Book 5, regarding the Senate:

> "The deed of the Fabii did not please them, and the Barbarians seemed to be demanding what was right; but lest the Senate decree that which was right, political ambition stood in the way among men of such great nobility."

Unless perhaps you say that the Romans, with great spirit, preferred to endure a war with the Gauls than to hand over men of such great name in the Republic to the enemy.

# CHAPTER XIX.

*The crimes of popular rule. Vicious liberty. The fraud of Manlius: Adjudicating a controversy between others for himself: And a brief discussion on whether Brutus rightly killed Caesar.*

<margin>Crimes of rule are most common in a popular state.</margin>
<margin>That the common people are prone to cruelty.</margin>
Indeed, almost all these crimes of rule are nowhere in greater use than in a popular state. Whatever that **Etruscan** <note>original: "Hetruscus"; referring to Niccolò Machiavelli, who was from Florence in Tuscany (ancient Etruria). Clapmar is critiquing Machiavelli’s preference for republics over princedoms</note> says to extol the virtue of the people and disparage Princes has already been refuted by others. For the common people are like a beast; and as Claudius <note>Likely referring to the Emperor Claudius or Appius Claudius</note> used to say, just as they are prone to mercy, so are they immoderate in cruelty. They are ruled by no reason but by unbridled impulse, having little regard for divine or human laws, provided they can protect that "liberty" of theirs—which is, in truth, a most dissolute license to do all things as they please. Regarding this, the Roman Lyric poet <note>Horace, in *Ars Poetica*</note> wrote:

> *But Liberty fell into vice, and a violence*
> *Deserving of being restrained by law.*

<margin>Under the pretext of liberty.</margin>
<margin>They hold a hereditary hatred for the Patricians.</margin>
And **Jovius** <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), an Italian physician and historian</note> says: "There was one particularly bitter pretext for cruelty and plundering—that liberty of a most sweet name (as they proclaimed it) which had been accepted for a long time." This is also what **Quinctius** <note>Titus Quinctius Capitolinus Barbatus, a Roman statesman</note>, that Roman Consul, says in **Livy**, book 3: *Under the title of equalizing the laws, we have borne and continue to bear our rights being oppressed.* Just as centurions, according to **Tacitus**, are the "oldest material of military hatred," so too was the hatred of the <term>plebs</term> <note>The common citizens of Rome</note> against the <term>Patricians</term> <note>The hereditary noble class of Rome</note> most deeply rooted in the Roman Republic. For where the rule of the common people exists, it is necessary for the Patricians and nobles to be afflicted with many great injuries, as **Aristotle** shows in the *Politics*, book 3, chapter 7. An example of this is found in **Manlius** <note>Marcus Manlius Capitolinus, who was accused of using the pretext of helping the poor to seize power</note>, who by making false accusations about the gold,

<margin>The subsequent condemnation of Sempronius, Virginius, Pomponius, and Furius.</margin>
The fact that the gold which the Romans had contributed to ransom themselves from the **Gauls** <note>Referring to the sack of Rome in 390 BCE</note> was taken back from the Gauls and then kept by the leading men [the Patricians] provoked the greatest hatred against them. **Machiavelli** cites a similar case in his *Florentine Histories*. Because of this "crime of rule," Gaius Sempronius was fined fifteen thousand copper coins <note>original: "æris"; referring to the *aes grave*, early Roman bronze or copper currency</note>, despite the Senate trying every possible means to soothe the common people (Livy, Book 4). Likewise, in Book 5, he writes of Virginius and Quintus Pomponius, who, by a most wretched example, were fined ten thousand heavy copper coins although they were innocent, simply because they had gratified the Senate by vetoing a proposal by the Tribunes. And regarding Furius <note>Referring to Marcus Furius Camillus, the hero who defeated the Gauls but was later driven into exile over the distribution of plunder</note> in Book 5, who went into exile after being condemned unjustly and without any probable cause.

<margin>Royal and Aristocratic crimes happen more frequently in a popular state.</margin>
Indeed, all the royal and aristocratic crimes we have listed—such as raging immoderately against those suspected of treason, breaking one’s word, plundering sacred temples, seizing the goods of others, and acting insolently or cruelly—all these, I say, also happen in a popular state, and much more so. For instance, when the Roman people were asked to judge a dispute over boundaries <note>The dispute between the cities of Aricia and Ardea over a piece of land</note>, they awarded the contested territory to themselves, acting like a common shyster or a thief of another’s lawsuit, as **Livy** says in Book 3. These crimes among the commoners were rebuked by the famous **Fabius** <note>Quintus Fabius Vibulanus, a Roman consul</note> in the same work:

> *The power of the tribunes was established to help individuals, not to destroy the community. You were created as Tribunes of the people, not as enemies of the Fathers [the Senate]. It is wretched for us and shameful for you that the abandoned Republic is being attacked; you should be lessening the envy against you, not undermining your own law, etc.*

There are monstrous examples of this in both the Florentine Republic and in certain cities of Germany described by **Crantz** <note>Albert Krantz (1448–1517), a historian who wrote on the history of the Saxons and the Vandals</note>, which I am ashamed and weary to recount. Truly, nothing is more cruel than the common people, especially when they have found a leader.

<page-num>266</page-num>
# Arnold Clapmarius, Book V. #

<margin>
The common people do not easily begin [an action], but follow immediately once a leader goes before them.
</margin>
Indeed, they do not easily begin; as the sharp historian <note>Likely referring to Tacitus</note> says, *the first cry of the common people is not easily raised* <note>original: "non facile prima vox plebis"</note>; but with a leader going before them, they follow in his footsteps immediately and go mad as if by contagion. Certainly, I do not deny that the people also have their own "rights of dominion" whenever someone, seized by a lust for power, invades the Republic and attempts to overturn liberty. In such an extraordinary time, there is occasionally a need for sudden judgment. Yet, truly, regard must be had for both honor and good faith; without these, it will no longer be a legitimate government, but a most shameful tyranny.

<margin>
Whether Brutus rightly killed Caesar.
</margin>
The question might be asked here regarding **Gaius Julius Caesar**: was he rightly killed by **Brutus**, **Cassius**, and the others? Indeed, I am not unaware of what learned and wise men think about this matter. But truly, it pleases me to <term>suspend judgment</term> <note>original: ἐπέχειν (*epechein*); a Greek philosophical term used by Skeptics to describe the withholding of assent when evidence is balanced</note> here. Certainly, according to the laws of liberty—or as **Cicero** calls them, the "rights of citizens"—it seems it was permitted for citizens (whose ancestors had sworn an oath to detest the rule of kings) to overthrow him who was trampling upon the laws of liberty. For if a Prince deservedly punishes a man who, out of a love for liberty, attempts to take away the Prince's power and life, why should it not also be permitted for the people to kill one who attempts to invade their liberty and impose slavery upon the citizens? **Tacitus** says this in the first book of his *Annals*: *when the Dictator Caesar was killed, it seemed to some a most foul deed, and to others a most beautiful one.* For in respect to the state of the Republic at that time, they acted wickedly. Indeed, such was the condition of the Republic that it could not have been kept safe unless the power devolved to a single man, as both Tacitus and **Cassius Dio** witness. This is also what **Pomponius** says in Book 2, Section 11 of *On the Origin of Law*: *It came to pass that it was necessary for the Republic to be looked after by a single person.* Although I do not know whether Caesar himself, and others, were the cause...

## CHAPTER XX.

### The rationale for the divisions and differences 
### in this matter is shown. The secrets of mixed
### Republics. The mixed Empire of the Germans.

<margin>The rationale for the division used by the author in this matter is shown.</margin>
And these are the **secret crimes of rule**, which are employed by those who hold sovereignty in a Republic, whether it be one person, a few, or many. In this matter, I am not unaware that judgments and censures are being prepared against me. Some will deny that differences should be derived from the number or multitude of those commanding; others will say there are more species of Republics, and therefore, according to my own opinion, more "secrets of empires" arise. <margin>What the essential differences of a Republic concern.</margin> I do not deny that the <term>essential differences</term> <note>original: *essentiales differentiæ*; a term from Scholastic logic referring to the fundamental nature that makes a thing what it is</note>, as they call them, look toward either the common or the private advantage. This distinction creates the declining Republics and <term>perversions</term> <note>original: παρεκϐάσεις (*parekbaseis*); Aristotle’s term for "deviations" from a correct form of government</note>, as Aristotle calls them, or the upright and good ones. In the latter, regard is had for virtue and wisdom; <margin>How the perversions of Republics vary according to these factors.</margin> in the former, regard is sometimes had for wealth, sometimes poverty, sometimes nobility, sometimes dignity, and sometimes even liberty. 

But truly, because the Patricians and Nobles are usually few, while the common people—the greatest part of humanity—are ignoble and needy, we have therefore begun our order of classification from the <term>accidental difference</term> <note>original: *accidentali differentia*; a classification based on observable traits (like number) rather than the inner "essence" of a thing</note>, seeing as it is joined with the essential one. For even though it sometimes happens that Patricians are poor and plebeians are rich, the Republic does not for that reason take on a different form. Therefore, that state is generally **Aristocratic** in which the few command, **Democratic** in which the many command, and a **Kingdom** in which one commands. Yet all and each, according to the condition of the place, the time, [and the state of the people...]

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 267, transitioning from the theoretical definition of states to the practical reality that most governments are "mixed" rather than pure forms. Clapmarius moves from a general defense of his classification system to a specific analysis of how power is shared among different social orders.</meta>

<page-num>268</page-num>
<header>Arnold Clapmarius, Book V.</header>

...and the nature of the people, <note>original: σπουδαῖοι (*spoudaioi*); a term used by Aristotle to describe excellent or virtuous citizens who are essential to a functioning state</note> excellent men. For I have positioned and considered Republics as most of them were, and still are.

<margin>Types of Republics</margin>
Which, to approach the second point, can be referred to three species: from which Cicero and Tacitus derive just as many methods of administration. The first is concerned with the nature and character of the **Nobility** or **Senators**. The second with the nature of the **common people**. The third with that of **Kings** and **Princes**. This last category encompasses not only Monarchy and Sovereign Rule, but also Tyranny; the second includes Democracy, Polity, and <term>Ochlocracy</term> <note>original: ὀχλοκρατία; "mob rule," the perverted form of democracy where the masses rule without regard for law</note>; and the first includes Aristocracy and Oligarchy.

<margin>The Mixed Republic</margin>
But mixed Republics are also formed from these; as most are, in which each part has either its own <term>arcana</term> <note>original: *arcana*; "secrets" or hidden techniques of power used to maintain control</note>, which it observes religiously; or <term>simulacra</term> <note>original: *simulacra*; "shadows" or pretenses of power, where one group appears to have authority that they do not actually possess</note>, which one part allows to another, as when the sovereign command is divided.

<margin>A pure Republic is rarely found</margin>
For I do not think a pure and simple Republic is easily found. For often one person holds some part of the command, the people another part, the Senate another; or the Senate and the people, or the Prince and the Senate, or the Prince and the people. Concerning this mixture, Livy says in Book 6: *Affairs cannot be conducted with equal right where power is in the hands of the patricians, and only the power of help is in the hands of the Tribunes, unless the command is shared; the common people will never have a part in the Republic.* For the opinion of those who deny that the rights of Command can be divided has long since been rejected.

<margin>The German Empire</margin>
This German Empire certainly, which the <term>Elector of Mainz</term> <note>original: *Moguntinus Elector*; the Archbishop of Mainz, traditionally the most powerful of the seven prince-electors of the Holy Roman Empire</note> said was Aristocratic in the Diet of Frankfurt, is rather a mixed one; as are many others: and so each part has its own [rights] of command and of liberty—

<meta>catchword: and [que]</meta>

<summary>Clapmarius argues that most actual governments are not "pure" forms of monarchy, aristocracy, or democracy, but are instead mixed systems where power and "secrets of state" are shared among different groups. He specifically cites the Holy Roman Empire as a prime example of such a mixed constitution.</summary>

...and the laws, and the <term>secrets</term> <note>original: *arcana*; the hidden techniques or strategies used by a government to maintain its power</note>, and even the <term>shadows</term> <note>original: *simulacra*; the outward appearances or "images" of authority that may not possess actual power</note>; which moderation I particularly gather from Aristotle, Book 4, chapter 9 of the *Politics*, and Book 4 of the *Politics*, chapter 13, where he treats secrets and <term>sophisms</term> <note>original: *sophismata*; political tricks or clever deceptions used to manage the state and its people</note>. <note>The Greek text here is from Aristotle’s *Politics*, 1297a</note> *Thus, he says, it is manifest that if one wishes to balance these things justly, it is necessary to take from both sides, and to establish wages for the one group <note>The poor, to encourage them to attend public assemblies</note>, but a penalty for the other <note>The wealthy, to ensure they do not skip their civic duties</note>.
