# ARNOLD CLAPMARIUS
### ON THE
# SECRETS OF
# STATES,
## BOOK SIX.

### *CHAPTER I.*

->*What the **Shadows of Power** <note>original: *Simulacra Imperii*</note> are, or empty secrets. How they differ from the secrets and the **Right of Sovereignty** <note>original: *Iure Imperii*</note>: likewise from the **secrets of dominion** <note>original: *arcanis dominationis*</note>. The shadow of liberty: the empty rights of commanding: the name of Power: sovereignty without the substance: an image without reality: allurements: force and true power: **representation** <note>original: ἀπεικόνισμα (*apeikonisma*); an image or a reflection</note>: **image** <note>original: εἴδωλον (*eidōlon*); a phantom or likeness</note>. How simulation has a place in a Republic.*<-

<margin>On the shadows of power.</margin>
<margin>The state of a Republic endures when all its parts love it. For this to occur, shadows must be presented to those who are excluded from the government.</margin>
It is a golden saying of Aristotle that the condition of a Republic remains safe and unharmed the longest when all parts of the city love it and wish it to endure. This is a difficult task indeed. However, for this to happen, it is necessary that certain <term>shadows</term> <note>original: *simulacra*; political illusions or "participation in name only" designed to appease the public</note> of power and liberty be presented to those who are otherwise barred from participating in the Republic. *For where*, as the same Aristotle says in Book 2 of the *Politics*, chapter 8, *the common people have no share in the Power, that is a sign of a poorly-ordered Republic.* Just as the <term>secrets of Power</term> <note>original: *arcana Imperii*; the practical, hidden techniques used by a state to maintain its specific form of government</note> are mostly concealed but effective arts used against rebellious men or those kept out of administration; so these shadows are hidden arts, but they are empty and hollow—or as Jovius <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), an Italian physician and historian known for his chronicles of his own time</note> calls them.

<meta>Catchword: 1. History [1. Histor.]</meta>

<summary>Clapmarius introduces the concept of "Shadows of Power" (simulacra imperii), which are political illusions used to make the common people feel they have a role in government to ensure state stability. He distinguishes these hollow "shadows" from the functional "secrets" of statecraft.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, shadows of power, political stability, simulation, secrets of state, Paolo Giovio, public participation, political illusions</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Chapter 1 of Book Six, following the introduction of "shadows of power" as a tool for political stability. Clapmarius is now distinguishing these "shadows" from other types of state secrets and providing historical examples of how authors have described these political illusions.</meta>

<header>On the Shadows of Power, Chapter 1.</header>
<page-num>271</page-num>

1. *History* shows us the **empty rights of commanding** <note>original: *inania jubendi jura*</note>, which are granted to those who are outside the Republic; and in which one thing is done, while another is simulated.

<margin>The difference between the force of power and of dominion. Their various names.</margin>
Rightly, however, these must be distinguished from the **Secrets of the State** <note>original: *arcanis Imperii*; the foundational strategies used to preserve the constitution</note>, and even more so from the **Right of Sovereignty**. In fact, they should rather be contrasted with those secrets. The former are used by Princes within the Republic; the latter are granted to those who are devoid of power. Likewise, they differ from the **secrets of dominion** <note>original: *arcanis dominationis*; the methods used by a ruler to maintain personal control over subjects</note>. For while the secrets of dominion are not permitted to citizens, the <term>shadows</term> <note>original: *simulacra*</note> are specifically granted to them. These are, at least, impressive in appearance, or as Tacitus calls them, **Empty Secrets** <note>original: *Arcana Inania*</note>; likewise, **empty and deceitful things of power**, or the **appearances and Shadows of Power**. Pliny calls them the **shadow of liberty**. Indeed, a shadow is often larger than the body it represents. Just as in Varro, *it horns the gold, it casts a shadow, it prepares to strike* <note>original: *cornuat aurum, umbram jacit, icere parat*</note>. Here, "shadow" refers to the weapon whose shadow was looming. The same Pliny elsewhere calls it a **name**. As in Book 1 of his *Epistles*: *It matters a great deal what you think the tribunate is; an empty shadow and a name without honor, or a Most Sacred power*, etc. So too Tacitus in Book 4 of his *Histories*: *to embrace the force of the principate, but to give up the name*. And Justin says: *Some hold the name of King, others the power*. Hence Caesar said: *The Republic is nothing more than a name without a body*. Velleius calls it **Power without substance** <note>original: *Imperium sine re*</note>. In Book 2: *In this consulship Pompey restored the tribunician power, of which Sulla had left only an image without the substance*. Otto of Freising writes that the heirs of Berthold of Zähringen, Duke of Swabia <note>original: *Sueciæ*; likely a transcription error for *Sueviæ* (Swabia), as the Zähringen family were Swabian dukes</note>, held a similar kind of power: *Princes without a principality, participating only in the name without the reality*. Livy, in Book 3, calls it an **artifice**. *Now liberty is not even brought forth by virtue, but is played with by artifice*. And Justin, in Book 14, calls them **allurements**. *Eumenes*, he says, *acted by allurements*. Others use different terms.

<margin>What is opposed to them.</margin>

# ARNOLD CLAPMARIUS
### ON THE
# SECRETS OF

## BOOK SIX.

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>
On the shadows of Power.
</margin>

*What the **Shadows of Power** <note>original: "Simulacra Imperii"</note>, or empty secrets, are. How they differ from State Secrets and the Right of Sovereignty; likewise, how they differ from the secrets of dominion. The shadow of liberty; the empty right of command; the name of Power; Power without substance; an image without reality; flatteries; force and true power; <term>likeness</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπεικόνισμα (apeikonisma)</note>; <term>phantom</term> <note>original Greek: εἴδωλον (eidolon)</note>. How simulation finds a place within a Republic.*

---

<margin>
The state of the Republic endures when all its parts love it. For this to happen, shadows must be presented to those who are excluded from its administration.
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'A' with floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

Aristotle’s saying is golden: that the condition of a Republic remains safe and unharmed for the longest time when all parts of the state love it and wish for it to endure. This is indeed a difficult task. However, to achieve this, it is necessary to present certain **shadows of power** and of liberty to those from whom the actual path to the State has been closed. For when the common people <note>original: "Plebs"</note> have no share in the government—as the same Aristotle says in the second book of his *Politics*, chapter 8—it is a bad sign for the Republic. Therefore, just as most **Secrets of State** <note>original: "arcana Imperii"</note> are hidden but substantial methods used against rebellious men who are kept from the administration of the State, so these "shadows" are hidden methods, yet they are empty and hollow, as Jovius <note>The Italian historian Paolo Giovio</note> calls them.

<meta>catchword: 1. Histor.</meta>

<summary>This page introduces Book Six, defining "Shadows of Power" as political illusions designed to satisfy the populace and maintain stability. Clapmarius argues, following Aristotle, that a state is only secure when all its citizens feel included, even if that inclusion is merely symbolic.</summary>
<keywords>Arnold Clapmarius, Shadows of Power, simulacra imperii, Aristotle, political stability, statecraft, simulation, public perception, Paolo Giovio</keywords>

--- Page 419 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to Book Six, specifically focusing on the definition and classification of "Shadows of Power." It follows the previous page’s discussion on Aristotle’s theory that a stable state requires the affection of all its citizens, which is often maintained through the strategic use of political illusions.</meta>

<header>On the Shadows of Power, Chapter 1.</header>

1. Historically, these are empty rights of command granted to those who are outside the administration of the Republic; they are mechanisms by which one thing is done, while another is feigned.

<margin>The difference between these and the secrets of state and dominion. Their various names.</margin>
Rightly, however, these must be distinguished from the **Secrets of State** <note>original: "arcana Imperii"</note>, and much more so from the **Right of Sovereignty** <note>original: "Iure Imperii"</note>; indeed, they should rather be seen as their opposites. Princes exercise the latter in a Republic; the former are used by those who are devoid of actual power. Likewise, they differ from the secrets of dominion. For secrets of dominion are not permitted to the citizens, but **shadows** <note>original: "simulacra"</note> are granted to them as concessions. These are at least visually impressive, or as Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian known for his analysis of power dynamics.</note> calls them, *Empty Secrets* <note>original: "Arcana Inania"</note>; likewise, *the empty and deceitful things of power* <note>original: "Imperii inania & subdola"</note>; and also *the appearances and Shadows of Power* <note>original: "species & Simulacra Imperii"</note>.

Pliny <note>Likely Pliny the Younger, a Roman author and administrator.</note> calls this the *shadow of liberty* <note>original: "libertatis umbram"</note>. For a shadow is often larger than the object it represents. As found in Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar.</note>: *the gold tosses its horns, casts a shadow, and prepares to strike.* <note>original: "cornuat aurum, umbram jacit, icere parat." This poetic metaphor refers to a weapon (the "gold") whose mere shadow is enough to threaten.</note> By "shadow," he means the weapon whose shadow was looming. The same Pliny elsewhere calls it a *name*. As in his first Letter: It matters greatly what you think the tribunate to be; whether it is an *empty shadow and a name without honor*, or a *Sacrosanct power*, etc. So Tacitus says in the fourth book of his *Histories*: *to embrace the force of the princedom, but to relinquish the name.* And Justin <note>A Roman historian who condensed the works of Pompeius Trogus.</note> writes: *Some hold the name of King, others hold the power.*

From this, Caesar <note>Julius Caesar.</note> concluded: *The Republic is nothing more, only a name without a body.* <note>original: "Nihil amplius Rempublicam esse, appellationem modo sine corpore."</note> Velleius <note>Velleius Paterculus, a Roman historian.</note> calls it *Power without the reality* <note>original: "Imperium sine re"</note> in his second book: *In this consulship, Pompey restored the tribunitian power, of which Sulla had left only an image without the reality.* Otto of Freising <note>A 12th-century German bishop and chronicler.</note> writes that the heirs of Berthold of Zähringen, Duke of Swabia, held a similar type of power: they were Princes without a principality, participating in the title alone, a name without the reality. Livy <note>Titus Livius, the primary historian of early Rome.</note> in his third book calls it an *art*: *Liberty is now no longer brought forth by virtue, but is played with by art.* <note>original: "arte ludi." Here "art" implies political maneuvering or deception.</note>

<margin>What is opposed to them.</margin>
And Justin, in his fourteenth book, calls them *flatteries* <note>original: "blandimenta"</note>: *Eumenes,* he says, *acted through flatteries.* Others describe them in other ways.

<meta>catchword: By which</meta>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the "shadows of power" (simulacra imperii). It elaborates on the distinction between the actual force and authority of a ruler versus the hollow appearances or titles granted to those without real influence. The author draws heavily on Roman historians and poets to define the nature of these political illusions.</meta>

<header>Arnold Clapmarius, Book VI.</header>

<margin>Force and true power are contrasted with the Prince and the State.</margin>
Against these shadows stands **force and true power** <note>original: "vis ac vera potentia"</note>; the force of the State; the force of the Prince; and the right of the State <note>original: "jus Imperii"</note>. No one speaks of these more clearly than Tacitus <note>A Roman historian famous for his cynical analysis of political power.</note>. Among the Romans, he says, *the right of the State prevails, while the empty things are passed over*. And elsewhere in the fourth book of his *Annals*: *once the pretenses were removed, true power increased*. But enough on these matters for now. Furthermore, they are called "shadows" <note>original: "simulacra"</note> because they present some external and grand appearance, much like the statues of the Gods. As Virgil <note>The Roman epic poet; this quote is from the Aeneid, describing a ghost.</note> wrote:

<margin>Why they are called "shadows."</margin>
> An image appeared before my eyes, larger than life.

Regarding this, as mentioned above: these shadows are "windy," like empty nutshells, and as Horace <note>A leading Roman lyric poet.</note> says, *void of substance, and melodious trifles*. Therefore, in an ancient glossary, a shadow <note>original: "simulacrum"</note> is defined as a *representation* <note>original: "ἀπεικόνισμα"</note>, an *image* <note>original: "εἴδωλον"</note>, or a *carved idol* <note>original: "ξύανον"</note>.

<margin>They are highly valued by those who lack power.</margin>
Furthermore, those who actually possess the State's power do not value these things much, for they are merely for show and exist in the shadows. On the other hand, those who lack the reality of power prefer to seem to have it, rather than both not having it and not appearing to have it. For this reason, the Roman soldiers acted imprudently when, not content with the victory they had won over the Germans, they built mounds inscribed with the names of the conquered nations. Regarding this, Tacitus says in the second book of his *Annals*: *The Germans were not moved by their wounds, their grief, or the destruction as much as they were by that display, which affected them with pain and rage.*

<margin>That they nevertheless wish to be seen as possessing it.</margin>
The jurist Modestinus <note>A celebrated Roman lawyer of the 3rd century AD.</note> argues shrewdly and appropriately to this subject in the *Digest* (Law 52, regarding conditions and demonstrations): It sometimes happens that certain things expressed by name are harmful, even though they could have been understood silently if omitted, and would not then have been an obstacle. And these shadows are almost always of this nature: one thing is being done, while another is feigned. It is feigned that others are participating in the Republic; but in truth, the exact opposite is being done.

<meta>catchword: But again</meta>

<summary>Clapmarius defines "shadows of power" as hollow titles or appearances used to pacify those without real authority, contrasting them with the "true power" held by the sovereign. He uses classical Roman examples to show how these illusions can sometimes provoke more resentment than actual force.</summary>
<keywords>simulacra, true power, Tacitus, Virgil, Horace, political illusion, Roman law, Modestinus, sovereignty</keywords>

<header>On the Shadows of Power, Chapter 2.</header>

<margin>Whether it is lawful to use them.</margin>
But you will say again that this is a form of deceit <note>original: "dolum"</note>, which exists not only in one who speaks obscurely for the sake of trickery, but also in one who insidiously and darkly conceals the truth, as noted in the *Digest of Roman Law* <note>original: "l. 43. D. de contrahen. empt." refers to Book 18, Title 1, Law 43 of the Corpus Juris Civilis, concerning contracts of sale.</note>. It is also said that he who speaks in a mocking or illusory way is deceiving others <note>original: "l. 69. de Eviction." refers to laws regarding the loss of property due to a third-party claim.</note>. However, you must not apply the rules of private contracts to public business. In the latter, the highest principle is the safety of the Republic; in the former, it is equity and justice. In public affairs, it is sometimes permitted to turn aside slightly from the "royal road" of virtue; in private matters, it is not. But these arguments have already been discussed by us above.

## CHAPTER II.

->*Shadows of other things. The meddlesome <note>original: "περίεργος" (periergos)</note>, the tasteless <note>original: "ἀπειρόκαλος" (apeirokalos)</note>, and the senseless. Grandiose titles of books. Poetic swellings. Empty fame, empty honors. The empty rumors of war <note>original: "τὰ κενὰ τοῦ πολέμου" (ta kena tou polemou)</note>, Panic terrors <note>original: "Πανικὰ" (Panika)</note>, and the shadows of war. Tutanus <note>A Roman deity believed to protect or provide safety.</note>.*<-

<margin>In every walk of life, there are those who wish to appear as such.</margin>
Examples of this tendency are found repeatedly in every walk of life. As Aeschines <note>An Athenian orator and statesman.</note> says: *He wishes not to seem the best, but to be so.* Indeed, the Greeks have elegant names for one who is captivated by the appearance and shadow of things: they call him *meddlesome* <note>original: "περίεργον"</note> or *tasteless* <note>original: "ἀπειρόκαλον"</note>. The Latins call such a person *senseless* <note>original: "infrunitum"</note> or an "ostentator" (a show-off). The most wise Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher famous for his "Characters," which categorized various personality types.</note> beautifully described such a person in his character sketches, as did Cicero in his work *To Herennius* and Ammianus Marcellinus. Of the latter, he writes: *Others, even when no one asks, puff up their patrimony to an immense degree with a stern expression, multiplying their annual harvests to make people believe they possess fertile lands that stretch from the rising to the setting sun.* And as a certain soldier remarks in the works of Livy <note>A famous Roman historian.</note>: *They show off war, rather than wage it.*

<margin>Even in literary matters.</margin>
In learning and literature, most people prefer to *seem* learned rather than actually *be* so; how few there are who follow a solid and rigorous method of study! Such people are rare.

<header>Arnold Clapmarius, Book VI.</header>

<margin>
Hence the showy and empty titles of books.
</margin>
...who embraces [the thing itself]? And what else do those words of Pliny to Vespasian suggest regarding inscriptions and showy titles? These are hung upon books just as ivy is hung to advertise wine <note>An ancient custom where an ivy wreath outside a tavern signaled that wine was for sale; hence the proverb "Good wine needs no bush."</note>: *The Greeks have a wonderful talent for titles. They have inscribed books as "The Honeycomb" <note>original: "κηρίον" (kerion)</note>, because they wanted them to be understood as full of sweetness; others use "The Horn of Plenty" <note>original: "κέρας ἀμαλθείας" (keras amaltheias)</note>, so that you might even expect to find a draft of "bird’s milk" <note>A proverbial expression for an impossible or rare luxury.</note> within the volume. Then there are titles like "The Muse," "The All-Receivers" <note>original: "πανδέκται" (pandektai), often translated as Pandects or Encyclopedias.</note>, "The Hand-dagger" <note>original: "ἐγχειρίδιον" (encheiridion), a double meaning referring to a handbook or a small dagger.</note>, "The Meadow" <note>original: "λειμὼν" (leimon)</note>, and "The Little Tablet" <note>original: "πινακίδιον" (pinakidion)</note>. These are titles for which a man might even skip a court date to read. But when you get inside, gods and goddesses, what a vacuum you will find in the center!*

<margin>
Poetic smoke.
</margin>
Horace also elegantly critiques this same "swelling" or pomposity in poets:
> ->What will this promiser produce worthy of such a wide-open mouth?<-

By contrast, he approves of the one who:
> ->Does not aim to produce smoke from a flash, but to give light from smoke,<-
> ->So that he may then produce showy wonders.<-

One may find this kind of "windy" ostentation most frequently in common daily life.

<margin>
The cheap and windy ostentation of Sejanus.
</margin>
A notable example is found in that famous Sejanus <note>Lucius Aelius Sejanus, the ambitious and ruthless commander of the Praetorian Guard under Emperor Tiberius.</note>. Since he was a haughty man, he behaved with magnificent pride, walking about with a large retinue of followers. He responded to those who addressed him with difficulty, and he became enraged and threatened the ultimate punishment against those who either failed to yield the path to him or did not repeat their salutations and marks of obedience. And yet, says Dio <note>Cassius Dio, a Roman historian who wrote in Greek.</note>, mocking Sejanus, *this is a sign of vanity; for a man who lacked the reality of power was captivated by this kind of "makeup" or disguise. For he who relies on his own genuine power,* he says, *cares little for these salutations and marks of obedience, and if they are omitted, he does not consider it a fault.*

<margin>
Chasing fame while neglecting reality.
</margin>
With similar folly, most people chase after fame while the reality itself is neglected. Whence Tacitus, in the second book of his *Annals*...

<page-num>275</page-num>
<header>On the Shadows of Power, Chapter 2.</header>

...seeks the emptiness of fame; likewise, games and the emptiness of honor.
<margin>The shadows of war are also noted.</margin>
Thus in war there are "the empty terrors of war" <note>original: "τὰ κενὰ τοῦ πολέμου" (ta kena tou polemou)</note>; likewise, "diversions" <note>original: "παίγνια" (paignia)</note>. Hence Lucretius speaks of the "shadows of war." And Curtius in Book 4: *And most things are empty, such as the shouting of men, the neighing of horses, and the flash of glinting weapons.* In the same place: *The soldier is moved more by vain and empty things than by just causes for fear.* And Livy in Book 3: *So that they might contend that it was not a war, but a vain image of war that had occupied the Capitol.* Yet these very shadows <note>The "shadows" here refer to psychological tactics and the mere appearance of a threat.</note> drove Hannibal away from Rome. Hence the god Tutanus was consecrated, as Varro mentions in his Satires <note>Tutanus was a minor Roman deity of protection, whose name derives from "tueri," meaning to watch over or defend; he was credited with turning Hannibal back from the gates of Rome.</note>.

<margin>Specifically regarding Rabirius, according to Cicero.</margin>
Marcus Tullius Cicero notes shadows of this sort regarding the Roman Knight Gaius Rabirius. He says: *You see, Judges, the shadow and image of a Roman Knight, preserved by the help and loyalty of a single friend. Nothing can be taken from this man except this shadow of his former dignity, which Caesar alone protects and sustains.* <note>Rabirius was an elderly senator defended by Cicero against a charge of high treason; Cicero argues that Rabirius has lost everything but the mere title or "shadow" of his former rank.</note>

<margin>Shadows of power are noted in the State.</margin>
Furthermore, by the same example, there are <term>shadows of power</term> <gloss>Simulacra Imperii: outward forms or titles of authority that lack actual political substance</gloss> in the State, which less-intelligent men gape at, and which leading men in the State easily and calmly allow others to have. Guicciardini, in Book 1 of his History, lists this among the praises of Louis XI, father of Charles VIII: that he always pursued the things themselves rather than the shadows of things.

### Book VI of Arnold Clapmarius ###

<header>Arnold Clapmarius, Book VI.</header>

...of forms, there are just as many <term>images of power</term> <note>original: "simulacra imperii"; these are the outward appearances or symbols of a government type used when the actual power structure has changed.</note>, and indeed they are threefold. There are images of kingship in an <term>aristocracy</term> <note>government by a small, elite class</note> and in a popular state; aristocratic images in a kingdom and in a people’s rule; and democratic images in a kingdom and an aristocracy. For there are just as many <term>secrets of state</term> <note>original: "arcana imperii"; the practical, often hidden methods used to maintain power</note> which are opposed to these images.

<margin>
*Hence there are as many species of these as there are secrets.*
</margin>

Royal images are like hidden privileges, yet they are empty and, as I have said, cheap <note>original: "hordeacea," literally "made of barley." In this context, it refers to something imitation or of low quality, like "straw" power.</note>, which are usurped by those who lack true power; they wish to appear to possess what they do not. I do not know if one could find more examples of this anywhere than among the Venetians, and even in this empire. 

<margin>
*Royal images. Most common among the Venetians.*
</margin>

For the Doge of Venice possesses for the most part only the images of power, and some secrets of state; such as the title of Duke, the first place in voting, a fortified residence, and other things of that kind. Regarding the Macedonians, Curtius writes in Book 4: *The Macedonians were indeed accustomed to royal rule, but with a greater shadow of liberty than other nations.*

<margin>
*Few in the Roman Republic.*
</margin>

I find few royal images in the Roman Republic. Is it because some writers have not searched for them carefully, or because after the <insert>kings</insert> Tarquins were expelled, they cut off the whole kingdom as if with a single blow? 

<margin>
*Such, however, was the creation of the King of Sacrifices.*
</margin>

Yet there is a notable instance reported by Livy in Book 2: *Care was then taken for divine matters,* he says, *and because certain public sacrifices had been performed by the Kings themselves, lest there be a longing for Kings anywhere, they created a **King of Sacrifices**.* <note>original: "Rex sacrificulus." After the Roman monarchy was abolished, this office was created to handle the religious duties the king used to perform, ensuring the gods weren't offended by the change in government, though the office-holder had no political power.</note> This is an image of royal power. For they made this priesthood subject to the Pontifex <note>The High Priest</note>, so that the honor added to the name would not hinder liberty, which was then the primary concern. 

<margin>
*Likewise the annual term of the two Consuls.*
</margin>

That creation of the two <term>Consuls</term> <note>The two highest-ranking elected officials in the Roman Republic</note> also introduced a certain liberty, more because it was an annual office than because...

# Concerning the Images of Empire, Chapter 3. #

...that anything was diminished from the royal power, as Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian</note> testifies in that same fifth book. Whence the Poet says:

> *The time when Rome first exchanged its haughty masters*
> *For peaceful consuls:*
<note>original: "Quo primum dominatus Roma superbos / Mutavit placidis tempore consulibus." This refers to the transition from the Roman Monarchy to the Republic, where the Consuls held the symbols of royal power but for limited terms.</note>

<margin>
Likewise, a species of empire in the Mufti under Selim, Prince of the Turks.
</margin>
The same species of <term>Empire</term> <note>original: "Imperii"; here referring to the appearance of supreme authority</note> was found in the Mufti <note>The highest religious authority in the Ottoman Empire</note>, who, under Selim, Prince of the Turks, was the foremost priest and interpreter of the Mohammedan superstition. He possessed such a great appearance of authority, as Lazzaro Soranzo <note>A Venetian diplomat and author of "L'Ottomano" (1598)</note> reports, that no one ever openly contradicted his opinion. However, whenever the Prince himself is present and commands something, the Mufti, as if thunderstruck, comes forward only to flatter and praise him.

<margin>
Burying one who is not a King in a royal manner.
</margin>
But that also seems to be a <term>royal image</term>: to be buried in a royal manner. Henry IV <note>Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1056–1105)</note> responded both sharply and wisely to someone asking why he allowed Rudolf <note>Rudolf of Rheinfelden, a rival "anti-king" who died in 1080</note>—who was not truly the King—to be buried with royal honors. He replied: *"I wish all my enemies lay so honorably."* Whence the German poet, writing on the deeds of Frederick I <note>Frederick Barbarossa</note>, in Book 7, says:

> *Foolish superstition; and what a just fate denied him*
> *While living, a stupid error bestowed upon him when dying.*
<note>original: "Stulta superstitio, quodque huic sors justa negarat / Viventi, stolidus morienti contulit error."</note>

Although that famous Theodora <note>Empress and wife of Justinian I</note> seemed to feel differently; she said to her husband, the Emperor Justinian, when he was trembling and hesitant to hold onto his power: "You do not know, my husband, how beautiful it is to have the name of 'Emperor' inscribed upon one's tomb." Nero felt otherwise toward his mother. Which, however, the Tragedian detests in the play *Octavia*:

> *He destroys the images and titles out of fear of death.*
<note>original: "Simulacra, titulos, destruit mortis metu."</note>

Moreover, Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle</note> laughs at that pride in burial in his work *On Ambition* <note>original Greek: "περὶ φιλοτιμίας" (peri philotimias)</note>: "If his wife dies, he inscribes on her monument not only her name, but the names of her husband, her father, and her mother..."

## CHAPTER IV.

->*The vain and smoky ambition of Tiridates, King of the Parthians: not to surrender his sword, to embrace the provincial governors, to be held in consular honor. Leaving the conquered their name, language, custom, and dress. Proud names, the hair-bands of women.*<-

<margin>To grant a favor to a king’s non-royal petition. An example in the petition of Vologeses, King of the Parthians, for his brother Tiridates, which the Romans humored.</margin>
I laughed (for I will not deny it) after I read in the 15th book of Tacitus's *Annals* about the windy and hardly royal—indeed, abject—ambition of that Vologeses <note>Vologeses I, King of the Parthian Empire (r. 51–78 AD)</note>. This Vologeses, through his own messengers, requested from the Roman general Corbulo <note>Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, a prominent Roman general under Claudius and Nero</note> that his brother Tiridates—after he had submitted his royal crown to Nero—should not have to surrender his sword <note>original: "ferrum"; literally "the iron." In this context, it refers to his sidearm or sword, a mark of status</note>, nor be barred from embracing those governing the provinces, nor be made to stand at their doors; and that he should be held in as much honor at Rome as the Consuls <note>The highest elected political office in Rome, which by this period was largely ceremonial but still prestigious</note>. 

Good gods, what kind of petition is this for a King? Except that it was considered shameful for a King to be unarmed <note>original: "discingi"; literally "to be ungirded"</note>, and especially for a King of the Parthians, who were always armed according to the custom of their nation (as Ammianus testifies in book 23) <note>Ammianus Marcellinus, a 4th-century Roman historian</note>. Furthermore, it was not permitted for other commoners to embrace Consuls or Envoys; as Severus, at that time the Envoy of Africa, says in Spartianus <note>Aelius Spartianus, one of the purported authors of the *Augustan History*</note>: *Do not, as a common man, rashly embrace an envoy of the Roman people.* 

But the dignity and authority of a Consul was not small, yet at that time it was hollow and without any real substance. Therefore the Romans, who made little of these <term>images</term> <note>original: "simulacra"; refers to the outward symbols or "shadows" of power that carry no real weight</note>, easily granted the favor of his petition. Thus Tacitus says: *Clearly, being accustomed to foreign pride and not knowing our ways—among whom the law of empire prevails—these hollow things are allowed to pass.* <note>original: "Scilicet externa superbia sueta, non notitia nostri, apud quos jus imperii valet, inania transmittuntur." Tacitus is mocking the Parthians for valuing ceremony over the actual legal power (jus imperii) that the Romans prioritized.</note> For in granting shadowy images of this kind, [they are] most indulgent—

### CHAPTER V.

->*Images of Aristocratic Rule: not changing everything at once; leaving the same titles for the magistrates; rising gradually and in a slow manner; initiating all business through the consuls; leaving the appearance of the former republic.*<-

<margin>
*Images of an Aristocratic Republic.*
</margin>
**I**t is the law and custom for such things, and others of that kind, to be thrust upon those who delight in the mere name of empire; this is done both so that, being occupied with these perceptions, they might neglect deeper matters, and also so that even when the form of government has changed, a shadow of the former Republic might remain.

<margin>

*When the Republic is changed, the Principate should be exercised gradually, leaving behind a shadow of the Republic.*
</margin>
And in the same way, when an Aristocratic republic is transformed into a kingdom, certain images of liberty are left behind. No historian or political thinker has expressed these more sharply or diligently than Cornelius Tacitus; those who have dared to prefer Sallust <note>Another Roman historian, often compared to Tacitus</note> to him certainly do not well understand these hidden and secret counsels of state. Thus, it is all the more absurd and—as the <term>legal scholars</term> <note>original: "ICti" (Iurisconsulti)</note> say—a "novelty" what is argued by that sharp writer from Tuscany <note>A reference to Niccolò Machiavelli, whose advice was often viewed as dangerously radical or cynical by later writers like Clapmarius</note>: that when a republic is changed, everything ought to be changed in a single moment. <margin>The prudence of Augustus, and his example.</margin>
In this, Augustus was more prudent, of whom Tacitus says: *Domestic affairs were peaceful; the names of the magistrates remained the same.* <note>original: "Domi res tranquillæ, eadem magistratuum vocabula"</note> And as a rule, as the jurist Ulpian says in the Digest: *In establishing new orders, there must be an evident utility to justify departing from what has long seemed equitable.* <note>original: "In rebus novis constituendis, evidentem utilitatem esse debere, ut recedatur ab eo quod diu æquum visum est."</note> Wherefore Tacitus says of the same Augustus in that same passage: *he rose up little by little, transferring to himself the duties of the senate, the magistrates, and the laws, with no one opposing him.* <note>original: "insurgere paulatim, munia senatus, magistratuum, legum in se transferre, nullo adversante."</note> And observe the cunning of Augustus. For he not only left the old customs in place; he even insisted that whenever a consulship was granted to him, he should have two colleagues instead of one, while everyone cried out that his majesty was being sufficiently diminished by the fact that he held that honor not alone, but with another. *Suetonius, Life of Augustus.*

<margin>Of Tiberius.</margin>
Tiberius followed this example and, as the same Suetonius says, exercised the power of the Prince gradually—that is, with a slow effort, and as Euripides elegantly says, *quietly with a slow foot.* <note>original Greek: "σιγᾷ ᾗ βραδεῖ ποδί"</note> And Tacitus says in the first book of his *Annals*: *He initiated all business through the Consuls, as if the old Republic still existed.* <note>original: "Cuncta per Consules incipiebat; tanquam vetere Republica."</note> And elsewhere he says: *The Consuls retained their own appearance, and the Praetors theirs.* <note>original: "Sua Consulibus, sua Prætoribus species."</note> Certainly, it was necessary to leave a shadow and appearance of the old Republic, by which the common people are wonderfully captivated. Tacitus says the same in the second book of his <margin>Annals, Book 2.</margin> *Annals*: *It was still a frequent occurrence for Senators, if anything seemed to be for the benefit of the state, to speak their opinion in their own place.*

### CHAPTER VI.

> *Not to usurp new or haughty titles. First of the Senate. First Citizen of the state or of the people. The Tribunate: to abstain from the titles of King, and Lord, and Jupiter. To call oneself the Servant of Servants. To profess oneself the Brother of the citizens. Superstition and curiosity regarding titles.*

And this is so true that even the first Princes and Roman Emperors did not usurp any titles other than those customary in the Roman Republic. For this, as Suetonius says, would be to *abuse one's mastery*. <margin>The name of "Prince" was very common among the Romans.</margin>
...[he said] that he was the master of his slaves, the General <note>original: "Imperatorem"</note> of his soldiers, and the Prince <note>original: "Principem"; in this context, it implies the 'First Citizen' rather than a hereditary monarch</note> of the rest. For the term **Prince** was most commonly used in the Roman Republic. Livy, in *Book 2*, writes: *Appius reached the rank of the Princes*; and in *Book 4*: *the Princes of the common people.* And throughout history, we find the "Prince of the Senate" and the "Prince of the City." Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar and writer</note> says: *he is questioned by the Prince of the city.*

<margin>The term "Lord," like that of "King," was hated.</margin>
On the other hand, the name of **Lord** <note>original: "Domini"</note>, just like that of **King**, was hated among the Romans. Martial <note>A Roman poet famous for his short, biting epigrams</note> alludes to this:

> *In vain, you flatterers, do you come to me*
> *With your wretched, worn-down lips,*
> *Intending to call me "Lord and God"—I am not he,*
> *There is no longer a place for you in this city.*
<note>original: "Frustra blanditiæ venitis ad me / Attritis miserabiles labellis, / Dicturus Dominum Deumque, non sum, / Iam non est locus hac in urbe vobis." These lines from Martial's Epigrams (10.72) celebrate the transition away from the megalomania of Emperor Domitian.</note>

<margin>The prudence of Tiberius is noted again in this matter.</margin>
Tacitus says the same of Tiberius: he sharply rebuked those who spoke of his "divine occupations" and called him "Lord." For he worked hard to ensure that the outward form of the Republic—which is the only thing the common people look at—was preserved for some time.

<margin>Augustus.</margin>
For this reason, Augustus <note>The first Roman Emperor, who famously claimed to have "restored the Republic" while actually holding total power</note> convened the Senate under no other authority than the title of the **Tribunician power** <term>Tribunicia potestas: An office originally designed to protect the common people, which gave the holder the power to veto any act of government</term>; and as Velleius <note>Velleius Paterculus, a Roman historian and soldier</note> more clearly states, he entered the tribunate as a way of fortifying his royal power. 

<margin>Philip of Macedon.</margin>
Similarly, King Philip of Macedon <note>Philip II, father of Alexander the Great</note>, after conquering Greece, ordered that he be called not the "King of Greece," but its "Leader" <note>original: "ducem"</note>, as Justin <note>A Roman historian who abridged the works of Pompeius Trogus</note> records in *Book 9*. 

<margin>The Princes of Macedon after the death of Alexander.</margin>
And after Alexander died, the Princes of Macedon did not desire to be called "Kings" until the entire lineage of Alexander had died out. Thus Justin writes in *Book 15*: *All of them abstained from the ornaments of royal honor for as long as the sons of their King could survive. Such was their modesty that, although they possessed royal wealth, they willingly lacked the titles of Kings as long as Alexander had a legitimate heir.* 

<margin>Vespasian.</margin>
And there was a singular quality in Vespasian—whether out of modesty or truly out of prudence—regarding Vologeses <note>Vologases I, the King of the Parthian Empire</note>, who had written to him in these words:

### C H A P T E R  V I I.

*How to make the Senate a participant in the assemblies; so that it may have the power to create and manage minor officials. The Roman Quæstorship. The Popes as masters of these political secrets.*

<margin>Returning the image of the assemblies to the Senate.</margin>
The right of the <term>assemblies</term> <note>original: "comitia"; the public gatherings where Romans voted on laws and elected officials</note>, as I stated in the first book, is a hallmark of supreme power. Therefore, the Roman Princes <note>The early Emperors, who used the title "Princeps" (First Citizen) to avoid the hated title of King.</note> drew that right to themselves by whatever art they could, but slowly and step by step. They left the *image* of the assemblies to the Senate. Julius Caesar, according to the historian Suetonius, divided this right with the people—except for the creation of Consuls, which he claimed for himself and the Senate. Augustus did the same. But Tiberius shared almost the entire right of the assemblies with the Senate, while excluding the common people.

<margin>Sharing the appearance of power with the Senate, while the Prince directs everything.</margin>
At this point, you might say: "These rights belonged to the supreme power, and therefore should not have been shared with the Senate at all." However, in truth, it was not the actual power that was being shared, but only the *appearance* of it, while the supreme Prince directed and managed everything behind the scenes. Furthermore, in a newly established government, certain concessions are necessary; these can easily be abolished later once the empire has been strengthened. As Tacitus writes in the first book of his *Annals*: *"Then, for the first time, the assemblies were transferred from the Field [of Mars] to the Senators."* <note>The Field of Mars was the traditional outdoor voting ground for the Roman citizenry; moving the vote to the Senate house effectively stripped the public of their voice.</note> For until that day, although the most important decisions were made at the Prince's whim, some things were still done through the enthusiasm of the tribes; (note this for me in this

## CHAPTER VIII.

### *Allowing arguments in the Senate. Referring all matters to the Conscript Fathers. Referring certain matters back to the Senate; such as the restraint of luxury, the petitions of the provinces; and even offering up greater matters for the sake of appearance.*

A debate was held in the Roman Senate regarding a riot of *actors*, and *opinions* were being voiced that the *Praetors* <note>High-ranking Roman magistrates</note> should have the right to use the rod <note>The right to administer corporal punishment</note> against *actors*. This was permitted in the past while the *Republic* was still standing. For that is how I understand that sentiment, quite differently than others do. Clearly, he conceded and handed back to the Senate those matters that were of no importance, such as the regulation of luxury in dishes, clothing, and the number of slaves; meanwhile, he himself held the actual force and right of Empire, which he claimed was something much greater and more lofty. For those smaller and inferior matters are safely committed to ministers. Hence <term>Horace</term> wrote:

### On the Facades of Empire. Chapter 10

...armies were hailed with the title of commander <note>original: "Imperator"</note>; and several people were called Commander at the same time, without any one being superior to the others in rank. Augustus also granted this title to certain individuals, as did Tiberius later for Blaesus. These things may seem to be of no consequence, yet the neglect of them brought the greatest hatred upon the Princes—as happened to Julius Caesar, because he did not rise to greet the Senate.

<margin>Rising for the seated Senate and bidding them farewell.</margin>
Suetonius says: "He stirred up for himself a particular and inexpiable hatred because, when all the Senators <note>original: "P. C." for *Patres Conscripti*</note> approached him with the most honorable decrees, he received them while remaining seated in front of the Temple of Venus the Mother." In this matter, Augustus was wiser; he greeted the Fathers <note>the Senators</note> while they were seated, addressing each by name without anyone prompting him, and upon departing, he would bid farewell to each while they remained seated. And regarding Tiberius, he rose for the Consuls and moved out of their way on the road.

<margin>Giving way on the road.</margin>
Does that speech of Tiberius to the Senate—or rather, that pretense—mean anything else? "Both now and often at other times, I have said, Senators, that a good and health-giving Prince, whom you have invested with such great and free power, ought to serve the Senate, and often the citizens as a whole, and frequently even individuals; nor do I regret having said this. I have had you as good, just, and favoring masters, and I have them still."

<margin>Calling the Senators "Masters."</margin>
Suetonius’s account of Tiberius is clearly modeled on the advice of the Elders to Rehoboam: *If today you will be a servant to this people, and will serve them, and speak good words to them, they will be your servants for all days.* <note>1 Kings 12:7</note> For this reason, Tiberius also never entered the senate house unless alone; and when he was carried in on a litter because he was ill, he dismissed his companions.

<margin>The establishment of taxes.</margin>
Of the same kind is that frequent occurrence where Nero granted the establishment of taxes to the Consuls and Tribunes. This power, as has been said and as Hermogenianus testifies, belongs to the supreme Prince; yet Nero granted it with what Tacitus calls a "sharp liberty"—plainly for appearance's sake and only for a time. Nor did it happen otherwise...

### On the Facades of Empire: Chapter 10.

<margin>
A passage from Tacitus pertains to this, in which there are also other marks of political wisdom <note>original: "prudentiæ" – here referring to statecraft or practical political skill</note>.
</margin>
There is a remarkable passage on this subject in Tacitus’s *Life of Agricola* <note>Agricola was a Roman general responsible for much of the conquest of Britain</note>, which I bring forward here not only because it is relevant to this matter, but also because of its many-sided observations on political wisdom. *The following winter,* he says, *was spent in most beneficial planning. For, in order that a people who were scattered, unrefined, and therefore prone to war, might grow accustomed to peace and leisure through pleasures, he encouraged them privately and aided them publicly to build temples, forums, and houses, by praising the ready*
<margin>
Firstly, he teaches how the common people are broken by pleasures, as if by a facade of liberty.
</margin>
*and punishing the slow. Thus, competition for honor took the place of compulsion. Furthermore, he began to educate the sons of the local chieftains in the liberal arts, and to prefer the natural talents of the Britons to the trained skills of the Gauls, so that those who recently rejected the Roman language began to crave its eloquence. From that followed a respect for our style of dress, and the toga became frequent; and little by little they slipped away into the allurements of vices—porticoes, baths,*
*and the elegance of banquets; and this, among the inexperienced, was called "civilization" <note>original: "humanitas"</note>, when it was actually a part of their servitude.*

First, he says that the common people are broken and held in check by pleasures. For this is a certain facade <note>original: "simulacrum"</note> of liberty. Indeed, when the common crowd enjoys such pleasures with impunity, they believe they have obtained everything they desire. For this reason, Tacitus writes concerning Augustus in the *Annals, Book 1*: "He himself did not shrink from such interests, and he believed it was a mark of a fellow-citizen <note>original: "civile" – acting like a citizen rather than a tyrant</note> to mingle in the pleasures of the common people"—even if legal scholars might consider this a vice of the mind. Therefore, when Augustus wished to restrain this license, that most wise Mæcenas <note>Augustus's influential political advisor</note> responded: *It is to your advantage, Caesar, that the common people be occupied with us* <note>original: "Συμφέρει σοι Καῖσαρ περὶ ἡμᾶς τὸ δῆμον ἀποτρίβεσθαι" – The author translates the Greek into Latin as "Expedit tibi Caesar plebem sic occupatam esse."</note>. And Livy writes in *Book 5* concerning the King of the Veientes, that he became an object of hatred because he had broken off the solemnity of the games, which it was a religious crime to interrupt.

<margin>Galba, Piso, Pertinax, and Hadrian VI are criticized for restoring discipline with too much severity.</margin>
For this reason, it seems to me that Galba, Piso, Pertinax, Hadrian VI <note>Hadrian VI was a 16th-century Pope known for his failed attempt to reform the Roman Curia through strict austerity</note>, and others acted most imprudently in restoring discipline too severely. Galba acted most disgracefully of all; at the very time he was designating an heir to the Empire—and thus to the whole world—he denied a gift <note>original: "donativum" – a customary cash bonus given to soldiers to secure their loyalty during a transition of power</note> to the soldiers, specifically the Praetorian Guard, in whose hands the safety of the Emperor rested. At such a time, they ought to have been indulged rather than given an occasion to break all discipline. *For it was certain*, says Tacitus, *that their loyalty could have been won over by even the smallest generosity from the stingy old man*. When Galba realized that the soldiers were offended by this severity, he only then considered a public handout <note>original: "congiario" – a distribution of money or goods to the people</note>; but it was too late, and therefore in vain. *Remedies come too late*, he says <note>quoting Tacitus</note>, *when the wound has already reached its final breath*. Concerning Otho, however, after he had conquered the soldiers’ hearts with gifts, Tacitus writes: *Nor was Otho lacking*, he says, *stretching out his hands, worshipping the common crowd, throwing kisses, and doing everything like a slave for the sake of Absolute Power <note>original: "Dominatione"</note>*. Regarding Piso, however: *Nor*, he says, *was anything else said or done in public by Piso during the following four days*. Let men like this Piso go to the "Utopia" of some Thomas More <note>Referring to Sir Thomas More’s famous work; the author suggests these rigid, idealistic leaders belong in a fictional world, not a real, turbulent empire</note>; they are unworthy and unequal to the task of a turbulent empire.

<margin>Another facade in Tacitus: the natural talents of the Britons were preferred by the Romans over those of the Gauls. False praises of mutinous and lazy soldiers.</margin>
But I return to the previous passage of Tacitus: that the Romans preferred the natural talents of the Britons over the Gauls. By my faith <note>original: "medius fidius" – a common Latin oath</note>, this was done astutely. The Roman Consul in Livy, Book 3, used the same art. *Come*, he said, *young men, surpass the infantry in valor, just as you surpass them in rank and honor*. And Otho, who called the soldiers’ mutiny "devotion." *Your excessive devotion*, he said, *is more fierce than it is well-considered.*

Truly, as Pliny says in Book 6 of his *Epistles*: *The same things do not suit everyone: furthermore, the true reason for doing something, or not doing it, is found both in the men themselves and in the circumstances and the times* <note>original: "Non omnibus eadem conveniunt: præterea faciendi aliquid, vel non faciendi, vera ratio tum hominum ipsorum, tum rerum ac temporum initur"</note>.

<margin>Likewise by most Roman Emperors.</margin>
Furthermore, many Roman Emperors allowed the people this license for speaking ill. <margin>The reason for this facade lies in the talkativeness of the common people.</margin>
For the common people, being talkative by nature, believe themselves to be faring excellently if they can use their tongues to find fault as they please; especially when their liberty has been lost and their servitude is still fresh. As Justin <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian</note> says in Book 9: *Since the people cannot avenge themselves with deeds, they desire to exercise their liberty in words.*

This aligns with what Tiberius says in Suetonius's biography: *In a free city, both the tongue and the mind ought to be free.* For what will be left for the common people if the exchange of speaking and hearing is taken away through inquisitions? On this point, the same Tiberius—who was otherwise most severe—said regarding insults thrown at him, *that he did not wish to be called to an investigation.* And Cremutius <note>Cremutius Cordus, a historian whose trial for treason became a symbol of the loss of free speech under the Empire</note> beautifully said in his or-

Add to this, that a slip of the tongue should not easily be pulled into punishment (Law 7 of the Digest on the Julian Law of Treason <term>Majestas: the crime of violating the majesty or dignity of the state or ruler</term>). Therefore, Augustus said to Tiberius: *Do not, my Tiberius, give in to your youth in this matter, nor be overly indignant that anyone speaks ill of me; it is enough that we have this: that no one is able to do us harm.* This was said prudently and rightly. For he who has a mind and a "nose" <note>original: "nasum"; a Latin idiom for a sharp wit or a sense of satire</note> considers these things again and again to be of no consequence, content with the actual power of Rule itself. And that famous Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Laurentius Medices, the Renaissance ruler of Florence</note> was accustomed to saying: *Let them talk, but we shall act.* And as Lycus says in Seneca’s *Hercules*: *The first art of kingship is to be able to endure envy.*

<margin>
The words of Lycus in Seneca. To punish words as though they were deeds is cruel and harmful. Coercion feeds rumors. Reason...
</margin>
But it is also cruel to punish words as if they were deeds, as Curtius notes in Book 8: *The King had taken up the detestable service of an executioner [punishing] a license of words that could have been blamed on wine.* And who has a neck so strong as to suppress such things? *A massive work,* sings the poet, *with no more than a double labor.* So much is excessive coercion the nourishment of rumors, as Tacitus writes. Yet a ruler will act cautiously if he studiously notes those whom he can, and guards himself from them with diligent watchfulness. For, as Alexander says in Curtius, Book 6: *The rashness of the tongue leads to swords.* This was the reason for the Constitution issued by Theodosius (the single law in the Code titled *If anyone speaks ill of the Emperor* <note>original: "Si quis Imperatori maledixerit"</note>). It is enough to mention it here; it has received light from others.

### CHAPTER XII.
### *To turn a blind eye to minor offenses. How offenses are inflamed by excessive remedies. To be content with the punishment of a few.*

<margin>The third facade: turning a blind eye to minor offenses. An example in the King of the Macedonians and in Tiberius.</margin>
It also does a great deal to infatuate <note>in this context: to render the public dull-witted or politically passive</note> and break the common people when those who hold power turn a blind eye to certain lighter offenses. ### On the Facades of Power, Chapter 12.
N 6

<margin>Annals [of Tacitus].</margin>
How unbecoming it is to disparage what cannot be obtained. *But if any of the magistrates promises such industry and severity that he is able to oppose [this vice], I both praise this man, and I confess that a part of my own labors is being lifted.* <note>original: "Quod si quis ex magistratibus tantam industriam ac severitatem pollicetur, ut ire obviam queat, hunc & laudo, & exonerari laborum meorum partem fateor." <margin>Offenses are never cured by excessive remedies.</margin>
For my part, I approve more of a man like Servilius, who was suited to mild remedies, than a man like Appius, who possessed a vehement nature. <note>The author contrasts the moderate Marcus Servilius with the famously harsh and arrogant Appius Claudius, two archetypes of Roman leadership.</note> This is because offenses are often increased by a great number of excessive remedies. Regarding certain people, Tacitus says, *he inflamed offenses with excessive remedies.* And from Livy, Book 6: *he provoked the sedition by the very remedy [intended to stop it].* I take this to be a **facade of liberty**: it is what the seditious Roman youths, who were hostile to the rule of the aristocrats, used to say over and over: *That a King is a human being, from whom you may obtain what you need, whether it involves the law or an injury; that there is a place for favor and for kindness; that he has the power to forgive and the power to be angry.* <note>Livy Book 2, Chapter 3. The young nobles preferred monarchy because a king could be swayed by personal influence, whereas they viewed the laws of a Republic as "deaf and inexorable."</note>

<margin>Terrible crimes must be punished entirely.</margin>
I am speaking here of minor offenses. It is another matter entirely regarding more atrocious crimes, which stir up seditions and ruin republics. Regarding these, Livy says: *The senators ordered the new praetor to cut it out, lest it creep further.* Which Guntherus also elegantly expressed: <note>Gunther of Pairis (c. 1150–1220), a Cistercian monk and Latin poet.</note>
> *It is safer for rotting limbs to be cut away with steel,*
> *Than for the whole body to waste away from the corruption of a part.*

<margin>But with the punishment of a few.</margin>
And yet even in these cases, the Romans were content with the punishment of a few. From Livy, Book 4: *The consuls, exercising the greatest moderation and mildness through the punishments of a few—who, it was sufficiently believed, had brought death upon themselves—having settled the matter, were nevertheless unable to ensure that the common people did not take it very poorly.* And Tacitus: *By the terror of this, and the punishment of a few, harmony returned to the townsfolk.* And Seneca in his play *Octavia*:
> *I bring word that the fury of the people, which rashly*
> *Resisted for a long time, has been suppressed by the slaughter of a few.*

<summary>Clapmarius argues that rulers should generally avoid harsh, "excessive" legal punishments for minor crimes, as over-regulation often provokes more rebellion. Even in cases of serious sedition, he suggests that punishing a small number of ringleaders is more effective and stable than mass execution.</summary>

<keywords>facades of power, leniency, punishment, sedition, Roman law, Tacitus, Livy, Seneca, political stability, mercy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Clapmarius’s analysis of political "facades" (simulacra)—the strategies used by rulers to maintain order and public favor. <margin>
By transferring the resentment of the act onto the guilty parties themselves.
</margin>
Moreover, in decreeing punishments, the safest method is that used by **Germanicus** <note>Germanicus (15 BCE – 19 CE) was a beloved Roman general and nephew of Emperor Tiberius. He was known for his charisma and effective leadership of the Rhine legions.</note> in punishing mutinous soldiers. He transferred the cruelty and resentment of the punishment onto the soldiers themselves. For when he was asked by certain people to punish the guilty, he ordered that the soldiers themselves carry out the execution. On this point, **Tacitus** writes: *The Caesar [Germanicus] stood aloof; since, as there was no order of his, the same cruelty and resentment belonged to the act [itself].* <note>original: "Cæsar arcebat; quando, nullo ipsius jussu, eadem sævitia facti & invidia erat." From Tacitus’s *Annals*, Book 1. By letting the soldiers kill their own mutinous leaders, Germanicus avoided being blamed for the bloodshed.</note> And the poet **Claudian** rightly says:

> *He who delights in punishment is a beast, and seems*
> *to provide the laws’ vengeance for his own sake.*

### C A P V T XIII.

*Regarding the granting of many other things to the common people, even if they are unworthy: taking care of the grain supply: freeing the people from customs duties: indulging many other things which can later be revoked. The great wealth of the German assemblies.*

<margin>
Various enticements given to the common people are noted from Livy. Care of the grain supply.
</margin>
The writings of **Livy**, Book 2, are the most full of this teaching. *Many enticements,* he says, *were given to the common people during that time: first of all, care was taken for the grain supply [annona]; some were sent to the Volscians, others to Cumae, to obtain grain; the right to sell salt was also granted to private individuals after all expense was removed, because it had been sold to the public at an excessive price; the people were also freed from customs duties and tribute.* <term>Annona</term> <note>The *annona* was the Roman state's department for the grain supply, crucial for feeding the urban poor and preventing riots.</note> *And a little later: This indulgence of the fathers [the Senators], later during harsh times of siege and famine, held the city in such harmony that the highest and lowest alike shuddered at the name of a King; nor was any single person afterwards so popular through wicked arts as the whole Senate was then by governing well.* Thus he writes. This is a massive **facade** <term>simulacrum</term> used upon the common people, for whom, as Tacitus writes in Book 4 of the *Histories*, *the care of the grain supply is their only concern regarding the State.* And the Satirist [Juvenal] says:

<margin>
As for one to whom this is the only concern.
</margin>

# Regarding the Facades of Power, Chapter 13.
N 7
<meta>catchword: is said,</meta>

->*He anxiously desires only two things,*<-
->*Bread and Circuses:*<-
<note>original: "Duas tantum res anxius optat, / Panem & Circenses." From Juvenal's *Satires*. It refers to the idea that the Roman public had traded their political freedom for food and entertainment.</note>

<margin>Even unfair things must be granted to the common people for the sake of retaining power.</margin>
For this reason, sometimes even the most unfair things must be granted to the common people. As **Livy** <note>Titus Livius (64 BCE – 17 CE), a Roman historian who wrote a monumental history of Rome.</note> says: *harmony must be maintained through both fair and unfair means.* <note>original: "per æqua & iniqua retinendam esse concordiam."</note> The Roman army, relying on a new and wavering Prince, demanded that they earn a single denarius <note>A standard silver Roman coin.</note> per day; that the sixteenth year of service should bring an end to their term; and that they should no longer be held under the standards, but be paid their reward in cash in those same camps. At such a time, it was better to grant these things voluntarily,
<margin>Livy says this should be done voluntarily rather than out of necessity.</margin>
rather than having them extorted by necessity. On this point, Livy writes in Book 2: *It was not sufficiently honorable for the Fathers [the Senate] to have looked out for the fortunes of their distressed citizens out of fear, rather than later out of goodwill.* And in Book 4: *The Senate acted opportunely; before the Tribunes of the plebs could stir up agrarian seditions by mentioning the division of the Lavican land, the Senate decreed in a crowded session that a colony should be led to Lavici.*

<margin>Objection based on the unworthiness of such concessions.</margin>
But you will say: it was unworthy to grant the petition for pay, and furthermore, the Republic was unequal to such great burdens.

<margin>Concessions can be revoked and favorable times must be seized.</margin>
But indeed, can these things not be reconsidered once the people have calmed down? For so says **Tacitus** <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56 – 120 CE), a senator and historian of the Roman Empire known for his cynical and deep psychological analysis of power.</note>: *Those things which had been wrung out through sedition,* he says, *were changed.* <note>original: "Mutata... quæ per seditionem expressa erant."</note> And elsewhere: *the poorly considered measures of the recent sedition were abolished for the future.* And Livy in Book 2: *Many thought the time had come when the rights which had been extorted from the Fathers by sedition and force could be recovered.* And besides this, is it not better to hand over a small part of the Republic to the common people than to call the entire Republic into extreme danger? **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), an ancient Roman scholar and writer.</note> said it beautifully: *A finger must be cut off if, by that act, gangrene is not going to spread to the arm.*

<margin>The Prudence of Charles...</margin>
By this same reasoning, **Charles V** <note>Charles V (1500–1558), Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain, who dealt with significant religious and political unrest in Germany.</note> is said to have granted many immunities to the Estates of the Empire...

<summary>This page argues that rulers must sometimes grant even unreasonable demands to the public to prevent total revolt, with the caveat that these concessions can often be revoked once order is restored. It uses historical examples from Roman mutinies and the strategies of the Roman Senate to illustrate the necessity of "Bread and Circuses" for political survival.</summary>

it is said, in order to collect money against the Turk, the common enemy of Germany. They do this with a bit applied, but held loosely, lest they be shaken from their seat of Power if they try to pull back with a violent jerk. **Alexander the Great** is quoted appropriately in **Quintus Curtius**, Book 6:

> *In a new and precarious Empire, while the Barbarians still submit to its yoke with stiff necks, time is needed; until they are imbued with gentler dispositions, and a milder custom soothes their wildness.*

<margin>
To grant according to custom.
To lower the symbols of authority (*fasces*).
To indulge in minor things so you may seize greater ones.

...to grant the custom that prevailed in the past. Thus, regarding the Holidays in the second book of **Livy** <note>Titus Livius, the premier historian of early Rome.</note>, the lowering of the *fasces* <term>fasces: a bundle of wooden rods with an axe, carried by attendants called lictors to symbolize a magistrate's power to punish and execute</term> called the common people back from sedition. **Livy** writes: <note>original: "Valerius... vocato in consilium populo submissis fascibus in concionem ascendit."</note> *Valerius, being suspected of aiming for kingship, called the people to a council and climbed the speaker's platform with lowered fasces. That was a pleasing sight to the multitude: that the symbols of power were lowered to them, and a confession was made that the majesty and power of the People were greater than those of the Consul.* Look how much this external and moderate appearance was able to bewitch the common people!

In the same vein, **Livy** writes in book 3: *There, the greatest progress was made because they tempered their impulses in a certain manner.* And in the same place: *By applying counsel and moderation where the situation required, they remained the leaders.*

To this point belong the words of **Velleius Paterculus** <note>A Roman soldier and historian of the early Empire.</note> in book 2: ***Marcus Livius Drusus*** <note>A reformist politician whose actions paved the way for the Social War.</note>*, even in those very things he was striving for on behalf of the Senate, found the Senate to be his adversary. They did not understand that if he did anything for the benefit of the common people, it was done as a way to bait and entice the multitude; so that once they had received minor things, he could promise greater ones.* And as **Cicero** says in book 3 of *On the Nature of the Gods*: *Many, while wishing to hinder, have helped; and while wishing to help, have hindered.*

<margin>
To flatter the common people with kind greetings, invitations, etc.
</margin>
Furthermore, nothing "dresses up" or cloaks the common people more than showy flattery. For example, when the Roman Fathers <note>The Senators.</note> noticed that the military levy was being blocked by the power of the Tribunes <note>Officials elected to protect the rights of the plebeians.</note>, they spontaneously flattered the Tribunes. **Livy** (book 2): *All the Fathers began to address the Tribunes courteously and kindly; and those of Consular rank—since each of them had some private legal standing against individuals—prevailed partly through favor and partly through authority, so that they made the powers of the tribunician office healthy for the Republic.* By this same art, the Roman Senators evaded the **Terentillian Law** <note>A proposed law intended to publish the laws and limit the arbitrary power of the consuls; it was fiercely resisted by the patricians.</note> for a whole year. **Livy** (book 3): *On the intervening days when the Tribunes were not acting upon the law, nothing was more peaceful or quiet than those very same men,*

### CHAPTER XV.

->*The force and dignity of these Facades in the Republic. Certain other Aristotelian, Democratic, and Aristocratic facades. The appearance of these Facades is great. However, it is not so great that they either establish or change the state of the Republic. # Of the Facades of Power, Chapter 15.
<meta>catchword: But</meta>

...[more] popular, than that one, and that one more royal, than this. For the method of governing sometimes consists in these **facades**; but the form of the State <note>original: "forma Reipublicae"</note> consists in the very power of the State <term>Imperium: supreme executive power or sovereignty</term>.

<margin>Facades passed down by Aristotle which exist in a popular state.</margin>
Moreover, certain great facades are handed down by **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher, particularly in his work *Politics*.</note>: such as in a popular state, to appoint advisors from the wealthy, and to spare them as much as possible; also to share with the wealthy or **Patricians** <note>The hereditary noble class of ancient Rome.</note> an equal or lesser share in all matters, except for the supreme Power: which must always remain in the hands of the people, or in the hands of the poor.

<margin>Those in an Aristocratic state. Sharing with those from [the people...]</margin>
In an **Aristocratic** state <note>A government ruled by a small, elite class of "best" citizens.</note>, these are the facades: to entrust to the **plebeians** <note>The common citizens of Rome, distinct from the elite Patricians.</note>, or the poor, those kinds of magistracies from which they can make a profit; to call certain individuals from the common people to deliberation; to create, from both commoners and patricians, those who may discuss matters, about which a few patricians afterwards decide according to their own judgment; likewise to entrust to the people the power of voting on those things which have previously been decreed by the elite. This is almost like that passage in **Livy**, Book 1: *The Fathers decreed that when the People had ordered a King, that should be ratified; if the Fathers became the authors of it.* <note>original: "Decreverunt Patres, ut cum Populus Regem jussisset, id sic ratum esset; si Patres autores fierent." This refers to the *Auctoritas Patrum*, the legal approval required from the Senate.</note> And today the same right is used in proposing laws and magistrates, though its force has been taken away; before the people enter their vote, into the uncertain outcome of the assemblies, the fathers become authors. Likewise, to leave to some of the people the power of acquitting, but not of condemning.

<margin>Facades in a popular state contrary to the Aristocratic one.</margin>
But on the contrary, in a popular state: that Patricians might be able to acquit, but not to condemn: just as at Rome a case concerning the life of a citizen could not be conducted except in the **centuriate assemblies** <note>original: "centuriatis... comitiis." These were the highest voting assemblies in Rome, organized by wealth and military rank.</note>, that is, the greatest and most full assemblies.

## CHAPTER XVI.

*Certain military secrets. Military laws. Laws of spoils: Disgraces of the military: military secrets; giving signals, addressing soldiers from the tribunal, military standards, seizing eagles. Military facades; calling soldiers "fellow soldiers," victors of nations. How military art differs from these secrets.*

<margin>The use of this doctrine is just as great in war as in peace. Secrets and facades. Also, examples of military disgraces illustrated by common military examples.</margin>
The use of this doctrine is very great not only in the business of peace, but also in matters of war. And I could without difficulty illustrate not only the laws of war, but also its **secrets** <term>arcana: hidden strategies or maneuvers used to maintain power</term> and **facades** <term>simulacra: appearances of power or legal right meant to influence morale</term>, as well as the **disgraces of the military** <note>original: "militiae flagitia," a phrase used by the historian Tacitus to describe shameful or criminal conduct by an army</note>, with military examples; except that most are quite obvious, such as the laws of spoils. As that famous Aemilius <note>Lucius Aemilius Paullus, the Roman general who conquered Macedon</note> says in the writings of Livy, *in the matter of spoils, the decision belongs to the Commanders, not the soldiers.* Likewise, driving off booty, ravaging fields, besieging, storming, and leveling great and vast cities to the ground—just as that Roman General Corbulo <note>Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, a prominent general under Claudius and Nero</note> destroyed the city of Artaxata in Armenia. Because, as Tacitus says: *It could neither be held without a strong garrison due to the size of its walls, nor did we have enough strength that it could be divided between reinforcing a garrison and prosecuting the war.* By this same right, Hannibal destroyed Saguntum, Scipio destroyed Carthage, Vespasian destroyed Jerusalem, and Dagobert <note>A 7th-century King of the Franks</note> destroyed **Pavia** <note>original: "Putavium," likely a variant of Papia (Pavia), though sometimes used for Padua (Patavium)</note>.

<margin>Such are the laws of spoils and the depopulation of fields.</margin>
But it is also a **disgrace of the military** to vent rage indiscriminately against walls and battlements. This is what Phaneas <note>An Aetolian statesman and general</note> reproached Philip, King of Macedonia, for: that he did not meet in battle on an open field, nor with joined

<margin>The destruction of cities, and cruelty against walls and battlements.</margin>

<margin>Military secrets differ from the technical arts of war.</margin>
...in the duty of keeping the soldier in his place. From these <note>the psychological "simulations" mentioned on the previous page</note> one must distinguish the actual military arts themselves. These include knowing the right time to begin a battle, strengthening the line with reserves when the situation requires it, bringing the cavalry down to support the infantry, restoring the fight, subvening those cut off from the battle line, and other things of that kind. Regarding all of these, the Tribune of the Plebs, Gaius Julius, accused Sempronius <note>Gaius Sempronius Atratinus, a Roman consul in 423 BCE who was blamed for a near-defeat against the Volscians</note>, as recorded in Book 4 of Livy. Modern military service is far different from our own ancient discipline; in ours, not even errors are punished, whereas in the past, if a recruit or a common soldier fell into such mistakes, it led to ruin and was worthy of punishment.
