# On the Simulations of Power. Chapter 17. #

<margin>Also the shames of life.</margin>Common life has its own shames, as when one person supplants another, either through envy or to secure their own position. Such are those who, by excusing the vices of others, actually manage to reproach them; they build up their own reputation at the expense of another’s name, striking "through the side" of their neighbor. Yet, while they hurry too much, they ultimately fail.

<margin>The example of a certain Brutidius.</margin>As the sharp writer <note>original: "acer scriptor" — a reference to the Roman historian Tacitus</note> reports, there was a certain Brutidius <note>Brutidius Niger, a rhetorician and politician mentioned in Tacitus's *Annals* 3.66</note> who was well-endowed with honorable skills; had he proceeded on the right path, he would have reached the highest honors. However, haste drove him to madness as he tried to surpass first his equals, then his superiors, and finally even his own prospects. This haste has ruined many good men who, scorning the slow path of safety, rush toward premature goals even at the cost of their own destruction.

<margin>A secret of civil life: turning chance occurrences to one's use by appearing to do something else.</margin>You must fortify yourself in marvelous ways against such people so that you are not deceived. This is my "secret of civil life": that you should turn whatever happens to you to your own advantage. Or, as Livy says, you should "bend things offered by chance to your own counsel" <note>original: "oblata casu, flectas ad consilium"</note>, and indeed do so while appearing to do something else <note>original: "aliud agendo" — a tactical maneuver where one achieves a goal while pretending to focus on a different task.</note>. If you wait every day for a better opportunity, you will wait in vain and find yourself stuck. At one time, the French feared a war with the English and saw it approaching. The Bretons <note>referring to the people of Brittany, who often navigated the conflicts between France and England</note>, seizing this opportunity to persuade the King of France to make peace—which they desired above all else—began to exaggerate the threat of the English war in many ways. They described the dangers and difficulties in vivid detail, making no mention of peace at all. By this simulation, they easily drew the King over to their own point of view. <margin>An example of this among the French.</margin> You should imitate this even in common life, especially against those who value none of their virtues more than the art of simulation—a habit famously associated with the Emperor Tiberius. As Marcus Tullius Cicero most truly wrote:

> *The nature of every man is covered by many layers of simulation, and shrouded as if by veils; the brow, the eyes, and the face often lie, but speech lies most often of all.* <note>original: "Multis simulationum involucris tegitur..." — quoted from Cicero's letter to his brother Quintus (*Ad Quintum Fratrem* 1.1.15).</note>

# Book VI of Arnoldus Clapmarius #

<margin>
To seem not to understand. To say less than one feels.
</margin>

To guard yourself against such people, you must take care to appear not to understand what you do understand, and so forth. Cicero writes to Atticus: *that you say less than you think* <note>original: "ut minus dicas, quam sentis"</note>. Tiberius, while seizing the Empire, introduced a sense of hesitation in order to peer into the minds of the Senators; the Senate, to mock this deception in turn, and to "play the fox with a fox," as the saying goes, feigned that they did not understand. Tacitus says, "The Fathers [Senators], whose only fear was that they might seem to understand, poured themselves out in complaints, tears, and vows." <note>A reference to the Senate's reaction to Tiberius's feigned reluctance to take power in *Annals* 1.11.</note> And regarding Agrippina <note>Agrippina the Younger, mother of Nero</note>: "The only remedy for plots was if they were not understood."

<margin>
To hide dangers.
</margin>

Seneca expresses this: "Some have taught others to deceive, while they themselves fear being deceived." And the tragic poet Seneca says in the play *Octavia*:

->*The wise compliance of the noble wife*<-
->*nevertheless prevailed, and her grief was suppressed.*<-

<margin>
To suppress grief. To be skeptical <note>original: "ἀπιστεῖν" (apistein)</note>.
</margin>

Therefore, what is a golden rule to Marcus Tullius [Cicero] is like the very apple of my eye: "Remember to be skeptical" <note>original: "μέμνησο ἀπιστεῖν" (memnēso apistein). This was a famous maxim of the Greek poet Epicharmus, often cited by Cicero, emphasizing that distrust is the sinew of the mind.</note>. For in this world, says Pliny the Younger in Book 2 of his *Letters*, a man who is otherwise very prudent is caught in an honorable but nonetheless mistaken error: that he thinks he has more friends than actually exist. "O friends, there is no friend" <note>original: "Ω φίλοι ὀδείς φίλος" (O philoi oudeis philos). A famous paradox attributed to Aristotle, suggesting true friendship is rare.</note>. For what else is this human life but deception and pretense? No one speaks from the heart; no one lies openly; but they mix truth with falsehood, embellish it, and thus more easily deceive the inexperienced. How few now harbor enmities openly; and alas, he who does so is how quickly overwhelmed by manufactured and hidden accusations!

<margin>
That friendships today are only for show.
</margin>

Tacitus notes this sharply in Book 4 of the *Histories*: "While the friendship remained in outward appearance" <note>original: "Manente... in speciem amicitia"</note>. And in Book 1 of the *Annals*: "Tiberius immediately attacked Haterius; Scaurus, against whom he was more implacably angry, he passed over in silence." And in Book 3 of the *Histories*: "From there came serious rivalries, which Antonius nurtured more simply, but Mutianus nurtured cunningly, and therefore more implacably."

Hidden hatreds...
</margin>

Against those who hate openly, you may easily fortify yourself. But even those do...

### CHAPTER XVIII.

*The difficulty of state secrets and the dangers surrounding these arts if they are discovered. How these secrets are to be masked so that they have a "color" <note>In this context, "color" refers to a plausible pretext or an outward appearance of legitimacy.</note> of truth: and a response to two objections.*

And these are most of the matters included by writers under the name of state secrets <note>original: "arcanorum"</note>. For as much as I am able to cover everything—"You ask me for a refusal?" <note>original Greek: "ἄρνησιν μ᾽ αἰτεῖς" (arnēsin m' aiteis)</note>; and as that man says,

->*For the reward of deep silence is without danger.*<-
-><note>original Greek: "Ἀκίνδυνον γὰρ ἐστὶ τῆς σιγῆς γέρας" (Akindynon gar esti tēs sigēs geras)</note><-

<margin>Mixed Republics can be adapted to these secrets. Great difficulty in accomplishing this matter.</margin>
Even mixed Republics <term>Respublica mixta</term> <note>A state that combines elements of monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy to achieve balance.</note>, as most are, can be adapted to these secrets. For it is possible that in a single Empire, in a single Republic, secrets of this kind may be found—whether royal, aristocratic, or democratic. And yet, there is great difficulty in properly executing this matter. As Aristotle says in Book 5 of the *Politics*, chapter 8: "One must not trust in tricks <note>original Greek: "σοφίσμασι" (sophismasi), referring here to political ruses or fallacies.</note> composed to deceive the multitude; for they are refuted by the facts." <note>original Greek: "Μὴ πισθύειν τοῖς σοφίσμασι χάριν πρὸς τὸ πλῆθος συγκειμένοις; ἐξελέγχεται γὰρ ὑπὸ τῶν ἔργων."</note> He is speaking here of these very secrets of state. And in Book 4, chapter 12: "For it is inevitable that in time, from false goods, a real evil will arise." <note>original Greek: "Ἀνάγκη γὰρ χρόνῳ πότ᾽ ἐκ τῶν ψευδῶν ἀγαθῶν, ἀγαθὲς συνβῆναι κακὸν."</note> Gunther <note>Gunther of Pairis (c. 1150–1220), a Cistercian monk and author of the *Ligurinus*, an epic poem about Frederick Barbarossa often cited by political theorists.</note> praises this principle in his *Prince*, Book 2.

> *The troupe performs a mime on stage; that one is called*
> ->the father,<-

> *Soon, when the script has closed the laughable roles,*
> *The true face returns, and the disguised one perishes.*

Therefore, concerning this very matter, a certain Roman Dictator in Livy says: *“As for what concerns me, I will neither deceive my fellow citizens further, nor will I myself be a dictator in vain.”* For if those against whom such snares are laid should sense the matter beforehand, they will overthrow the Republic in a single impulse. That famous Appius, the Decemvir <note>One of a ten-man commission appointed to reform Roman law; Appius Claudius was the most notorious member.</note>, wanted his term as Decemvir to be extended. To prevent this, the others devised a trick and assigned to him the duty of holding the elections. On this, Livy writes in *Book 3*: *“This was the artifice: that he might not be able to elect himself.”* But he noticed the trick and elected himself anyway, casting aside those who were most steadfast in the cause of the aristocrats.

# On the Simulations of Empire. Chapter 18. 315

*And thus he lies, so mixing the false with the true,*
*That the beginning fits the middle, and the middle the end.*
<note>original: "Atque ita mentitur, sic veris falsa remiscet. Primo ne medium, medio ne discrepet imum." This is a famous quote from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, advising poets on how to create a believable fiction. Clapmarius applies this to politics: a lie must be consistent to be believed.</note>

Following this advice, Ligurinus <note>Gunther of Pairis (c. 1150–1220), a Cistercian monk and poet who wrote the *Ligurinus*, an epic poem about Frederick Barbarossa.</note> says in Book 3, even if he speaks of a wicked matter:

> He knew the beautiful art of deceiving,
> Proving false things with the true; because no one 
> Can deceive by speaking only falsehoods. 
> Under the image of the truth, the false 
> Flows in, and stealthily occupies the ears it has deceived.

I must not overlook the fact at this point that many people believe some of these simulations are of little importance. Yet Aristotle says in Book 5 of the *Politics*, Chapter 8:

The mind is misled <note>original: "Παραλογίζεται... ἡ διάνοια." Clapmarius uses Greek to cite Aristotle’s technical term for a logical fallacy.</note> by these small changes, just as in the sophistical argument: "if each part is small, then the whole is also small." This is true in one sense, but not in another; for the whole and the sum are not small, but are composed of small parts.

*The mind is deceived by them, as by that sophistical reasoning: if every single thing is tiny, then the whole is also tiny. This is so in one way, and not so in another. For the whole, and the sum of all things, is not small; rather, it is composed of small things.*

<margin>Caution is needed, lest you concede too much.</margin>
And so much caution is needed that you are not too lenient in indulging these sorts of simulations. For once people have attained small things, they always strive for greater ones. They proceed to infinity, as the Philosopher <note>A common title for Aristotle in Renaissance and Early Modern texts.</note> relates in *Politics* Book 1, Chapter 5. And Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> writes in Book 3: *By conceding everything, the Senate would find the common people <term>plebs</term> <note>The general body of free Roman citizens who were not patricians.</note> not more gentle toward them, but more harsh; for having obtained their first requests, they would demand one thing after another, each more unjust than the last.*

<margin>The author explains why he distinguishes between different kinds of secrets.</margin>
Furthermore, certain things are introduced by me here and there which do not strictly belong to those "sophistical secrets" <gloss>deceptive political maneuvers</gloss>; and others will criticize this. To them I answer again that I take the "Secrets of the State" <term>arcana Rerumpubl.</term> in two ways. Some secrets are simulations and are "sophistical" <note>original: "σοφιστικὰ." Clapmarius uses the Greek term to imply a "crafty" or "deceptive" trick.</note>; others are not. And yet they often aim at the same target: the safety of those who hold the

# On the Simulacra of Empire. Chapter 19.

...there is no doubt that the Commonwealth <note>original: *Respublica*</note> suffers harm.

<margin>Harmony among the orders of the Empire.</margin>
The greatest philosopher and statesman [Aristotle] once proved this through the art of harmony; in this art, the choir master will not allow one member of the choir to strain his voice too much, nor to emit a sound too high and sharp that it deafens the others. Rather, he ensures that the melody is balanced, which Aristotle elegantly calls "harmonizing" <note>original: "συμφωνεῖν" (symphōnein)</note>. 
<margin>This harmony must be entirely preserved.</margin>
Therefore, primary care must be taken so that these members do not become alienated from one another, and that neither side is too heavily oppressed. For instance, that famous Gracchus <note>Tiberius or Gaius Gracchus, Roman reformers whose populist measures often bypassed the Senate, leading to political instability.</note>, by depressing the senatorial order and excessively exalting the others, dealt the first blow to the Roman Republic. For this structure joined together—as Tacitus <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56 – 120 AD), the Roman historian.</note> said of the Roman Republic—through the fortune and discipline of many years; it is a structure that cannot be torn apart without the destruction of those doing the tearing. Cicero speaks appropriately on this in a Letter to his brother Quintus:

<margin>There must be one head of this Empire.</margin>
> If we oppose these tax collectors <note>original: *publicanis* — private contractors who collected taxes for the Roman state.</note>, we shall alienate from ourselves an order that has deserved very well of us and which has been joined to the Republic through us; we ought to serve not only their safety, but even their interests.

<margin>No foreigner is to be elevated to the Empire.</margin>
For this reason, it is of the greatest importance that there be one head of this empire; if this head were cut off (which may the gods forbid), what else would exist but wars of all the members against each other? As a Roman General once said. By this same counsel, care has been taken that no foreigner <note>original: *externus*</note> be elevated to the Empire. For such a person, relying on external power and impatient of sharing authority, would easily bring the liberty of Germany to ruin. 
<margin>The King of Bohemia's role in electing the Emperor.</margin>
From this, it was also prudently established that in electing an Emperor, if the votes are in disagreement, the King of Bohemia <note>One of the seven Prince-electors of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> holds the prerogative <note>The deciding or tie-breaking vote.</note>, so that if they disagree equally, he himself...

# On the Simulations of Empire. Chapter 20.

...to Constantinople; to keep the sons and heirs of the Empire in such close custody that they do not break out and plot revolutions; to grant great outward displays of honor to the Pashas <note>original: *Bassis*</note> and Viziers; even to honor them with marriage alliances; and to keep the common people occupied with either trade or military affairs.

<margin>A singular point is noted: that no one from the conquered nations is permitted to offer prayers in their temples for the safety of the Prince.</margin>

Furthermore, I consider this a great secret of state <note>original: *imperii arcano*</note>: that no one among the conquered peoples is allowed to offer prayers for the Prince’s safety in their temples. This was once the duty of the high priests and other priests under the Roman Emperors. *Tacitus, Annals, Book 4: The high priests, and other priests following their example, when they took up vows for the safety of the Prince, etc.* Privately, however, it was permitted to all. As Martial <note>A Roman poet known for his epigrams.</note> wrote to Jupiter:

> Do not be angry with me, Jupiter, as if I were proud
> When I ask nothing for myself;
> I ought to petition you on behalf of Caesar,
> And I ought to petition Caesar on behalf of myself.

<margin>Every single law of the Quran contains secrets of domination.</margin>

And Pliny in his *Panegyric* <note>original: *Panegyricus*, a famous speech of praise by Pliny the Younger to the Emperor Trajan.</note>: *The one prayer of all is the safety of the Prince.* Moreover, nearly every single law of the Quran <note>original: *Alcorani*</note> contains nothing other than secret counsels for preserving or increasing dominion. For this reason, there was a need for greater wisdom and diligence against such a powerful and well-fortified Empire. And yet, that enemy has become famous through our dissensions and discords; as that former leader of the Britons, Galgacus <note>A Caledonian chieftain who opposed the Roman conquest.</note>, used to say, *he turns our vices to the glory of his own army.* Why, then, do you German Princes not settle matters with your military expeditions? After so many years, set a great day for this; prove to the State that neither the delays of war nor the reasons for making peace could ever be blamed on the army. For thus spoke the famous Agricola <note>The Roman general and father-in-law of Tacitus who campaigned in Britain.</note> long ago to his Roman soldiers.

# Arnold Clapmarius, Book V.

<margin>
The secrets of the Venetian Republic.
</margin>
...simulations and the external appearance of the Empire rest with the Doge <note>original: *Duce*; the elected leader of Venice</note>; however, the actual power of the Empire rests with the Senate. The Venetians do not easily resort to arms, for they strive for neutrality; nevertheless, they send aid to various factions. They allow the common people <note>original: *plebi*</note> to hold the lowlier offices, such as those of Chancellors, Scribes, and so on.

<margin>
The author calls another place the "jewel" of Germany.
</margin>
In that Republic which is the jewel <note>original: *ocellum*, literally "little eye," a term of endearment for something precious or beautiful</note> of Germany <note>Clapmarius is likely referring to the Free Imperial City of Nuremberg, often praised for its governance</note>, there is a great care for the census and the dignity of the leading families. There are ranks of dignity, clear distinctions, and a constant presence of Senators in the court, as if from a watchtower over the whole city. This is arranged so that those who hold the actual empire and the force of power may abstain from those external simulations by living sparingly and frugally in private, both in food and clothing, and also in their dwellings. It ensures that the Senators are humane and civil toward the common people, but severe toward the wicked; that the commoners are occupied either with official duties or notable trade, and that they are admitted to minor magistracies. Furthermore, the sons of the Aristocracy <note>original: *Optimatum*</note> are expected to surpass the common crowd in the equestrian, military, and literary arts, as well as through various travels abroad. Indeed, it is common in our Republics—and a notable simulation of empire—to report matters to the people for a vote only after they have already been decided by decree. But once again, that Helenus <note>A Trojan seer in Virgil's Aeneid</note> in the poet's work pulls my ear:

> *For the Fates prevent Helenus from knowing the rest,*
> *and Saturnian Juno forbids him to speak.* <note>original: *Prohibent nam cætera Parcæ, / Scire Helenum, farique vetat Saturnia Iuno.* Quoted from Virgil's Aeneid, 3.379-80.</note>

# BY CHRISTOPHORUS BESOLDUS, JURIST.

## Concerning the Secrets of States,

### CHAPTER I.

->Concerning Secrets suitable to every state.<-

<margin>The necessity of Secrets of State.</margin>
Subjects must be guided toward political happiness not only through religion, education, laws, and other similar means; but because the Majesty of the Empire serves as the guardian of safety, the ruler must also protect the state’s condition, its form, and his own authority through certain means. These are commonly called "secrets of the republic" or "secrets of the empire"; Aristotle, in Book 5, Chapter 8 of his *Politics*, calls them "political sophisms" <note>original Greek: *tōn politeiōn sophismata* — clever maneuvers used by a government to maintain its power</note>, and elsewhere "hidden things" <note>original Greek: *kryphia*</note>, and also "contrivances" <note>original Greek: *kataskeuasmata*</note>. See Conrad Cerneman in the *Works of Julius Caesar*, number 214, and Facius in the preface to *Livian Politics*. Consequently, these matters also concern the safety of the people, since the safety of the Prince and the stability of the state are primarily focused on public peace.

<margin>Praise for Arnold Clapmarius.</margin>
These matters were first organized into a system by *Arnold Clapmarius*, a most prudent young man, in that brilliant work he titled *Concerning the Secrets of States*. However, most of its contents are claimed by *Waremund von Ehrenberg* (also known as *Eberhard von Weihe*) in a plagiarizing manner <note>Besoldus uses the phrase *conditione suppilatoria*, accusing Weihe of "pilfering" or "thieving" Clapmarius's ideas</note> within his *Treatise on Subsidies*, Chapter 3, number 4, Chapter 6, number 26, and also Chapter 7, number 31. It also contributes to these...

<summary>In this opening chapter, Besoldus defines "Secrets of State" (Arcana) as necessary tools for a ruler to maintain authority and public peace, citing Aristotle and discussing the academic history of the topic.</summary>

# THE DISCOURSE OF CHRISTOPHORUS BESOLDUS

...to the knowledge of these secrets, **Tacitus** is especially useful, as is **Suetonius** as well; (whom I believe it would benefit the world of letters if the most distinguished **Berneggerus** <note>Matthias Bernegger (1582–1640) was a renowned professor at Strasbourg known for his editions of classical historians.</note> continues to further illustrate with his most learned commentary); among more recent authors, however, **Guicciardini** and **Machiavelli** are of note.

<margin>
What the
Secret of 
Empire 
once was.
</margin>
II. The *Secret of Empire* <note>original Latin: *Arcanum Imperii*</note> among the ancients was once a kind of inner sanctuary for superstitions: it consisted of ceremonies, rites, and the most ancient statues of the Gods, by which foolish paganism believed Empires were preserved and, once preserved, kept stable. For most of these kingdoms cultivated such fictions of human design in the innermost recesses of their temples; they persuaded the common people that public safety was, as it were, dependent on these things, so that no one would investigate the foundations of their religions, or, having investigated them, would dare to betray them, deterred by a preconceived sense of sanctity. **Caspar Barthius** <note>A German philologist and scholar (1587–1658).</note> on **Rutilius**, Book 2, verse 42. And thus it was considered a sin to make public the name of the guardian God of the city of Rome, under whose auspices it had reached such height, as **Plutarch** and **Macrobius** testify.

<margin>
Secrets of 
the Republic
are different 
and are defined.
</margin>
The secrets of the Republic, of which I speak here, are something else; and I define them, following **Clapmarius** <note>Arnold Clapmarius (1573–1604) wrote a foundational text on the "secrets" or maneuvers used to maintain political power.</note> (in this work, Book 1, Chapter 4), as: the intimate and hidden reasons or counsels of those who hold the leadership in a Republic, for the sake of both their own tranquility and the preservation of the current state of the Republic, and generally for the public good. And these **Lipsius** <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606) was a highly influential philosopher whose "Politics" sought to combine moral philosophy with practical governance.</note> calls "sharp counsels," deviating from virtue or the laws for the good of the ruler and the Empire, which you might even call "good deceit" <note>original Latin: *dolum bonum*—a legal and ethical term for a lie or trick used for a beneficial or necessary end.</note>; to God, however, they are hidden arts. For indeed, if the secrets of any particular government were known by the common people, much of their authority would be taken away. And certainly, to discuss them, even in general, with the favor of political...

# On the Simulations of Empire. Chapter 21.

<margin>The preservation of Republics.</margin>
...preserved. For unless the Roman Consuls—after the Kings had been driven out and the Republic was thus transformed—and later the Roman Emperors had been instructed in these secrets, they could never have laid such strong and long-lasting foundations for their rule. Yet, in truth, few people understand these things. Therefore, the historian Sallust <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus (86–35 BC), a celebrated Roman historian known for his accounts of the Catiline conspiracy and the Jugurthine War.</note> spoke truly: *To me,* he said, *as I read and heard much regarding the illustrious deeds the Roman people performed at home and in war, and as I pondered what quality above all else had sustained such great affairs, it finally became clear that the outstanding virtue of a few citizens had accomplished everything.* <note>original Latin: "Mihi... multa legenti... constitit tandem, paucorum civium egregiam virtutem cuncta patravisse."</note>

<margin>Who may be fit for these things.</margin>
But not everyone is fit for this task; rather, only those who are <term>most skillful masters of their craft</term> <note>original Greek: τεχνώτατοι (technōtatoi)</note>, versatile, and possessing a practiced countenance and mind. Such men are those who do not wish to appear as they truly are; they are not overly cautious or blunt in all matters, but rather they allow certain things that are merely for show so that they may draw out greater results. It is a matter of great talent to take counsel in public affairs based on the specific situation and the timing.

<margin>A clever counsel of civility given by Seneca to Nero is noted.</margin>
While Nero was listening to the ambassadors of the Armenians delivering their speeches, his mother Agrippina prepared to ascend the Emperor’s platform and to rule alongside him, while the Senate looked on in stunned silence. In that moment, Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (4 BC–65 AD), the Stoic philosopher and advisor to the Emperor Nero.</note> whispered into Nero's ear that he should go out to meet his mother as she approached the public council, under the appearance of filial piety. In this way, he blocked both the woman's ambition and a public disgrace. Thus, both Nero’s reverence toward his mother and the majesty of the Prince remained unharmed.

<margin><term>Bad Governance</term> <note>original Greek: Κακο-πολιτεία (Kakopoliteia)</note> of Johannes Victorius, Jurist.</margin>

An example of this was given in the Florentine Republic by that Johannes Victorius <note>Giovanni Vittorio, a legal scholar and politician in Renaissance Florence.</note>, a man otherwise skilled in the laws...

# On the Simulations of Power, Chapter 21.

<margin>
To rule in the forum and to handle public business are distinct duties.
</margin>
In his *Letter to his brother Quintus* <note>original: "Epistola ad Quintum Fratrem"; Cicero’s letters to his brother often contain advice on administration and provincial governance.</note>, Cicero says: "In making agreements, they are able to look not to the strict censorial law <note>original: "legem censuriam"; referring to the rigid rules or contracts overseen by the Censors in Rome.</note>, but rather to the convenience of completing the business and the relief from trouble." For this reason, it was necessary that the duties of those who rule in the forum <note>The "forum" here represents the arena of public leadership and politics.</note> be distinct from the duties of those who handle public affairs and business. Cicero says the same thing in his speech *In Defense of Cornelius Balbus*. Indeed, that famous Scaevola the Augur <note>Quintus Mucius Scaevola (c. 159–88 BCE), a renowned authority on Roman law.</note>, though he was a man most skilled in the law, when he was consulted regarding the law of estates <term>jus praediatorium</term> <note>The specific area of law dealing with land ownership and state-guaranteed properties.</note>, he would sometimes refer his clients to Furius and Cascellius, who were specialists in estates. He did this because a mind devoted to one specific thing through constant use often surpasses both natural talent and theoretical art.

<margin>
Commanders are to be preferred over legal experts in these matters.
</margin>
Who would doubt that, regarding treaties—that is, regarding the entire law of peace and war—our Commanders <note>original: "Imperatores"; while often translated as Emperors, in this context it refers to high-ranking military and civil leaders who possess "imperium" or the right to command.</note> are to be preferred over even the most skilled legal experts? And indeed, by these and similar methods, the Roman Princes obtained much more and much faster than if they had snatched power <term>imperium</term> <note>The supreme authority of the state.</note> away from the people in a single moment or with a single impulse. As Tacitus elegantly and truly wrote:

> *They were specious in words, but empty or deceitful in reality; the more they were covered by a grand image of liberty, the more they were destined to break out into a more bitter servitude.* <note>original: "Speciosa verbis, re inania aut subdola..." from Tacitus, *Annals* 1.81. Tacitus is describing the "simulations" of Augustus, who kept the outward forms of the Republic while centralizing all power.</note>

[...I may be permitted] to do so: for there are those who perhaps do not wish the innermost chambers of political science to be revealed (as the legal expert <term>Govianus</term> <note>Likely referring to a jurist such as Gulielmus Govanus or a similar legal commentator</note> says in a similar context). Indeed, even God himself has his own secret counsels, into which it is acknowledged as a sin for man to inquire. <margin>Divine Secrets.</margin> *For the searcher of Majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory.* <note>original: "Scrutator enim Majestatis opprimetur à gloria," a Latin rendering of Proverbs 25:27, often used to warn against over-curiosity regarding the divine or the sovereign.</note> Such is that secret concerning the time of the world's end, which not even the Angels themselves know; and other Mysteries, shared only with the saints. Just as Paul boasts that, having been caught up into the third heaven, he heard secret words which a man is not permitted to speak. <margin>Sacred secrets.</margin> And likewise Princes and court politicians (whose greatest secret is that their secrets must not be revealed) take it badly when such things are published; they pursue with hatred those books where such matters are discussed. This is what the most witty <term>Boccalini</term> <note>Trajano Boccalini (1556–1613), an Italian satirist famous for his "News from Parnassus," a work that critiqued the politics of his day</note> also notes, who in his *first century, report 89*, relates that Machiavelli was expelled from Parnassus for the reason that he "restored sight to the moles"; and in his *second century, report 71*, he imagines Tacitus being accused by Princes because he manufactured "political spectacles." <note>A metaphor for analytical tools that allow the public to see through the deceptions of rulers</note> Add also *century 1, report 86, folio 400.* But in truth, Guevara, Julius Bellus, Lipsius, and others advise that one should investigate the secrets of every Republic while traveling abroad. And even in theory, it would be useful to investigate the secrets of politicians as far as literature allows, lest they overwhelm the unwary when one moves from the school to the forum—as if into another world—to take action. For *weapons that are foreseen cause less harm.* <note>original: "tela praevisa minus nocent," a common legal and political maxim suggesting that being forewarned is being forearmed.</note> To suppress these things would perhaps be an act of envy, just as a certain <term>legal expert</term> <note>The text uses the abbreviation "ICtus" for "Iureconsultus," meaning a professional lawyer or scholar of the law</note> revealed that there are secrets of Jurisprudence which Doctors hide from their students so that they may always seem wiser than them. Neither <term>Sirach</term> <note>The author of the biblical Book of Sirach or Ecclesiasticus, associated with wisdom literature</note> nor the Great <term>Scaliger</term> <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), one of the most famous scholars of the Renaissance</note> approves of this, nor did Aristotle imitate it when he published his *Politics* against the will of Alexander the Great.

### Discourse of Christoph Besold

Mr. Johannes Gryphiander <note>Johann Gryphiander (1580–1641) was a German jurist known for his works on law and history.</note>, in his *Juridical-Political Skirmish on Political Secrets, thesis 12*.

<margin>The distinction of secrets according to Clapmarius.</margin>
III. Clapmarius <note>Arnoldus Clapmarius (1574–1604) was a prominent political scientist; his work "On the Secrets of Republics" was a standard text on "Reason of State."</note> subtly distinguishes these secrets in Book 1, Chapter 8. He divides them into the **secrets of the Republic**, namely those which concern the preservation of the present form and appearance of the Republic, and **secrets of Domination**, which pertain to the security of those who hold the first rank in the state. This is also suggested by Mr. Gryphiander in the aforementioned place, thesis 64, etc., where he writes that some secrets tend primarily toward the public utility, while others do so only as a consequence. The former are said to pertain to the health of the Empire itself; the latter to the health of those who preside over the state. Those who are more discerning know that these two things are distinct, and it is manifest enough whenever the Estates of the Empire <note>The "Ordines Imperii," or the representative ranks of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> disagree with the Emperor himself in the assemblies, should they divide into opposing parties. This happened in the Protestant War <note>Likely referring to the Schmalkaldic War (1546–1547), a conflict between the forces of Emperor Charles V and the Lutheran Schmalkaldic League.</note>, when the Princes protested that they were taking up arms against Charles, but not against the Empire.

<margin>The person of the Emperor is distinct from the Empire.</margin>
For the person of the Emperor is distinct from the Empire, so that if the former is removed, the latter remains no less. Just as Tiberius Caesar used to say that "Princes are mortal, but the Republic is eternal" <note>original: "Principes mortales esse, Rempublicam æternam dicebat"</note>; and in a similar legal case, Alfenus <note>Alfenus Varus, a famous Roman jurist of the 1st century BC.</note> responded that although the persons of individual judges may be changed, the court itself remains the same.

<margin>Likewise the crime of rebellion and high treason.</margin>
Hence, although the crime of rebellion <term>perduellio</term> <note>A specific Roman law term for treasonous acts that treat the state as an enemy.</note> and high treason <term>crimen majestatis</term> <note>An offense against the dignity or "majesty" of the sovereign.</note> are often confused by legal experts, Cujas <note>Jacques Cujas (1522–1590), a leading French legal humanist who sought to restore Roman law to its original context.</note> and Vultejus <note>Hermann Vultejus (1555–1634), a German jurist and influential professor at Marburg.</note> have taught that, strictly speaking, the former is committed against the state of the Republic itself, while the latter is committed against the Prince. Indeed, great consideration must also be given to those who rule, since the safety of the Republic rests for the most part upon their safety; this has appeared as often as a most powerful army has been easily defeated once its leader was slain. # On the Secrets of Republics.

Whatever contributes to their tranquility must be believed to benefit the community at large. Because if the head is cut off, the other members cannot remain safe. <note>A common metaphor in early modern political thought, where the King or Ruler is the head and the citizens are the limbs of the "Body Politic."</note> Nevertheless, by these rulers, private desires are often veiled under the pretext of public utility. So it was with Augustus; although Pompeius the Jurist <term>ICtus</term> <note>Abbreviation for *Jurisconsultus*, a legal expert or counselor.</note> says that, with the facts themselves dictating, it was necessary for the Republic to be managed by one man because of the factions which then frequently distracted the Republic; yet, says Tacitus <note>Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), a Roman historian known for his cynical view of the transition from Republic to Empire.</note>, it was said on the contrary: *the times of the Republic were taken as a pretext, but all things were done with a lust for power.* <note>original: "tempora Reipub. obtentui sumpta, cæterum dominandi cupidine acta omnia."</note> Hence, since the nature of mortals is greedy for power and headlong to fulfill the soul's desire, as Sallust <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus, a Roman historian who wrote on the corruption of the late Republic.</note> admits, cautious politicians should know how to separate that personal ambition from public utility.

<margin>The secrets of power must not be confused with the rights of power.</margin>
And furthermore, the secrets of power <note>original: "Imperii arcana."</note> should by no means be confused with the rights of Majesty, or of the state. For these secrets are nothing other than hidden arts, through which seditious men are prohibited from the right of power and from domination itself. *Clapmarius, Book 1, Chapter 9.* Certain clever devices, or reasons, introduced to turn away those who oppose the intention of the Politician, as *Gryphiander* notes in the same place, thesis 1. In turn, the rights of power are open, and the Republic can do without them less than it can without secrets. These secrets are the "Reason of State." <note>original: "ratio Status."</note> *See my own work, Politics, Book 1, Chapter 2, number 37.* This is what Botero <note>Giovanni Botero (1544–1617), an Italian thinker whose "Della ragion di Stato" (1589) argued that statecraft could be compatible with Christian morality.</note> describes in his *Reason of State* at the beginning: The knowledge of the means and reasons by which a State is founded, strengthened, and increased. Under that name, he was criticized by Trajano Boccalini <note>A famous Italian satirist (1556–1613) who was far more critical of the "Reason of State" than Botero.</note> using a pseudonym. Boccalini, in his *Century 2, Report 86*, defines it as *being a law useful to states, but in everything contrary to the law of God and of men.* <note>original: "essere una legge utile à gli stati, ma in tutto contraria alla legge d'Iddio, è de gli huomini."</note>

# The Discourse of Christopher Besold

<margin>The judgment of political thinkers regarding secrets.</margin>
...[these secrets] are usually spoken of very poorly by the most serious political thinkers. Therefore, the most wise Paruta <note>Paolo Paruta (1540–1598) was a Venetian diplomat and historian who wrote on the tension between Christian morality and political necessity.</note> in his *Soliloquy* says: *In this corrupt age, under the certain empty name of "reason of state," human and divine matters are often being disturbed and confounded.* <note>original Italian: "In questo corrotto secolo, con certo vano nome di ragion di stato, si vanno spesso perturbando, è confondendo le cose humane, è le Divine."</note> And while these reasons are sometimes not to be neglected, as Kirchner <note>Hermann Kirchner (1562–1620), a professor of history and poetry.</note> discusses in his *Political Disputations* (20, in the note to thesis 3), they should not be held as the primary consideration. For there is no greater secret of state than to rule justly and not to offend God, as argued in the Book of Proverbs, chapter 18. See also Nicolaus Betsius in his treatise *On Family Pacts*, page 747. A citizen is one who loves his fatherland and desires all good people to be safe and unharmed, as Cicero wrote in his *Against Verres*; he who neglects this is not a good Prince.

<margin>The foundation of secrets.</margin>
Nevertheless, out of two evils, the lesser must sometimes be chosen. It is upon this principle that these secrets of state are founded: we are accustomed to use them as one uses poisons in medicine—employing them as if by a right of defense. This is supported by Gryphiander <note>Johannes Gryphiander, a 17th-century German jurist.</note> in thesis 20. It is evident that this is done for defense, because by these secrets, <term>political men</term> <note>original Greek: πολιτικοὶ (politikoi). In this context, it refers to those skilled in the art of statecraft.</note> deceive factious people and protect the peace of the Republic from injuries. Enticed by these charms—especially by the "shadows of power" <note>The "simulacra imperii" are political maneuvers that give the appearance of liberty or shared power while the ruler maintains actual control.</note>—such men might voluntarily abandon their greed for power, which they otherwise would not have done except by force or the fear of punishment.

<margin>The double duty of prudence.</margin>
Indeed, this is the double duty of civil prudence: to keep citizens in their duty not only by force and fear of punishment, but also by cunning, by the encouragement of rewards, and by small persuasions. The former is considered the proper domain of the <term>legal experts</term> <note>original: ICti (Jurisconsulti). Professional lawyers and judges who rely on the letter of the law.</note>, while the latter belongs to the political thinkers.

<margin>It is defended.</margin>
I know that this is not approved by certain theologians, who, <term>straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel</term> <note>original Greek: διυλίζοντες τὸν κώνωπα, τὴν δὲ κάμηλον καταπίνοντες. A biblical idiom (Matthew 23:24) criticizing those who obsess over tiny details while ignoring major moral failings.</note>, will object to us that saying of Saint Paul,
<meta>catchword: not</meta>

<summary>Besold argues that while "reason of state" is often a mask for corruption, the "secrets of power" are necessary tools for a ruler to maintain peace without resorting to violence. He distinguishes between the rigid application of law (the jurist's role) and the flexible, sometimes deceptive, management of the public (the politician's role).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that while "reason of state" and political secrets are often viewed with suspicion, they are sometimes necessary for the survival of the state, particularly as a form of "blameless defense."</meta>

# On the Secrets of Republics.

<margin>Even from the Sacred Scriptures.</margin>
It is argued that evil things must not be done so that good may come. <note>original: "non esse facienda mala, ut eveniant bona." A reference to the Pauline principle in Romans 3:8.</note> We easily grant this to those critics: provided the actions are evil in their entire kind and nature, such that they could not be excused by any pretext of the public good. The rest—which Justus Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606) was a hugely influential Flemish humanist whose work *Politica* attempted to reconcile Machiavellian realism with Christian ethics.</note> in his *Politics* correctly separates from the former—are not simply evil, but are judged by the intention of harming. If that intention is absent, they are like the stings of little bees, which, once the stinger is removed, contain no poison. And even if some poison remains, it is nevertheless absorbed by the necessity of defense; for this reason, even a homicide committed within the limits of blameless self-defense is considered excusable in the court of law regarding deceit. <note>The author is comparing political maneuvering to the legal concept of *inculpatae tutelae* (blameless self-defense), where an otherwise criminal act is excused by necessity.</note> This is also the reason why civil laws permit deceit to be avenged with deceit, so that a compensation or balance is made on both sides. Hence, against an action for deceit, a defense of deceit is not granted (just as a reply is not given against a defense); it is as if the one who alleges it later was the one who committed the deceit first. 

Such secrets are suggested by Biblical history as well. Thus David did not kill Joab, <note>Joab was King David's general who committed several murders; David felt unable to punish him during his own reign due to Joab's power.</note> though he was many times over guilty of death; but David commanded his son [Solomon] in his Last Will and Testament that he should do it, etc. Therefore, a true "reason of state" is not contrary to religion. Philips van Marnix <note>Philips van Marnix (1540–1598) was a Dutch statesman and key figure in the Dutch Revolt.</note> in section 1, resolution 5, writes: "One must sometimes sail, not by the first navigation—or that which is first desired—but by the second, or that which is sought in the second place." <note>This "second sailing" is a classical proverb referring to taking the next best course (like using oars) when the wind (the ideal situation) fails.</note> See also Aristotle, *Politics* Book 8, chapter 9, where Sepúlveda <note>Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda (1494–1573), a Spanish philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> comments. Thus, some deceit is considered "good." <note>original: "dolus aliquis est bonus." In Roman law, *dolus bonus* referred to permissible trickery, such as outsmarting an enemy or standard commercial puffery.</note> As Plautus says:

> It is fitting for an honest man to be versatile,
> He whose heart is wise: let him be good to the good. <note>original Latin: "Versipellem frugi convenit esse hominem, / Pectus cui sapit: bonus sit bonis." From the play *Miles Gloriosus*.</note>

<margin>Suspicion as a secret.</margin>
The people either sharpen or soften the manners of Kings, and even compel them to use secret arts. And thus, Princes are accustomed to count suspicion as a secret of state, nor should they neglect it...

# Christoph Besold’s Discourse

...which concerns safety: *Botero’s Sayings, book 1, page 2 and page 17.* <note>Giovanni Botero (1544–1617) was a former Jesuit and influential Italian thinker whose work *The Reason of State* argued that a ruler must occasionally use "secret" means to preserve the state.</note> Especially here, it is safer to prevent a problem than to search for a remedy once the cause has been ruined.

<margin>Legal experts also have their secrets.</margin>
But even legal experts <note>original: "ICti," an abbreviation for *Jurisconsulti*.</note> have their own secrets, which the Roman jurists Pomponius and Ulpian call "remedies." Herennius calls them *εὑρήματα* <note>Greek: *euremata*, meaning "discoveries" or "inventions."</note> or *Eurematica*, about which he wrote a specific book. Practitioners call them "Cautions" (*Cautelas*), which are certain clever methods or subtle inventions of legal experts—as Brederode explains—intended to obtain victory in a case. A collection of these has been passed down by Baldus, Cepolla, Durantes, and others. These are "secrets of the courts," as Ulpian calls them elsewhere, in which the "nerve" or (as the Emperors put it) the "ambiguous fates of cases" <note>original: "ambigua fata cauffarum"</note> reside; if these are neglected, the case itself is easily lost. And some of these are so devised that they seem to tend toward a "fraud against the law" and indirectly oppose the strict right. Even the ancient legal experts themselves admitted such things, as Johannes Fichard demonstrates with examples. This was done to mitigate the hardness and rigor of the old law, which the ancients considered "supreme law, supreme torture," <note>original: "summum jus, summa crux." This is a variation of the legal proverb *summum ius, summa iniuria*, suggesting that the most rigid application of the law can result in the greatest injustice or "torture" for the subjects.</note> as Columella recorded. For this purpose, "legal fictions" were also invented—namely, legal constructs adapted for the use of common life, even if they go against nature and the truth of the matter, as Hotman <note>François Hotman (1524–1590) was a French legal scholar and humanist.</note> defines them. *See Gryphiander, thesis 51, etc.*

<margin>And Doctors.</margin>

For God, who established Kingdoms, also knows the just and lawful methods for maintaining them against hardships (which men sometimes believe must be removed even through evil arts for the sake of a greater good), and He is accustomed to provide these in a timely manner. *Trust in the Lord, and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land. # Discourse of Christoph Besold

...blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord: the people whom he hath chosen for his own inheritance. The king is not saved by a great army: and a giant shall not be delivered by the help of his great strength. A horse is a deceitful thing for safety: neither shall he be delivered by the abundance of his strength. Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon them that fear him: and on them that hope in his mercy. Besold uses this scripture to emphasize that ultimately, the security of a state depends on Divine Providence rather than mere military might or human cunning.</note>

<margin>The limits of this art.</margin>
And therefore, along with Clapmarius <note>Arnoldus Clapmarius (1574–1604) was a German jurist and political theorist who wrote extensively on "Secrets of Empire."</note>, limits must be set for this art of statecraft: namely, Religion, faith, and decency <note>original: "pudor"; refers to a sense of shame or moral integrity that prevents one from acting dishonorably.</note>, which one is not permitted to transgress.

<margin>Machiavelli is noted.</margin>
In this regard, Machiavelli departs from us; he teaches that for the safety of the Prince, these limits need not even be observed. *A Prince,* he says, *should protect his life and see to the preservation of his rule: by what means that is done does not matter, provided they present some appearance of honor. Nor should he worry much if he incurs the infamy of those vices without which he could not easily protect his Dominion.* <note>Besold is summarizing the core thesis of Machiavelli's *The Prince*, specifically the idea that the "end justifies the means."</note>

This is exactly what Tigellinus <note>Ofonius Tigellinus, the notorious prefect of the Praetorian Guard under Emperor Nero, known for his cruelty and unscrupulousness.</note> suggested to Nero: that he did not look toward various hopes like others, but only to the safety of the Prince; for whom it is useful to be guarded against plots by any means necessary, even through crimes. *Gryphiander, thesis 43.* And I myself shall say more below, God willing, when I deal with the outrages of Dominion.

<margin>To what extent it is expedient to know the outrages of rule.</margin>
These outrages are not to be learned for any other reason than how Saint Jerome advises that the opinions of Heretics should be learned: not so that we may follow them, but so that we may refute and judge them. Just as in Ethics, instruction is given not only regarding virtues, but also regarding vices. Likewise, from a <term>ICto: an abbreviation for *Iurisconsulto*, a legal consultant or expert learned in the law.</term>, Ulpian <note>One of the most famous Roman jurists; his writings make up a large portion of the *Digest*.</note> requires knowledge not only of what is just, lawful, or equitable, but also of the unjust, the unlawful, and the inequitable, so that in the act of choosing, one might distinguish the one from the other, good from evil (which is the proper function of prudence...

# Christoph Besold’s Discourse

...they are zealous: those who think themselves so bound to their Prince that they seek only to be of benefit to him, rather than to counsel what is just. It is helpful to add here a judgment on these matters by the most astute Tommaso Campanella <note>An Italian philosopher and theologian (1568–1639) known for his work on political theory, *Politics*.</note> in his *Politics*, chapter 4, section 6 and following.

<margin>*A judgment on political reason, which is called "reason of state."*</margin>
Political reason, which they now call "reason of state" (formerly known as equity and *epieikeia* <note>original: "ἐπιείκεια"; a Greek term referring to the spirit of the law or fairness that tempers the harshness of the literal written law.</note>), goes beyond the letter of the law promulgated in writing or by voice, following instead its spirit and purpose. It does this only for the sake of a better and more common good, when it abrogates, interprets, or grants exemptions from the law. This occurred when the Roman Senate granted life to Fabius Rullianus <note>A Roman general who won a great victory but faced execution for engaging the enemy against his commander's orders; the Senate intervened to save him.</note>, who by the letter of the law ought to have died, and also to Horatius, who had killed the three Curiatii, for the sake of the Roman Empire. However, modern "reason of state" is an invention of tyrants designed to mimic equity: they believe that for the sake of acquiring or preserving even the smallest power, they can transgress all laws—not only their own, but even divine ones.

<margin>*Reason of state and equity differ.*</margin>
Truly, there is a difference between reason of state and equity: for equity looks toward the true public good, while the former looks only to the private and apparent benefit of the Ruler. However, so that they might cover this name—which has been recognized as impious ever since Machiavelli "acted the part of Ahithophel" <note>original: "Achitophelizavit"; a reference to Ahithophel, the biblical counselor who betrayed King David with cunning, wicked advice. Besold uses this to describe Machiavelli's influence.</note>—Princes now speak of "reason for good governance." These terms can indeed contain a positive meaning, even if they were coined by a wicked person. For example: by a *right* reason of state, Cleonymus killed the Ephors <note>High-ranking officials in Sparta; Cleonymus was a Spartan prince.</note> in Sparta; but the King of the Persians did not act rightly in killing his brothers. For although the Persian King might seem to do this for the common good, it is against the law of God; since other ways could be found to prevent them from seizing the Kingdom, his actions are irrational. A good Prince does not need this "reason of state," because he protects himself through perpetual integrity.

<summary>Besold distinguishes between "equity," which adjusts laws for the public good, and the modern "reason of state," which he condemns as a Machiavellian tool for tyrants to bypass divine and human laws for personal gain.</summary>

<margin>*The authority of those who command protects the Empire.*</margin>
V. Every Empire, and every form of Republic, is protected by a most powerful bulwark: the **authority** of those who hold supreme power. This authority is described as the distinguished esteem and veneration held by both subjects and foreigners toward the high rank of the rulers. Just as a physician in whom the patient trusts heals more successfully than another <note>Galeotto Marzio (1427–1497), an Italian humanist and physician whose work *De doctrina promiscua* is cited here.</note>, so too does a distinguished reputation (or "Reputation") for an Empire accomplish much—and sometimes more than even arms <note>Trajano Boccalini (1556–1613), a satirist whose *Ragguagli di Parnaso* (Dispatches from Parnassus) used fictional news reports to critique 17th-century politics.</note>. This reputation is the "patrimony of the Prince" <note>Giovanni Bottero (1544–1617), an influential theorist who argued that a ruler’s power was built on the well-being and admiration of his people rather than mere force.</note>. It is the most certain protection of the State and of public safety; nothing is more powerful against hatred and contempt—those fatal plagues of governance that usually bring defiance and rebellion in their wake <note>Hermann Kirchner (1562–1620), a German jurist and professor of history and rhetoric.</note>. Through false reputation, you may do nothing purely, provided you do it cautiously; you may be most foul in private, provided you are publicly praised. > *But what is more frequent in courts today than this perverse Reputation? Its characteristics are: to strive for a reputation for virtue while hating true virtue; to lie about one’s status; to cast off humility and humanity; to desire the friendship of no one, but the admiration, fear, and respect of all; and to seek the devotion of only a few. The consequences are a swelling of titles, the emptying of one’s inheritance, the hatred of good men, the anger of superiors, the contempt of inferiors, and finally, to buy and sell smoke,* <note>original: "fumos emere & vendere"; a common historical idiom for selling false promises or charging for influence that one does not actually possess.</note> *etc.*

### VII. The second general defense of any Empire is the Love of the subjects.

# On the Secrets of State Affairs.

<margin>The love of subjects is the other fortification of Rule.</margin>
Other titles we grant more for the sake of honor: we speak of the **Great**, the **Fortunate**, and the **August**, and we heap upon ambitious Majesty whatever titles we are able. But we call him the **Father of the Country** <note>original: "Patrem patriae"</note>, who exercises a fatherly power—which is the most moderate of all—consulting the interests of his children and putting their needs before his own. Just as a father is slow to cut off his own limbs, and even when he has cut them away, he desires to put them back, and groans during the cutting, having hesitated much and for a long time. For this reason, the fatherly love of Kings toward their citizens has such power that they often possess their hearts and innermost affections entirely; and often, by a single kind little word and a gentle look—as if by some most powerful charm <note>The author uses the word "fascino," referring to a psychological or almost magical attraction that a beloved leader exerts over people.</note>—they capture their wills, their chests, and their strongboxes. *Lord Lansius, in defense of France, folio 19.*

And the reputation for equity, gravity, constancy, and wisdom has greater force for keeping even fierce men in their duty than the royal scepter; even more than prison, the confiscation of goods, banishment, or finally, the rods and axes <note>The "virgae and secures" were the traditional Roman symbols of a magistrate’s power to punish and execute.</note>. *Jan Herburt of Fulstin, Polish Histories, book 20, chapter 2.* That **State** <note>original: "Respublica"</note> is ultimately judged to be the strongest where the **Prince** or those ruling are loved by the citizens. *See Seneca, 1st Declamation, third.*

Indeed, no **Rule** <note>original: "Imperium"</note> is safe unless it is fortified by goodwill, as Aemilius Probus <note>A reference to Cornelius Nepos, whose biographical works were long misattributed to the 4th-century editor Aemilius Probus.</note> says in his life of Dion. And no one can call himself the Master of another through violence. *Pérez in Aphorisms, folio 246; Boccalini, Reports from Parnassus, report 99; and the same in The Political Touchstone, folio 20.* A King can do much by commanding, but more by loving: Love and Obedience are true brothers. *Antonio Pérez, folio 21, number 105.* The ungodly, and even the impure spirits themselves, fear God; but because they do not love Him, they do not offer Him obedience...

VIII. That love, however, must be joined with a certain reverence and fear. The Emperor Sigismund <note>Sigismund of Luxembourg (1368–1437), Holy Roman Emperor, noted for his efforts to end the Papal Schism.</note> explained this skillfully: hearing some people debating whether it was better for a ruler to be loved or feared by his subjects, he replied: just as the powers above <note>original: "superi," referring to the divine or the gods.</note> wish to be both loved and feared, so do Kings. For you cannot love well unless you also fear. But it also lies with Kings to be both loved and feared: they should moderate their lives so that they are neither a source of terror to those below them, nor an object of contempt to those above. Aeneas Sylvius <note>Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini (1405–1464), later Pope Pius II; he was a prolific humanist author.</note>, *Commentary on the deeds of Alfonso, Book 4.* Therefore, a familiarity that carries frivolity <note>original: "levitatem," meaning a lack of dignity or seriousness.</note> as its companion must be avoided; this is what once brought down John d’Albret, King of Navarre <note>John III of Navarre (1469–1516), who lost much of his kingdom to Ferdinand II of Aragon.</note>: *History of Navarre, folio 603 and following,* and he was bitterly tormented by his wife on that account. *Ibid. folio 623.* Familiar drinking parties should be avoided, etc. *Kirchner, Disputation on the Republic 20, thesis 1, corollary.* Olaus Magnus <note>A Swedish historian and cleric (1490–1557) famous for his descriptions of Northern European life.</note> *Book 13, chapter 34.* The lure of love lies not only in caring for the whole population, but for individuals as well (for he must also fear even the smallest person. *Perez, folio 39, n. 217 and following.*) and so he himself should hear the complaints of individuals. *See Justus Lipsius <note>A famous Flemish humanist (1547–1606) whose political theories influenced much of early modern Europe.</note> in his short dissertation where he discusses Rudolph of Austria.* <note>Rudolph I (1218–1291), the first Habsburg King of the Romans.</note> Furthermore, it is a barbaric way of acquiring authority if the Prince is never seen. *Kirchner, Disputation on the Republic 20, thesis 2. b. ( 2 ) Conversely, he himself—not through an intermediary—ought to offer rewards. <margin>3. He should strive for the subjects to love the present state.</margin>
( 5 ) Above all, effort must be made so that subjects are content with the present state of affairs and do not become weary of the Government. For that rule is the most stable. Antonio Pérez, *folio 155.* For subjects who are poorly satisfied are desperate men. Francesco Guicciardini, *Political Reminders, number 56.* And kingdoms full of "malcontents," as they are called, are like a tower built upon quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo," referring to mercury. A building on mercury would have no solid foundation and would shift or collapse.</note>. Pérez, *folio 22, number 113.* It is therefore a great secret <term>arcanum|In this context, a "secret of state" refers to a strategic principle of governance known to the ruler but perhaps not obvious to the public.</term> not to have dissatisfied subjects; a kingdom is easily overturned where the subjects are ready to change not just the Lord, but the very system of Government. Boccalini, *Century 2, report 6, folio 21.*

<margin>He should punish spreaders of new rumors.</margin>
But nothing disturbs the minds of subjects more than those who spread new rumors—whether they are uncertain or fabricated out of personal bias. Therefore, such people are especially to be punished.

### Christoph Besold’s Discourse

<margin>Let him satisfy just petitions. Let him not violate privileges.</margin>
Languet <note>Hubert Languet (1518–1581) was a French diplomat and advisor.</note> says it best in *Semestria*, book 8, chapter 11: Just like those who today spread the "New Newspapers" <note>original German: *Newe Zeitungen spargiren*. This refers to the early printed news-sheets that circulated sensationalist or political information.</note>, they strive to make both Princes and subjects lean toward one side or the other. This is a most vain and wicked class of men. The desire for liberty is innate in all mortals, and for those who endure misery unwillingly and under compulsion, any occasion—even the slightest—seems a suitable opportunity for revolution <term>res novas: literally "new things," a classical idiom for political upheaval or regime change</term>. *Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 4.* Therefore, the just petitions of the people must be satisfied. *Perez, folio 160, Aphorism 8.* Much less should their privileges be violated. *Pierre Mathieu, book 6, narrative 1, note 4, folio 452.* And thus Trajan wrote back to Pliny in *Book 10, Letter 110*, that the laws of each individual city must be followed. For (speaking of the cities of Bithynia and Pontus), if they possess a privilege by which they are preferred over other creditors, it must be upheld; but if they do not, I ought not to grant it to the injury of private citizens. And in *Letter 114*: "Therefore, I think that which is always safest should be followed: the law of each city."

<margin>So that the party which wants the State safe may prevail.</margin>
But if it is impossible for everyone to be content with the present state of affairs, that part of the city which desires the Republic <term>Respublica: the state or the "common weal"</term> to be safe must nevertheless remain the more powerful. *Aristotle, Politics, book 4, chapter 12.* This is what Lysander <note>A Spartan admiral and politician.</note> always looked toward. *Æmilius Probus in his Life.* <note>Æmilius Probus was the name historically attributed to the biographer Cornelius Nepos.</note> And likewise, although a Prince ought to fear the curses of his subjects more than the weapons of his enemies—which was the aphorism of King Henry of Castile: *Botero, On Sayings, folio 3*—nevertheless, the gentleness of Emperor Frederick III is to be imitated. <margin>The most general secret: pretense.</margin>
X. But among the secrets <term>arcana: literally "hidden things," referring to the confidential strategies of statecraft</term> which I am now treating, some are general, which can be applied to all business in every Republic according to the circumstances of time and place, and from which specific secrets are derived. Among these, *pretense* <term>simulatio: the act of feigning or making a false show of intentions</term> leads the first rank. This is the most general secret, from which all others descend, like streams from their source.

<margin>What is pretense?</margin>
The Jurist <term>ICtus: short for *Iurisconsultus*, a legal scholar or expert in law</term> calls pretense "deceit" <term>dolus: a legal term for intentional fraud or trickery</term>, when one thing is done and another is feigned. By this name, I do not mean shameful pretense, nor the kind an arrogant man is accustomed to use: such as *Nero* was for five years, or *Herod the Younger* for six years, after which time their pretense was detected, and their nature—hitherto hidden—broke forth. Although *Aristotle* says this is very necessary for a Tyrant (such as *Tiberius* was, an artist in hiding his vices), I nevertheless approve of *Cato*, of whom *Velleius* <note>Velleius Paterculus (c. 19 BC – c. AD 31) was a Roman historian.</note> writes, that he never did right just so that he might merely *seem* to have done it. Nevertheless, *Saint Jerome* <note>B. Hieronymus: Saint Jerome (c. 347–420) was a prominent early Christian scholar and theologian.</note> teaches that "honest pretense," which does not depart far from virtue, is useful and should be adopted at the right time; even righteous men have used it for their own safety and that of others.

What "feigning" means to political thinkers.

...what lies beneath in truth; this is what the playwright *Plautus* calls "throwing dust in one's eyes" <note>original: "glauco oculis objicere." This Latin idiom literally means to cast a film or cataract over someone's vision to blind them to the truth.</note>; the jurist *Ulpian* calls it acting "under a guise" or "under a pretext"; and *Marcianus* refers to it as acting "under a color." In the same way, *Marcellus* calls it a "color" or a "contrived title," a false explanation that *Quintilian* also interprets in this sense. All such acts are "imaginary," occurring when the appearance of a fact is simulated without the truth being present, as *Modestinus* <note>Herennius Modestinus was a celebrated Roman jurist of the 3rd century AD.</note> defines it. This is entirely necessary when it is in the interest of the State for its plans to be kept secret; otherwise, if the true cause is discovered, the plans might be nipped in the bud <note>original: "in herbâ supprimantur," literally "suppressed while still in the blade of grass."</note> before they reach maturity. "I have seen many things done by others under such pretexts, and I have sometimes done them myself, cunningly and insidiously," says *Comines* <note>Philippe de Comines (1447–1511) was a diplomat and historian whose memoirs are a classic of Renaissance political realism.</note>.

<margin>
The pretense of Princes regarding ambassadors.
</margin>
By this same artifice, Princes are often accustomed to deceive even their own ambassadors. They send them away under one pretext while concealing the true reason for the mission. This is done because if the ambassadors knew the truth, they might act with less zeal, as I mentioned above in the *dissertation on ambassadors*. This strategy has a place whenever one cause is offered as a front, so that we do not appear to be doing what we are actually doing. See *Gryphander* <note>Johannes Gryphiander (1571–1641) was a German jurist and academic.</note>, thesis 70 and following.

The most powerful pretext of all is that of religion. *Bodin* <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596) was a French political philosopher who famously defined the concept of sovereignty.</note> writes that this is the sole means by which Southern peoples keep their subjects in their duty. For "the highest reason is that which works for Religion," as *Papinian* <note>Aemilius Papinianus was one of the most revered Roman legal experts.</note> says. Indeed, the Roman state considered that all things should be placed after religion, according to the testimony of *Valerius Maximus*, even in matters where they wished the glory of the State's Majesty to be most visible. Human minds are struck by this as if by a ritual staff <note>original: "thyrso," the staff of Bacchus, used here to suggest a kind of divine or overwhelming influence.</note>, so that the common people easily accept even a false and simulated image. *Tacitus* <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56 – c. 120 AD) was a Roman historian known for his analysis of the psychology of power.</note> says that nothing rules the multitude more effectively than superstition, and when their minds are once struck...

### On the Secrets of States
<page-num>25</page-num>

...lest superstition should rule. From this, even Gaius the Jurisconsult <note>Gaius was a celebrated Roman jurist of the 2nd century AD whose works became a primary source for Roman law.</note> calls it the greatest remedy for expediting legal actions. See Gryphiander <note>Johannes Gryphiander (1580–1652) was a German jurist known for his work on the law of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, thesis 77, etc., and my own work, Book 2 of *Politics*, chapter 1.

<margin>Also the law.</margin>
Likewise, the pretext of the law is so very commonly used that it has almost lost its value through excessive use. For there is no man—and certainly no Prince—who does not wish to appear to act lawfully in whatever he does. A politician would seem quite foolish if, like the brigand mentioned by the jurist Ulpian, when asked why he does a thing, he were to answer simply, "Because I am doing it," <note>original: "quia facio." This refers to a legal scenario where a person acts by mere force without any "title" or legal right.</note> and could provide no reason for his action, not even a foolish or silly one. Indeed, he should know a plausible reason—one that might even deceive those who are more expert.

<margin>A note on Machiavelli and other unjust defenders.</margin>
This is what Machiavelli suggests to his Prince: that one must look at least to utility and the preservation of power, for reasons will never be lacking to cast some "color" of law <note>original: "color juris." In legal rhetoric, a "color" is a plausible but potentially deceptive appearance of legality.</note> over one's actions. He argues that men are moved and judge more by the appearance and "color" of things than by the things themselves; this is especially true of the common people, who are perpetually held captive by the appearance of right and by the final outcome of events. And since almost the whole world is comprised of the common people, the opinions of the few wise men need not be taken into account. 

Indeed, there will always be "defenders" who offer themselves for such tasks, just as a certain philosopher argued that Alexander the Great’s murder of Cleitus <note>Alexander killed his friend Cleitus the Black in a drunken rage in 328 BC; the philosopher Anaxarchus reportedly comforted Alexander by telling him that the King's will is the law.</note>—though committed in a drunken stupor—was done rightly, and he even managed to have the act declared lawful by the soldiers. Cardinal Thomas Wolsey likewise attempted to excuse the incest and frequent divorces of King Henry of England before the Pope. Truly, this is what Cicero complained of in a similar vein: that nothing can be said or imagined so monstrously that some philosopher has not already asserted it. See Gryphiander, thesis 96, etc. Few men today follow the example of Papinian the Jurisconsult <note>Aemilius Papinianus was a Roman jurist who was reportedly executed by Emperor Caracalla in 212 AD because he refused to write a legal justification for the Emperor's murder of his own brother, Geta.</note>, who, they say, preferred to die rather than provide an excuse for the Emperor’s act of fratricide.

# Christoph Besold’s Discourse
<page-num>26</page-num>

<margin>The concealment of emotions, which is rather a part of dissimulation.</margin>
And likewise, it is a general secret of state: the concealment of hatred, anger, sorrow, joy, and other emotions, so that they are not noticed. This falls under the category of dissimulation, which is like the inseparable sister and companion of simulation: because by this very act, while we dissimulate (hide) what truly is, we also simulate (pretend) what is not. This is considered so highly necessary for a Politician <note>In this context, "Politician" refers to a statesman or ruler engaged in the practical art of governing.</note> that the Great King <note>Referring to King Louis XI of France (1423–1483), famously known as "the Universal Spider" for his web of intrigues.</note> did not rashly say, "He who knows not how to dissimulate, knows not how to rule" <note>original: "qui nescit dissimulare, nescit regnare." This was Louis XI's most famous maxim on statecraft.</note>: indeed, such a person knows not how to live. For since many things occur in the life of a Politician which he would not want, in order to achieve the goals of his plans, he must pretend many things against his will and hide his true feelings even when in pain, as Marcus Tullius Cicero says somewhere. See Gryphiander <note>Johannes Gryphiander (1580–1652), a German legal scholar.</note>, thesis 134, etc. In this way, it is necessary to hide injuries sometimes, at least for a time. And although in the case of private citizens, the Jurisconsult <note>original: "ICtus" (Jurisconsultus), a legal expert.</note> says that an injury is abolished by dissimulation—meaning if you ignore it, you lose the right to sue—in the case of Princes,

<margin>The necessity of which is demonstrated.</margin>
it nevertheless remains "stored deep in the mind" <note>original: "altâ mente reposta." A famous quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, describing Juno’s long-held grudge.</note> until an opportunity for "recalling to mind" (as the legal experts call it) presents itself. Thus, for the present, Tiberius <note>The second Roman Emperor, known for his secretive and suspicious nature.</note> handled the injury "civilly," as Tacitus says, but in a mind revolving its angers; even if the initial impulse of the offense had faded, the memory remained strong. In the same way, Saul hid his feelings regarding the contempt shown by the "sons of Belial" <note>A biblical term for wicked or worthless men; see 1 Samuel 10:27.</note> and acted as if he were deaf. David, finally, when he was about to die, commanded his son to take vengeance for the injuries of Shimei <note>Shimei had cursed David during Absalom's rebellion; David did not punish him immediately but advised Solomon to do so later.</note>.

<margin>5. Deceiving with false hope.</margin>
It is equally common for Politicians to deceive others with false hope. One can see in the writings of Commines <note>Philippe de Commines (1447–1511), a diplomat and historian whose memoirs are a primary source for the reign of Louis XI.</note> how Louis XI and Charles of Burgundy fed each other with such hopes. Similarly, in Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a French historian and statesman.</note>, one reads how Charles V vainly held out hope to Francis I regarding the restoration of Milan.

To this belongs persuasion, by which we cunningly entice the minds and efforts of those who are estranged...
