# On the Secrets of Republics
<page-num>27</page-num>
<header>On the Secrets of Republics.</header>

<margin>
6. To win over the minds of those who are under the jurisdiction of another.
</margin>
...jurisdiction, as Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606) was a Flemish philosopher and humanist whose works on political "prudence" were foundational for 17th-century rulers.</note> defines it. Cicero established that it is a characteristic of prudence to win over the hearts of men and turn them to one’s own use. Thus Metellus, in the writings of Sallust <note>The Roman historian Sallust describes how the general Metellus fought the Numidian King Jugurtha using psychology as much as force.</note>, approached the ambassadors of Jugurtha one by one; by gradually testing them and promising many things once he knew they were vulnerable, he persuaded them.

<margin>
7. To divide adversaries.
</margin>
Just as, conversely, it is a secret of state to divide adversaries, sow hatred and rumors, and nourish factions. In this way, Cato <note>Cato the Elder, a Roman statesman known for his strictness and pragmatism.</note> used to nurture feuds among his slaves, lest they conspire together against their master. Louis XI <note>King Louis XI of France (r. 1461–1483), often called "The Universal Spider" for his complex diplomacy.</note> was highly skilled in this art; he would sometimes assist both sides in a war with money or soldiers, and he kept his "ear-listeners" <note>original: "ωτακουστας" (otakoustas). This is a term used by Aristotle to describe spies or eavesdroppers who report back to a tyrant.</note>—as the Philosopher <note>A common reference to Aristotle.</note> calls them—in almost every court of the Princes. These were chosen from among the ruler's most intimate advisors, to whom Louis secretly paid an annual salary so they would favor his cause.

<margin>
Nevertheless, a Prince must absolutely keep his word.
</margin>
But if faith has been pledged on both sides, we ought not to be the authors of treachery or perjury to anyone, as the Emperor Alexander [Severus] wrote in a similar legal response. For, as the Jurisconsult <term>ICto</term> <note>original: "ICto" (Iurisconsulto), a professional legal scholar or expert in Roman law.</note> testifies, it is a grave matter to break one's word, as it is the most sacred thing in life, according to Cicero. This is agreed upon by all peoples under the Law of Nations <note>original: "Iure gentium." This refers to the legal principles considered common to all mankind, the precursor to modern international law.</note>; without it, neither human commerce nor civil society itself could stand.

This principle ought to hold true in all men, but most especially in Princes, whose simple assertion is held in the place of an oath—as I have stated in my *Discourse on the Law of Treaties*. For this reason, Cacheranus and Baldus <note>Octavianus Cacheranus and Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400) were highly influential legal commentators and jurists.</note> want Princes to be far removed from all malice; they should have "one tongue and one pen" and remain immovable, like a cornerstone. Truly, however, how many are there today for whom there is no faith in words or promises, except insofar as it is expedient? This was said of the Par- <note>The text likely refers to the "Parthians," a people often cited by Roman authors as examples of treachery and broken promises.</note>

The quote is actually a Latin translation of a famous line from Euripides' *Hippolytus*.</note> says: *I have sworn with my tongue, but I carry a mind unsworn.* But Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an influential scholar and bishop whose work on ethics and law was standard for centuries.</note> conveniently blocks this path: *With whatever art of words one may swear, God nonetheless, who is the witness of conscience, accepts it in the way that the one to whom the oath is made understands it.* Others are accustomed to be entangled in another way: *a pact is not a pact, and a non-pact is a pact, when it pleases them;* <note>A reference to the Roman comedian Plautus, highlighting the absurdity of legalistic double-talk.</note> Indeed, *when the tablets are marked and twelve witnesses are present, nonetheless a speaker is found who denies what was done.* If not openly, then at least secretly at times. Gryphiander <note>Johann Gryphiander (1580–1652), a German jurist.</note> discusses this at length in thesis 196 and following. Thus, utility is usually substituted for justice. Master Christoph Forstner <note>Christoph Forstner (1598–1667) was an Austrian diplomat and political theorist.</note> in his *Political Reminders*, 27.

# Concerning the Secrets of States

Chapter 19. And to this point belong the secondary ends of States <term>States: the Latin "Rerumpublicarum" here refers generally to any organized political community or commonwealth, not just republics.</term>, about which Aristotle writes in Book 3 of his *Politics*, Chapter 5. Thus, the end <note>The "end" (finis) in classical philosophy refers to the ultimate goal or purpose of a thing.</note> of an **Oligarchy** is wealth; for a **Democracy**, it is equality. These ends are less primary and concern the state specifically. Therefore, **Secrets of State** are the methods for attaining these ends.

<margin>The secrets of a kingdom governed by succession are fewer, and what they are.</margin>
11. The **Secrets of a Kingdom** that is acquired by succession are fewer. For it is sufficient that the Prince does not overstep the institutions of his ancestors; and then, that he adapts himself to the times in the face of new circumstances. Thus, if a Prince of this kind is gifted with at least common and ordinary diligence in his conduct, he can always maintain himself in his Principality. Unless he falls into the hatred and offense of the people through extraordinary and very powerful vices, he is deservedly loved by his own through a certain natural right. In the very antiquity of a coherent and continued rule, the memory of all previous changes <note>Referring to the political upheavals that might have occurred when the dynasty first took power.</note> lies buried. 

See Niccolò Machiavelli in *The Prince*, chapter 2, and his *Discourses*, book 3, chapter 5. Also John Barclay’s *The Mirror of Minds* <note>original: "Icon animorum"</note>, chapter 13; Hænnonius in his *Political Disputations* 9, theses 26, 27, and 29; Antonio Pérez, folio 180, number 124. I also discuss this in my *Preliminary Treatise on Succession and Election*, folio 15, number 13. 

Although the greater part of Kings prefer to follow a different reasoning and detest this common and popular way of ruling—as the same Pérez testifies in his *Aphorisms from the Second Letters*, number 5; see also folio 153, aphorism 74. Hence, a Prince ought not to change or dismiss the advisors of such a predecessor. See 1 Kings 12 <note>original: "3. Reg. 12." In the Vulgate Bible, 1 Kings is titled the Third Book of Kings.</note>; Philippe de Comines in the place cited, chapter 3; the Most Serene King of Great Britain <note>Referring to King James I (r. 1603–1625), who wrote extensively on the divine right of kings.</note> in his *The King's Gift* <note>original: "Instit. Regiae," referring to the Basilikon Doron.</note>, my edition page 69; Johann Gerhard, *Decade 4*, question 6; and my own work, *On Political Counsel*, chapter 6. 

If, however, someone follows a Prince who was hated, and whose rule is regretted...

### On the Secrets of Republics.

...[lest they] should seek the command of those provinces which they administered; just as Justinian humbled Belisarius <note>Belisarius (c. 500–565 AD) was a legendary Byzantine general under Emperor Justinian I. Indeed, in matters of state, whatever *can* happen must be feared *lest* it happen. For the human disposition is so constituted that where there is ability and opportunity, ambition usually takes hold of them. And he who is able to command hardly neglects opportunities, even if it is done against the law.

<margin>To halt the recklessness of ministers through marriage.</margin>
A "secret" of the Prince used against such great ministers is to compel them toward marriage. Henry IV, King of France, incautiously neglected this in the case of Biron <note>Charles de Gontaut, Duke of Biron, was a close friend and general of Henry IV who was eventually executed for conspiring with Spain. The text suggests that a man with a family is less likely to risk everything on a treasonous gamble.</note>. *French Mercury, volume 1, folio 111.* For those who must fear for themselves and their children are not so reckless.

For this reason, the crime of Treason <note>original: "crimen Majestatis," referring to *crimen laesae maiestatis*, or "injured majesty," the highest crime against the state.</note> also affects the children with punishment. This is done, clearly, so that no one commits that crime out of fear of the punishment passing to their children, even if they are innocent. Thus also, under the guise of honor, rivals are removed. *Lord Gruter, Discourses, part 2, folios 124 and 132.*

<margin>Other secrets are added.</margin>
Certain Princes, for that reason, were also accustomed to choose magistrates who were equal to their tasks, but not superior to them. *Tacitus, Annals, Book 6*, where he speaks of Poppaeus Sabinus <note>Poppaeus Sabinus was a Roman governor under Augustus and Tiberius; Tacitus famously remarked that he was chosen for high office because he was "competent for his business and not above it" (*par negotiis neque supra*).</note>.

To this belongs what political theorists <term>Statists; those who study the "reason of state"</term> advise: not to continue the terms of magistrates, nor to give offices to great families. *Botero, On the Sayings [of Great Men], folio 14. b. Perez, folio 10, numbers 43, 44, 46.* One should commit the conduct of war to a foreigner, since obedience is rendered solely out of respect for the Prince, and not out of consideration for the commander's own greatness; *Boccalini, 1st Report, folio 127.* Great men should not be sent far away (Perez, folio 11, number 48), so that their actions might be more easily kept in sight. *The Secrets of Rule* by Barnabé Brisso—

### 35 On the Secrets of Republics.

<header>On the Secrets of Republics.</header>
<sig>Q</sig>

<margin>Secrets regarding Aristocracy, both against the common people and against the rule of a single monarch.</margin>
Concord and equality protect an Aristocratic government. For a harmonious rule by the few does not easily perish from within. <note>original: "Arist. 5. pol. 6." Referring to Aristotle’s *Politics*, Book 5, Chapter 6, which discusses the causes of revolution in aristocracies.</note> Care must also be taken that great powers of command are not monopolized by a single family. See Clapmarius, Book 6, chapter 20 <note>Arnoldus Clapmarius (1573–1604) was a legal scholar famous for his work on the "secrets" of statecraft.</note>, where he reviews the secrets of a certain Republic which is the jewel <note>original: "ocellus," literally "little eye" or "darling."</note> of Germany (I mean Nuremberg). Boccalini relates many secrets and unique features of the Venetian Republic in report 5 of his first century. <note>Trajano Boccalini, an Italian satirist. His "reports" from Parnassus were a popular way to critique contemporary politics.</note> This same Republic does not entrust the conduct of wars to its own Patricians <note>term: "Patricians" refers to the hereditary ruling noble class of Venice.</note>, lest any one individual grow too powerful. See Commines, book 7, last chapter, folio 685. <note>Philippe de Commines (1447–1511) was a diplomat and historian; he noted that Venice often hired foreign mercenaries (condottieri) to lead their armies to prevent successful generals from seizing political power at home.</note> Every free Republic must also observe this: that it does not govern its subject provinces with a slave-like rule, but allows them also to feel the benefits of their shared liberty. The neglect of this principle overthrew the Roman Democracy. For as Tacitus writes in the first book of his *Annals*:
> Nor did the provinces reject that state of affairs <note>The transition from the Republic to the rule of Augustus Caesar.</note>, for they were suspicious of the rule of the Senate and the People because of the conflicts among the powerful and the greed of the magistrates; the protection of the laws was ineffective, as they were thrown into chaos by force, political maneuvering, and finally by money.

In the same way, the oppression of the citizens of Pisa gave the occasion for the ruin of the Florentines. See Commines, book 8, chapter 3, folio 709.

Free cities likewise ought to help one another, not destroy each other. It is similarly advisable not to extend the boundaries of the empire too far. And wisely, as he does in all things, Boccalini writes in report 6 of his second century, folio 20: *The best political precept that one can admire in the German Republics is that they hold the conquest of other nations in the highest horror.* <note>original Italian: "Il miglior precetto Politico, che altri possa ammirare nelle Republiche Alemane, sia l'haver in sommo horrore gli acquisti delle Nationi."</note> Thus, Felix Fabri, in his *History of Swabia*, seems to unfairly criticize the people of Ulm because they were unwilling to acquire neighboring territories by right of purchase. For that was a State Secret, lest [to themselves...] <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page. The "secret" implies that small city-states remain stable by not over-extending or becoming targets of envy through expansion.</note>

### 36 Christoph Besold’s Dissertation

they would bring upon themselves troubles and the envy of their neighbors. On the other hand, the Rule of the Best <note>original: "Aristia," here referring to Aristocracy or the rule of the elite.</note> is defended if some duties are given to the common people, provided that no actual power is granted to them. *Adam Contzen, Politics, book 1, chapter 17, number 4 and following.* The main point here is that even if someone has suffered a specific injury, they should not harbor feelings against the Senate or attempt any revolutionary schemes; instead, they should value the interests of the Republic and the peace of the Citizens more than their own affairs, more than their children, or even their own lives. *Aonius Palearius, in defense of Antonio Bellante, page 298.* <note>Aonius Palearius was an Italian humanist; Antonio Bellante was a client he defended against charges of sedition.</note>

<margin>
*The foundation and goal of popular administration.*
</margin>
**VII.** The foundation and goal of **Popular Administration** <note>term: "Popular administration" (administratio popularis) refers to a democratic system of government.</note> are **liberty** and **equality**. The people achieve liberty easily enough, but equality is more difficult to obtain. For although they are equal in the sense that everyone commands and obeys in turn, the actual opportunity to command falls to very few.

Liberty consists not in living according to your own whim, or being entirely without any authority over you, but in living according to the laws, being subject to your **Magistrate** <note>term: "Magistrate" refers to a high-ranking civil officer or government official.</note>, and under the condition that you also have the power to command. This is the equal right and honor of the City for everyone. *Contzen, book 2, chapter 19, number 2.*

<margin>
*How it is preserved against a single ruler.*
</margin>
And thus the popular state (which requires the greatest wisdom in its governance) is preserved against the rise of a single ruler: if no single person is given infinite power or a term of office that is too long. *Werner, Disputation on the Republic, 20, thesis 4. b. and note 1, discourse 1, folio 11.* It was precisely by such indulgence that Caesar wrongly seized the path to **Monarchy**. <note>The author refers to Julius Caesar’s transition from a Roman magistrate to a perpetual dictator, effectively ending the Republic.</note> Likewise, one must diligently guard against giving any one of the Magistrates so...

Let the **Jewel of Europe** note this! <note>original: "Europæ ocellus" – This likely refers to Venice, which was often called the "eye" or "jewel" of Europe and was famous for its stable republican system.</note> Thus, by the warning of **Tacitus**, the people must always beware of those who—falsely putting forward the name of liberty—are privately degenerate and publicly destructive, having no hope except through discord. <note>A paraphrase of Tacitus, *Annals* 11.23.</note>

By what means the Romans prevented the tyranny of the **Magistrate** is related by Caspar Ens, *Convivialium*, book 1, page 146.

<margin>How Democracy is defended against the powerful.</margin>
Plutarch, in *On the Fortune of Alexander*, defends Democracy against the powerful; he does not allow the wealth and power of a few to grow at the expense of the whole community. For this reason, the <term>Ostracism</term> of the Athenians and the <term>Petalism</term> <note>term: "Ostracism" and "Petalism" were practices where citizens voted to temporarily exile a prominent individual who was deemed a threat to democratic equality.</note> of others were established in former times. For they believe that, in such a way, popular governments are converted into an Aristocracy over the course of time. Hence in Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentinæ" — the Latin name for Strasbourg.</note>, the **Ammeister** <note>The chief magistrate representing the guilds and commoners.</note> (whose power is greater than that of the **Stadtmeister** <note>The representative of the nobility.</note>) is chosen only from a commoner’s family. Likewise in Genoa, no one was formerly elected Doge unless he was a commoner; and he was nominated by the Nobles. *Philippe de Commines, book 8, chapter 15, page 820.*

<margin>How the people are to be defended against the common folk themselves.</margin>
But the people must be defended not only against a single ruler or the aristocrats, but also against the common folk <note>original: "plebem"</note> themselves. This is achieved through equality and by ensuring each social rank maintains its own dignity. And thus, in the past, the "Best Men" <note>term: The "Optimates" were a traditionalist senatorial faction in the late Roman Republic that favored the authority of the Senate over populist reforms.</note> of Rome defended the state against the common folk, specifically the best among the Senators. Hence Cicero writes in his speech *For Sestius*: *Because they conducted themselves in such a way that their counsels were approved by every good man, they were considered the "Optimates"* <note>original: "Optimates habebantur"</note>. Consequently, those standing on the side of the *Optimates* seem to defend liberty more effectively than those who merely protect the interests of the common folk. Sulla, who was counted among the *Optimates*, acted with much unrestrained power, yet he did not extinguish the Republic. Caesar, however—in whom Sulla, with sharp judgment, quickly perceived there were "many Mariuses" <note>note: Gaius Marius was a populist general and Sulla's rival; Sulla saw in the young Julius Caesar a similar threat to the established order. See Suetonius, *Life of Caesar*, 1.</note>—craftily used a show of clemency to overthrow both liberty and the Republic.

<margin>In what liberty consists.</margin>
VIII. Skillfully does Aonius Palearius <note>note: Antonio della Pagliara (1503–1570) was an Italian humanist and orator known for his defense of civic harmony.</note> write in his *Oration for the Harmony of Citizens* (page 410): *The essence of liberty is to live as you wish.* If people interpret this as they usually do, what a plague! What destruction! What a ruin of true liberty that would be! How much more seriously and wisely did a Decemvir <note>term: A "Decemvir" was a member of a ten-man administrative council in certain Italian Republics, like Lucca.</note> of the Republic of Lucca respond to a bold and reckless foreigner, who was boasting that in a free city one should act according to one's own feelings and will: "If you are in a free city, be free, provided that you live as you *ought*." For since the natures and wills of men are diverse, it cannot be said what discords, what losses, and what evils arise where anyone is allowed to do anything. I could scarcely believe that even in the forests, when men lived like wild beasts, such a definition could have been tolerated by those interpreters. Yet almost the single greatest evil of democracies is immoderate liberty and the unrestrained license of public assemblies <note>original: "concionum"</note>. In this one way...

But the people must be defended not only against a single ruler and the patricians <note>The hereditary aristocrats of Rome.</note>, but also against the common folk themselves. This is achieved through equality and by preserving for each social order its own dignity. And so, in former times, the state was defended against the common folk by the *Optimates* <term>Optimates: Literally "the best men," the traditionalist senatorial faction in the Roman Republic who favored the authority of the Senate over popular assemblies.</term> of Rome—the most excellent of the senators. Hence Cicero says in *For Sestius*: <note>original: "Quia ita se gerebant, ut sua consilia optimo cuique probarentur, Optimates habebantur."</note> *Because they conducted themselves in such a way that their counsels were approved by every good man, they were considered the Optimates.* And thus, those standing with the party of the Optimates seem to defend liberty more than those who protect the interests of the common folk. Sulla <note>Lucius Cornelius Sulla (138–78 BCE), a general who seized power to restore the Roman Senate's supremacy.</note>, who was counted among the Optimates, acted with much lack of restraint, yet he did not extinguish the Republic. Caesar—in whom Sulla, with sharp judgment, quickly guessed there were many like Marius <note>Gaius Marius was a populist general and Sulla's rival; Sulla famously warned that the young Julius Caesar had "many a Marius" in him.</note> (*Suetonius, Life of Caesar, 1*)—by craftily using clemency, overthrew both liberty and the Republic.

<margin>
In what liberty consists.
</margin>

VIII. Cleverly, Aonius Palearius <note>An Italian humanist and orator (1503–1570).</note> writes in his *Oration for the Harmony of Citizens*, page 410: <note>original: "Libertatis proprium est, sic vivere ut velis."</note> *The characteristic of liberty is to live as you wish.* Yet if people interpret this as they usually do, what a plague! What destruction! What a ruin of true liberty! How much more seriously and wisely did a Decemvir <term>Decemvir: A member of a ten-man governing council.</term> of the Republic of Lucca <note>A powerful independent city-state in Tuscany known for its long-standing republican constitution.</note> respond to a bold and reckless foreigner, who was boasting that in a free city one should look to one's own feelings and will. He replied: "If you are in a free city, be free—provided you live as you ought." For since the natures and wills of men are so diverse, one cannot say what discords, what losses, and what evils would arise where anyone is permitted to do anything. I can scarcely believe that even in the forests, when men lived like wild beasts, such a sentiment could have been tolerated by those who interpret it this way. But almost the one evil of democracies is immoderate liberty and the license of public assemblies <term>Conciones: Formal public gatherings where orators addressed the people, often a site of political agitation.</term>. In this one way,

# A Dissertation by Christoph Besold #

...ing, <note>The fragment "do" from the original Latin likely completes a word from the previous page such as "ruendo" (falling) or "succumbendo" (succumbing).</note> that ancient Greece perished, which once flourished in wealth, dominion, and glory. In noble contrast was the custom of the Romans, who willed that no power of an assembly <term>concio: An informal gathering or speech to the people, which in Greece could lead to immediate legislative action, but in Rome was strictly separated from the formal voting process.</term> should exist to decree anything for the plebeians, or which the people might command. They willed that once the assembly was dismissed, the parts distributed by tribe and century <note>The Roman "Comitia" or voting assemblies were organized by geographic tribe or by wealth-based "centuries" to ensure a structured, rather than chaotic, vote.</note>, the ranks described, the authors of a proposal heard, and the matter proclaimed and examined for many days, only then should the law be ordered or forbidden. *Cicero, For Flaccus, leaf 50.* It is a great secret <term>Arcanum: A "secret of state" or a foundational principle of power that is often kept from the general public to ensure stability.</term> that in a Democracy, the people should not know they possess all power, but should believe themselves subject to the Laws, the Magistrate, and the Senate. The Fathers <note>The "Patres," or the early Roman Senators.</note> at Rome once determined to achieve this studiously. Petty legalists <term>Leguleji: A derogatory term for lawyers who are obsessed with the letter of the law but lack political wisdom.</term> are not capable of grasping this secret; they untunefully argue that the Roman Prince <note>Referring here to the leader of the state during the Republic.</note> held greater power than the people while liberty was in its prime. I have already warned of this in my *Economics, Title 3 and 4, book 1, question 9 at the end, and specific disputations on book 1, thesis 11.*

<margin>
The Senate is necessary in a free Republic.
</margin>
Hence, in a free Republic, a Senate must exist; the lack of one harmed the Athenian Republic. It would likewise have benefited the Roman Republic if there had been more Senators of greater authority, and if the people had possessed only the power of the Magistrate, election, and correction <note>Meaning the power to elect and hold officials accountable, rather than making every day-to-day decision.</note>. *Paruta, Discourse 1, leaf 38.*

<margin>
The Nobles ought not to flatter the common people.
</margin>
The high-born likewise ought not to flatter the common people. Regarding the Roman *Optimates* <note>The traditionalist senatorial faction.</note>, see *Discourse 9, book 1, Paruta:* <note>original: "Et si vede havere per l'ordinario tenuto quiei Nobili strada diversa da quella, che si conviene usare con la plebe, con la quale molto più giova l'usar verso lei certa maniera grave e severa, che la dolce, & humile non fa. Ma l'ambitione acciecò talmente egli animi loro, che tale errore non conoscendo, ò non curando, cercavano l'u..."</note> *And it is seen that those Nobles usually held a path different from that which is appropriate to use with the common folk, with whom it is far more beneficial to use a certain grave and severe manner, rather than a sweet and humble one. # On the Secrets of Republics #

...not one outdoing the other in competition, with donations, spectacles, and with a humble demeanor, to ingratiate themselves into the favor of the People. <note>original Italian: "no l'uno a gara dell' altro, condoni, conspettacoli, & con procedere dimesso, di insinuarsi nella gratia del Popolo." This is likely a quote from Trajano Boccalini, an Italian satirist and political commentator popular in the 17th century.</note>

<margin>The Common People</margin>
An equal to this secret is to ensure that citizens are skilled in the affairs of the Republic. For although in knowledgeable democracies, the virtue of a few usually accomplishes everything—as *Aemilius Probus* <note>Now known as the Roman biographer Cornelius Nepos.</note> defines in his life of *Epaminondas*—nevertheless, the judgment of the people regarding those few should be sharp and well-informed. Likewise, in a free Republic, it is fitting for the tongue to be free: and for this reason, in Rome and Athens, comedies, satires, and the like were frequent; even in triumphs, there was the greatest liberty of speech. See *Suetonius, Life of Caesar, 49,* and the commentators on that passage.

<margin>*Secrets in a Mixed State.*</margin>
IX. In a mixed state <term>Mixed State: A form of government that combines elements of monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy to prevent any one from becoming tyrannical.</term>, it is a secret to have powerful Estates <term>Estates: These are the "Orders" or organized social classes (such as the nobility, clergy, and commons) that hold representative power.</term>; and to avoid those things that can accelerate the ruin of this state. These include: the supine negligence of the Estates, ignorance of the Republic, timidity, flattery of superiors, discord, private interest, and the betrayal of secrets. It is also dangerous to admit to the number of such Estates men who are base, mercenary, or bound to a superior for many reasons—those whom the Prince can deprive of their office (which they hold within the Estates or elsewhere) whenever he pleases. Those who wish to harm a mixed state do not offend the common people and the nobility at the same time. *Boccalini, Century 1, Report 35, page 145 and following.* Therefore, the two classes should not allow themselves to be separated.

<margin>*Secrets of Rule and Secrets of Dominion are compared.*</margin>
X. It has already been said above (Chapter 1, section 3) that the "Secrets of Rule" <term>Arcana Imperii: Legal but hidden strategies used to maintain a legitimate government.</term> differ from the "Rights of Rule," and this matter does not seem to present any difficulty. But the "Secrets of Rule" and the "Secrets of Dominion" <term>Arcana Dominationis: Shady or tyrannical tactics used by a ruler to maintain personal power over the state.</term> are very closely related and connected, so much so that the distinction seems more subtle than political discourse usually allows. See *Clap-* <note>A reference to Arnoldus Clapmarius (1574–1604), a famous theorist on the "Secrets of Empire."</note>

# CHAPTER III.
## On the Crimes of Domination.

<margin>
Crimes of
domination
to be
avoided.
</margin>
One must avoid here those foul and barbaric methods, as well as the crimes used for preserving and increasing domination; or, to use the word we use today, "Machiavellian Counsels," <note>Referring to the political theories of Niccolò Machiavelli, often interpreted in this period as endorsing immoral actions for political gain.</note> which a Prince should avoid as much as possible. Livia said something manly and beyond her gender to Augustus: "It is necessary for you," she said, "to do nothing through injury, but also to not even *appear* to do so." <note>Livia Drusilla, wife of the first Roman Emperor, Augustus Caesar.</note> For to private men, it is enough not to commit a crime; but Princes are not even allowed to be under suspicion. Just as it is sometimes permissible to heal using poison, cauterization, or surgery, but never with sorcery, conspiracies, and the like: so we may legitimately use secrets at times, but never crimes.

<margin>
Hated
even by
the Pagans.
</margin>
And certainly these crimes haunted the consciences of even the Pagans. Sallust, in his *Jugurthine War*, chapter 72, writes: "After Bomilcar and many others whom he knew to be his accomplices in the conspiracy were put to death, [Jugurtha's] anger was suppressed, lest some sedition should arise from that business. But after those events, no day or night for Jugurtha was..." <note>Sallust was a Roman historian; Jugurtha was the King of Numidia who fought Rome and was known for his ruthless tactics.</note>

### CHAPTER IV and Final.
#### Concerning the Images of Power.

<margin>
What the
Images of
Power are.
</margin>
The *Images of Power* <note>original: "Simulacra Imperiorum." This refers to the hollow forms or symbols of authority that lack actual governing power.</note> also pertain to the administration of a Commonwealth. However, just as the secrets of State <term>arcana Imperii</term> are mostly hidden but effective tactics used against rebellious men or those removed from the administration of the State: so these "images" are hidden arts, but they are empty and hollow; or as Paolo Giovio <note>A 16th-century Italian physician and historian.</note> calls them, "empty rights of commanding." These are granted to those who are outside of the government, and for whom one thing is done while another is pretended. Clapmarius, book 6, chapter 1. Gryphiander says this best in his *Disquisition on Secrets, thesis 110.*

<margin>
Their
difference
from the
secrets.
</margin>
Furthermore, the secrets remain in the hands of the Prince, while the "images" are in the hands of the subjects—though in respect to the Prince, these too are secrets. The subjects believe they possess the reality, when they only have an Idol or a phantom. <note>original: "Idolon seu simulacrum."</note> Moreover, those who hold the actual Rule do not value these things very highly, as they are merely showy and shadowy. On the contrary, those who lack the reality of power prefer to seem to have it, rather than both to not have it and not to seem to have it. Hence Tacitus says: *Among the Romans, the right of Rule prevails; empty things are handed over.* <note>original: "Apud Romanos... jus Imperii valet, inania transmittuntur."</note> And here, that saying especially holds its place: *In governing a Commonwealth, opinion and pretense carry no less weight (and perhaps I know not if more) than the reality itself.* This is most true in the transitions of States, which do not happen suddenly,

Those who strive for changes of this sort change the Commonwealth; and for that reason, even the ancient laws remain: but those who have diverted the Commonwealth are the ones who truly dominate. *Aristotle, Politics, book 4, chapter 5, at the end; Machiavelli, Discourses, book 1, chapter 25.* <note>The author cites Aristotle and Machiavelli to argue that a revolution is often more successful if it maintains the "image" of the old government while the actual power shifts to new hands.</note>

<margin>Images to be observed when introducing a new religion.</margin>
And there are certainly also "images" <note>original: "simulacra," meaning semblances, shadows, or pretenses.</note> which are usually observed when introducing a new religion: since one must act differently and much more gently with those who are recent and weak in the faith; and differently with adults, and those already strengthened in the faith, or those who have been solidified with a firm root in the faith, as the text speaks there; which correctly accommodates the saying of Paul: *2 Corinthians 3. I gave you milk to drink, not meat, or more solid food.* <note>The author cites Paul the Apostle, though the "milk and meat" metaphor is traditionally found in 1 Corinthians 3:2. The point is that new converts should not be overwhelmed with difficult doctrines immediately.</note> And for the same reason, the Pope <term>P.M.</term> <note>Pontifex Maximus</note> accommodated himself to the Norwegians, as new Christians, and condescended to their weakness, as Cujacius <note>Jacques Cujas, a famous 16th-century French legal scholar.</note> teaches regarding chapter 3 of *Consanguinity and Affinity.* And even the Theologians concede: Sometimes it is more advisable to defer—that is, to indulge the multitude and observed custom somewhat—rather than to decree something else that leads to dissension and the scandal of the people by introducing some novelty. *Rittershusius, On the Differences between Civil and Canon Law, book 1, chapter 9.*

<margin>To what extent the remains of the old Roman Republic belong to the images of the Empire.</margin>
II. To these "images" belong all those things which were left over from the ancient Roman Republic into the Principate, and because the Princes <note>referring to the early Roman Emperors, who used the title "Princeps" or "First Citizen."</note> sometimes offered even the greater matters to the people or the Senate in appearance. For this reason, some wrongly wish to separate a Kingdom from a Principate. See my *Discourse on Monarchy, chapter 4, number 2, etc.* Caesar shared the elections <term>comitia</term> with the people, and yet he forbade the gatherings and assemblies of the people: Suetonius, *Life of Julius Caesar, chapter 41.* He increased the punishments, etc. Sue-

And so it was a mere semblance <note>original: "simulacrum," a recurring theme in this text referring to an outward appearance that masks a different reality.</note> that he left certain provinces to the people—namely, the weak and peaceful ones, not suited for starting revolutions—as noted by **Strabo**, toward the end. # On the Secrets of States.

...once a great power; now an empty name. But concerning the **Secrets of the Roman Princes**, Gryphiander speaks shrewdly in the cited passage, thesis 113. So too the Florentine Principality has its own outward shows <note>original: "simulacra," referring to political facades that hide the true nature of power.</note>: see the *Political Treasure*, part 1, page 283. And even in Rome itself, the Roman Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> maintains such forms: *Political Treasure*, part 1, page 24, etc. Likewise, in Rome there is a certain appearance of liberty in the "license of the Pasquils" <note>The "Pasquilli" were statues in Rome where citizens would anonymously post satirical poems or "pasquinades" criticizing the government, a tolerated outlet for public frustration.</note>. See the *Spanish Forest*, part 1, chapter 1, final entry. Just as Augustus and Tiberius allowed the greatest freedom of speech so that the Republic might still seem to be free. See **Pierre Matthieu** in his work on *Sejanus*, page 103, etc.

<margin>Privileges are also mere semblances.</margin>
Privileges granted to subjects are also "simulacra" or outward shows. **So that great lords may silence their troublesome subjects, like crying children with dolls, and then afterwards take those same things away again with a clever hand.** <note>Translated from the original German: "Damit grosse Herren ihre schwürige Vnderthanen / wie die weinende Kinder mit den Docken geschweygen / vnd selbige hernacher mit sonderbarer manier wieder hinwegnemen."</note> As **Boccalini** writes in his *Reports from Parnassus*, century 2, report 1. It is pleasing to add the judgment of **Gryphiander** in his *Political Skirmishes on Secrets*, thesis 127 and following, who says: To this category belong the granting of privileges, the remission of taxes, immunities, and other favors by which the common people are soothed, so that they might willingly acquiesce to the rule of the Sovereign. In granting these things, Princes are not usually stubborn, especially in a new reign; so that subjects, enriched by these new conditions, might prefer "safe and present things rather than the old and dangerous ones," <note>original: "tuta & præsentia, quàm vetera & periculosa," a reference to Tacitus’s *Annals* 1.2 describing how the Romans accepted the peace of the Empire over the bloody civil wars of the Republic.</note> as **Tacitus** says.

<margin>To gradually accustom the common people to pleasures through luxuries.</margin>
For **Aristotle** taught that such is the nature of the common crowd: if they perceive a personal benefit, they are not greatly led by a desire for political power. Using—or rather abusing—this generosity, the Roman Princes bestowed banquets, public spectacles, <term>congiaria</term> <note>Official distributions of money or food to the Roman citizenry.</note>, <term>missilia</term> <note>Gifts or tokens thrown to the crowds during games.</note>, and other "allurements of vice," as Tacitus calls them, upon the commoners and the soldiers, beyond all strength and measure.

...while what they called "civilization" was actually a part of their servitude, as the same author <note>Referring to the historian Tacitus.</note> observed. By these delights, the people were gradually accustomed to bodily pleasures and voluntarily cast all care for the Republic into the lap of the Princes. Just as the Satirist <note>The Roman poet Juvenal in his *Satires*.</note> lamented: the people who once bestowed military commands, high offices, legions, everything, now restrains itself and anxiously desires only two things: **Bread and Circuses**. <note>original: "Panem ac Circenses."</note>

<margin>To offer a shadow of liberty.</margin>
And the same Gryphiander, in thesis 91 and following, writes prudently: *The pretext of liberty in conducting affairs is also held in high favor; for the legal expert <note>original: "ICtus," an abbreviation for Jurisconsultus.</note> Gaius calls it more favorable than all other things, and Paulus calls it an inestimable thing <note>original: "rem inaestimabilem," a famous Roman legal principle.</note>, than which nothing more pleasing can happen to a man. Just as, on the other hand, all servitude is miserable, and its yoke is heavy for all those educated in liberty, as Cicero confesses.* And by this pretext, the people are often deceived, while sometimes a mere appearance of liberty is offered which in itself contains nothing but servitude—what Pliny calls the **shadow of liberty**. This will break out into a more bitter service the more it is covered by a greater image of liberty, as Tacitus foresaw. We see this also in certain Hanseatic and Belgian <note>In this period, "Belgic" often referred generally to the Low Countries or the Dutch Republic.</note> cities; under the appearance of liberty in a popular state <note>A democracy.</note>, the citizens are treated more harshly than if they lived under a Prince.

<margin>A healthy balance is noted as distinct from mere pretenses.</margin>
III. It must be noted above all that these outward shows <note>simulacra</note> are to be properly distinguished from a **healthy balance**, by which the force of a Monarchy is tempered and leans toward a mixed form of government through fundamental laws. Thus, sometimes even a Democracy is best ruled by Aristocratic principles. Just as in the Roman Republic, while the supreme power belonged to the people, it was nevertheless governed aristocratically through the Consulship and especially the Senato-

<meta>This is the title page of a seventeenth-century legal and political treatise. Arnold Clapmarius (1574–1604) was a notable German jurist, and this work represents a standard text on the "secrets" of statecraft and public law during the Baroque period.</meta>

### ARNOLD
# CLAPMARIUS,
## FRANCIS
## ROSELLE
<note>original: "Francisci Roselli"</note>
->AND<-
## WOLFGANG HEINRICH
## RUPRECHT
### *Conclusions*
->ON<-
# PUBLIC LAW.
<note>Public Law <term>Ius Publicum</term> in this era referred to the laws governing the state itself, its sovereignty, and the relationship between the ruler and the subjects.</note>

<image-desc>A woodcut of an armillary sphere, showing various celestial rings including the zodiac belt, mounted on a small ornamental pedestal.</image-desc>

->*Amsterdam,*<-
->By Louis Elzevir, 1644.<-
<note>The Elzevirs were a world-renowned Dutch family of printers and booksellers. Their pocket-sized editions of scholarly works were prized for their portability and clear typography.</note>

<summary>This is the title page of a 1644 Amsterdam edition of a legal treatise on public law authored by Arnold Clapmarius and contributed to by Francis Rosellus and Wolfgang Heinrich Ruprecht. It was published by the prestigious Elzevir press, a mark of high academic quality for the time.</summary>
<keywords>Public Law, Arnold Clapmarius, Louis Elzevir, Amsterdam, 17th century, political science, jurisprudence</keywords>
